breaths.text: Come thou hither, I implore thee, To deliver me from trouble,
Come I pray thee, hither hasten, Hasten more that thou art needed,
When she ceased her supplications,
Ere a beauteous duck descending, Hastens toward the water-mother,
Seeks herself a place for nesting. Flies she eastward, flies she westward,
Cannot find a grassy hillock, Not the smallest bit of verdure;
Cannot find a place befitting, Where to make her nest in safety.
She descries no place for resting, Thinking loud and long debating,
“Build I in the winds my dwelling, On the floods my place of nesting?
Far away the waves would wash it.”
Now the hapless water-mother, Raised her shoulders out of water,
That the duck might build her dwelling, Build her nesting-place in safety.
Flying slowly, looking round her, Spies the shoulders of the maiden,
Now the hapless water-mother, Thinks them to be grassy hillocks,
Thence she flies and hovers slowly, Lightly on the knee she settles,
Where to lay her eggs in safety. Here she builds her humble dwelling,
Six, the golden eggs she lays there, Then a seventh, an egg of iron;
Quickly warms them on the knee-cap Of the hapless water-mother;
Then a third day sits and hatches. Warmer grows the water round her,
While her knee with fire is kindled, And her shoulders too are burning,
Quick the maiden moves her shoulders, Shakes her members in succession,
And the eggs fall into ocean, Dash in pieces on the bottom
In the sand they do not perish, Not the pieces in the ocean;
All the fragments come together Forming pieces two in number,
Equal to the one, the other. From one half the egg, the lower,
From the upper half remaining, Grows the upper vault of Heaven;
From the yellow part the sunshine, From the motley part the starlight,
And the days speed onward swiftly, Quickly do the years fly over,
From the lighting of the full moon.
Swims the sea as water-mother, With the floods outstretched before her,
Finally about the ninth year, In the summer of the tenth year,
Lifts her forehead from the waters, And begins at last her workings,
On the azure water-ridges, On the mighty waste before her.
There arose a fertile hillock; Wheresoe’er her foot she rested,
Where she dived beneath the waters, Fell the many deeps of ocean;
There the level banks have risen; Where her head was pointed landward,
When from shore she swam a distance, And upon her back she rested,
And the hidden reefs created, Where the ships are wrecked so often,
Thus created were the islands,
Pillars of the sky were planted, Fields and forests were created,
Gleaming in the silver sunlight, All the rocks stood well established;
Had not yet beheld the sunshine, Had not seen the golden moonlight,
Wainamoinen, old and trusty,
Thirty summers altogether, And of winters, also thirty,
On the broad-sea’s yielding bosom, Well reflected, long considered,
In the spaces wrapped in darkness, In uncomfortable limits,
Had not seen the silver sunshine. Thereupon these words he uttered,
“Take, O Moon, I pray thee, take me, Take me, thou, O Sun above me,
From this dark and dreary prison, From these unbefitting portals,
From this dark and gloomy dwelling, Hence to wander from the ocean,
On the dry land walk and wander, Like an ancient hero wander,
Thus to see the moon at evening, Thus to see the silver sunlight,
That the stars I may consider.”
And the Sun would not deliver, Nor the Great Bear give assistance,
And his life but an annoyance, Bursts he then the outer portals
With his strong, but unnamed finger, Opens he the lock resisting;
With the fingers of his right hand, Creeps he through the yielding portals
On his knees across the threshold, Throws himself head foremost, forward
Plunges hither, plunges thither, Turning with his hands the water;
Swims he eastward, swims he westward, Studying his new surroundings.
Rested five years in the ocean, Six long years, and even seven years,
When at last he leaves the waters, Stops upon a promontory,
On his knees he leaves the ocean, On the land he plants his right foot,
Quickly turns his hands about him, Stands erect to see the sunshine,
That he may behold the Great Bear, That he may the stars consider.
Thus the wonderful enchanter Was delivered from his mother,
Wainamoinen’S Sowing.
With his feet upon the island, On the island washed by ocean,
There remained he many summers, There he lived as many winters,
Well considered, long reflected, Who for him should sow the island,
Thought at last of Pellerwoinen, First-born of the plains and prairies,
Who should sow the vacant island, Who the forest seeds should scatter.
Sows with diligence the island, Seeds upon the lands he scatters,
Forest seeds upon the loose earth, On the firm soil sows the acorns,
Pine-trees also on the hill-tops, Many shrubs in every valley,
In the loose soil sows the alders, In the lowlands sows the lindens,
Mountain-ash in virgin places, On the banks of streams the hawthorn,
This the work of Pellerwoinen, Slender Sampsa, in his childhood.
Soon the forest trees were growing, Soon appeared the tops of fir-trees,
Birches rose from all the marshes, In the loose soil grew the alders,
Junipers were also growing, Junipers with clustered berries,
Now the hero, Wainamoinen,
How the Sampsa-seeds are growing, How the crop of Pellerwoinen;
Sees the forest rise in beauty; But the oak-tree has not sprouted,
Still within the acorn sleeping, Its own happiness enjoying.
And as many days he waited, Waited till a week had vanished,
But the oak-tree was not growing, Had not left her acorn-dwelling.
Spies four maidens in the distance, Water-brides, he spies a fifth-one,
In the dewy grass and flowers, On a point extending seaward,
Some were mowing, some were raking, Raking what was mown together,
From the ocean rose a giant,
Pressed compactly all the grasses, That the maidens had been raking,
And the flames shot up to heaven, Till the windrows burned to ashes,
Of the grasses raked together. In the ashes of the windrows,
In the leaves he plants an acorn, From the acorn, quickly sprouting,
From the ground enriched by ashes, Newly raked by water-maidens;
Rounds itself a broad corona, Raises it above the storm-clouds;
Stops the white-clouds in their courses, With its branches hides the sunlight,
And the starlight dies in heaven.
Thought awhile, and well considered, How to kill the mighty oak-tree,
How to fell the tree majestic, How to lop its hundred branches.
Sad the homes of ocean-dwellers, If the sun shines not upon them,
Is there not some mighty hero, Was there never born a giant,
That can lop its hundred branches? Wainamoinen, deeply thinking,
“Kapé, daughter of the Ether, Ancient mother of my being,
Loan to me the water-forces, Great the powers of the waters;
To upset this mighty oak-tree, To uproot this tree of evil,
That the moon once more may glimmer.”
Rose a hero from the waters, Nor belonged he to the largest,
Long was he as man’s forefinger, Taller than the hand of woman;
Boots upon his feet were copper, Gloves upon his hands were copper,
Belt around him made of copper, Hatchet in his belt was copper;
Was as long as hand of woman, Of a finger’s breadth the blade was.
Thought awhile and well considered, And his measures are as follow: “Art thou, sir, divine or human?
Tell me what thy name and station. Very like a man thou lookest,
Though the length of man’s first finger, Scarce as tall as hoof of reindeer.”
To the form from out the ocean: “Verily I think thee human,
Might as well be dead or dying, Fit for nothing but to perish.”
Spake the small one from the ocean To the valiant Wainamoinen: “Truly am I god and hero,
Come I here to fell the oak-tree, Lop its branches with my hatchet.”
Answers thus the sea-born hero: “Never hast thou force sufficient,
To uproot this mighty oak-tree, To upset this thing of evil,
Scarcely had he finished speaking,
Ere the pigmy full unfolding, Quick becomes a mighty giant.
Plants himself, a mighty hero, On the forest-fields surrounding;
To his knees his beard extending, And his locks fall to his ankles;
Far apart his feet are stationed, Farther still his mighty shoulders.
Quickly to an edge he whets it, Using six hard blocks of sandstone,
Straightway to the oak-tree turning, Thither stalks the mighty giant,
Flapping in the winds of heaven; With his second step he totters
With his third stop firmly planted, Reaches he the oak-tree’s branches,
With one mighty swing he strikes it, With a second blow he cuts it;
From his axe the sparks fly upward, From the oak-tree fire outshooting;
Yields the oak with hundred branches, Shaking earth and heaven in falling.
Far to westward flew the tree-tops, To the South the leaves were scattered,
Whosoe’er a branch has taken, Has obtained eternal welfare;
He has gained the master magic; Who the foliage has gathered,
Of the chips some had been scattered, Scattered also many splinters,
Of the ocean smooth and mirrored, Rocked there by the winds and waters,
Storm-winds blew them to the Northland, Some the ocean currents carried.
Washing on the shore a head-dress, Beating on the rocks her garments,
In the waters of Pohyola, There beheld the chips and splinters,
In a bag the chips she gathered, Took them to the ancient court-yard,
Arrows for the great magician, There to shape them into weapons,
Since the mighty oak has fallen, Now has lost its hundred branches,
See the gentle gleam of moonlight, That the clouds may keep their courses,
Over every lake and river, O’er the banks of every island.
Beautifully grew the forests, And again, the vines and flowers.
Noisily the merry thrushes, And the cuckoos in the birch-trees;
Golden flowers in the meadows, And the herbs of many colors,
But the barley is not growing.
Goes away and well considers, By the borders of the waters,
Finds six seeds of golden barley, Even seven ripened kernels,
In the sand upon the sea-shore, Hides them in his trusty pouches,
Some were made from skin of marten; Hastens forth the seeds to scatter,
On the brinks of Kalew-waters, On the Osma-hills and lowlands.
From the aspen, words as follow: “Osma’s barley will not flourish,
If the soil be not made ready, If the forest be not levelled,
Wainamoinen, wise and ancient,
Then began to clear the forest, Then began the trees to level,
Only left the birch-tree standing For the birds a place of resting,
Sacred bird in sacred branches. Down from heaven came the eagle,
That he might this thing consider; And he spake the words that follow: “Wherefore, ancient Wainamoinen,
Left the birch-tree only standing?” Wainamoinen thus made answer: “Therefore is the birch left standing,
That the eagle there may rest him, There may sing the sacred cuckoo.”
“Good indeed, thy hero-judgment, That the birch-tree thou hast left us,
As a resting-place for eagles, And for birds of every feather,
Quickly then this bird of heaven, Kindled fire among the branches;
And the east-winds lend their forces, Burn the trees of all descriptions,
Only is the birch left standing.
Brings his magic grains of barley, Brings he forth his seven seed-grains,
Fashioned from the skin of squirrel, Some were made from skin of marten.
Hastes the barley-grains to scatter, Speaks unto himself these measures: “I the seeds of life am sowing,
From the hand of my Creator, In this soil enriched with ashes,
Ancient mother, thou that livest Far below the earth and ocean,
Bring the rich soil to producing, Bring the seed-grains to the sprouting,
Never will the earth unaided, Yield the ripe nutritious barley;
If the givers give assistance, If the givers grace the sowing,
Rise, O earth, from out thy slumber, From the slumber-land of ages,
Let the blades themselves be starting, Let the verdant stalks be rising,
And a hundredfold producing, From my plowing and my sowing,
Ukko, thou O God, up yonder, Thou O Father of the heavens,
Curbest all the clouds of heaven, Holdest in the air thy counsel,
From the East dispatch a cloudlet, From the North-east send a rain-cloud,
From the North-west, still another, Quickly from the South a warm-cloud,
That the clouds may drop their honey, That the ears may fill and ripen,
Thereupon benignant Ukko,
Held his counsel in the cloud-space, Held good counsel in the Ether;
From the North-east, sent a rain-cloud, From the West another sent he,
Quickly from the South a warm-cloud; Joined in seams the clouds together,
Grasped the cloud, and hurled it earthward. Quick the rain-cloud drops her honey,
That the ears may quickly ripen, That the barley crop may rustle.
From the germ the blade unfolding, Richly colored ears arising,
From the work of Wainamoinen.
And as many nights fly over. When the seventh day had journeyed,
Wainamoinen, wise and ancient, Went to view his crop of barley,
How his labors were resulting; Found his crop of barley growing,
And the ears he found six-sided.
Turned his face, and looked about him, Lo! there comes a spring-time cuckoo,
Rests upon it, sweetly singing: “Wherefore is the silver birch-tree
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Therefore I have left the birch-tree,
Home for thee for joyful singing. Call thou here, O sweet-voiced cuckoo,
Sing thou here with voice of silver, Sing the cuckoo’s golden flute-notes;
Call within the hour of noontide, For the better growth of forests,
For the richness of, the Northland, For the joy of Kalevala.”
Wainamoinen and Youkahainen.
Passed his years in full contentment, On the meadows of Wainola,
Singing ever wondrous legends, Songs of ancient wit and wisdom,
Singing in the dusk of evening, Singing till the dawn of morning,
Tales of ages long forgotten, Now the legends of creation,
By our children sung no longer, Sung in part by many heroes,
Evil days our race befallen. Far and wide the story travelled,
Of the chanting of the hero, Of the song of Wainamoinen;
All of Northland heard the story.
Lived the singer, Youkahainen, Lapland’s young and reckless minstrel.
Dining with his friends and fellows, Came upon his ears the story,
On the meadows of Wainola, On the plains of Kalevala,
Better skilled than Youkahainen, Better than the one that taught him.
Envy rose within his bosom, Envy of this Wainamoinen,
Hastes he angry to his mother, To his mother, full of wisdom,
Hie him southward and betake him To the dwellings of Wainola,
There as bard to vie in battle, With the famous Wainamoinen.
“Nay,” replies the anxious father, “Do not go to Kalevala.”
“Nay,” replies the fearful mother, “Go not hence to Wainamoinen,
He will charm thee with his singing Will bewitch thee in his anger,
Sink thee in the fatal snow-drift, Turn to ice thy pliant fingers,
These the words of Youkahainen: “Good the judgement of a father,
Best of all one’s own decision. I will go and face the minstrel,
Challenge him as bard to battle, Sing to him my sweet-toned measures,
Chant to him my garnered wisdom, That this best of boasted singers,
Shall be worsted in the contest, Shall become a hapless minstrel;
That his feet shall be as flint-stone, And as oak his nether raiment;
Thus bewitched, shall carry ever, In his heart a stony burden,
On his hand a flint-stone gauntlet, On his brow a stony visor.”
Heeding not advice paternal, Heeding not his mother’s counsel,
Fire outstreaming from his nostrils, From his hoofs, the sparks outshooting,
To his golden sledge, the courser, Mounts impetuous his snow-sledge,
Strikes his courser with his birch-whip, With his birch-whip, pearl-enamelled.
Springs away upon his journey; On he, restless, plunges northward,
All the next day, onward, onward, So the third from morn till evening,
To the meadows of Wainola, To the plains of Kalevala.
Wainamoinen, the magician, Rode that sunset on the highway,
Down Wainola’s peaceful meadows, O’er the plains of Kalevala.
Urging still his foaming courser, Dashes down upon the singer,
Meeting thus in full collision; Shafts are driven tight together,
Tangled are the reins and traces. Thus perforce they make a stand-still,
Water drips from hame and collar, Vapors rise from both their horses.
“Who art thou, and whence? Thou comest Driving like a stupid stripling,
Thou hast ruined shafts and traces; And the collar of my racer
And my golden sleigh is broken, Box and runners dashed to pieces.”
Spake at last the words that follow: “I am youthful Youkahainen,
Whence thou comest, where thou goest, From what lowly tribe descended?”
Answered thus the youthful minstrel: “If thou art but Youkahainen,
I am many years thy senior.”
Spake again to Wainamoinen: “Young or ancient, little matter,
He that higher stands in wisdom, He whose knowledge is the greater,
He alone shall keep the highway, And the other take the roadside.
Famous sorcerer and minstrel? Let us then begin our singing,
Let us chant our garnered wisdom, That the one may hear the other,
In a war of wizard sayings.”
Thus replied in modest accents: “What I know is very little,
Neither is my singing wondrous: All my days I have resided
In a desert land enchanted, In my cottage home for ages;
Are the cuckoo’s simple measures, Some of these I may remember;
I accept thy boastful challenge. Tell me now, my golden youngster,
Open now thy store of wisdom.”
Lapland’s young and fiery minstrel: “Know I many bits of learning,
Every roof must have a chimney, Every fire-place have a hearth-stone;
Merry is the life of walrus, Feeding on incautious salmon,
Whitings live in quiet shallows, Salmon love the level bottoms;
And defies the storms of winter. Slowly perches swim in Autumn,
Spawn in shallows in the summer, Bounding on the shore of ocean.
I can tell thee other matters, Sing thee other wizard sayings:
Mother-horses plow the Southland, Inner Lapland plows with oxen;
Know I well in all their grandeur; On the Horna-rock are fir-trees,
Slender grow the trees on mountains. Three, the water-falls in number,
Three in number, lofty mountains, Shooting to the vault of heaven.
Katrakoski in Karyala; Imatra, the falling water,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen: “Women’s tales and children’s wisdom
Hero, old enough for wedlock; Tell the story of creation,
Tell me of the creatures in it, And philosophize a little.”
Thus replied to Wainamoinen: “Know I well the titmouse-fountains,
And the viper, green, a serpent; Whitings live in brackish waters;
Iron rusts, and rusting weakens; Bitter is the taste of umber;
Fire is ever full of danger; First physician, the Creator;
Magic is the child of sea-foam; God the first and best adviser;
Fire descended first from heaven; Iron from the rust was fashioned;
Marshes are of lands the oldest; First of all the trees, the willow;
Hollowed stones the first of kettles.”
Thus addresses Youkahainen: “Canst thou give me now some wisdom,
Youkahainen thus made answer: “I can tell thee still a trifle,
When I plowed the salt-sea’s bosom, When I raked the sea-girt islands,
Hollowed out the deepest caverns, When I all the lakes created,
When I piled the rocks about them. I was present as a hero,
Seventh of all primeval heroes, When the heavens were created,
When the sky was crystal-pillared, When was arched the beauteous rainbow,
When the silver Sun was planted, When the Bear was firmly stationed,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Thou art surely prince of liars,
Never wert thou in existence, Surely wert thou never present,
When were raked the sea-girt islands, When were dug the salmon-grottoes,
When the lakes were all created, When were heaped the mountains round them,
Thou wert never seen or heard of When the earth was first created,
When the air was crystal-pillared, When the Moon was placed in orbit,
When the Bear was firmly stationed, When the skies with stars were sprinkled.”
Answered ancient Wainamoinen: “Then, sir, since I fail in wisdom,
Come thou, famous bard and minstrel, Thou the ancient wonder-singer,
Let our blades be fully tested.” Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Not thy sword and not thy wisdom,
Do I fear a single moment. Let who may accept thy challenge,
Not with one so vain and paltry, Will I ever measure broadswords.”
Mouth awry and visage sneering, Shook his golden locks and answered: “Whoso fears his blade to measure,
Into wild-boar of the forest, Swine at heart and swine in visage,
I will hurl such hero-cowards, This one hither, that one thither,
In the rubbish of the stable.”
Wrathful waxed, and fiercely frowning, Self-composed he broke his silence,
Sang he not the tales of childhood, Children’s nonsense, wit of women,
That the children never heard of, That the boys and maidens knew not,
Known in part by many heroes, In these mournful days of evil,
Grandly sang wise Wainamoinen, Till the copper-bearing mountains,
Heard his magic tones and trembled; Mountain cliffs were torn to pieces,
And the distant hills re-echoed. Lo! the boastful Youkahainen
And his sledge with golden trimmings Floats like brushwood on the billows;
Sings his reins to twigs of willow, And to shrubs his golden cross-bench.
Floats a reed upon the border; Lo! his steed with golden forehead,
Hames and traces are as fir-boughs, And his collar, straw and sea-grass.
Sings his sword with golden handle, Sings it into gleam of lightning,
Sings his cross-bow, gaily painted, To a rainbow o’er the ocean;
Into hawks and screaming eagles; Sings his dog with bended muzzle,
Sings his cap from off his forehead, Sings it into wreaths of vapor;
Into rushes on the waters; Sings his vesture, purple-colored,
Sings his girdle, set with jewels, Into twinkling stars around him;
Sings him into deeps of quick-sand; Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
To his belt in mud and water. Now it was that Youkahainen
What his folly, what the end was, Of the journey he had ventured,
For the glory of a contest With the grand, old Wainamoinen.
Pohyola’s old and sorry stripling, Strives his best to move his right foot,
When he strives to move his left foot, Lo! he finds it turned to flint-stone.
In the deeps of desperation, And in earnest supplication,
“O thou wise and worthy minstrel, Thou the only true magician,
Only turn away thy magic, Let me leave this slough of horror,
Free me from this killing torment, I will pay a golden ransom.”
“What the ransom thou wilt give me If I cease from mine enchantment,
Lift thee from thy slough of horror, Loose thee from thy stony prison,
Answered youthful Youkahainen: “Have at home two magic cross-bows,
One so light a child can bend it, Only strength can bend the other,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen: “Do not wish thy magic cross-bows,
Thine to me are worse than useless; I have bows in great abundance,
Bows that laugh at all the hunters, Bows that go themselves a-hunting.”
Sang alas! poor Youkahainen Deeper into mud and water,
Youkahainen thus made answer: “Have at home two magic shallops,
One rides light upon the ocean, One is made for heavy burdens;
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Do not wish thy magic shallops,
All my bays are full of shallops, All my shores are lined with shallops,
Some were built to sail against them.”
Sings again poor Youkahainen Deeper, deeper into torment,
Till the Lapland bard in anguish Speaks again to Wainamoinen: “Have at home two magic stallions,
One was born for heavy burdens; Take of these the one that pleases.”
“Neither do I wish thy stallions, Do not need thy hawk-limbed stallions,
Magic stallions swarm my stables, Eating corn at every manger,
Water on each croup in lakelets.”
Sings the hapless Lapland minstrel Deeper, deeper into torment,
Spake again young Youkahainen: “O thou ancient Wainamoinen,
Cease I pray thee thine enchantment, Only turn away thy magic,
Countless stores of shining silver; From the wars my father brought it,
Spake the wise, old Wainamoinen: “For thy gold I have no longing,
Have enough of each already; Gold abundant fills my chambers,
Gold that glitters in the sunshine, Silver shining in the moonlight.”
Deeper in his slough of torment, To his chin in mud and water,
“O thou ancient Wainamoinen, Greatest of the old magicians,
From this prison-house of torture; I will give thee all my corn-fields,
Thus my hapless life to ransom, Thus to gain eternal freedom.”
“Take thy corn to other markets, Give thy garners to the needy;
Fields have I in every quarter, Corn in all my fields is growing;
One’s own grain is much the sweeter.”
Sorrow-laden, thus enchanted, Deeper sinks in mud and water,
In the mire, his beard bedrabbled, Mouth once boastful filled with sea-weed,
Youkahainen thus beseeches: “O thou ancient Wainamoinen,
Cease at last thine incantations, Only turn away thy magic,
Lift me from this stifling torment, Free mine eyes from sand and water,
Fairest daughter of my mother, Bride of thine to be forever,
Sweep the rooms within thy cottage, Keep thy dwelling-place in order,
Spread thy couch with finest linens, For thy bed, weave golden covers,
Wainamoinen, old and truthful,
Lapland’s young and fairest daughter, Sister dear of Youkahainen;
In his age a beauteous maiden, Bride of his to be forever,
Now the happy Wainamoinen, Sits upon the rock of gladness,
Sings a little, sings and ceases, Sings again, and sings a third time,
Thus to lessen the enchantment, Thus the potent charm to banish.
Youkahainen, sad, but wiser, Drags his feet from out the quicksand,
From the rocks leads forth his courser, Brings his sledge back from the rushes,
Sets his golden sledge in order, Throws himself upon the cross-bench,
Hastens homeward, heavy-hearted, Sad indeed to meet his mother,
Careless thus he hastens homeward, Nears his home with noise and bustle,
Breaks the shafts against the portals, Breaks his handsome sledge in pieces.
Would have chided him for rashness, But the father interrupted: “Wherefore dost thou break thy snow-sledge,
Wherefore comest home so strangely, Why this rude and wild behavior?”
Cap awry upon his forehead, Falls to weeping, broken-hearted,
Eyes and lips expressing sadness, Answers not his anxious father.
Sought to find his cause for sorrow: “Tell me, first-born, why thou weepest,
Why thy mind is so dejected, Why thine eyes express such sadness.”
“Golden mother, ever faithful, Cause there is to me sufficient,
Bitter cause for this my sorrow, Cause for bitter tears and murmurs:
Since, O mother of my being, I have promised beauteous Aino,
Aino, my devoted sister, To decrepit Wainamoinen,
Roof above him, prop beneath him, Fair companion at his fire-side.”
Clapped her hands in glee together, Thus addressing Youkahainen: “Weep no more, my son beloved,
Hast no reason for thy sorrow, Often I this hope have cherished;
That this mighty bard and hero, Wise and valiant Wainamoinen,
Son-in-law to me, her mother.”
Sister dear of Youkahainen, Straightway fell to bitter weeping,
Wept all day and all the night long, Wept a second, then a third day,
On her youthful heart had fallen. Then the gray-haired mother asked her: “Why this weeping, lovely Aino?
Thou wilt rule his spacious dwelling, At his window sit and rest thee,
Walk a queen within his dwelling.” Thus replied the tearful Aino: “Mother dear, and all-forgiving,
Cause enough for bitter weeping: I must loose my sunny tresses,
Cannot deck my hair with jewels, Cannot bind my head with ribbons,
Underneath the linen bonnet That the wife must wear forever;
Weep alas! for waning beauty, Childhood vanished, youth departed,
Hope and pleasure of my childhood, Taken from me now forever,
At the tool-bench of my brother, At the window of my sister,
Spake again the gray-haired mother
“Cease thy sorrow, foolish maiden, By thy tears thou art ungrateful,
Not the slightest cause for weeping; Everywhere the silver sunshine
Not alone the moonlight glimmers Through thy father’s open windows,
Flowers bloom in every meadow, Berries grow on every mountain;
All the day long go and find them; Not alone thy brother’s meadows
Not alone thy father’s mountains Yield the ripe, nutritious berries;
Berries grow on other mountains, There as here, my lovely Aino.”
THE Fate OF Aino.
Sister fair of Youkahainen, Hastened early to the forest,
Went to gather birchen tassels; Bound a bundle for her father,
Silken tassels for her sister. Straightway then she hastened homeward,
As she neared the woodland border, Lo! the ancient Wainamoinen,
As she left the birchen woodland, Trimly dressed in costly raiment,
“Aino, beauty of the Northland, Wear not, lovely maid, for others,
Golden cross upon thy bosom, Shining pearls upon thy shoulders;
Wear for me thy golden braidlets.” Thus the maiden quickly answered: “Not for thee and not for others,
Deck my hair with silken ribbons; Need no more the many trinkets
Sooner wear the simplest raiment, Feed upon the barley bread-crust,
In the cabin with my father.”
Tore the jewels from her fingers, Quickly loosed her shining necklace,
Cast them all away indignant Into forest ferns and flowers.
Hastened to her mother’s cottage.
Whittling on an oaken ax-helve: “Wherefore weepest, beauteous Aino,
“Cause enough for weeping, father,
This, the reason for my weeping, This, the cause of all my sorrow:
From my belt, the clasp of copper, From my waist, the belt of silver,
Near the door-way sat her brother,
“Why art weeping, lovely Aino, Aino, my devoted sister?”
“Cause enough for weeping, brother,
Therefore come I as thou seest, Rings no longer on my fingers,
Golden were the rings thou gavest, And the necklace, pearls and silver!”
Weaving her a golden girdle: “Why art weeping, beauteous Aino,
“Cause enough for weeping, sister,
Therefore come I as thou seest, On my head no scarlet fillet,
On mine arms no purple ribbons, Round my neck no shining necklace,
In mine ears no golden ear-rings.”
Skimming cream, sat Aino’s mother. “Why art weeping, lovely Aino,
Thus the sobbing maiden answered: “Loving mother, all-forgiving,
Good the reasons for my sorrow, Therefore do I weep, dear mother:
Brooms to bind and shoots to gather, There to pluck some birchen tassels;
Bound a second for my mother, Bound a third one for my brother,
Straightway then I hastened homeward, By a foot-path left the forest;
Spake Osmoinen from the cornfield, Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: ‘Wear not, beauteous maid, for others,
On thy breast a golden crosslet, Shining pearls upon thy shoulders,
Weave for me thy silver braidlets.’ Then I threw the gold-cross from me,
Quickly loosed my shining necklace, Quick untied my silken ribbons,
Into forest ferns and flowers. Then I thus addressed the singer: ‘Not for thee and not for others,
Deck my hair with silken ribbons; Need no more the many trinkets,
Sooner wear the simplest raiment, Feed upon the barley bread-crust,
In the cabin with my father.’”
Aino, her beloved daughter: “Weep no more, my lovely maiden,
One year eat thou my sweet butter, It will make thee strong and ruddy;
It will make thee tall and queenly; Eat a third year only dainties,
Now make haste to yonder hill-top, To the store-house on the mountain,
Thou will find it filled with boxes, Chests and cases, trunks and boxes;
Lift away the gaudy cover, Thou will find six golden girdles,
Woven by the Moon’s fair daughters, Fashioned by the Sun’s sweet virgins.
As a maiden on the mountains, In the happy days of childhood,
There by chance I heard the daughters Of the Moon as they were weaving;
Of the Sun as they were spinning On the red rims of the cloudlets,
On the border of the pine-wood, On a high and distant mountain.
Stole myself within their hearing, Then began I to entreat them,
‘Give thy silver, Moon’s fair daughters, To a poor, but worthy maiden;
To this maiden, young and needy.’ Thereupon the Moon’s fair daughters
And the Sun’s sweet shining virgins Gave me gold from their abundance,
For my hair the shining silver. Then I hastened joyful homeward,
Happy to my mother’s cottage; Wore them one day, than a second,
Took the gold then from my temples, From my hair I took the silver,
Many seasons have they lain there, Have not seen them since my childhood.
Trim with gold thy throbbing temples, And thy neck with pearly necklace,
Robe thyself in pure, white linen Spun from flax of finest fiber;
Fasten it with golden girdle; On thy feet, put silken stockings,
Deck thy hair with golden braidlets, Bind it well with threads of silver;
And thy hands with dainty ruffles; Come bedecked then to thy chamber,
To the greeting of thy kindred, To the joy of all that know thee,
Coming as thy father’s sunbeam, Walking beautiful and queenly,
Thus she spake to weeping Aino,
But the maiden, little hearing, Does not heed her mother’s wishes;
There to weep in bitter sorrow, All alone to weep in anguish.
Thus at last soliloquizes: “Unto what can I now liken
Like the waters in the river, Like the waves in yonder lakelet,
Unto what, the biting sorrow Of the child of cold misfortune?
Like the icicle in winter, Water in the well imprisoned.
When a maiden free and merry, Happily through fen and fallow,
Lingered with the ferns and flowers, Knowing neither pain nor trouble;
Wanders though the bog and stubble, Wanders weary through the brambles,
Till my life is filled with darkness, And my spirit white with anguish.
Had she never seen the sunlight, Or if born had died an infant,
In these days of sin and sorrow, Underneath a star so luckless.
Had she died upon the eighth day After seven nights had vanished;
Needed but a little coffin, And a grave of smallest measure;
Father too perhaps a trifle, Sister would have wept the day through,
Thus had ended all the mourning.”
Wept one day, and then a second, Wept a third from morn till even,
“Why this weeping, fairest daughter, Darling daughter, why this grieving?”
“Therefore do I weep and sorrow, Wretched maiden all my life long,
Since thy daughter thou hast promised To the aged Wainamoinen,
Prop to stay him when he totters, In the storm a roof above him,
Better far if thou hadst sent me Far below the salt-sea surges,
And the friend of perch and salmon; Better far to ride the billows,
And the friend of nimble fishes, Than to be an old man’s solace,
Hand to aid him when he trembles, Arm to guide him when he falters,
Better be the whiting’s sister And the friend of perch and salmon,
Ending thus she left her mother,
To the store-house on the summit, Opened there the box the largest,
Found therein six golden girdles, Silken dresses seven in number.
She adorned herself as bidden, Robed herself to look her fairest,
In her hair the shining silver, On her shoulders purple ribbons,
Golden cross, and rings, and jewels, Fitting ornaments to beauty.
Leaves the store-house on the mountain, Filled with gold and silver trinkets,
Over stone-fields waste and barren, Wanders on through fen and forest,
Wanders hither, wanders thither, Singing careless as she wanders,
“Woe is me, my life hard-fated! Woe to Aino, broken-hearted!
Yet the sting would not be deeper, Nor the pain and anguish greater,
In my saddened heart’s dejection, I should yield my life forever,
Lo! the time has come for Aino From this cruel world to hasten,
To the realm of the departed, To the isle of the hereafter.
Mother dear, withhold thy censure, Lovely sister, dry thine eyelids,
When I sink beneath the sea-foam, Make my home in salmon-grottoes,
Water-ferns my couch and pillow.”
All the next day, sad and weary, So the third from morn till evening,
As she reached the sandy margin, Reached the cold and dismal sea-shore,
Sat alone in cold and darkness, Listened only to the music
Singing all the dirge of Aino. All that night the weary maiden
Through the sand and sea-washed pebbles.
She beholds three water-maidens, On a headland jutting seaward,
Sitting on the wave-lashed ledges, Swimming now upon the billows,
Quick the weeping maiden, Aino, Hastens there to join the mermaids,
Weeping Aino, now disrobing, Lays aside with care her garments,
Drops her gold-cross on the sea-shore, On the aspen hangs her ribbons,
On the grass her shoes of deer-skin, In the sand her shining necklace,
Out at sea a goodly distance,
Glittering in silver sunlight. Toward it springs the hapless maiden,
Up the standing-stone has clambered, Wishing there to rest a moment,
When upon a sudden swaying To and fro among the billows,
Falls the stone of many colors, Falls upon the very bottom
With the stone of rainbow colors, Falls the weeping maiden, Aino,
Sinking far below the surface, To the bottom of the blue-sea.
Thus poor Aino sank and perished, Singing as the stone descended,
“Once to swim I sought the sea-side, There to sport among the billows;
Sank poor Aino to the bottom Of the deep and boundless blue-sea,
Never come a-fishing, father, To the borders of these waters,
As thou lovest daughter Aino.
“Mother dear, I sought the sea-side,
With the stone of many colors, Sank poor Aino to the bottom
Like a pretty song-bird perished. Never mix thy bread, dear mother,
Never during all thy life-time, As thou lovest daughter Aino.
“Brother dear, I sought the sea-side,
With the stone of many colors Sank poor Aino to the bottom
Like a pretty song-bird perished. Never bring thy prancing war-horse,
Never bring thy steeds to water, To the borders of the blue-sea,
As thou lovest sister Aino.
“Sister dear, I sought the sea-side,
With the stone of many colors Sank poor Aino to the bottom
Like a pretty song-bird perished. Never come to lave thine eyelids
Never during all thy life-time, As thou lovest sister Aino.
Shall be blood of Aino’s body; All the fish that swim these waters
All the willows on the sea-side Shall be Aino’s ribs hereafter;
Will have grown from Aino’s tresses.”
Thus the lovely Aino perished. Who will tell the cruel story,
To the cottage of her mother, Once the home of lovely Aino?
Tell the tidings to her mother? Nay, the bear must not be herald,
Who then tell the cruel story, Who will bear the evil tidings
Once the home of lovely Aino? Shall the wolf repeat the story,
Nay, the wolf must not be herald, He would eat the gentle lambkins.
Who will bear the evil tidings. To the cottage of her sister?
Tell the tidings to her sister? Nay, the fox must not be herald,
Who then tell the cruel story,
To the cottage of her brother, Once the home of lovely Aino?
Bear the sad news to her brother? Yea, the hare shall be the herald,
Thus the harmless hare makes answer: “I will bear the evil tidings
Tell the story to her kindred.”
Like the winds he hastened onward, Galloped swift as flight of eagles;
Till he gained the wished-for cottage, Once the home of lovely Aino.
So he hastened to the bath-house, Found therein a group of maidens,
Sat the hare upon the threshold, And the maidens thus addressed him: “Hie there, Long-legs, or we’ll roast thee,
Roast thee for our lady’s breakfast, Stew thee for our master’s dinner,
And her brother, Youkahainen! Better therefore thou shouldst gallop
Than be roasted for our dinners.”
Chanting thus the fate of Aino: “Think ye not I journey hither,
To be stewed in yonder kettle; Let fell Lempo fill thy tables!
Come to tell the cruel story Of the flight and death of Aino,
With the stone of many colors Sank poor Aino to the bottom
Like a pretty song-bird perished; Hung her ribbons on the aspen,
Silken robes upon the alders, On the rocks her silken stockings,
In the sand her shining necklace, In the sand her rings and jewels;
Sleeping on the very bottom Of the deep and boundless blue-sea,
There to be the whiting’s sister And the friend of nimble fishes.”
From her blue-eyes bitter tear-drops, As in sad and wailing measures,
“Listen, all ye mothers, listen, Learn from me a tale of wisdom:
From the dwellings of their fathers, To the bridegrooms that they love not,
Drove away my lovely Aino, Fairest daughter of the Northland.”
And the tears that fall are bitter, Flowing down her wrinkled visage,
Then across her heaving bosom, Till they reach her garment’s border;
Till they touch her shoes of deer-skin; Then beneath her shoes of deer-skin,
Part to earth as its possession, Part to water as its portion.
Form they streamlets three in number, And their source, the mother’s eyelids,
Flowing on like little rivers, And each streamlet larger growing,
In each rushing, roaring torrent, There a cataract is foaming,
From the cataract’s commotion Rise three pillared rocks in grandeur;
Grow three hillocks clothed in verdure; From each hillock, speckled birches,
On the summit of each birch-tree Sits a golden cuckoo calling,
“Love! O Love!” the first one calleth; Sings the second, “Suitor! Suitor!”
“Consolation! Consolation!” He that “Love! O Love!” is calling,
For the love-rejecting maiden Sleeping in the deep sea-castles.
Sings six moons and sings unceasing For the suitor that forever
He that sadly sings and echoes, “Consolation! Consolation!”
For the broken-hearted mother That must mourn and weep forever.
Heard the sacred cuckoo singing, Spake she thus, and sorely weeping: “When I hear the cuckoo calling,
Tears unlock my heavy eyelids, Flow adown my furrowed visage,
Older grow my wearied elbows, Weaker ply my aged fingers,
Does my body shake in palsy, When I hear the cuckoo singing,
Wainavoinen’S Lamentation.
Far away men heard the story Of the flight and death of Aino,
Fairest daughter of creation.
Straightway fell to bitter weeping, Wept at morning, wept at evening,
That his Aino had departed, That the maiden thus had vanished,
Of the blue-sea, deep and boundless.
Wainamoinen of the Northland, Heavy-hearted, sorely weeping,
This the suitor’s prayer and question: “Tell, Untamo, tell me, dreamer,
Where the water-gods may linger, Where may rest Wellamo’s maidens?”
Lazily he told his dreamings: “Over there, the mermaid-dwellings,
On the headland robed in verdure, On the forest-covered island,
On the purple-colored sea-shore; Yonder is the home of sea-maids,
Live there in their sea-side chambers, Rest within their water-caverns,
On the juttings of the sea-cliffs.”
To a boat-house on the sea-shore, Looks with care upon the fish-hooks,
Lines, and hooks, and poles, and fish-nets, Places in a boat of copper,
To the forest-covered island, To the point enrobed in verdure,
Where the sea-nymphs live and linger. Hardly does he reach the island
Far away he throws his fish-hook, Trolls it quickly through the waters,
Dangling from a silver fish-line, Golden is the hook he uses.
Angles long, and angles longer, Angles one day, then a second,
Angles at the hour of noontide, Many days and nights he angles,
Strikes a fish of magic powers, Plays like salmon on his fish-line,
Till at length the fish exhausted Falls a victim to the angler,
Of the hero’s boat of copper.
Speaks these words in wonder guessing: “This the fairest of all sea-fish,
Smoother surely than the salmon, Brighter-spotted than the trout is,
Has less fins than any female, Not the fins of any male fish,
Not the belt of any mermaid, Not the ears of any song-bird,
From the blue-sea’s deepest caverns.”
Wore a knife insheathed with silver; From its case he drew the fish-knife,
Dress the nameless fish for roasting, Make of it a dainty breakfast,
Make for him a toothsome supper, Make the later meal at evening.
Touches with his knife of silver, Quick it leaps upon the waters,
From the boat with copper bottom, From the skiff of Wainamoinen.
Quickly from the sea it rises On the sixth and seventh billows,
Out of reach of fishing-tackle, Then addresses Wainamoinen,
“Wainamoinen, ancient minstrel, Do not think that I came hither
Only to be chopped in pieces, Dressed and eaten like a whiting
Make for thee a meal at midday, Make for thee a toothsome supper,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Wherefore didst thou then come hither,
Thus the nameless fish made answer: “Hither have I come, O minstrel,
And thyself to love and cherish, At thy side a life-companion,
Deck thy couch with snowy linen, Smooth thy head upon the pillow,
Keep thy dwelling-place in order, Build a fire for thee when needed,
Fill thy cup with barley-water, Do for thee whatever pleases.
“I am not a scaly sea-fish,
Not a whiting from the waters, Not a salmon of the North-seas,
Friend and sister of the fishes, Youkahainen’s youngest sister,
I am Aino whom thou lovest.
“Once thou wert the wise-tongued hero,
Scant of insight, scant of judgment, Didst not know enough to keep me,
Tried to kill me with thy fish-knife, So to roast me for thy dinner;
Once the fair and lovely Aino, Sister dear of Youkahainen.”
Filled with sorrow, much regretting: “Since thou’rt Youkahainen’s sister,
Come to me again I pray thee!”
“Nevermore will Aino’s spirit Fly to thee and be ill-treated.”
From the surface of the billow To the many-colored pebbles,
Where the mermaids live and linger.
Thought afresh and well reflected, How to live, and work, and win her;
To and fro through foam and billow, Through the bays and winding channels,
Drew it through the salmon-dwellings, Through the homes of water-maidens,
Through the blue-back of the ocean, Through the lakes of distant Lapland,
Through the seas of Kalevala, Hoping thus to find his Aino.
Every form of fish-like creatures, But he did not catch the sea-maid,
Fairest daughter of the Northland.
Mind depressed, and heart discouraged, Spake these words, immersed in sorrow: “Fool am I, and great my folly,
Surely once I had some knowledge, Had some insight into wisdom,
But my virtues all have left me In these mournful days of evil,
Insight gone, and sense departed, All my prudence gone to others!
All these years have sought to honor, Aino, now Wellamo’s maiden,
Promised bride of mine forever, Once I had within my power,
Led her to my boat of copper, With my fish-line made of silver;
Did not know that I had caught her Till too late to woo and win her;
To the home of water-maidens, To the kingdom of Wellamo.”
Empty-handed, heavy-hearted, Straightway hastened to his country,
Spake these words upon his journey: “What has happened to the cuckoo,
In the morning, in the evening, Often bringing joy at noontide?
What has changed the cuckoo’s calling? Sorrow must have stilled his singing,
As I hear him sing no longer, For my pleasure in the morning,
Never shall I learn the secret, How to live and how to prosper,
How upon the seas to wander! Only were my ancient mother
Surely she would well advise me, What my thought and what my action,
That this sorrow might escape me, And this darkened cloud pass over.”
From her tomb she spake as follows: “Only sleeping was thy mother,
What thy thought and what thine action, That this cup of grief may pass thee,
And this darkened cloud pass over. Hie thee straightway to the Northland,
Thou wilt find them wise and lovely, Far more beautiful than Aino,
Not such silly chatter-boxes, As the fickle Lapland maidens.
From the honest homes of Suomi, One of Northland’s honest daughters;
Make thee happy through her goodness, Form perfection, manners easy,
Full of wit and good behavior, Honor to thy home and kindred.”
Wainamoinen’S Hapless Journey.
Now arranges for a journey To the village of the Northland,
To the land of little sunshine, To the land of worthy women;
Then adjusts the golden bridle, Lays upon his back the saddle,
Seats himself upon his courser, And begins his journey northward;
Galloping along the highway, In his saddle, gaily fashioned,
Plunging through Wainola’s meadows, O’er the plains of Kalevala.
Galloped far beyond Wainola, Bounded o’er the waste of waters,
Wetting not the hoofs in running.
Nursed a grudge within his bosom, In his heart the worm of envy,
Of this wonderful enchanter. He prepares a cruel cross-bow,
Paints the bow in many colors, Molds the top-piece out of copper,
Gold he uses too in trimming. Then he hunts for strongest sinews,
Interweaves the flax of Lempo. Ready is the cruel cross-bow,
Beautiful the bow and mighty, Surely cost it not a trifle;
On each end a colt of beauty, Near the curve a maiden sleeping,
Wonderful the bow thus fashioned; Cuts some arrows for his quiver,
From the oak the shafts he fashions, Makes the tips of keenest metal.
Then he feathers well his arrows From the plumage of the swallow,
Hardens well his feathered arrows, And imparts to each new virtues,
In the virus of the adder.
Ready strung, his cruel cross-bow, Waiting for wise Wainamoinen.
Waits a long time, is not weary, Hopes to spy the ancient singer;
Spies he ceaselessly at noontide, Lies in wait for the magician,
Sits he at the open window, Stands behind the hedge, and watches;
Spies along the balks of meadows; On his back he hangs his quiver,
Dipped in virus of the viper, On his arm the mighty cross-bow,
Listens from the boat-house window, Lingers at the end of Fog-point,
Near the holy stream and whirlpool, Near the sacred river’s fire-fall.
Youkahainen of Pohyola, At the breaking of the day-dawn,
Fixed his gaze upon the North-east, Turned his eyes upon the sunrise,
Something blue upon the waters, And soliloquized as follows: “Are those clouds on the horizon,
Neither clouds on the horizon, Nor the dawning of the morning;
The renowned and wise enchanter, Riding on his way to Northland;
Magic courser of Wainola.”
Lapland’s vain and evil minstrel, Filled with envy, grasps his cross-bow,
For the death of Wainamoinen.
Spake these words to Youkahainen: “For whose slaughter is thy cross-bow,
Youkahainen thus made answer: “I have made this mighty cross-bow,
For the death of Wainamoinen, Thus to slay the friend of waters;
The eternal bard and hero, Through the heart, and through the liver,
With this bow and feathered arrows Thus destroy my rival minstrel.”
Thus reproving, thus forbidding: “Do not slay good Wainamoinen,
From a noble tribe descended, He, my sister’s son, my nephew.
Ancient son of Kalevala, Then alas! all joy will vanish,
Better on the earth the gladness, Better here the magic music,
In the kingdom of Tuoni, In the realm of the departed,
Then the youthful Youkahainen
Ere he made a final answer.
But the other seemed to weaken, As he drew the cruel bow-string.
As his bosom swelled with envy: “Let all joy forever vanish,
Disappear earth’s sweetest music, Happiness depart forever;
Little heeding what the end is.”
On his left knee rests the weapon, With his right foot firmly planted,
Takes three arrows from his quiver, Choosing well the best among them,
Sets with care the feathered arrow, To the flaxen string he lays it,
Aiming well along the margin, At the heart of Wainamoinen,
In the shadow of a thicket, Speaks these words while he is waiting “Be thou, flaxen string, elastic;
Swiftly speed, thou deadly missile, Quick as light, thou poisoned arrow,
If my hand too low should hold thee, May the gods direct thee higher;
May the gods direct thee lower.”
Like the lightning flies the arrow O’er the head of Wainamoinen;
And the highest clouds it pierces, Scatters all the flock of lamb-clouds,
Not discouraged, quick selecting,
Quickly aiming, shoots a second. Speeds the arrow swift as lightning;
Into earth the arrow plunges, Pierces to the lower regions,
Nothing daunted, Youkahainen,
Swift as light it speeds its journey, Strikes the steed of Wainamoinen,
Strikes him near his golden girdle, Through the shoulder of the racer.
Headlong fell upon the waters, Plunged beneath the rolling billows,
From his dappled steed of magic. Then arose a mighty storm-wind,
Bore away old Wainamoinen Far from land upon the billows,
On the broad sea’s great expanses.
Thinking Waino dead and buried, These the boastful words he uttered: “Nevermore, old Wainamoinen,
While the golden moonlight glistens, Nevermore wilt fix thy vision
On the plains of Kalevala; Full six years must swim the ocean,
Eight years ride the foamy billows, In the broad expanse of water;
Seven winters as a pebble, Eight long summers as an aspen.”
Hastened to his room delighting, When his mother thus addressed him “Hast thou slain good Wainamoinen,
Youkahainen thus made answer: “I have slain old Wainamoinen,
That he now may plow the ocean, That he now may sweep the waters,
In the salt-sea plunged he headlong, In the deep sank the magician,
On his back to rock forever, Thus the boundless sea to travel,
This the answer of the mother: “Woe to earth for this thine action,
Vanished is the wit of ages! Thou hast slain good Wainamoinen,
Slain the pride of Suwantala, Slain the hero of Wainola,
Wainamoinen’S Rescue.
Swam through all the deep-sea waters, Floating like a branch of aspen,
Swam six days in summer weather, Swam six nights in golden moonlight;
And behind him sky and ocean. Two days more he swam undaunted,
On the evening of the eighth day, Wainamoinen grew disheartened,
For his feet had lost their toe-nails, And his fingers dead and dying.
Sad and weary, spake as follows: “Woe is me, my old life fated!
Fool was I when fortune favored, To forsake my home and kindred,
Here beneath the starry heavens, In this cruel waste of waters,
Here to struggle with the storm-winds, To be tossed by heaving billows,
In this ocean vast and boundless.
“Cold my life and sad and dreary,
Evermore within these waters, Thus to struggle for existence!
How to find me food and shelter, In these cold and lifeless waters,
Build I in the winds my dwelling? It will find no sure foundation.
Surely would the waves destroy it.”
From the occident, an eagle, Is not classed among the largest,
One wing touches on the waters, While the other sweeps the heavens;
Strikes his beak upon the sea-cliffs, Flies about, then safely perches,
There beholds brave Wainamoinen, On the blue-back of the ocean,
“Wherefore art thou, ancient hero, Swimming in the deep-sea billows?”
“I am ancient Wainamoinen, Friend and fellow of the waters,
Went to woo a Northland maiden, Maiden from the dismal Darkland,
Riding on the plain of ocean. I arrived one morning early,
At the bay of Luotola, Near Youkola’s foaming river,
Slew my steed with bow and arrow, Tried to slay me with his weapons.
Plunged beneath the salt-sea’s surface, From the saddle of the courser,
“Then arose a mighty storm-wind,
Washed me seaward on the surges, Seaward, seaward, further, further,
Swam and rocked upon the billows, Where as many nights I struggled,
With the angry winds and waters.
“Woe is me, my life hard-fated!
How to live nor how to perish In this cruel salt-sea water.
It will find no sure foundation. Build my home upon the waters?
Must I swim the sea forever, Must I live, or must I perish?
If I sink below the billows, Perish here from cold and hunger?”
“Be not in the least disheartened, Place thyself between my shoulders,
I will lift thee from the waters, Bear thee with my pinions upward,
Well do I the day remember Where thou didst the eagle service,
Thou didst leave the birch-tree standing, When were cleared the Osmo-forests,
As a home for weary song-birds, As a resting-place for eagles.”
Lifts his head above the waters, Boldly rises from the sea-waves,
Seats himself upon the eagle, On the eagle’s feathered shoulders.
Bears the ancient Wainamoinen, Bears him on the path of zephyrs,
To the distant shore of Northland, To the dismal Sariola,
Flies away to join his fellows.
Straightway fell to bitter weeping, Wept and moaned in heavy accents,
On a cheerless promontory, With a hundred wounds tormented,
With his hair and beard dishevelled By the surging of the billows.
Wept as many nights in anguish, Did not know what way to journey,
That would point him to the highway, To his home in Kalevala,
Northland’s young and slender maiden,
With the Sun had laid a wager, With the Sun and Moon a wager,
On the morning of the morrow. And the maiden rose in beauty,
Long before the Moon had wakened, From their beds beneath the ocean.
Ere the Sun had broken slumber; She had sheared six gentle lambkins,
Hence to make the rolls for spinning, Hence to form the threads for weaving,
Ere the morning dawn had broken, Ere the sleeping Sun had risen.
Then she scrubbed the birchen tables, Sweeps the ground-floor of the stable,
From the birches of the Northland, Scrapes the sweepings well together
Carries them beyond the stable, From the doorway to the meadow,
Near the surges of the great-sea, Listens there and looks about her,
Hears a weeping from the sea-shore, Hears a hero-voice lamenting.
Hastens to her mother’s dwelling, These the words the maiden utters: “I have heard a wail from ocean,
On the shore some one lamenting.”
Ancient, toothless dame of Northland, Hastens from her door and court-yard,
Listens well for sounds of weeping, For the wail of one in sorrow;
Hears a hero-cry of anguish. Thus the ancient Louhi answers: “This is not the wail of children,
In this way weep bearded heroes; This the hero-cry of anguish.”
To the floods her goodly vessel, Straightway rows with lightning swiftness,
Gives the hero consolation, Comfort gives she to the minstrel
In his piteous condition, Mid the alder-trees and aspens,
Visage trembling, locks dishevelled, Ears, and eyes, and lips of sadness.
Thus addresses Wainamoinen: “Tell me what has been thy folly,
Old and truthful Wainamoinen
“Well I know that it is folly That has brought me all this trouble,
To these regions unbefitting; Happy was I with my kindred,
There my name was named in honor.”
Thus replied to Wainamoinen: “I would gain the information,
Who thou art of ancient heroes, Who of all the host of heroes?”
“Formerly my name was mentioned, Often was I heard and honored,
In the long and dreary winters, Called the Singer of the Northland,
On the plains of Kalevala; No one thought that such misfortune
Louhi, hostess of Pohyola,
“Rise, O hero, from discomfort, From thy bed among the willows;
Come with me to yonder dwelling, There relate thy strange adventures,
Now she takes the hapless hero,
In her boat she safely seats him, And begins at once her rowing,
To her home upon the sea-shore, To the dwellings of Pohyola.
Rests the ancient Wainamoinen, Gives him warmth, and food, and shelter,
Then the hostess of Pohyola
“Wherefore didst thou, Wainamoinen, Friend and fellow of the waters,
On the border of the ocean, Mid the aspens and the willows?”
“Had good reason for my weeping, Cause enough for all my sorrow;
Had been buffeting the billows, In the far outstretching waters.
I have lived in toil and torture, Since I left my home and country,
Came to this the land of strangers, To these unfamiliar portals.
All thy branches, spines to pierce me, Even birches give me trouble,
My companions, winds and waters, Only does the Sun seem friendly,
Near these unfamiliar portals.”
“Weep no longer, Wainamoinen, Grieve no more, thou friend of waters,
At our friendly homes and firesides; Thou shalt live with us and welcome,
Eat the salmon from our platters, Eat the sweetest of our bacon,
Answers thus old Wainamoinen,
“Never do I court strange tables, Though the food be rare and toothsome;
One’s own table is the sweetest, One’s own home, the most attractive.
Thou Creator, full of mercy, Grant that I again may visit
Better dwell in one’s own country, There to drink its healthful waters
Than in foreign lands to wander, There to drink the rarest liquors
Louhi, hostess of Pohyola,
“What reward wilt thou award me, Should I take thee where thou willest,
To thy much-loved home and fireside, To the meadows of Wainola,
These the words of Wainamoinen: “What would be reward sufficient,
To my home and distant country, To the borders of the Northland,
Hear the sacred cuckoo calling? Shall I give thee golden treasures,
This is Louhi’s simple answer: “O thou ancient Wainamoinen,
Never will I ask for riches, Never ask for gold nor silver;
Silver for the stallion’s jewels. Canst thou forge for me the Sampo,
From the tips of white-swan feathers From the milk of greatest virtue,
From the finest wool of lambkins?
“I will give thee too my daughter,
Take thee to thy much-loved home-land, To the borders of Wainola,
Hear the sacred cuckoo calling.”
Gave this answer to her question: “Cannot forge for thee the Sampo,
Take me to my distant country, I will send thee Ilmarinen,
Hammer thee the lid in colors, He may win thy lovely maiden;
In this art is first and master; He, the one that forged the heavens.
Nowhere see we hammer-traces, Nowhere find a single tongs-mark.”
“Him alone I’ll give my daughter, Promise him my child in marriage,
Hammer me the lid in colors, From the tips of white-swan feathers,
From a single grain of barley, From the finest wool of lambkins.”
Harnessed quick a dappled courser, Hitched him to her sledge of birch-wood,
Placed the hero on the cross-bench, Made him ready for his journey;
These the words that Louhi uttered: “Do not raise thine eyes to heaven,
While thy steed is fresh and frisky, While the day-star lights thy pathway,
If thine eyes be lifted upward, While the day-star lights thy pathway,
Some sad fate will overtake thee.”
Fleetly drove upon his journey, Merrily he hastened homeward,
From the ever-darksome Northland From the dismal Sariola.
Maiden of the Rainbow.
Glory of the land and water, Sat upon the bow of heaven,
In a gown of richest fabric, In a gold and silver air-gown,
Interlacing threads of silver; Weaving with a golden shuttle,
Merrily flies the golden shuttle, From the maiden’s nimble fingers,
Swiftly flies the comb of silver, From the sky-born maiden’s fingers,
Came the ancient Wainamoinen,
From the ever sunless Northland, From the dismal Sariola;
Driven but a little distance, When he heard the sky-loom buzzing,
Quick the thoughtless Wainamoinen Lifts his eyes aloft in wonder,
There beholds the bow of beauty, On the bow the maiden sitting,
Glory of the earth and ocean, Weaving there a golden fabric,
Wainamoinen, ancient minstrel,
Looks upon the charming maiden, Then addresses her as follows: “Come, fair maiden, to my snow-sledge,
Thus the Maid of Beauty answers: “Tell me what thou wishest of me,
Speaks the ancient Wainamoinen, Answers thus the Maid of Beauty: “This the reason for thy coming:
Shalt prepare me barley-water, Thou shalt fill my foaming beer-cups,
Shalt rejoice within my portals, Walk a queen within my dwelling,
In the courts of Kalevala.”
From her throne amid the heavens: “Yesterday at hour of twilight,
There to rock upon the common, Where the Sun retires to slumber;

“Then I asked the pretty songster,
‘Sing to me, thou pretty song-bird, Sing that I may understand thee,
How to live in greatest pleasure, And in happiness the sweetest,

“Thus the song-bird gave me answer,
‘Bright and warm are days of summer, Warmer still is maiden-freedom;

Not to wives are favors given.’”
Answers thus the Maid of Beauty: “Foolish is the thrush thus singing,
Like to babes are maidens treated, Wives are queens and highly honored.
I am not despised as hero, Not the meanest of magicians;
Wife and queen in Kalevala.” Thus the Maid of Beauty answered: “Would consider thee a hero,
When a golden hair thou splittest, Using knives that have no edges;
With a snare that I can see not.”
Split a golden hair exactly, Using knives that had no edges;
With a snare the maiden saw not.
“Come, sweet maiden, to my snow-sledge,
Thus the maiden wisely answered: “Never enter I thy snow-sledge,
Till thou cuttest me a whip-stick From the ice, and make no splinters,
Wainamoinen, true magician,
Deftly peeled the rounded sandstone, Deftly cut from ice a whip-stick,
Losing not the smallest fragment. Then again he called the maiden,
But the Maid or Beauty answered,
“I will go with that one only That will make me ship or shallop,
From the fragments of my distaff, In the waters launch the vessel,
Using not the knee to push it, Using not the arm to move it,
Using not the foot to turn it, Using nothing to propel it.”
These the words the hero uttered: “There is no one in the Northland,
Who like me can build a vessel, From the fragments of the distaff,
Then he took the distaff-fragments,
Hastened off the boat to fashion, Hastened to an iron mountain,
Full of zeal he plies the hammer, Swings the hammer and the hatchet;
Works one day and then a second, Works with steady hand the third day;
Evil Hisi grasps the hatchet, Lempo takes the crooked handle,
Strikes the rocks and breaks to pieces; From the rocks rebound the fragments,
Cut the knee of Wainamoinen. Lempo guides the sharpened hatchet,
Quickly gushes forth a blood-stream, And the stream is crimson-colored.
The renowned and wise enchanter, Thus outspeaks in measured accents: “O thou keen and cruel hatchet,
Thou shouldst cut the trees to fragments, Cut the pine-tree and the willow,
Cut the juniper and aspen, Shouldst not cut my knee to pieces,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen
Thus begins his magic singing, Of the origin of evil;
Makes no effort to remember, Sings the origin of iron,
Thus prepare a lock for surety, For the wounds the axe has given,
But the stream flows like a brooklet, Rushing like a maddened torrent,
Scarcely is a bit of verdure That the blood-stream does not cover
From the knee of the magician, From the veins of Wainamoinen.
Gathers lichens from the sandstone, Picks them from the trunks of birches,

Feeling pain and fearing languor, Falls to weeping, heavy-hearted;
Hitches to the sledge of birch-wood, Climbs with pain upon the cross-bench,
Snaps his whip above the racer, And the steed flies onward swiftly;
Till he nears a Northland village, Where the way is triple-parted.
Takes the lowest of the highways, Quickly nears a spacious cottage,
“Is there any one here dwelling, That can know the pain I suffer,
That can check this crimson streamlet?”
On a bench beside a baby, And he answered thus the hero: “There is no one in this dwelling
That can heal the wounds of hatchet, That can check the crimson streamlet;
That perchance can do thee service.”
Whips his courser to a gallop, Dashes on along the highway;
On the middle of the highways, To a cabin on the road-side,
Questions all through open windows, These the words the hero uses: “Is there no one in this cabin,
That can heal this wound of hatchet, That can check this crimson streamlet?”
Near the fire-place lay the beldame, Thus she spake to Wainamoinen,
“There is no one in this cabin That can know the pain thou feelest,
That can check the crimson streamlet; Some one lives in yonder cottage,
Wainamoinen, nothing daunted,
Dashes on along the highway; Only drives a little distance,
Gallops to a humble cottage, Asks one standing near the penthouse,
“Is there no one in this cottage, That can know the pain I suffer,
That can check this crimson streamlet?”
On the hearthstone sat the gray-beard, Thus he answered Wainamoinen: “Greater things have been accomplished,
Through but three words of the master; Through the telling of the causes,
River cataracts been lessened, Bays been made of promontories,
Origin OF Iron.
Quickly rises in his snow-sledge, Asking no one for assistance,
Takes a seat within the dwelling. Come two maids with silver pitchers,
Dip they up a very little, But the very smallest measure
From the wounds of Wainamoinen.
Thus the gray-beard asks the minstrel: “Tell me who thou art of heroes,
Lo! thy blood fills seven sea-boats, Eight of largest birchen vessels,
From the wounds of some magician. Other matters I would ask thee;
Sing to me the source of metals, Sing the origin of iron,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen
“Know I well the source of metals, Know the origin of iron;
Of the mothers air is oldest, Water is the oldest brother,
And the youngest brother, iron; Ukko is the first creator.
Cut apart the air and water, Ere was born the metal, iron.
Firmly rubbed his hands together, Firmly pressed them on his knee-cap,
Three most beautiful of daughters; These were mothers of the iron,
Tremblingly they walked the heavens, Walked the clouds with silver linings,
With the milk of future iron, Flowing on and flowing ever,
To the earth, the valleys filling, To the slumber-calling waters.
“Ukko’s eldest daughter sprinkled
And the second daughter sprinkled White milk over hills and mountains,
Red milk over seas and oceans. Where the black milk had been sprinked,
Where the white milk had been sprinkled, Grew the iron, lighter-colored;
Grew the red and brittle iron.
“After Time had gone a distance,
His beloved elder brother, Thus to know his brother better.
Labored to consume his brother, His beloved younger brother.
Saves himself by fleetly fleeing, From the fiery flame’s advances,
Fleeing still and taking shelter In the swamps and in the valleys,
By the rivers winding seaward, On the broad backs of the marshes,
Where the wild geese hatch their goslings.
“Thus is iron in the swamp-lands,
Hidden well for many ages, Hidden in the birchen forests,
From the searchings of his brother; Here and there the fire has caught him,
That the spears, and swords, and axes, Might be forged and duly hammered.
From the heath the bears came ambling, And the wolves ran through the marshes.
Where the feet of wolves had trodden, Where the paws of bears had trampled.
“Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
He was born upon the Coal-mount, Skilled and nurtured in the coal-fields;
In the other, tongs of iron; In the night was born the blacksmith,
Sought with care a favored hillock, Where the winds might fill his bellows;
Where the iron hid abundant; There he built his smelting furnace,
Hastened where the wolves had travelled, Followed where the bears had trampled,
In the wolf-tracks of the marshes, In the foot-prints of the gray-bear.
“Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
‘Thou most useful of the metals, Thou art sleeping in the marshes,
Where the wolf treads in the swamp-lands, Where the bear sleeps in the thickets.
What would be thy future station, Should I place thee in the furnace,
“Then was Iron sorely frightened,
When of Fire he heard the mention, Mention of his fell destroyer.
“Then again speaks Ilmarinen,
‘Be not frightened, useful metal, Surely Fire will not consume thee,
Will not harm his nearest kindred. Come thou to my room and furnace,
Thou wilt live, and grow, and prosper, Wilt become the swords of heroes,
“Ere arose the star of evening,
From the water-beds had risen, Had been carried to the furnace,
Laid it in his smelting furnace. Ilmarinen starts the bellows,
And the iron flows in streamlets From the forge of the magician,
Soft as dough for bread of barley. Then out-screamed the metal, Iron: ‘Wondrous blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
From this fire and cruel torture.’
“Ilmarinen thus made answer: ‘I will take thee from my furnace,
Thou shalt be a mighty power, Thou shalt slay the best of heroes,
“Straightway Iron made this promise,
By the furnace, by the anvil, By the tongs, and by the hammer,
‘Many trees that I shall injure, Shall devour the hearts of mountains,
Shall not kill the best of heroes, Shall not wound my dearest brother;
Happier would be my life-time, Should I serve my fellow-beings,
Than as implements of warfare, Slay my friends and nearest kindred,
“Now the master, Ilmarinen,
From the fire removes the iron, Places it upon the anvil,
Hammers many fine utensils, Hammers spears, and swords, and axes,
Hammers tools of all descriptions.
“Many things the blacksmith needed,
Could not make the tongue of iron, Could not hammer steel from iron,
Well considered Ilmarinen, Deeply thought and long reflected.
Steeped the ashes in the water, Made a lye to harden iron,
With his tongue he tests the mixture, Weighs it long and well considers,
‘All this labor is for nothing, Will not fashion steel from iron,
“Now a bee flies from the meadow,
Flies about, then safely settles Near the furnace of the smithy.
“Thus the smith the bee addresses,
‘Little bee, thou tiny birdling, Bring me honey on thy winglets,
Sweetness from the fragrant meadows, From the little cups of flowers,
That we thus may aid the water To produce the steel from iron.’
“Evil Hisi’s bird, the hornet,
Looking from the cottage gable, Flying to the bark of birch-trees,
While the steel was being tempered; Swiftly flew the stinging hornet,
Brought the blessing of the serpent, Brought the venom of the adder,
Brought the stings of all the insects, Mixed them with the ore and water,
“Ilmarinen, skilful blacksmith,
Thought the bee had surely brought him Honey from the fragrant meadows,
From the tips of seven petals, And he spake the words that follow: ‘Welcome, welcome, is thy coming,
Thou hast brought to aid the water, Thus to form the steel from iron!’
“Ilmarinen, ancient blacksmith,
Water mixed with many poisons, Thought it but the wild bee’s honey;
When he plunged it into water, Water mixed with many poisons,
Angry grew the hardened iron, Broke the vow that he had taken,
Mercilessly cut his brother, Madly raged against his kindred,
From the wounds of man and hero. This, the origin of iron,
From the hearth arose the gray-beard,
“Now I know the source of iron, Whence the steel and whence its evils;
Curses on the steel thou givest, Curses on thee, tongue of evil,
Once thou wert of little value, Having neither form nor beauty,
When in form of milk thou rested, When for ages thou wert hidden
Hidden in their heaving bosoms, On the borders of the cloudlets,
“Thou wert once of little value,
Neither strength nor great importance, When like water thou wert resting
On the steep declines of mountains, When thou wert but formless matter,
“Surely thou wert void of greatness,
When the moose was trampling on thee, When the roebuck trod upon thee,
And the bear-paws scratched thy body. Surely thou hadst little value
First of all the iron-workers, Brought thee from the blackened swamp-lands,
Placed thee in his fiery furnace. Truly thou hadst little vigor,
When thou in the fire wert hissing, Rolling forth like seething water,
When thou gavest oath the strongest, By the furnace, by the anvil,
By the dwelling of the blacksmith, By the fire within the furnace.
“Now forsooth thou hast grown mighty,
Thou hast broken all thy pledges, All thy solemn vows hast broken,
Shamest both thyself and kindred, Tainted all with breath of evil.
Tell who taught thee all thy malice, Tell who gavest thee thine evil!
Did the eldest of thy brothers, Did the youngest of thy sisters,
Give to thee thine evil nature? Not thy father, nor thy mother,
Not the youngest of thy sisters, Not the worst of all thy kindred,
Thou the cause of all our trouble. Come and view thine evil doings,
Ere I tell thy gray-haired mother, Ere I tell thine aged father.
Great indeed a father’s sorrow, When a son does something evil,
“Crimson streamlet, cease thy flowing
Blood of ages, stop thy coursing From the veins of the magician;
Stand like columns in the ocean, Stand like birch-trees in the forest,
Like the high-rocks on the sea-coast, Stand by power of mighty magic!
“Should perforce thy will impel thee,
Through the veins of Wainamoinen, Through the bones, and through the muscles,
Of the mighty sage and singer; Better be the food of heroes,
On the meadows and the woodlands, And be lost in dust and ashes.
Thou must cease this crimson out-flow; Stain no more the grass and flowers,
Pride and beauty of our heroes. In the veins of the magician,
Is thy rightful home and storehouse. Thither now withdraw thy forces,
Flow no more as crimson currents, Fill no longer crimson lakelets,
Nor meander like the rivers.
“Cease thy flow, by word of magic,
As the rivers of Tuoni, When the sky withheld her rain-drops,
In the famine of the seasons, In the years of fire and torture.
I shall offer other measures, Know I well of other forces;
In them I shall boil and roast thee, Thus to check thy crimson flowing,
“If these means be inefficient,
I shall call omniscient Ukko, Mightiest of the creators,
Wiser than the world-magicians; He will check the crimson out-flow,
“Ukko, God of love and mercy,
Come thou hither, thou art needed, Come thou quickly I beseech thee,
Touch this wound with healing fingers, Stop this hero’s streaming life-blood,
Mingle with them healing flowers, Thus to check this crimson current,
Save the life of Wainamoinen.”
As the magic words were spoken. Then the gray-beard, much rejoicing,
There to make a healing balsam, From the herbs of tender fibre,
From the stalks secreting honey, From the roots, and leaves, and blossoms.
And the oak the son addresses: “Hast thou honey in thy branches,
Thus the oak-tree wisely answers: “Yea, but last night dripped the honey
And the clouds their fragrance sifted, Sifted honey on my leaflets,
Then the son takes oak-wood splinters,
Gathers many healing grasses, Gathers many herbs and flowers,
Places them within the furnace In a kettle made of copper;
Bits of bark chipped from the oak-tree, Many herbs of healing virtues;
Three long days of summer weather, Days and nights in quick succession;
Looks to see if it is ready, If his remedy is finished;
Then he added other grasses,
That were brought from distant nations, Many hundred leagues from Northland,

Found at last that it was ready, Found the magic balm was finished.
On the border of the meadow, Wickedly it had been broken,
Quick he takes his balm of healing, And anoints the broken branches,
Thus addresses then the birch-tree: “With this balsam I anoint thee,
Cover well thine injured places; Now the birch-tree shall recover,
True, the birch-tree soon recovered,
Grew more uniform its branches, And its bole more strong and stately.
Thus the magic salve he tested, Touched with it the splintered sandstone,
Touched the fissures in the mountains, And the broken parts united,
Then the young boy quick returning
To the gray-beard gave the ointment, And the boy these measures uttered: “Here I bring the balm of healing,
It will join the broken granite, Make the fragments grow together,
And restore the injured birch-tree.”
Tested thus the magic balsam, Found the remedy effective,
Then anointed he the minstrel, Touched the wounds of Wainamoinen,
With the balm of many virtues; Speaking words of ancient wisdom,
“Do not walk in thine own virtue, Do not work in thine own power,
Do not speak in thine own wisdom, Speak with tongue of mighty Ukko.
It has come from my Creator; If my hands are filled with beauty,
When the wounds had been anointed,
Straightway ancient Wainamoinen Suffered fearful pain and anguish,
Turning one way, then another, Sought for rest and found it nowhere,
Banished by the aid of magic, Drove away his killing torment
To the highest hill of torture, To the distant rocks and ledges,
To the realm of wicked Hisi. Then he took some silken fabric,
Making equal strips for wrapping, Tied the ends with silken ribbons,
Then he wrapped with skilful fingers Wainamoinen’s knee and ankle,
And this prayer the gray-beard uttered “Ukko’s fabric is the bandage,
These have served the wounded hero, Wrapped the wounds of the magician.
Come and guard us, kind Creator, And protect us from all evil!
Guard our lives from every danger, From the wicked wilds of Hisi.”
Felt the mighty aid of magic, Felt the help of gracious Ukko,
Straightway were the wounds united, Quick the fearful pain departed.
Straightway walked in perfect freedom, Turned his knee in all directions,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen
Looked with gratitude to heaven, Looked on high, in joy and gladness,
This the prayer the minstrel uttered: “O be praised, thou God of mercy,
Since thou gavest me assistance, And vouchsafed me thy protection,
Banished all my pain and trouble, Caused by Iron and by Hisi.
People of this generation, And the folk of future ages,
River boat, nor ocean shallop, Boasting of its fine appearance;
Give to cause its perfect ending, Never hand of man can find it,
Ukko is the only Master.”
Ilmarinen Forges the Sampo.
Takes his steed of copper color, Hitches quick his fleet-foot courser,
Straightway springs upon the cross-seat, Snaps his whip adorned with jewels.
Like a lightning flash, the racer Makes the snow-sledge creak and rattle,
Dashes on through fen and forest, Over hills and through the valleys,
Over fertile plains and meadows; Journeys one day, then a second,
Till the third day evening brings him To the endless bridge of Osmo,
To the plains of Kalevala; When the hero spake as follows: “May the wolves devour the dreamer,
May disease destroy the braggart, Him who said that I should never
Nevermore behold my kindred, Never during all my life-time,
Never while the moonlight glimmers On the meadows of Wainola,
Then began old Wainamoinen,
To renew his incantations; Sang aloft a wondrous pine-tree,
With its golden top and branches, Till it touched the very heavens,
In the ever-shining sunlight.
Sings the Moon to shine forever In the fir-tree’s emerald branches;
Then he quickly journeys homeward, Hastens to his golden portals,
Crooked cap upon his forehead, Since as ransom he had promised
Thus to save his life from torture On the distant fields of Northland,
