When his stallion he had halted
Quickly rising in his snow-sledge, The magician heard one knocking,
Beating with a heavy hammer. Wainamoinen, famous minstrel,
Found the blacksmith, Ilmarinen, Knocking with his copper hammer.
“Welcome, brother Wainamoinen, Old and worthy Wainamoinen!
Where hast thou so long been hiding?”
These the words of the magician: “Long indeed have I been living,
Many cheerless nights have lingered, Floating on the cruel ocean,
Of the never-pleasant Northland, In the dismal Sariola;
With the people filled with witchcraft.”
These the words the blacksmith uses: “O thou ancient Wainamoinen,
Tell me of thy journey northward, Of thy wanderings in Lapland,
Spake the minstrel, Wainamoinen: “I have much to tell thee, brother,
In the Northland lives a virgin, In a village there, a maiden,
That a hero’s hand refuses, That a wizard’s heart disdaineth;
Sings her worth and magic beauty, Fairest maiden of Pohyola,
From her temples beams the moonlight, From her breast, the gleam of sunshine,
On her neck, the seven starlets, And the Great Bear from her shoulder.
“Ilmarinen, worthy brother,
Go and see her wondrous beauty, See her gold and silver garments,
See her sitting on the rainbow, Walking on the clouds of purple.
Forge the lid in many colors, Thy reward shall be the virgin,
Go and bring the lovely maiden To thy home in Kalevala.”
“O thou cunning Wainamoinen, Thou hast promised me already
Thy devoted head to ransom, Thus to rescue thee from trouble.
Shall not go to see thy maiden, Do not love the Bride of Beauty;
Shall I go to dreary Pohya, To the plains of Sariola,
Sink their heroes in the ocean, Not for all the maids of Lapland.”
“I can tell thee greater wonders, Listen to my wondrous story:
Seen its flowers with emerald branches, On the Osmo-fields and woodlands;
And the Bear lives in its branches.” Ilmarinen thus made answer: “I cannot believe thy story,
Till I see the blooming fir-tree, With its many emerald branches,
This is Wainamoinen’s answer: “Wilt thou not believe my story?
If my lips speak fact or fiction.”
Haste to view the wondrous fir-tree; Wainamoinen leads the journey,
As they near the Osmo-borders, Ilmarinen hastens forward
Spies the Bear within the fir-top, Sitting on its emerald branches,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen:,
“Climb this tree, dear Ilmarinen, And bring down the golden moonbeams,
From the fir-tree’s lofty branches.”
Straightway climbed the golden fir-tree, High upon the bow of heaven,
Thence to bring the Bear of heaven, From the fir-tree’s topmost branches.
Spake these words to Ilmarinen: “O thou senseless, thoughtless hero,
Thou dost climb my golden branches, Like a thing of little judgment,
Take away my silver starlight, Steal my Bear and blooming branches.”
Sang again in magic accents, Sang a storm-wind in the heavens,
And the singer spake as follows: “Take, O storm-wind, take the forgeman,
Quickly hence, and land the hero On the ever-darksome Northland,
Now the storm-wind quickly darkens,
Makes of air a sailing vessel, Takes the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Toward the never-pleasant Northland, Toward the dismal Sariola.
Fast and far the hero travelled, Sweeping onward, sailing northward,
O’er the Moon, beneath the sunshine, On the broad back of the Great Bear,
Neared the homes of Sariola, And alighted undiscovered,
Was not scented by the watch-dogs.
Ancient, toothless dame of Northland, Standing in the open court-yard,
As she spies the hero-stranger: “Who art thou of ancient heroes,
Coming here upon the storm-wind, O’er the sledge-path of the ether,
This is Ilmarinen’s answer: “I have surely not come hither
At these unfamiliar portals, At the gates of Sariola.”
Asks again the hero-stranger: “Hast thou ever been acquainted
With the hero, Ilmarinen, With the skilful smith and artist?
Long this one has been expected, On the borders of the Northland,
Spake the hero, Ilmarinen: “Well indeed am I acquainted
I myself am Ilmarinen, I, the skilful smith and artist.”
Toothless dame of Sariola, Straightway rushes to her dwelling,
“Come, thou youngest of my daughters, Come, thou fairest of my maidens,
Deck thy hair with rarest jewels, Pearls upon thy swelling bosom,
Bind thy head with silken ribbons, Make thy cheeks look fresh and ruddy,
Since the artist, Ilmarinen, Hither comes from Kalevala,
Hammer us the lid in colors.”
Honored by the land and water, Straightway takes her choicest raiment,
Finest of her silken wardrobe, Now adjusts her silken fillet,
Round her waist a golden girdle, Round her neck a pearly necklace,
In her hair the threads of silver. From her dressing-room she hastens,
Full of beauty, full of joyance, Ears erect and eyes bright-beaming,
Waiting for the hero-stranger.
Leads the hero, Ilmarinen, To her dwelling-rooms in Northland,
Seats him at her well-filled table, Gives to him the finest viands,
Then addresses him as follows: “O thou blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Canst thou forge for me the Sampo, Hammer me the lid in colors,
From the milk of greatest virtue, From a single grain of barley,
Thou shalt have my fairest daughter, Recompense for this thy service.”
“I will forge for thee the Sampo, Hammer thee the lid in colors,
From the milk of greatest virtue, From a single grain of barley,
Since I forged the arch of heaven, Forged the air a concave cover,
Thereupon the magic blacksmith
Went to find a blacksmith’s workshop, Went to find the tools to work with;
Found no smithy, found no bellows, Found no chimney, found no anvil,
Then the artist, Ilmarinen.
“Only women grow discouraged, Only knaves leave work unfinished,
Nor the Gods of greater knowledge.”
Sought a place to build a smithy, Sought a place to plant a bellows,
On the Pohya-hills and meadows; Searched one day, and then a second;
Came a rock within his vision, Came a stone with rainbow-colors.
Set at work to build his smithy, Built a fire and raised a chimney;
On the third day built his furnace, And began to forge the Sampo.
Ancient blacksmith, Ilmarinen, First of all the iron-workers,
Put the mixture in the caldron, Laid it deep within the furnace,
Skilfully they work the bellows, Tend the fire and add the fuel,
Three short nights of bright midsummer, Till the rocks begin to blossom,
From the magic heat and furnace.
Downward bent and well examined, On the bottom of his furnace,
From the magic fire and metals. From the fire arose a cross-bow,
Golden bow with tips of silver; On the shaft was shining copper,
But alas! it was ill-natured, Asking for a hero daily,
Ilmarinen, skilful artist,
Broke the bow in many pieces, Threw them back within the furnace,
Tried to forge the magic Sampo.
Downward bent and well examined, On the bottom of the furnace;
Came a boat of purple color, All the ribs were colored golden,
Thus the skiff was full of beauty, But alas! a thing of evil;
Hastens into every quarrel, Hastes without a provocation
Ilmarinen, metal artist,
Breaks the skiff in many fragments, Throws them back within the furnace,
Thus to forge the magic Sampo.
First of all the metal-workers, Downward bent and well examined,
There he saw a heifer rising, Golden were the horns of Kimmo,
On her brow a disc of sunshine, Beautiful the cow of magic;
Rushes headlong through the forest, Rushes through the swamps and meadows,
Ilmarinen, the magician,
Cuts the magic cow in pieces, Throws them in the fiery furnace,
Thus to forge the magic Sampo.
Downward bent and well examined, To the bottom of the furnace;
Rising from the fire of metals, Golden was the point and plowshare,
And the handles, molten silver, Beautiful the plow and wondrous;
Plows up fields of corn and barley, Furrows through the richest meadows.
Is not pleased with this creation, Quickly breaks the plow in pieces,
Lets the winds attend the bellows, Lets the storm-winds fire the metals.
East-wind rushing, West-wind roaring, South-wind crying, North-wind howling,
Blow the third from morn till even, When the fire leaps through the windows,
Clouds of smoke arise to heaven; With the clouds the black smoke mingles,
On the third night Ilmarinen,
On the bottom of the furnace, Sees the magic Sampo rising,
Quick the artist of Wainola Forges with the tongs and anvil,
Forges skilfully the Sampo; On one side the flour is grinding,
On a third is money forging, And the lid is many-colored.
To and fro the lid in rocking, Grinds one measure at the day-break,
Grinds a second for the market, Grinds a third one for the store-house.
Louhi, hostess of Pohyola, Takes away the magic Sampo,
To the copper-bearing mountains, Puts nine locks upon the wonder,
In the earth they grow nine fathoms, One large root beneath the mountain,
One beneath the mountain-dwelling.
For the maiden’s willing answer, These the words of the magician: “Wilt thou come with me, fair maiden,
I have forged for thee the Sampo, Forged the lid in many colors.”
Answers thus the metal-worker: “Who will in the coming spring-time,
Guide the cuckoo’s song and echo? Who will listen to his calling,
Should I go to distant regions, Should this cheery maiden vanish
From Pohyola’s fens and forests, Where the cuckoo sings and echoes?
Should my mother’s berry vanish, Should these mountains lose their cherry,
All the birds would leave the forest, Leave the summit of the mountain,
Never shall I, in my life-time, Say farewell to maiden freedom,
Lest the harvest be ungarnered, Lest the berries be ungathered,
Lest the mermaids leave the waters, Lest I sing with them no longer.”
The eternal metal-forger, Cap awry and head dejected,
Empty-handed, well considers, How to reach his distant country,
Gain the meadows of Wainola, From the never-pleasant Northland,
Louhi thus addressed the suitor: “O thou blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Why thy visage so dejected? Hast thou in thy mind to journey
To the meadows of Wainola, To thy home in Kalevala?”
“Thitherward my mind is tending, To my home-land let me journey,
Be at rest in mine own country.”
Gave the hero every comfort, Gave him food and rarest viands,
In a copper-banded vessel, Called the winds to his assistance,
Thus the skilful Ilmarinen Travels toward his native country,
Travels one day, then a second, Till the third day evening brings him
To his home in Kalevala.
Thus addresses Ilmarinen: “O my brother, metal-artist,
Didst thou forge the magic Sampo, Forge the lid in many colors?”
These the words the master uttered: “Yea, I forged the magic Sampo,
To and fro the lid in rocking Grinds one measure at the day-dawn,
Grinds a second for the market, Grinds a third one for the store-house.
I have not the Bride of Beauty.”
Lemminkainen’S Lament.
Son of Lempo, Kaukomieli, Also known as Lemminkainen.
Grew amid the island-dwellings, At the site of his dear mother,
On the points of promontories. Ahti fed upon the salmon,
Thus became a mighty hero, In his veins the blood of ages,
Growth of mind and body perfect; But alas! he had his failings,
Roaming in unworthy places, Staying days and nights in sequence
At the dances of the virgins, With the maids of braided tresses.
Lived the fair and winsome Kulli, Lovely as a summer-flower,
Grew to perfect form and beauty, Living in her father’s cottage,
Beautiful was she and queenly, Praised throughout the whole of Ehstland;
To the birthplace of the virgin, To the household of her mother.
But she will not go to Sun-land, Will not shine beside the Day-star,
For her son, the bright Moon wooes her, But she will not go to Moon-land,
Will not run through boundless ether.
But she will not go to Star-land, Will not twinkle in the starlight,
Lovers come from distant Ehstland,
But they cannot win the maiden, This the answer that she gives them “Vainly are your praises lavished
Wealth and praise are no temptation; Never shall I go to Ehstland,
On the waters of the Ingern, Shall not cross the Sahri-waters,
Never taste the Ehstland viands. Ingerland shall never see me,
Will not step within her borders; Hunger there, and fell starvation,
Neither water, wheat, nor barley, Even rye is not abundant.”
Warlike hero, Kaukomieli, Undertakes to win the maiden,
Win a bride so highly honored, Win the maid with golden tresses,
But his mother gives him warning: “Nay,” replies his gray-haired mother, “Do not woo, my son beloved,
She will never make thee happy With her lineage of Sahri.”
These the words of Kaukomieli: “Should I come from lowly station,
I shall woo to please my fancy, Woo the maiden fair and lovely,
This the anxious mother’s answer: “Lemminkainen, son beloved,
Do not go to distant Sahri, To her tribe of many branches;
All the women will deride thee.”
Answers thus his mother’s pleading: “I will still the sneers of women,
I will crush their haughty bosoms, Smite the hands and cheeks of infants;
Fitting ending to derision!” This the answer of the mother: “Woe is me, my son beloved!
Shouldst thou taunt the Sahri daughters, Or insult the maids of virtue,
There will rise a great contention, Fierce the battle that will follow.
Armed in thousands will attack thee, And will slay thee for thy folly.”
Heeding not his mother’s warning, Led his war-horse from the stables,
Fleetly drove upon his journey, To the distant Sahri-village,
There to win the Bride of Beauty.
All the young and lovely maidens Laughed to scorn the coming stranger
Wildly driving through the court-yard, Now upsetting in the gate-way,
Then the fearless Lemminkainen,
Shook his sable locks and answered: “Never in my recollection
Never have I been derided, Never suffered sneers of women,
Not in my immortal life-time. Is there any place befitting
Where to join in songs and dances? Is there here a hall for pleasure,
Merry maids with braided tresses?”
Answered from their promontory: “Room enough is there in Sahri,
Room for pleasure-halls and dances; Sing and dance upon our meadows,
Shepherd-boys have room for dancing; Indolent the Sahri-children,
Little caring, Lemminkainen
In the daytime on the pastures, In the evening, making merry
At the dances with the virgins, With the maids with braided tresses.
Thus the shepherd, Kaukomieli, Quickly hushed the women’s laughter,
Quickly silenced their derision. All the dames and Sahri-daughters
At his side they danced and lingered. Only was there one among them,
Harbored neither love nor wooers, Favored neither gods nor heroes,
This the Sahri’s fairest flower. Lemminkainen, full of pleasure,
Rowed a hundred boats in pieces, Pulled a thousand oars to fragments,
Tried to win the fair Kyllikki.
Fairest daughter of the Northland, Thus addresses Lemminkainen: “Why dost linger here, thou weak one,
Why come wooing at my fireside, Wooing me in belt of copper?
Rather give this stone its polish, Rather would I turn the pestle
Rather sit beside my mother In the dwellings of my father.
Neither wights nor whisks I care for, Sooner have a slender husband
Wish to have him fine of figure, Since perchance I am well-shapen;
Since my form perchance is queenly; Never waste thy time in wooing
Time had gone but little distance,
When upon a merry evening, Where the maidens meet for dancing,
On a level patch of verdure, Came too soon the maid Kyllikki,
Quickly followed Lemminkainen, With his stallion proudly prancing,
Fleetly drives beyond the meadow, Where the maidens meet for dancing,
On the settle seats the maiden, Quickly draws the leathern cover,
Whips his courser to a gallop. With a rush, and roar, and rattle,
Speaks these words to those that listen: “Never, never, anxious maidens,
That I carried off Kyllikki To my distant home and kindred.
Ye shall badly fare as maidens; I shall sing to war your suitors,
That for months, and years, and ages, Never ye will see their faces,
Never will they tread these uplands, Never will they join these dances,
Sad the wailing of Kyllikki,
Listen to her tearful pleading: “Give, O give me back my freedom,
Let this maiden wander homeward, By some foot-path let me wander
To my mother who is weeping; Let me go or I will curse thee!
Wilt not let me wander homeward, Where my loved ones wait my coming,
Seven sons of father’s brother, Seven sons of mother’s sister,
Hunt the hare upon the heather; They will follow thee and slay thee,
Lemminkainen, little heeding,
Would not heed her plea for mercy.
Pride and beauty of the Northland: “Joyful was I with my kindred,
Merrily I spent my childhood, Happy I, in virgin-freedom,
By the bedside of my mother, With my lineage in Sahri;
All my happiness departed, All my maiden beauty waneth
Shameless hero of dishonor, Cruel fighter of the islands,
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen,
“Dearest maiden, fair Kyllikki, My sweet strawberry of Pohya,
Be thou free from care and sorrow, Never shall I do thee evil,
Never will mine arms abuse thee, Never will my tongue revile thee,
“Tell me why thou hast this anguish,
Why this sighing and lamenting, Tell me why this wail of sadness?
Dry thy tears and still thine anguish, I have cattle, food, and shelter,
Kine upon the plains and uplands, In the marshes berries plenty,
I have kine that need no milking, Handsome kine that need no feeding,
Need not tie them up at evening, Need not free them in the morning,
Need not give them salt nor water.
“Thinkest thou my race is lowly,
Does my lineage agrieve thee? Was not born in lofty station,
From a worthy race descended; But I have a sword of fervor,
Surely these are well descended, These were born from hero-races,
By the gods were forged and burnished; Therefore will I give thee greatness,
With my broadsword filled with fervor, With my spear still filled with courage.”
Thus addresses Lemminkainen: “O thou Ahti, son of Lempo,
As thy faithful life-companion, Take me under thy protection,
Swear to me an oath of honor, That thou wilt not go to battle,
When thou wishest gold and silver?” This is Lemminkainen’s answer: “I will swear an oath of honor,
When for gold I feel a longing, When I wish for gold and silver.
Thou wilt go not to the village, When desire for dance impels thee,
Thus the two made oath together,
Vowed before omniscient Ukko, Ne’er to go to war vowed Ahti,
Lemminkainen, full of joyance,
Whipped his racer to a gallop, And these words the hero uttered: “Fare ye well, ye Sahri-meadows,
That I wandered through in summer, That I travelled o’er in winter,
At the evening hour I lingered, When I sought to win the virgin,
Fairest of the Sahri-flowers. Fare ye well, ye Sahri-woodlands,
Vales and mountains, isles and inlets, Once the home of fair Kyllikki!”
Galloped on along the highway, Toward the meadows of Wainola,
As they neared the Ahti-dwellings,
“Cold and drear is thy cottage, Seeming like a place deserted;
Who the one so little honored?”
These the words that Ahti uttered: “Do not grieve about my cottage,
I shall build thee other dwellings, I shall fashion them much better,
Fashioned from the sacred birch-wood.”
Lemminkainen’s home and birthplace, Enter they his mother’s cottage;
These the words the mother uses: “Long indeed hast thou been absent,
Long in Sahri thou hast lingered!” This is Lemminkainen’s answer: “All the host of Sahri-women,
All the maids with braided tresses, Well have paid for their derision,
That they basely heaped upon me. I have brought the best among them
Well I wrapped her in my fur-robes, Kept her warm enwrapped in bear-skin,
As my faithful life-companion; Thus I paid the scornful maidens,
“Cherished mother of my being,
I have won the Maid of Beauty. Spread our couch with finest linen,
On our table rarest viands, So that I may dwell in pleasure
With the pride of distant Sahri.” This the answer of the mother: “Be thou praised, O gracious Ukko,
Since thou givest me a daughter, Ahti’s bride, my second daughter,
Who can weave me finest fabrics, Who can twirl the useful spindle,
Who can full the richest garments.
“Son beloved, praise thy Maker,
Pride and joy of distant Sahri! Kind indeed is thy Creator,
Pure the snow upon the mountains, Purer still thy Bride of Beauty;
Whiter still her virgin-spirit; Graceful on the lakes, the white-swan,
Beautiful the stars in heaven, Still more beautiful, Kyllikki.
Wider build the doors and windows, Fashion thou the ceilings higher,
Now that thou a bride hast taken From a tribe of higher station,
From the meadow-lands of Sahri, From the upper shores of Northland.”
Kyllikki’S Broken Vow.
Reckless hero, Kaukomieli, Constantly beside his young wife,
And the years rolled swiftly onward; Ahti thought not of the battles,
Once upon a time it happened
Went upon the lake a-fishing, Was not home at early evening,
To the village went Kyllikki, To the dance of merry maidens.
Who will bear the information To the husband, Lemminkainen?
And the sister’s name, Ainikki.
Straightway gives the information, Of Kyllikki’s perjured honor,
“Ahti, my beloved brother, To the village went Kyllikki,
To the plays and village dances, With the young men and the maidens,
To the halls of joy and pleasure.”
Broken-hearted, flushed with anger, Spake these words in measured accents: “Mother dear, my gray-haired mother,
In the blood of poison-serpents, In the black blood of the adder?
To the camp-fires of the Northland, To the battle-fields of Lapland;
To the play of merry maidens, To the games and village dances,
Straightway speaks the wife, Kyllikki: “My beloved husband, Ahti,
In the evening I lay sleeping, Slumbering I saw in dream-land
Flames arising, mounting skyward, From the windows of this dwelling,
Piercing through our upper chambers, Roaring like the fall of waters,
Darting from the halls and doorways.”
Makes this answer to Kyllikki: “I discredit dreams of women,
Faithful mother of my being, Hither bring my mail of copper;
For the cup of deadly combat, For the mead of martial conquest.”
“Lemminkainen, son beloved, Do not go to war I pray thee;
In our vessels beer of barley, Held in casks by oaken spigots;
Let us drink of it together.” Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “I shall taste no more the viands,
Rather would I drink the water From the painted tips of birch-oars;
Than the beverage of dishonor, At my mother’s home and fireside!
“Hither bring my martial doublet,
Bring my father’s sword of honor; I must go to upper Northland,
There to win me gold and silver.” This the anxious mother’s answer: “My beloved Kaukomieli,
Gold and silver in the store-room; Recently upon the uplands,
Toiled the workmen in the corn-fields, Plowed the meadows filled with serpents,
From a chest of gold and silver, Countless was the gold uncovered,
This the treasure I have brought thee, Take the countless gold in welcome.”
“Do not wish thy household silver, From the wars I’ll earn my silver;
Are to me of greater value Than the wealth thou hast discovered.
Bring me too my spear and broadsword; To the Northland I must hasten,
Thither does my pride impel me, Thitherward my heart is turning.
“I have heard a tale of Lapland,
That a maid in Pimentola Lives that does not care for suitors,
This the aged mother’s answer: “Warlike Athi, son beloved,
Fairest wife of all the islands; Strange to see two wives abiding
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “To the village runs Kyllikki;
Let her sleep in other dwellings, With the village youth find pleasure,
Seeks the mother to detain him,
“Do not go, my son beloved, Ignorant of Pohya-witchcraft,
Till thou hast the art of magic, Till thou hast some little wisdom;
To the fires of Northland’s children, To the slaughter-fields of Lapland,
There the Lapland maids will charm thee, Turyalanders will bewitch thee,
Head and shoulders to the furnace, Into ashes sing thy fore-arm,
Spake the warlike Lemminkainen: “Wizards often have bewitched me,
Lapland wizards, three in number, On an eve in time of summer,
Not a garment to protect them, Once bewitched me with their magic;
This the sum of all my losses: What the hatchet gains from flint-stone,
What the heel chips from the iceberg, And what death purloins from tomb-stones.
“Horribly the wizards threatened,
In the water of the marshes, In the mud and treacherous quicksand,
But I too was born a hero, Born a hero and magician,
“Straightway I began my singing,
Sang the spearmen with their weapons, Sang the swordsmen with their poniards,
The enchanters with their magic, To the rapids of the rivers,
To the all-devouring whirlpool, To the deepest depths of ocean,
Sleeping till the grass shoots upward Through the beards and wrinkled faces,
As they sleep beneath the billows.”
Still beseeches Lemminkainen, Trying to restrain the hero,
This the language of the mother: “Do not go, my son beloved,
Nor to Lapland’s frigid borders; Dire misfortune will befall thee,
Lemminkainen’s end, destruction.
“Couldst thou speak in tongues a hundred,
Through the magic of thy singing, To enchant the sons of Lapland
Dost not know the Tury-language, Canst but speak the tongue of Suomi,
Lemminkainen, reckless hero,
Stood beside his mother, combing Out his sable locks and musing,
Steadfast still in his decision, Quickly hurls his brush in anger,
Gives his mother final answer, These the words that Ahti uses: “Dire misfortune will befall me,
Evil come to Lemminkainen, When the blood flows from that hair-brush,
Thus the warlike Lemminkainen Goes to never-pleasant Lapland,
Heeding not her prohibition.
Quick equips himself for warfare, On his head a copper helmet,
On his body iron armor, Steel, the belt around his body;
Ahti thus soliloquizing: “Strong the hero in his armor,
Powerful in mail of iron, Stronger far than any hero
Need not fear their wise enchanters, Need not fear their strongest foemen,
Grasped he then the sword of battle,
That Tuoni had been grinding, That the gods had brightly burnished,
Tied the scabbard to his armor.
Where protect themselves from evil? Heroes guard their homes and firesides,
Guard the posts that hold the torch-lights, Guard the highways to the court-yard,
Heroes guard themselves from women, Carefully from merry maidens;
Easy fall the heroes, victims To the snares of the enchanters.
Of the tribes of warlike giants, Where the highway doubly branches,
On the marshes filled with evil, Near the mighty fall of waters,
Near the fiery springs and rapids. Spake the stout-heart, Lemminkainen: “Rise ye heroes of the broadsword,
From the deeps, ye sickle-bearers, From the brooks, ye crossbow-shooters,
Come, ye thickets, with your armies, Mountain spirits, with your powers,
Water-mother, with thy dangers, Come, Wellamo, with thy mermaids,
Come, ye nymphs from winding rivers, Be protection to this hero,
Body-guard to Lemminkainen, Thus to blunt the spears of wizards,
That the spears of the enchanters, That the arrows of the archers,
May not harm this bearded hero.
“Should this force be insufficient,
I can call the gods above me, Call the great god of the heavens,
Him who rules through boundless ether, Who directs the march of storm-winds.
“Ukko, thou O God above me,
Thou that speakest through the thunder, Thou whose weapon is the lightning,
Grant me now thy mighty fire-sword, Give me here thy burning arrows,
Thus protect me from all danger, Guard me from the wiles of witches,
Help me conquer the enchanters, Help me drive them from the Northland;
Those that fill the ranks behind me, Those around me, those above me,
With their knives, and swords, and cross-bows, With their spears of keenest temper,
Help me drive these Lapland wizards To the deepest depths of ocean,
Then the reckless Lemminkainen
Called the racer from the hurdles, Called his brown steed from the pasture,
Hitched the fleet-foot to the snow-sledge, Leaped upon the highest cross-bench,
And the steed flies onward swiftly, Bounds the sleigh upon its journey,
Travels one day, then a second, Travels all the next day northward,
To a sorry Northland village, On the dismal shores of Lapland.
Drove along the lowest highway, Through the streets along the border,
Asked one standing in the doorway: “Is there one within this dwelling,
That can lift his heavy collar, That these shafts can rightly lower?”
And the young child gave this answer: “There is no one in this dwelling
That can lift his heavy collar, That the shafts can rightly lower.”
Whips his racer to a gallop, Rushes forward through the village,
To the court-yard in the centre, Asks one standing in the threshold,
“Is there any one here dwelling That can slip my stallion’s bridle,
That can tend my royal racer?”
From her bench the witch made answer: “Thou canst find one in this dwelling,
That can loose his heavy breastplate, That can tend thy royal racer.
That can make thee hasten homeward, That can give thee fleet-foot stallions,
Reckless rascal and magician, To thy home and fellow minstrels,
To the cabins of thy mother, To the work-bench of thy brother,
Ere the evening star has risen, Ere the sun retires to slumber.”
Gives this answer to the wizard: “I should slay thee for thy pertness,
Then he whipped his fiery charger,
On the upper of the highways, To the court-yard on the summit.
Had approached the upper court-yard, Uttered he the words that follow: “O thou Hisi, stuff this watch-dog,
Close the mouth of this wild barker, Bridle well the vicious canine,
While the hero passes by him.”
With his whip he struck the flooring, From the floor arose a vapor,
Who unhitched the royal racer, From his back removed the harness,
Then the hero, Lemminkainen, Carefully advanced and listened.
No one heard his cautious footsteps; Heard he songs within the dwelling,
Through the walls he heard them singing, Through the doors the peals of laughter.
Lurking slyly in the hall-ways, Found the court-rooms filled with singers,
Near the doors the wise men hovered, Skilful ones upon the benches,
All were singing songs of Lapland, Singing songs of evil Hisi.
Changes both his form and stature, Passes through the inner door-ways,
And these words the hero utters: “Fine the singing quickly ending,
Better far to keep thy wisdom Than to sing it on the house-tops.”
Fleetly rushing through the door-way, To the centre of the court-room,
“Formerly a dog lay watching, Was a cur of iron-color,
Loved to lick the blood of strangers. Who then art thou of the heroes,
That thou art within my court-rooms, That thou comest to my dwelling,
Was not scented by my watch-dogs?” Spake the reckless Lemminkainen: “Do not think that I come hither
Having neither art nor power, Wanting in ancestral knowledge,
That thy watch-dogs may devour me.
“My devoted mother washed me,
Three times in the nights of summer, Nine times in the nights of autumn,
I might sing the ancient wisdom, Thus protect myself from danger;
As the minstrels of thy hamlet.”
Ancient hero, Kaukomieli, Quick began his incantations,
From his fur-robe darts the lightning, Flames outshooting from his eye-balls,
From his wonderful enchantment. Sang the very best of singers
Filled their mouths with dust and ashes, Piled the rocks upon their shoulders,
Stilled the sorcerers and wizards. Then he banished all their heroes,
This one hither, that one thither, To the lowlands poor in verdure,
To the oceans wanting whiting, To the waterfalls of Rutya,
To the waters decked with sea-foam, Into fires and boiling waters,
Then the hero, Lemminkainen,
Sang the heroes with their weapons, Sang the eldest, sang the youngest,
Only one he left his senses, He a poor, defenseless shepherd,
And the old man’s name was Nasshut. Spake the miserable shepherd: “Thou hast old and young enchanted,
Why hast spared this wretched shepherd?” This is Lemminkainen’s answer: “Therefore have I not bewitched thee:
Feeble-minded thou, and harmless, Loathsome now without my magic.
When a shepherd filled with malice, Ruin all thy mother’s berries,
Ruin all thy brother’s cattle, Drive to death thy father’s stallions,
Through the lowlands, o’er the mountains, Heeding not thy mother’s counsel.”
Angry grew and swore for vengeance, Straightway limping through the door-way,
O’er the meadow-lands and pastures, To the river of the death-land,
To the kingdom of Tuoni, To the islands of Manala;
Listened long for Lemminkainen, Thinking he must pass this river
On the highway to the islands, From the upper shores of Pohya,
Lemminikainen’S Second Wooing.
To the hostess of Pohyola: “Give to me thy lovely daughter,
Bring the best of Lapland virgins, Fairest virgin of the Northland.”
Answered thus the wild magician: “I shall never give my daughter,
Not the best one, nor the worst one, Not the largest, nor the smallest;
Thou has taken hence one hostess, Carried off the fair Kyllikki.”
“To my home I took Kyllikki, To my cottage on the island,
Now I wish a better hostess, Straightway bring thy fairest daughter,
Fairest maid with sable tresses.” Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Never will I give my daughter
To a minstrel vain and evil; Therefore, pray thou for my maiden,
When thou bringest me the wild-moose From the Hisi fields and forests.”
Deftly whittled out his javelins, Quickly made his leathern bow-string,
And soliloquized as follows: “Now my javelins are made ready,
And my oaken cross-bow bended, But my snow-shoes are not builded,
Lemminkainen, grave and thoughtful,
Where the snow-shoes could be fashioned, Who the artist that could make them;
To the smithy of Lylikki, Thus addressed the snow-shoe artist: “O thou skilful Woyalander,
Make me quick two worthy snow-shoes, Smooth them well and make them hardy,
Roaming through the Hisi-forests, I may catch and bring to Louhi,
Then Lylikki thus made answer,
“Lemminkainen, reckless minstrel, Thou wilt hunt in vain the wild-moose,
In the Hisi fens and forests.”
Spake these measures to Lylikki: “Make for me the worthy snow-shoes,
Go I will and catch the blue-moose Where in Tapio it browses,
Then Lylikki, snow-shoe-maker,
Whittled in the fall his show-shoes, Smoothed them in the winter evenings,
All the next day making stick-rings, Till at last the shoes were finished,
Then he fastened well the shoe-straps, Smooth as adder’s skin the woodwork,
Oiled he well his wondrous snow-shoes With the tallow of the reindeer;
These the accents of Lylikki: “Is there any youth in Lapland,
That can travel in these snow-shoes, That can move the lower sections?”
Full of hope, and life, and vigor: “Surely there is one in Lapland.
That can travel in these snow-shoes, That the right and left can manage.”
Placed the bow upon his shoulder, With both hands he grasped his snow-cane,
“There is nothing in the woodlands, Nothing in the world of Ukko,
In the uplands, in the lowlands, Nothing in the snow-fields running,
That could not be overtaken With the snow-shoes of Lylikki,
Wicked Hisi heard these measures,
Straightway Hisi called the wild-moose, Juutas fashioned soon a reindeer,
Horns of naked willow branches, Feet were furnished by the rushes,
Veins were made of withered grasses, Eyes, from daisies of the meadows,
And the skin of tawny fir-bark, Out of sappy wood, the muscles,
Juutas thus instructs the wild-moose,
“Flee away, thou moose of Juutas, Flee away, thou Hisi-reindeer,
To the snow-homes of the ranger, To the ridges of the mountains,
That thy hunter may be worn out, Thy pursuer be tormented,
Thereupon the Hisi-reindeer,
Fleetly ran through fen and forest, Over Lapland’s hills and valleys,
Through the penthouse doors and gate-ways, Turning over tubs of water,
And upset the dishes cooking. Then arose a fearful uproar,
Lapland-dogs began their barking, Lapland-children cried in terror,
And the Lapland-heroes shouted.
Followed fast, and followed faster, Hastened on behind the wild-moose,
Over snow-fields vast and pathless, Over high uprising mountains,
Smoke arising from his snow-cane: Could not hear the wild-moose bounding,
Glided on through field and forest, Glided over lakes and rivers,
Through the desert plains of Hisi, Glided o’er the plains of Kalma,
To the end of Kalma’s empire, Where the jaws of Death stand open,
Ready to devour the stranger, To devour wild Lemminkainen;
Kalma cannot overtake him.
Far away a woodland corner Stands unsearched by Kaukomieli,
In the realm of dreary Lapland. Now the hero, on his snow-shoes,
There to hunt the moose of Piru. As he nears the woodland corner,
From the Northland’s distant borders, From the dreary fields of Lapland,
Hears the children loudly screaming, Hears the laughter of the women,
Thereupon wild Lemminkainen Hastens forward on his snow-shoes,
To the distant woods of Lapland.
Had approached this Hisi corner, Straightway he began to question: “Why this laughter of the women,
Why the shouting of the heroes, Why this barking of the watch-dogs?”
“This the reason for this uproar, Women laughing, children screaming,
Hisi’s moose came running hither, Hither came the Piru-Reindeer,
Through the open fields and court-yards, Through the penthouse doors and gate-ways,
Threw the kettles from the fire-pole, And upset the dishes cooking.”
Straightway summoned all his courage, Pushed ahead his mighty snow-shoes,
Levelled bushes in the marshes, Like the swift and fiery serpents,
Keeping balance with his snow-staff: “Come thou might of Lapland heroes,
Come thou strength of Lapland-women, And prepare the boiling caldron;
Bring together fire and fuel; Come, thou strength of Lapland-kettles,
Then with mighty force and courage,
Striking backward, shooting forward; With a long sweep of his snow-shoe,
With the second, shooting further, Was the hunter out of hearing;
On the shoulders of the wild-moose; Took a pole of stoutest oak-wood,
Wherewithal to bind the moose-deer, Bind him to his oaken hurdle.
“Here remain, thou moose of Juutas Skip about, my bounding courser,
Captive from the fields of Piru, From the Hisi glens and mountains.”
Patted him upon his forehead, Spake again in measured accents: “I would like awhile to linger,
In the cottage of my maiden, With my virgin, young and lovely.”
Stamped his feet and shook his antlers, Spake these words to Lemminkainen: “Surely Lempo soon will got thee,
Shouldst thou linger by the virgin.”
Tears in two the bands of willow, Breaks the oak-wood pole in pieces,
Quickly leaping from his captor, Bounds away with strength of freedom,
Over swamps and over snow-fields, Over mountains clothed in heather,
Nor the hero’s ear detect him.
Angry grows, and much disheartened, Starts again the moose to capture,
With his might he plunges forward; At the instep breaks his snow-shoe,
On the mountings breaks his javelins, In the centre breaks his snow-staff,
Through the Hisi-woods and snow-fields, Out of reach of Lemminkainen.
Looked with bended head, ill-humored, One by one upon the fragments,
“Northland hunters, never, never, Go defiant to thy forests,
There to hunt the moose of Juutas, Like this senseless, reckless hero;
Ruined too my useful snow-staff, And my javelins I have broken,
Through the Hisi fields and forests.”
Death of Lemminkainen.
Deeply thought and long considered, What to do, what course to follow,
In the fastnesses of Hisi, And return to Kalevala,
Hoping thus to bring him captive, Thus return at last a victor
To the joy of all her daughters, To the wood-nymph’s happy fireside.
Spake these words in supplication: “Ukko, thou O God above me,
Put my snow-shoes well in order, And endow them both with swiftness,
Over marshes, over snow-fields, Over lowlands, over highlands,
Through the distant plains of Lapland, Through the paths of Lempo’s wild-moose,
To the snow-fields shall I journey, Leave the heroes to the woodlands,
Into Tapio’s wild dwellings.
“Greeting bring I to the mountains,
Greet ye, heights with forests covered, Greet ye, ever-verdant fir-trees,
Greetings bring to those that greet you, Fields, and streams, and woods of Lapland.
Lapland-deserts, show me kindness, Mighty Tapio, be gracious,
Let me glide along thy rivers, Let this hunter search thy snow-fields,
Where the bounding reindeer lingers.
“O Nyrikki, mountain hero,
Hero with the scarlet head-gear, Notches make along the pathway,
That this hunter may not wander, May not fall, and falling perish
Hunting for the moose of Hisi, Dowry for the pride of Northland.
“Mistress of the woods, Mielikki,
Let thy gold flow out abundant, Let thy silver onward wander,
For the wild-moose of thy kingdom; Bring me here thy keys of silver,
Open Tapio’s rich chambers, And unlock the forest fortress,
While I hunt the moose of Lempo.
“Should this service be too menial
Send at once thy servant-maidens, And command it to thy people.
If thou hast not in thy service, Maidens ready by the hundreds,
Who thy herds may watch and nurture, Tend the game of thy dominions.
“Tall and slender forest-virgin,
Blow thou now thy honey flute-notes, Play upon thy forest-whistle,
For thy charming woodland-mistress, Make her hear thy sweet-toned playing,
Should thy mistress not awaken At the calling of thy flute-notes,
Make the golden tongue re-echo.”
Steadfast prays upon his journey, Calling on the gods for succor,
Passes on through cruel brush-wood, To the colliery of Hisi,
Glided one day, then a second, Glided all the next day onward,
Climbed upon its rocky summit, Turned his glances to the north-west,
There appeared the Tapio-mansion. All the doors were golden-colored,
Through the thickets on the mountains, Through the distant fields of Northland.
Hastens onward from his station Through the lowlands, o’er the uplands,
Under snow-robed firs and aspens, Hastens forward, happy-hearted,
Halts without at Tapio’s windows, Slyly looks into her mansion,
Forest-dames outstretched before him, All are clad in scanty raiment,
Spake the stranger Lemminkainen: “Wherefore sit ye, forest-mothers,
In your soiled and ragged linen? Ye, forsooth! are too untidy,
In your tattered gowns appareled. When I lived within the forest,
One of horn and one of ivory, And the third of wood constructed;
Six the windows in each castle, Through these windows I discovered
Saw its fair and stately hostess; Saw great Tapio’s lovely daughter,
With her train of charming maidens; All were dressed in golden raiment,
Then the forest’s queenly hostess, Still the hostess of these woodlands,
Golden rings upon her fingers, In her hair were sparkling jewels,
In her ears were golden ear-rings, On her neck a pearly necklace,
“Lovely hostess of the forest,
Fling aside thine ugly straw-shoes, Cast away the shoes of birch-bark,
Doff thy gown of shabby fabric, Don the bright and festive raiment,
While I stay within thy borders, While I seek my forest-booty,
Here my visit will be irksome, Here thy guest will be ill-humored,
Hunting here the moose of Lempo, Finding not the Hisi-ranger,
Should I find no joy, nor respite. Long the eve that gives no pleasure,
“Sable-bearded god of forests,
Robe thy trees in finest fibers, Deck thy groves in richest fabrics,
Deck with gold the slender balsams, Give the spruces copper belting,
Give the birches golden flowers, Deck their stems with silver fret-work,
When the days and nights were brighter, When the fir-trees shone like sunlight,
Honey breathed throughout the forest, Settled in the glens and highlands
Oil out-pouring from the lowlands.
“Forest daughter, lovely virgin,
Second of the Tapio-daughters, Drive the game within these borders,
Should the reindeer be too sluggish, Should the moose-deer move too slowly
Whip them hither in their beauty, Drive the wild-moose to my hurdle,
To the hunter who is watching, Waiting in the Hisi-forests.
“When the game has started hither,
Hold thy magic hands before them, Guard them well on either road-side,
May not dart adown some by-path. Should, perchance, the moose-deer wander
Take him by the ears and antlers, Hither lead the pride of Lempo.
“If the path be filled with brush-wood
If the branches cross his pathway, Break the branches into fragments;
Cross the way that leads him hither, Make an opening within it,
If the way be crossed by streamlets, If the path be stopped by rivers,
Weaving webs of scarlet color, Drive the deer-herd gently over,
O’er the rivers of thy forests, O’er the streams of thy dominions.
“Thou, the host of Tapio’s mansion,
Sable-bearded god of woodlands, Golden lord of Northland forests,
Queen of snowy woods, Mimerkki, Ancient dame in sky-blue vesture,
Come I to exchange my silver, To exchange my gold and silver;
Silver of the age of sunshine, In the first of years was gathered,
It will rust within my pouches, Soon will wear away and perish,
Long the hunter, Lemminkainen,
Sang his songs throughout the woodlands, Through three mountain glens he sang them,
Sang he, also, Tapio friendly, Friendly, all the forest virgins,
Now they start the herds of Lempo,
In the realms of evil Hisi, Tapio’s highest mountain-region;
To the open courts of Piru, To the hero that is waiting,
When the herd had reached the castle,
O’er the antlers of the blue-moose, Settled on the neck and shoulders
Then the hunter, Kaukomieli, Stroked his captive’s neck in safety,
Thereupon gay Lemminkainen
“Pride of forests, queen of woodlands, Metsola’s enchanted hostess,
Mother-donor of the mountains, Take the gold that I have promised,
Spread thy kerchief well before me, Spread out here thy silken neck-wrap,
Underneath the shining silver, That to earth it may not settle,
Then the hero went a victor
And addressed these words to Louhi: “I have caught the moose of Hisi,
Give, O hostess, give thy daughter, Give to me thy fairest virgin,
Louhi, hostess of the Northland,
“I will give to thee my daughter, For thy wife my fairest maiden,
On the flaming horse of Hisi, Rapid messenger of Lempo,
Nothing daunted, Lemminkainen
Louhi’s second test of heroes, On the cultivated lowlands,
Everywhere he sought the racer, Sought the fire-expiring stallion,
Lemminkainen, fearless hunter, Bearing in his belt his bridle,
Sought one day, and then a second, Finally, upon the third day,
Climbed, and struggled to the summit; To the east he turned his glances,
There beheld the flaming courser, On the heath among the far-trees.
Fire and mingled smoke out-shooting From his mouth, and eyes, and nostrils.
This the hero’s supplication: “Ukko, thou O God above me,
Open thou the vault of heaven, Open windows through the ether,
Lot the heavy hailstones shower On the flaming horse of Hisi,
Ukko, the benign Creator,
Broke apart the dome of heaven, Rent the heights of heaven asunder,
Smaller than the heads of horses, Larger than the heads of heroes,
On the fire-expiring stallion, On the terror of the Northland.
Looked with care upon the courser, Then he spake the words that follow: “Wonder-steed of mighty Hisi,
Bring thy mouth of gold, assenting, Gently place thy head of silver
In this silver-mounted bridle. I shall never harshly treat thee,
On the way to Sariola, On the tracks of long duration,
To her magic courts and stables, Will not lash thee on thy journey;
Drive thee with the reins of kindness, Cover thee with silken blankets.”
Flaming horse of mighty Hisi, Put his head of shining silver,
In the silver-mounted bridle. Thus the hero, Lemminkainen,
Flaming horse of evil Piru; Lays the bits within his fire-mouth,
Mounts the fire-expiring courser, Brandishes his whip of willow,
Bounding o’er the hills and mountains, Dashing through the valleys northward,
To the courts of Sariola.
Stepped within the court of Louhi, Thus addressed the Northland hostess: “I have bridled Lempo’s fire-horse,
Caught the fire-expiring stallion, In the Piru plains and pastures,
I have caught the moose of Lempo, I have done what thou demandest;
Give to me thy fairest maiden, Bride of mine to be forever.”
Made this answer to the suitor: “I will only give my daughter,
Bride of thine to be forever, When for me the swan thou killest
Swimming in the black death-river, In the sacred stream and whirlpool;
But one arrow from thy quiver.”
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli, Braved the third test of the hero,
Hunt the long-necked, graceful swimmer, In Tuoni’s coal-black river,
Quick the daring hunter journeyed, Hastened off with fearless footsteps,
To the sacred stream and whirlpool, With his bow upon his shoulder,
Nasshut, blind and crippled shepherd,
Stood beside the death-land river, Near the sacred stream and whirlpool,
Waiting there for Lemminkainen, Listening there for Kaukomieli,
Finally he hears the footsteps Of the hero on his journey,
As he journeys nearer, nearer, To the river of Tuoni,
To the sacred stream and whirlpool. Quick the wretched shepherd, Nasshut,
Like an arrow from a cross-bow, To the heart of Lemminkainen,
Lemminkainen, little conscious,
Spake these measures as he perished: “Ah! unworthy is my conduct,
That I did not heed my mother, Did not take her goodly counsel,
Oh! for three words with my mother, How to live, and how to suffer,
How to bear the stings of serpents, Tortures of the reed of waters,
“Ancient mother who hast borne me,
Learn, I pray thee, where I linger, Where alas! thy son is lying,
Come, I pray thee, faithful mother, Come thou quickly, thou art needed,
From the death-jaws of Tuoni, From the sacred stream and whirlpool.”
Nasshut, the despised protector Of the flocks of Sariola,
Throws the hero of the islands, Into Tuonela’s river,
To the worst of fatal whirlpools. Lemminkainen, wild and daring,
Floating down the coal-black current, Through the cataract and rapids
There the blood-stained son of death-land,
Cuts in pieces Lemminkainen, Chops him with his mighty hatchet,
From the rocks within his chamber, Chops the hero into fragments,
Throws each portion to Tuoni, In Manala’s lowest kingdom,
“Swim thou there, wild Lemminkainen, Flow thou onward in this river,
With thy cross-bow and thine arrow, Shoot the swan within this empire,
Thus the hero, Lemminkainen,
The untiring suitor, dieth In the river of Tuoni,
Lemminkainen’S Restoration.
Anxious roams about the islands, Anxious wonders in her chambers,
Why her son so long has tarried; Thinks that something ill has happened
Sad, indeed, the mother’s anguish, As in vain she waits his coming,
Where her daring son is roaming, Whether to the fir-tree mountain,
Or upon the broad-sea’s ridges, On the floods and rolling waters,
To the heat and din of battle, Steeped in blood of valiant heroes,
Daily does the wife Kyllikki
In the home of Lemminkainen, At the court of Kaukomieli;
Looks, perchance, upon his hair-brush, Sees alas! the blood-drops oozing,
And the blood-drops, scarlet-colored.
Spake these words in deeps of anguish: “Dead or wounded is my husband,
Lost perhaps in Northland forests, In some glen unknown to heroes,
From the brush of Lemminkainen, Red drops oozing from the bristles.”
Looks upon the bleeding hair-brush And begins this wail of anguish: “Woe is me, my life hard-fated,
For alas! my son and hero, Valiant hero of the islands,
Some sad fate has overtaken My ill-fated Lemminkainen!
Oozing from its golden bristles, And the drops are scarlet-colored.”
On her arm she throws her long-robes, Fleetly flies upon her journey;
Mountains tremble from her footsteps, Valleys rise and heights are lowered,
All the hills and valleys levelled. Soon she gains the Northland village,
These the words the mother utters: “O thou hostess of Pohyola,
Tell me of my son and hero!”
Gives this answer to the mother: “Nothing know I of thy hero,
Where thy son may be I know not, Cannot lend the information;
Hitched the racer to his snow-sledge, This the last of Lemminkainen;
Frozen in the icy ocean, Fallen prey to wolves in hunger,
Lemminkainen’s mother answers: “Thou art only speaking falsehoods,
Nor the bears kill Kaukomieli; He can slay the wolves of Pohya
Bears of Northland he would silence With the magic of his singing.
“Hostess of Pohyola, tell me
I shall burst thy many garners, Shall destroy the magic Sampo,
Where to find my Lemminkainen.” Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “I have well thy hero treated,
Gave him of my rarest viands, Fed him at my well-filled tables,
Thus to float adown the current, This the last of Lemminkainen;
Whether in the foam of waters, Whether in the boiling torrent,
Lemminkainen’s mother answers: “Thou again art speaking falsely;
Make an end of thy deception, Where is now my Lemminkainen,
Young and daring son of Kalew? If a third time thou deceivest,
I will send thee fell destruction, Certain death will overtake thee.”
“This the third time that I answer, This the truth that I shall tell thee:
To the Hisi-fields and forests, There to hunt the moose of Lempo;
Catch the fire-expiring stallion, On the distant plains of Juutas,
Then I sent him to the Death-stream, In the kingdom of Tuoni,
There to shoot the swan as dowry For my best and fairest daughter;
Since he left for Tuonela; May in misery have fallen,
Has not come to ask my daughter, Has not come to woo the maiden,
Now the mother seeks her lost one,
Like the wolf she bounds through fenlands, Like the bear, through forest thickets,
Like the hare, along the sea-coast, To the sea-point, like the hedgehog,
Casts the rubbish from her pathway, Tramples down opposing brush-wood,
Seeks a long time for her hero, Seeks, and seeks, and does not find him.
And the forest gives this answer: “We have care enough already,
Cruel fates have we to battle, Pitiful our own misfortunes!
Cut in blocks for hero-fancy, We are burned to death as fuel,
Now again the mother wanders,
Seeks, and seeks, and does not find him. Paths arise and come to meet her,
“Paths of hope that God has fashioned, Have ye seen my Lemminkainen,
Travelled through thy many kingdoms?” Sad, the many pathways answer: “We ourselves have cares sufficient,
Wretched are the lives of pathways, Deep indeed our own misfortunes;
By the wolves, and bears, and roebucks, Driven o’er by heavy cart-wheels,
Trodden under foot of heroes, Foot-paths for contending armies.”
Seeks her long-lost son and hero, Seeks, and seeks, and does not find him;
Asks the Moon in pleading measures: “Golden Moon, whom God has stationed
Hast thou seen my Kaukomieli, Hast thou seen my silver apple,
Thus the golden Moon makes answer: “I have trouble all-sufficient,
Long the journey I must travel, Sad the fate to me befallen,
All alone the nights to wander, Shine alone without a respite,
In the summer sink and perish.”
Seeks, and does not find her hero; Sees the Sun in the horizon,
“Silver Sun, whom God has fashioned, Thou that giveth warmth and comfort,
Hast thou seen my Lemminkainen, Wandering in thy dominions?”
“Surely has thy hero perished, To ingratitude a victim;
In Tuoni’s fatal river, In the waters of Manala,
In the cataract and rapids, Sank within the drowning current
To Manala’s lower regions.”
Wailing in the deeps of anguish, Mourns the fate of Kaukomieli,
To the forge of Ilmarinen, These the words the mother utters: “Ilmarinen, metal-artist,
Forging earth a concave cover, Yesterday wert forging wonders,
Forge a rake with shaft of copper, Forge the teeth of strongest metal,
And five hundred long the handle.”
Makes the rake in full perfection.
Takes the magic rake and hastens To the river of Tuoni,
“Thou, O Sun, by God created, Thou that shinest on thy Maker,
Give me warmth, and strength, and courage, Shine a third time full of power,
Still the people of Manala, Quiet all Tuoni’s empire.”
Dearest child of the Creator, Flying through the groves of Northland,
Shines a little while in ardor, Shines again in greater fervor,
Lulls to sleep the wicked people In the Manala home and kingdom,
Makes the lancers halt and totter, Stills the stoutest of the spearmen,
Now the Sun retires in magic, Hovers here and there a moment
Hastens upward to his station, To his Jumala home and kingdom.
Takes the rake of magic metals, Rakes the Tuoni river bottoms,
Rakes the swift and boiling current Of the sacred stream of death-land,
Searching for her long-lost hero, Rakes a long time, finding nothing;
To her belt in mud and water, Deeper, deeper, rakes the death-stream,
Raking up and down the current, Till at last she finds his tunic,
Rakes again and rakes unceasing, Finds the hero’s shoes and stockings,
Now she wades the river deeper, Rakes the Manala shoals and shallows,
As she draws the rake the third time From the Tuoni shores and waters,
Of her long-lost Lemminkainen, In the metal teeth entangled,
Thus the reckless Lemminkainen,
Was recovered from the bottom Of the Manala lake and river.
Half the head, a hand, a fore-arm, Many other smaller portions,
Then the mother, well reflecting, Spake these words in bitter weeping: “From these fragments, with my magic,
Hearing this, the raven answered,
“There is not in these a hero, Thou canst not revive these fragments;
On his eyes have fed the whiting; Cast the dead upon the waters,
Let him there become a walrus, Or a seal, or whale, or porpoise.”
Cast the dead upon the waters, On the streams of Tuonela;
Rakes the river lengthwise, crosswise, Through the Manala pools and caverns,
Finds a hand and half the back-bone, Many other smaller portions;
Shapes anew her Lemminkainen, Flesh to flesh with skill she places,
Binds one member to the other, Joins the ends of severed vessels,
Knits the parts in apposition; Then this prayer the mother offers:
“Suonetar, thou slender virgin,
Skilful spinner of the vessels, With thy slender, silver spindle,
Set in frame of molten silver, Come thou hither, thou art needed;
Firmly knit the veins together, At the end join well the venules,
In the members that are injured.
“Should this aid be inefficient,
In a boat enriched with silver, In a copper boat, a maiden,
Come, O maiden, from the ether, Virgin from the belt of heaven,
Row through all these lifeless members, Through the channels of the long-bones,
Set the vessels in their places, Lay the heart in right position,
Join the smallest of the veinlets, And unite with skill the sinews.
Silken thread within its eyelet, Ply the silver needle gently,
“Should this aid be inefficient,
Come and give us thine assistance, Harness thou thy fleetest racer,
In thy scarlet sledge come swiftly, Drive through all the bones and channels,
Drive thy courser through each vessel, Bind the flesh and bones securely,
Purest gold in all the fissures.
“Where the skin is broken open,
Mend these injuries with magic; Where the blood has left the body,
Where the bones are rudely broken, Set the parts in full perfection;
Touch the wounds with magic balsam, Do not leave a part imperfect;
Heart, and brain, and gland, and vessel, Heal as Thou alone canst heal them.”
Thus she joins the lifeless members, Thus she heals the death-like tissues,
To his former life and likeness; All his veins are knit together,
All the parts in apposition, Life returns, but speech is wanting,
Now the mother speaks as follows: “Where may I procure the balsam,
To anoint my son and hero, Thus to heal my Lemminkainen,
May again begin his singing, Speak again in words of wonder,
“Tiny bee, thou honey-birdling,
Fly away and gather honey, Bring to me the forest-sweetness,
And in Tapio’s fragrant meadows, From the petals of the flowers,
Thus to heal my hero’s anguish, Thus to heal his wounds of evil.”
Flies away on wings of swiftness, Into Metsola’s rich gardens,
Gathers sweetness from the meadows, With the tongue distills the honey
From the bloom of countless grasses; Quick from Metsola returning,
With his winglets honey-laden, With the store of sweetest odors,
Lemminkainen’s anxious mother Takes the balm of magic virtues,
Heals his wounds and stills his anguish; But the balm is inefficient,
Then again out-speaks the mother: “Little bee, my honey-birdling,
Fly across the seven oceans, In the eighth, a magic island,
To the distant Turi-castles, To the chambers of Palwoinen;
There, the wonder-working balsam, This may heal the wounded hero;
That I may anoint his eyelids, May restore his injured senses.”
Flies away o’er seven oceans, To the old enchanted island;
On the verdure does not settle, Does not rest upon the flowers;
Till a third day evening brings him To the island in the ocean,
To the cataract and fire-flow, To the sacred stream and whirlpool.
There the magic balm distilling In the tiny earthen vessels,
Smaller than a maiden’s thimble, Smaller than the tips of fingers.
Gathers the enchanted honey From the magic Turi-cuplets
Time had gone but little distance,
Flying fleetly, honey-laden; In his arms were seven vessels,
All were filled with honey-balsam, With the balm of magic virtues.
Quick anoints her speechless hero, With the magic Turi-balsam,
Nine the times that she anoints him With the honey of Palwoinen,
But the balm is inefficient, For the hero still is speechless.
“Honey-bee, thou ether birdling, Fly a third time on thy journey,
Fly thou to the seventh heaven, Honey there thou’lt find abundant,
Only used by the Creator, Only made from the breath of Ukko.
With the honey of his wisdom, When they feel the pangs of sorrow,
Dip thy winglets in this honey, Steep thy plumage in His sweetness,
Balsam of the great Creator; This will still my hero’s anguish,
This restore his long-lost vision, Make the Northland hills re-echo
With his wonderful enchantment.” Thus the honey-bee made answer: “I can never fly to heaven,
To the distant home of Ukko, With these wings of little virtue.”
“Thou canst surely fly to heaven, To the seventh of the heavens,
Through the dim and distant starlight. On the first day, flying upward,
Fan the brow of Kootamoinen; On the second thou canst rest thee
On the third day, flying higher, Rest upon the seven starlets,
Short the journey that is left thee, Inconsiderable the distance
To the dwellings of the blessed.”
From the earth flies swiftly upward, Hastens on with graceful motion,
In the paths of golden moonbeams, Touches on the Moon’s bright borders,
Rests upon Otava’s shoulders, Hastens to the seven starlets,
Flies to the Creator’s castle, To the home of generous Ukko,
Finds the balm of life distilling, In the silver-tinted caldrons,
On one side, heart-easing honey, On a second, balm of joyance,
Here the magic bee, selecting, Culls the sweet, life-giving balsam,
Heavy-laden hastens homeward.
Ere the busy bee came humming To the anxious mother waiting,
And a thousand other vessels, Filled with honey, filled with balsam,
Lemminkainen’s mother quickly
Finds a balsam all-sufficient. Then the mother spake as follows: “I have found the long-sought balsam,
Wherewith God anoints his people, Gives them life, and faith, and wisdom,
Makes them strong against temptation, Guards them from the evil-doers.”
Heals her son, the magic singer, Eyes, and ears, and tongue, and temples,
Touching well the life-blood centres, Speaks these words of magic import
“Wake, arise from out thy slumber, From the worst of low conditions,
Quickly wakes the son and hero,
Speaks again in magic accents, These the first words of the singer: “Long, indeed, have I been sleeping,
But my sleep was full of sweetness, Sweet the sleep in Tuonela,
This the answer of his mother: “Longer still thou wouldst have slumbered,
Tell me now, my son beloved, Tell me that I well may hear thee,
To the river of Tuoni, To the fatal stream and whirlpool?”
Gave this answer to his mother: “Nasshut, the decrepit shepherd
Blind, and halt, and poor, and wretched, And to whom I did a favor;
Nasshut sent me to Manala, To the river of Tuoni;
Sent an adder from the death-stream, Through the heart of Lemminkainen;
Could not speak the serpent-language, Did not know the sting of adders.”
“O thou son of little insight, Senseless hero, fool-magician,
To enchant the wise enchanters, On the dismal shores of Lapland,
From the borders of Pohyola; Didst not know the sting of serpents,
Nor the magic word-protector! Learn the origin of serpents,
“In the floods was born the serpent,
From the brain of ocean-swallows; Suoyatar had made saliva,
Currents drove it outward, onward, Softly shone the sun upon it,
Gently nursed by winds and waters, By the waves was driven shoreward,
Thus the serpent, thing of evil, Filling all the world with trouble,
Born from Suoyatar, its maker.”
Rocked her son to rest and comfort, Rocked him to his former being,
Into greater magic powers; Wiser, handsomer than ever
But his heart was full of trouble, And his mother, ever watchful,
This is Lemminkainen’s answer: “This the cause of all my sorrow;
All my thoughts forever wander To the Northland’s blooming virgins,
Northland’s ugly hostess, Louhi, Will not give to me her daughter,
Till I kill the swan of Mana, With my bow and but one arrow,
Lemminkainen’s mother answers, In the sacred stream and whirlpool. “Let the swan swim on in safety,
In the river of Manala, In the whirlpool of Tuoni;
With her charms and fading beauty; With thy fond and faithful mother,
To thy native fields and fallows. Praise thy fortune, all sufficient,
Ukko gave thee aid when needed, Thou wert saved by thy Creator,
In the waters of Tuoni, In the chambers of Manala.
Could not give the least assistance; God alone, omniscient Ukko,
Can revive the dead and dying, Can protect his worthy people
From the fatal stream and whirlpool, In the kingdom of Tuoni.”
With his fond and faithful mother, Hastened straightway on his journey
To the Wainola fields and meadows, To the plains of Kalevala.
Leave my hero Lemminkainen, Long I leave him from my singing,
Send it forth on other pathways, Sing some other golden legend.
Wainamoinen’S Boat-Building.
The eternal wisdom-singer, For his boat was working lumber,
On a fog-point jutting seaward, On an island, forest-covered;
Beams were wanting for his vessel, Beams and scantling, ribs and flooring.
Who procure the timber needed For the boat of Wainamoinen,
Pellerwoinen of the prairies,
He will seek the needful timber, He procure the beams of oak-wood
For the bottom of his vessel.
To the eastern fields and forests, Hunts throughout the Northland mountain
To a third he hastens, searching, Golden axe upon his shoulder,
Comes an aspen-tree to meet him Of the height of seven fathoms.
Starts to fell the stately aspen, But the aspen quickly halting,
“Tell me, hero, what thou wishest, What the service thou art needing?”
“This indeed, the needed service That I ask of thee, O aspen:
For the boat of Wainamoinen, Wisest of the wisdom-singers.”
Thus its hundred branches answer: “All the boats that have been fashioned
Such a vessel floats a distance, Then it sinks upon the bottom
All my trunk is filled with hollows, Three times in the summer seasons
Feed upon my heart and tissues.”
Hunts again through all the forest, Wanders through the woods of Northland,
Of the height of fourteen fathoms.
Strikes it with his axe of copper, As he asks the pine this question: “Will thy trunk give worthy timber
Wisest of the wisdom-singers?” Loudly does the pine-tree answer: “All the ships that have been fashioned
I am full of imperfections, Cannot give thee needed timber
Ravens live within my branches, Build their nests and hatch their younglings,
Sampsa leaves the lofty pine-tree,
To the woods of gladsome summer, Where an oak-tree comes to meet him,
And the oak he thus addresses: “Ancient oak-tree, will thy body
Build a boat for Wainamoinen, Master-boat for the magician,
Thus the oak replies to Sampsa: “I for thee will gladly furnish
I am tall, and sound, and hardy, Have no flaws within my body;
In the warmest of the seasons, Does the sun dwell in my tree-top,
In my branches sings the cuckoo, In my top her nestlings slumber.”
Takes the hatchet from his shoulder, Takes his axe with copper handle,
Well he knows the art of chopping. Soon he fells the tree majestic,
With his magic axe and power. From the stems he lops the branches,
Fashions lumber for the bottom, Countless boards, and ribs, and braces,
For the boat of the magician.
The eternal wonder-worker, Builds his vessel with enchantment,
From the timber of the oak-tree, From its posts, and planks, and flooring.
Sings a second, sets the siding; Sings a third time, sets the row-locks;
Joins the sides and ribs together. When the ribs were firmly fastened,
Then alas! three words were wanting, Lost the words of master-magic,
How the stern should be completed, How complete the boat’s forecastle.
Wise and wonderful enchanter, Heavy-hearted spake as follows: “Woe is me, my life hard-fated!
Pass in safety o’er the water, Never ride the rough sea-billows.”
Where to find these words of magic, Find the lost-words of the Master: “From the brains of countless swallows,
From the plumage of the gray-duck?”
Kills of swans a goodly number, Kills a flock of fattened gray-duck,
Cannot find the words of magic, Not the lost-words of the Master.
Still reflected and debated: “I perchance may find the lost-words
In the mouth of the white squirrel.”
Hastes to find the magic sayings, Kills a countless host of reindeer,
Finds of words a goodly number, But they are of little value,
Long he thought and well considered: “I can find of words a hundred
In the Manala fields and castles.”
To the kingdom of Tuoni, There to find the ancient wisdom,
Hastens on through fen and forest, Over meads and over marshes,
Journeys one week through the brambles, And a second through the hazels,
When appear Tuoni’s islands, And the Manala fields and castles.
Calls aloud in tones of thunder, To the Tuonela deeps and dungeons,
“Bring a boat, Tuoni’s daughter, Bring a ferry-boat, O maiden,
O’er this black and fatal river.”
Magic maid of little stature, Tiny virgin of Manala,
Tiny cleaner of the dresses, At the river of Tuoni,
Speaks these words to Wainamoinen, Gives this answer to his calling: “Straightway will I bring the row-boat,
Why thou comest to Manala In a hale and active body.”
Gives this answer to the maiden: “I was brought here by Tuoni,
Speaks the maiden of Manala: “This a tale of wretched liars;
Mana raised thee from the coffin, Then Tuoni would be with thee,
With Tuoni’s hat upon thee, On thy hands, the gloves of Mana;
What has brought thee to Manala?”
Gives this answer, still finessing: “Iron brought me to Manala,
Speaks the virgin of the death-land,
“Well I know that this is falsehood, Had the iron brought thee hither,
Blood would trickle from thy vesture, And the blood-drops, scarlet-colored.
This the third time that I ask thee.”
Still finesses to the daughter: “Water brought me to Manala,
This the tiny maiden’s answer: “Well I know thou speakest falsely;
If the cataract and whirlpool, Or the waves had brought thee hither,
Water drip from all thy raiment. Tell the truth and I will serve thee,
Then the stubborn Wainamoinen
“Fire has brought me to Manala, To the kingdom of Tuoni.”
“Well I know the voice of falsehood. If the fire had brought thee hither,
Singed would be thy locks and eyebrows, And thy beard be crisped and tangled.
If I row thee o’er the ferry, Thou must speak the truth in answer,
Make an end of thy deception. What has brought thee to Manala,
Still untouched by Death’s dark angels?” Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “At the first I spake, not truly,
I a boat with ancient wisdom, Fashioned with my powers of magic,
Sang the third day until evening, When I broke the magic main-spring,
Of my song the fleetest runners; Then I come to Mana’s kingdom,
Thus to mend my sledge of magic, Thus to join the parts together.
Send me, quick, Tuoni’s row-boat, Help me cross this fatal river,
Spake the daughter of Tuoni,
“Thou art sure a stupid fellow, Foresight wanting, judgment lacking,
Coming here without a reason, Coming to Tuoni’s empire;
To thy distant home and kindred; Many they that visit Mana,
Spake the good old Wainamoinen: “Women old retreat from danger,
Not the weakest of the heroes. Bring thy boat, Tuoni’s daughter,
Come and row me o’er the ferry.”
Brings her boat to Wainamoinen, Quickly rows him through the channel,
To the kingdom of Manala, Speaks these words to the magician: “Woe to thee! O Wainamoinen!
Since thou comest to Manala, Comest neither dead nor dying.”
Ancient hostess of Tuoni, Brings him pitchers filled with strong-beer,
Speaks these measures to the stranger: “Drink, thou ancient Wainamoinen,
Wainamoinen, wise and cautious,
Looks a long time in the pitchers, Sees the spawning of the black-frogs,
Lizards, worms, and writhing adders, Thus addresses Tuonetar: “Have not come with this intention,
Drink the beer of Tuonela; Those that drink Tuoni’s liquors,
Court the Devil and destruction, End their lives in want and ruin.”
“Ancient minstrel, Wainamoinen, Tell me what has brought thee hither,
To the courts of Tuonela, Ere Tuoni sent his angels
There to cut thy magic life-thread.” Spake the singer, Wainamoinen: “I was building me a vessel,
Needed three words of the Master, How to fasten in the ledges,
How complete the boat’s forecastle. This the reason of my coming
To the castles of Manala: Came to learn these magic sayings,
Spake the hostess, Tuonetar: “Mana never gives these sayings,
Not the lost-words of the Master; Thou shalt never leave this kingdom,
Never go to Kalevala, To Wainola’s peaceful meadows.
Quick the hostess, Tuonetar,
O’er the head of Wainamoinen, Puts to rest the wisdom-hero,
In the robes of living heroes, Deep the sleep that settles o’er him.
In the kingdom of Tuoni, Evil witch and toothless wizard,
Moulder of the bands of copper, Weaver of a hundred fish-nets,
Spinning in the days of summer, Weaving in the winter evenings,
In the kingdom of Tuoni
Three the fingers of the hero, Spinner he of iron meshes,
Countless were his nets of metal, Moulded on a rock in water,
Mana’s son with crooked fingers,
Pulls of nets, at least a thousand, Through the river of Tuoni,
In the fatal, darksome river, That the sleeping Wainamoinen,
May not leave the isle of Mana, Never in the course of ages,
Never while the moonlight glimmers On the empire of Tuoni.
Rising from his couch of slumber, Speaks these words as he is waking: “Is there not some mischief brewing,
In the chambers of Tuoni, In the Manala home and household?”
Changes too his form and feature, Slips into another body;
Rolls black-dyed upon the waters; Like a snake among the willows,
Like an adder through the grasses, Through the coal-black stream of death-land,
Interlaced with threads of iron, From the kingdom of Tuoni,
Mana’s son, the wicked wizard,
In the early morning hastens To his thousand nets of copper,
Finds therein a countless number Of the death-stream fish and serpents;
Wainamoinen, wise and wary, Friend and fellow of the waters.
Had escaped from Tuonela, Spake he thus in supplication: “Gratitude to thee, O Ukko,
Never suffer other heroes, Of thy heroes not the wisest,
Never let another singer, While he lives within the body,
As thou lovest thy creations. Many heroes cross the channel,
Few return to tell the story, Few return from Tuonela,
Wainamoinen calls his people,
Speaks these words of ancient wisdom, To the young men, to the maidens,
“Every child of Northland, listen: If thou wishest joy eternal,
Never evil treat the guiltless, Never wrong the feeble-minded,
Never stain thy lips with falsehood, Never cheat thy trusting neighbor,
Lest thou surely payest penance In the kingdom of Tuoni,
There, the home of all the wicked, There the couch of the unworthy,
Underneath Manala’s fire-rock Are their ever-flaming couches,
Vipers green their writhing covers, For their drink the blood of adders,
Pain and agony their solace; If thou wishest joy eternal,
Wainamoinen Finds the Lost-Word.
Did not learn the words of magic In Tuoni’s gloomy regions,
Thereupon he long debated, Well considered, long reflected,
When a shepherd came to meet him, Speaking thus to Wainamoinen: “Thou canst find of words a hundred,
In the mouth of wise Wipunen, In the body of the hero;
To his tomb the magic highway, Trodden by a host of heroes;
On the sharpened points of needles; Then a long way thou must journey
Thirdly thou must travel farther On the edges of the hatchets.”
Well considered all these journeys, Travelled to the forge and smithy,
“Ilmarinen, worthy blacksmith, Make a shoe for me of iron,
Mold a staff of strongest metal, Lay the steel upon the inside,
I am going on a journey To procure the magic sayings,
From the mouth of the magician, From the tongue of wise Wipunen.”
“Long ago died wise Wipunen, Disappeared these many ages,
Sets no longer traps of iron, Cannot learn from him the wisdom,
Wainamoinen, old and hopeful,
In his metal shoes and armor, Hastens forward on his journey,
On the sharpened points of needles; Wearily he strides the second,
Swings himself the third day forward, On the edges of the hatchets.
Ancient bard, and great magician, With his magic songs lay yonder,
On his shoulder grew the aspen, On each temple grew the birch-tree,
From his beard grew willow-bushes, From his mouth the dark green fir-tree,
Wainamoinen, coming closer,
From his magic leathern scabbard, Fells the aspen from his shoulder,
From his chin he fells the alder, From his beard, the branching willows,
Fells the oak-tree from his forehead.
Through the mouth of wise Wipunen, Pries his mighty jaws asunder,
“Rise, thou master of magicians, From the sleep of Tuonela,
Wise Wipunen, ancient singer,
Keenly feels the pangs of torture, From the cruel staff of iron;
Bites in twain the softer iron, Cannot bite the steel asunder,
Wainamoinen of Wainola, In his iron-shoes and armor,
In the spacious mouth and fauces Of the magic bard, Wipunen.
Opens wide his mouth and swallows Wainamoinen and his magic,
Then outspeaks the wise Wipunen: “Many things before I’ve eaten,
Bear, and ox, and wolf, and wild-boar, Never in my recollection,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Now I see the evil symbols,
In the darksome Hisi-hurdles, In the catacombs of Kalma.”
How to live and how to prosper, How to conquer this condition.
With a handle hewn from birch-wood, From the handle builds a vessel,
In this vessel rows he swiftly Through the entrails of the hero,
Of the wisest of magicians. Old Wipunen, master-singer,
Gives no heed to Wainamoinen. Then the artist of Wainola
Sets at work to hammer metals; Makes a smithy from his armor,
Makes the air-valve from his fur-coat, From his stockings, makes the muzzle,
Makes a hammer of his fore-arm; Like the storm-wind roars the bellows,
Forges one day, then a second, Forges till the third day closes,
In the sorcerer’s abdomen.
Speaks these words in wonder, guessing: “Who art thou of ancient heroes,
Many heroes I have eaten, And of men a countless number,
Smoke arises from my nostrils, From my mouth the fire is streaming,
“Go, thou monster, hence to wander,
Ere I go to seek thy mother, Tell the ancient dame thy mischief;
Great the burden she shall carry; Great a mother’s pain and anguish,
Cannot comprehend the meaning, Nor this mystery unravel,
Camest here to give me torture. Art thou Hisi sent from heaven,
Art, perchance, some new creation, Ordered here to do me evil?
Some calamity from Ukko, Sent to me by my Creator,
God does not forsake the worthy, Does not ruin those that trust him,
If by man thou wert created, If some hero sent thee hither,
Shall destroy thy wicked tribe-folk.
“Thence arose the violation,
Thence came all the evil-doings: From the neighborhood of wizards,
From the caves of vicious spirits, From the haunts of fortune-tellers,
From the castles of Tuoni, From the bottom of Manala,
From Ingratitude’s dominions, From the rocky shoals and quicksands,
From the cataract’s commotion, From the bear-caves in the mountains,
From the roarings of the pine-tree, From the burrows of the fox-dog,
From the caves and Hisi-hurdles, From the battles of the giants,
From the billows of the oceans, From the streams of boiling waters,
From the limits of the storm-clouds, From the pathways of the thunders,
From the distant plains of Pohya, From the fatal stream and whirlpool,
“Art thou coming from these places?
To the heart of sinless hero, To devour my guiltless body,
Get thee hence, thou dog of Lempo, Leave, thou monster from Manala,
Leave my liver, thing of evil, In my body cease thy forging,
Let me rest in peace and slumber.
“Should I want in means efficient,
To outroot thine evil genius, I shall call a better hero,
To remove this dire misfortune, To annihilate this monster.
From the fields, the old-time heroes, Mounted heroes from the sand-hills,
From these pains and ceaseless tortures.
“If this force prove inefficient,
Come, thou forest, with thy heroes, Come, ye junipers and pine-trees,
Come, ye mountains, with your wood-nymphs, Come, ye lakes, with all your mermaids,
Come, torment this son of Hisi, Come and kill this evil monster.
“If this call is inefficient,
Rise, thou ancient water-mother, With thy blue-cap from the ocean,
Bring protection to thy hero, Comfort bring and full assistance,
