May not perish prematurely.
“Shouldst thou brave this invocation,
Come, thou beauteous, golden maiden, Oldest of the race of women,
Come and turn away this evil, Come, remove this biting torment,
“If this call be disregarded,
Ukko, on the arch of heaven, In the thunder-cloud dominions,
Come, protect thy tortured hero, Drive away this magic demon,
With his sword and flaming furnace, With his fire-enkindling bellows.
“Go, thou demon, hence to wander,
Never come again for shelter, Nevermore build thou thy dwelling
Take at once thy habitation To the regions of thy kindred,
When thy journey thou hast ended, Gained the borders of thy country,
Give a signal of thy coming, Rumble like the peals of thunder,
Knock upon the outer portals, Enter through the open windows,
Seize the host and seize the hostess, Knock their evil heads together,
To the black-dogs of the forest.
“Should this prove of little value,
O’er the dwellings of the master, Scare the horses from the mangers,
Twist their tails, and horns, and forelocks, Hurl their carcasses to Lempo.
“If some scourge the winds have sent me,
Brought me by the frosts of winter, Quickly journey whence thou camest,
Perching not upon some aspen, Resting not upon the birch-tree;
That the copper-winds may nurse thee, Waves of ether, thy protection.
“Didst those come from high Jumala,
Quick ascend beyond the cloud-space, Quickly journey whence thou camest,
To the twinkling stars of heaven; There thy fire may burn forever,
In the Sun’s undying furnace.
“Wert thou sent here by the spring-floods,
Quickly journey whence thou camest, Quickly hasten to the waters,
To the ancient water-mountain, That the floods again may rock thee,
“Didst thou come from Kalma’s kingdom,
Haste thou back to thine own country, To the Kalma-halls and castles,
Where contending armies perish.
“Art thou from the Hisi-woodlands,
From the thickets of the pine-wood, From the dwellings of the fir-glen?
To the dwellings of thy master, To the thickets of thy kindred;
Till thy house decays about thee, Till thy walls shall mould and crumble.
“Evil genius, thee I banish,
To the caverns of the white-bear, To the deep abysm of serpents,
To the ever-silent waters, To the hot-springs of the mountains,
To the lifeless lakes and rivers, To the sacred stream and whirlpool.
“Shouldst thou find no place of resting,
To the Northland’s distant borders, To the broad expanse of Lapland,
To the unproductive prairies, Sunless, moonless, starless, lifeless,
This for thee, a place befitting, Pitch thy tents and feast forever
“Shouldst thou find no means of living,
To the cataract of Rutya, To the fire-emitting whirlpool,
To the windfalls of the forest; Swim hereafter in the waters
Whirl thou ever in the current Of the cataract’s commotion,
“Should this place be unbefitting,
To Tuoni’s coal-black river, To the endless stream of Mana,
Thou canst never leave Manala, Should I not thy head deliver,
Thou canst never safely journey Through nine brother-rams abutting,
Through nine brother-stallions thwarting, Thou canst not re-cross Death-river
Interlaced with threads of copper.
“Shouldst thou ask for steeds for saddle,
I will give thee worthy racers, I will give thee saddle-horses;
Crimson mane, and tail, and foretop, Fire emitting from his nostrils,
Hoofs are made of strongest iron, Legs are made of steel and copper,
Darts like lightning through the valleys, When a skilful master rides him.
“Should this steed be insufficient,
Give thee Hisi’s shoes of elm-wood, Give to thee the staff of Piru,
Into Hisi’s courts and castles, To the woods and fields of Juutas;
Dash the flinty rocks in pieces, Hurl the fragments to the heavens;
Make them turn aside in greeting; If some mighty hero hail thee,
“Hasten hence, thou thing of evil,
Ere the breaking of the morning Ere the Sun awakes from slumber,
Haste away, thou plague of Northland, Haste along the track of moonbeams,
To the darksome fields of Pohya.
“If at once thou dost not leave me,
Send to thee the beaks of vultures, To devour thine evil body,
Much more quickly cruel Lempo Left my vitals when commanded,
Called the help of my Creator. Flee, thou motherless offendant,
Flee, thou hound without a master, Ere the morning sun arises,
Wainamoinen, ancient hero,
“Satisfied am I to linger In these old and spacious caverns,
For my meat I have thy tissues, Have thy heart, and spleen, and liver,
Goodly home for Wainamoinen.
“I shall set my forge and bellows
I shall swing my heavy hammer, Swing it with a greater power
I shall never, never leave thee Till I learn thine incantations,
Learn the lost-words of the Master; Never must these words be hidden,
Though the wisdom-singers perish.”
Ancient prophet, filled with power, Opens full his store of knowledge,
Filled with old-time incantations, Filled with songs of times primeval,
Sings the very oldest folk-songs, Sings the origin of witchcraft,
Sings the first of all creations, Sings the source of good and evil,
Only sung in part by heroes In these days of sin and sorrow.
Sings the orders of enchantment. How, upon the will of Ukko,
How the air was first divided, How the water came from ether,
How from earth came vegetation, Fish, and fowl, and man, and hero.
How the Moon was first created, How the Sun was set in heaven,
Whence the ether’s crystal pillars, How the skies with stars were sprinkled.
Sings in miracles of concord, Sings in magic tones of wisdom,
Songs he sings in countless numbers, Swift his notes as tongues of serpents,
Sings one day, and then a second, Sings a third from dawn till evening,
Listen all the stars of heaven, And the Moon stands still and listens
In the bay the tides cease rising, Stop the rivers in their courses,
Even Jordan ceases flowing, And the Wuoksen stops and listens.
Well had learned the magic sayings, Learned the ancient songs and legends,
Learned the lost-words of the Master, Well had learned the secret doctrine,
Of the wisdom-bard, Wipunen, Leave the bosom of the master,
Spake the hero, Wainamoinen: “O, thou Antero Wipunen,
I have found the magic lost-words, I will leave thee now forever,
Will return to Kalevala, To Wainola’s fields and firesides.”
“Many are the things I’ve eaten, Eaten bear, and elk, and reindeer,
Eaten man, and eaten hero, Never, never have I eaten
Thou hast found what thou desirest, Found the three words of the Master;
Take my blessing on thy going.”
Opens wide his mouth, and wider; And the good, old Wainamoinen
Leaves Wipunen’s great abdomen; From the mouth he glides and journeys
Swift as red-deer of the forest, Swift as yellow-breasted marten,
To the plains of Kalevala.
Of his brother, Ilmarinen, Thus the iron-artist greets him: “Hast thou found the long-lost wisdom,
Hast thou learned the master magic, How to fasten in the ledges,
How complete the ship’s forecastle?” Wainamoinen thus made answer: “I have learned of words a hundred,
Hidden deep for many ages, Learned the words of ancient wisdom,
Found the lost-words of the Master.”
Straightway journeys to his vessel, To the spot of magic labor,
Firmly binds the stern together And completes the boat’s forecastle.
Built the boat with magic only, And with magic launched his vessel,
Using not the foot to move it, Using not the knee to turn it,
Thus the third task was completed, For the hostess of Pohyola,
Sitting on the arch of heaven, On the bow of many colors.
THE Rival Suitors.
Long considered, long debated, How to woo and win the daughter
How to lead the Bride of Beauty, Fairy maiden of the rainbow,
From the dismal Sariola.
Paints the boat in blue and scarlet, Trims in gold the ship’s forecastle,
Sings his magic ship down gliding, On the cylinders of fir-tree;
On each mast the sails of linen, Sails of blue, and white, and scarlet,
Wainamoinen, the magician,
Steers the bark across the waters, On the blue back of the broad-sea,
Sailing to the dark Pohyola: “Come aboard my ship, O Ukko,
To protect thine ancient hero, To support thy trusting servant,
On the far out-stretching waters.
“Rock, O winds, this wondrous vessel,
Rolling waves, bear ye me northward, That the oar may not be needed
O’er this mighty waste of waters.”
Fair and goodly maid, Annikki, Of the Night and Dawn, the daughter,
Rises long before the daylight, Stood one morning on the sea-shore,
Rinsing out her silken ribbons, On the bridge of scarlet color,
On a headland jutting seaward, On the forest-covered island.
Looking through the fog and ether, Looking through the clouds of heaven,
Sees the morning sun arising, Glimmering along the billows,
Toward the sunrise on the waters, Toward the winding streams of Suomi,
There she sees, on the horizon,
Something blue upon the billows, Speaks these words in wonder guessing: “What is this upon the surges,
What this darkling in the sunlight? ’Tis perhaps a flock of wild-geese,
Then upon thy wings arising, Fly away to highest heaven.
“Art thou then a shoal of sea-trout,
Dive then to the deep sea-bottom, In the waters swim and frolic.
“Art thou then a cliff of granite,
Floating on the rough sea-billows? May the floods then wash and beat thee,
Wainamoinen, sailing northward,
Toward the headland jutting seaward, Toward the island forest-covered.
Sees it is the magic vessel Of a wonderful enchanter,
And she asks this simple question: “Art thou then my father’s vessel,
Haste away then to thy harbor, To thy refuge in Wainola.
Sail then farther on thy journey, Point thy prow to other waters.”
Not a sail-boat from the distance, ’Twas the ship of Wainamoinen,
Sails within a hailing distance, Swims still nearer o’er the waters,
Brings a third of magic import.
Of the Night and Dawn, the daughter, To the sailor of the vessel: “Whither sailest, Wainamoinen,
Pride and joy of Kalevala?”
Gives this answer to the maiden: “I have come to catch some sea-trout,
Hiding in these reeds and rushes.” This the answer of Annikki:
“Do not speak to me in falsehood,
Long ago my honored father Was a fisherman in Northland,
Fished within these seas and rivers. Very well do I remember
How he rigs his fishing vessel, Lines, and gaffs, and poles, and fish-nets;
Whither goest, Wainamoinen, Whither sailest, friend of waters?”
“I have come to catch some wild-geese, Catch the hissing birds of Suomi,
In the Sachsensund dominions.” Good Annikki gives this answer: “Know I well a truthful speaker,
Formerly my aged father Often came a-hunting hither,
Hunt the red-bill of these waters. Very well do I remember
Bows, and arrows, knives, and quiver, Dogs enchained within the vessel,
Setters seeking in the marshes; Tell the truth now Wainamoinen,
Spake the hero of the Northland: “To the wars my ship is sailing,
Where the streams run scarlet-colored, Where the paths are paved with bodies.”
“Know I well the paths to battle; Formerly my aged father
Often led the hosts to conquest; In each ship a hundred rowers,
On the prow a thousand cross-bows, Swords, and spears, and battle-axes;
Speak no longer fruitless falsehoods, Whither sailest, Wainamoinen,
These the words of Wainamoinen: “Come, O maiden, to my vessel,
Then I’ll give thee truthful answer.”
Answers ancient Wainamoinen: “With the winds I’ll fill thy vessel,
And capsize thy ship of magic, Break in pieces its forecastle,
If thou dost not cease thy falsehoods, If thou dost not tell me truly
These the words of Wainamoinen: “Now I make thee truthful answer,
I am sailing to the Northland To the dismal Sariola,
Where they drown the worthy heroes, There to woo the Maid of Beauty
Woo and win the fairy virgin, Bring her to my home and kindred,
Then Annikki, graceful maiden,
As she heard the rightful answer, Knew the truth was fully spoken,
Left unwashed her linen garments, Left unrinsed her silks and ribbons
On the bridge of scarlet color; On her arm she threw her long-robes,
To the shops of Ilmarinen, To the iron-forger’s furnace,
Here she found the hero-artist, Forging out a bench of iron,
Soot lay thick upon his forehead, Soot and coal upon his shoulders.
These the words his sister uses: “Ilmarinen, dearest brother,
Forge me now a loom of silver, Golden rings to grace my fingers,
Six or seven golden girdles, Golden crosslets for my bosom,
And I’ll tell a tale surprising, Tell a story that concerns thee
Then the blacksmith Ilmarinen
“If thou’lt tell the tale sincerely, I will forge the loom of silver,
Forge thee gold and silver ear-rings, Six or seven golden girdles,
For thy head forge golden trinkets; But if thou shouldst tell me falsely,
Break thine ornaments in pieces, Hurl them to the fire and furnace,
This the answer of Annikki: “Ancient blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Her already thine affianced, Beauteous Maiden of the Rainbow,
Chosen bride of Sariola? Shouldst thou wish the Maid of Beauty,
Hammering the days and nights through; Forge the summer hoofs for horses,
In the long nights forge the snow-sledge, Gaily trim it in the daytime,
To thy wooing in the Northland, To the dismal Sariola;
Sails another now before thee, There to woo thy bride affianced,
Woo and win the Maid of Beauty; Three long years thou hast been wooing.
On the blue back of the waters, Sitting at his helm of copper;
Beautiful his boat of magic, Sailing fleetly o’er the billows,
To the dismal Sariola.”
Stood a statue at the story; Silent grief had settled o’er him,
From one hand the tongs descended, From the other fell the hammer,
“Good Annikki, worthy sister, I shall forge the loom of silver,
Forge thee gold and silver ear-rings, Six or seven golden girdles,
Go and heat for me the bath-room, Fill with heat the honey-chambers,
Lay the smaller woods around them, Pour some water through the ashes,
Thus to cleanse my blackened visage, Thus to cleanse the blacksmith’s body,
Then Annikki, kindly sister,
Warmed it with the knots of fir-trees, That the thunder-winds had broken;
Threw them in the heating waters; Broke the tassels from the birch-trees,
Made a lye from milk and ashes, Made of these a strong decoction,
Of the reindeer of the mountains, Made a soap of magic virtue,
Thus to beautify the suitor, Thus to make the hero worthy.
The eternal metal-worker, Forged the wishes of his sister,
Rings, and bracelets, pins and ear-drops, Forged for her six golden girdles,
While the maid prepared the bath-room, Set his toilet-room in order.
Gave the loom of molten silver, And the sister thus made answer: “I have heated well thy bath-room,
Everything as thou desirest; Go prepare thyself for wooing,
Make thy cheeks look fresh and ruddy, Lave thyself in Love’s aroma,
Ilmarinen, magic artist,
Bathed his head to flaxen whiteness, Made his cheeks look fresh and ruddy,
Like the moonlight on the waters; Wondrous were his form and features,
These the words of Ilmarinen: “Fair Annikki, lovely sister,
Bring my best and richest vesture, Bring me now my softest linen,
Straightway did the helpful sister
Bring the softest of his linen, Raiment fashioned by his mother;
Brought him shoes of marten-leather, Brought a vest of sky-blue color,
Brought a coat with scarlet trimming, Brought a red shawl trimmed in ermine
Brought a fur-coat made of seal-skin, Fastened with a thousand bottons,
Brought for him his magic girdle, Fastened well with golden buckles,
Brought him gloves with golden wristlets, That the Laplanders had woven
Brought the finest cap in Northland, That his ancient father purchased
Ilmarinen, blacksmith-artist,
When he thus addressed a servant: “Hitch for me a fleet-foot racer,
For I start upon a journey To the distant shores of Pohya,
Spake the servant thus in answer: “Thou hast seven fleet-foot racers,
Which of these shall I make ready?” Spake the blacksmith, Ilmarinen: “Take the fleetest of my coursers,
Hitch him to my sledge of magic; Place six cuckoos on the break-board,
Thus to charm the Northland maidens, Thus to make them look and listen,
Bring me too my largest bear-skin, Fold it warm about the cross-bench;
As a cover and protection.”
Of the blacksmith, Ilmarinen, Put the gray steed in the harness,
Placed six cuckoos on the break-board, Seven bluebirds on the cross-bars,
Then he brought the largest bear-skin, Folded it upon the cross-bench;
Warm protection for the master.
The eternal metal-worker, Earnestly entreated Ukko: “Send thy snow-flakes, Ukko, father,
Let them cover all the heather, Let them hide the berry-bushes,
O’er the hills to Sariola!”
Gently dropped the crystal snow-flakes, Lending thus his kind assistance
On his journey to the Northland.
Seats him in his metal snow-sledge, And beseeches thus his Master: “Good luck to my reins and traces,
God protect my magic snow-sledge, Be my safeguard on my journey
Now the ancient Ilmarinen
Snaps his whip above the courser, To the gray steed gives this order,
“Haste away, my flaxen stallion, Haste thee onward, noble white-face,
To the dreary Sariola!”
On the curving snow-capped sea-coast, On the borders of the lowlands,
Merrily the steed flies onward, Bluebirds singing, cuckoos calling,
Through the sand and falling snow-flakes Blinding winds, and snow, and sea-foam,
As he glides upon his journey, Looking seaward for the vessel
Travels one day, then a second, Travels all the next day northward,
Overtakes old Wainamoinen, Hails him in his magic vessel,
“O thou ancient Wainamoinen, Let us woo in peace the maiden,
Sitting on the bow of heaven, Let each labor long to win her,
Him selecting, let her follow.” Wainamoinen thus makes answer: “I agree to thy proposal,
Not by force, nor faithless measures, Shall we woo the Maid of Beauty,
Let the unsuccessful suitor Harbor neither wrath nor envy
Thus agreeing, on they journey,
Fleetly does the steed fly onward, Quickly flies the magic vessel,
Ilmarinen’s fleet-foot racer Makes the hills of Northland tremble,
To the dismal Sariola.
And they fly to his assistance; Swiftly sails his ship of beauty,
In her pathway to Pohyola.
Scarce a moment had passed over, Ere the dogs began their barking,
In the courts of Sariola, Watch-dogs of the court of Louhi;
Never had they barked so loudly, Never with their tails had beaten
Spake the master of Pohyola: “Go and learn, my worthy daughter,
Why the black-dog signals danger.” Quickly does the daughter answer: “I am occupied, dear father,
I must tend my flock of lambkins, I must turn the nether millstone,
Run the grindings through the sifter, Only have I time for grinding.”
Seldom does he growl so strangely. Spake the master of Pohyola: “Go and learn, my trusted consort,
Why the black-dog signals danger.” Thus his aged wife makes answer: “Have no time, nor inclination,
Must prepare a worthy dinner, I must bake the toothsome biscuit,
Only have I strength for kneading.” Spake the master of Pohyola: “Dames are always in a hurry,
Whether warming at the oven, Or asleep upon their couches;
Why the black-dog growls displeasure.” Quickly does the son give answer: “Have no time, nor inclination,
I must chop this log to cordwood, For the fire must cut the faggots,
Large the pile and small the fire-wood, Only have I strength for chopping.”
Growl the whelps within the mansion, Growl the dogs chained in the kennel,
Setting Northland in an uproar. Spake the master of Pohyola: “Never, never does my black-dog
Never does he bark for nothing, Does not growl at angry billows,
Then the master of Pohyola
For the barking of the watch-dogs; Strode he through the spacious court-yard,
To the summit of the uplands. Looking toward his black-dog barking,
To a distant, stormy hill-top, To a mound with alders covered;
Why his dogs had barked so loudly, Why had growled the wool-tail bearer,
At full sail, he saw a vessel, And the ship was scarlet-colored,
Saw a sledge of magic colors, Gliding up the curving sea-shore,
Then the master of the Northland
Hastened forward to his court-room, These the accents of the master: “Often strangers journey hither,
Sailing in a scarlet vessel, Rocking in the bay of Lempo;
To the honey-lands of Louhi.”
“How shall we obtain a token Why these strangers journey hither?
Lay a branch upon the fire-place, Let it burn with fire of magic;
War and bloodshed do they bring us; If it trickle drops of water,
Northland’s fair and slender maiden,
Lays a sorb-branch on the fire-place, Lights it with the fire of magic;
Trickles neither blood, nor water, From the wand come drops of honey.
This the language of the wizard: “If the wand is dripping honey,
Are but worthy friends and suitors.”
With the daughter of the hostess, Straightway left their work, and hastened
Looked about in all directions, Turned their eyes upon the waters,
Rocking slowly in the harbor, Having sailed the bay of Lempo,
Sable was the nether portion, And the upper, scarlet-colored,
Leaning on his oars of copper; Saw a fleet-foot racer running,
Saw the magic sledge emblazoned, Guided toward the courts of Louhi;
Sitting on the break-board, calling, Seven bluebirds richly colored
In the sledge a magic hero, Young, and strong, and proud, and handsome,
Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Dearest daughter, winsome maiden,
Should these heroes come to woo thee, Wouldst thou leave thy home and country,
Be his faithful life-companion?
“He that comes upon the waters,
Having sailed the bay of Lempo, Is the good, old Wainamoinen;
Richest presents from Wainola.
“He that rides here in his snow-sledge
With the cuckoos and the bluebirds, Is the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Only brings some wisdom-sayings. When they come within the dwelling,
Bring a pitcher with two handles, Give to him that thou wouldst follow;
Him that brings thee countless treasures, Costly presents in his vessel,
Spake the Northland’s lovely daughter,
“Good, indeed, advice maternal, But I will not wed for riches,
For his worth I’ll choose a husband, For his youth and fine appearance,
In the olden times the maidens Were not sold by anxious mothers
I shall choose without his treasures Ilmarinen for his wisdom,
Him that forged the wondrous Sampo, Hammered thee the lid in colors.”
“Senseless daughter, child of folly, Thus to choose the ancient blacksmith,
Evermore to rinse his linen, Lave his hands, and eyes, and forehead,
Little use his wit and wisdom When compared with gold and silver.”
“I will never, never, never, Wed the ancient Wainamoinen
Never will I be a helpmate To a hero in his dotage,
Wainamoinen, safely landing
Pulls his gaily-covered vessel From the waves upon the sea-beach,
On the rollers copper-banded, Straightway hastens to the guest-room
Of the master of the Northland, Speaks these words upon the threshold
“Come with me, thou lovely virgin, Be my bride and life-companion,
Be my honored wife hereafter!” This the answer of the maiden: “Hast thou built for me the vessel,
From the fragments of the distaff, From the splinters of the spindle?”
“I have built the promised vessel, Built the wondrous ship for sailing,
It will weather roughest billows, Will outlive the winds and waters,
Of the deep and boundless ocean; It will ride the waves in beauty,
Like a cork on lake and river, Through the angry seas of Northland,
Northland’s fair and slender daughter
“Will not wed a sea-born hero, Do not care to rock the billows,
Storms would bring us pain and trouble, Winds would rack our hearts and temples;
Cannot keep thy home in order, Cannot be thy life-companion,
Ilmarinen’S Wooing.
The eternal metal-worker, Hastens forward to the court-room
Of the master of the Northland, Hastens through the open portals
Servants come with silver pitchers, Filled with Northland’s richest brewing;
To the blacksmith of Wainola, Ilmarinen thus replying: “I shall not in all my life-time
Till I see the Maid of Beauty, Fairy Maiden of the Rainbow;
For whose hand I journey hither.” Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Trouble does the one selected
Not yet are her feet in sandals, Thine affianced is not ready.
Only canst thou win the maiden, When thou hast by aid of magic
Plowed the field of hissing vipers, Touching neither beam nor handles.
Lempo furrowed it with horses, With a plowshare made of copper,
Never since has any hero Brought this field to cultivation.”
Straightway hastens to the chamber Of the Maiden of the Rainbow,
“Thou of Night and Dawn the daughter, Tell me, dost thou not remember
Hammered thee the lid in colors? Thou didst swear by oath the strongest,
By the tongs and by the hammer, In the ears of the Almighty,
Thou wouldst follow me hereafter, Be my bride, my life-companion,
Now thy mother is exacting, Will not give to me her daughter,
I have plowed the field of serpents, Plowed the hissing soil of Hisi.”
Gives this answer to the suitor: “O, thou blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Forge thyself a golden plowshare, Forge the beam of shining silver,
Then with ease, by aid of magic, Thou canst plow the field of serpents,
Ilmarinen, welcome suitor,
Places gold within the furnace, In the forge he lays the silver,
Forges, too, a beam of silver, Forges handles out of copper,
Forges him a mail of metal, For his limbs a safe protection,
Then a horse of fire selecting, Harnesses the flaming stallion,
Plow the viper-lands of Hisi. In the field were countless vipers,
Crawling, writhing, hissing, stinging, Harmless all against the hero,
“Vipers, ye by God created, Neither best nor worst of creatures,
And whose venom comes from Hisi, Ukko is your greater Master,
Get ye hence before my plowing, Writhe ye through the grass and stubble,
Keep your heads beneath the heather, Hunt your holes to Mana’s kingdom
Then will mighty Ukko smite them With his iron-pointed arrows,
Thus the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Lifts the vipers in his plowing, Buries them beneath the furrow,
When the task had been completed, Ilmarinen, quick returning,
“I have plowed the field of Hisi, Plowed the field of hissing serpents,
Give me, ancient dame, thy daughter, Fairest maiden of the Northland.”
“Shall not grant to thee my daughter, Shall not give my lovely virgin,
Till Manala’s wolf is conquered, In the forests of the Death-land,
Hundreds have been sent to hunt him, So one yet has been successful,
Thereupon young Ilmarinen
Thus addresses his affianced: “Still another test demanded,
Bridle there the bear of Mana, Bring him from the Death-land forests,
This advice the maiden gives him: “O thou artist, Ilmarinen,
Forge of steel a magic bridle, On a rock beneath the water,
Make the straps of steel and copper, Bridle then the bear of Mana,
Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
On a rock beneath the water, In the foam of triple currents;
Straightway went the bear to muzzle, In the forests of the Death-land,
“Terhenetar, ether-maiden, Daughter of the fog and snow-flake,
O’er the hills and lowland thickets, Where the wild-bear feeds and lingers,
May not hear my stealthy footsteps!”
Makes the fog and snow-flake settle On the coverts of the wild-beasts;
Fetters him in chains of magic, In the forests of Tuoni,
When this task had been completed,
Thus addressed the ancient Louhi: “Give me, worthy dame, thy daughter,
I have brought the bear of Mana From Tuoni’s fields and forests.”
To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen: “I will only give my daughter,
When the monster-pike thou catchest In the river of Tuoni,
Using neither hooks, nor fish-nets, Neither boat, nor fishing-tackle;
No one yet has been successful, All have perished in Manala.”
Hastened to the maiden’s chamber, Thus addressed the rainbow-maiden: “Now a third test is demanded,
I must catch the pike of Mana, In the river of Tuoni,
Hard the third test of the hero!” This advice the maiden gives him: “O thou hero, Ilmarinen,
In thy furnace, forge an eagle, From the fire of ancient magic;
Catch the monster-fish in safety, From the death-stream of Tuoni,
Then the suitor, Ilmarinen,
In the furnace forged an eagle From the fire of ancient wisdom;
Forged he talons out of iron, And his beak of steel and copper;
On his back between the wing-bones, Thus addresses he his creature,
“Mighty eagle, bird of beauty, Fly thou whither I direct thee,
To the blue deeps of the Death-stream, Seize the mighty fish of Mana,
Swiftly flies the magic eagle,
To the river of Tuoni, There to catch the pike of Mana;
While the other sweeps the heavens; In the ocean dips his talons,
Safely landing, Ilmarinen,
Hunts the monster of the Death-stream, While the eagle hunts and fishes
From the river rose a monster, Grasped the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Quick the eagle pounced upon him, With his metal-beak he seized him,
Hurled him back upon the bottom Of the deep and fatal river,
Then arose the pike of Mana,
Of the pikes was not the largest, Nor belonged he to the smallest;
Teeth as long as fen-rake handles, Mouth as broad as triple streamlets,
Tried to snap the magic blacksmith, Tried to swallow Ilmarinen.
Of the birds was not the largest, Nor belonged he to the smallest;
Mouth as wide as seven streamlets, Tongue as long as seven javelins,
Swoops upon the pike of Mana. Quick the giant fish endangered,
Dragging down the mighty eagle, Lashing up the very bottom
When the mighty bird uprising Leaves the wounded pike in water,
To his home in upper ether; Soars awhile, and sails, and circles,
Swoops again on lightning-pinions, Strikes with mighty force his talons
Strikes the second of his talons On the flinty mountain-ledges,
From the cliffs rebound his talons, Slip the flinty rocks o’erhanging,
Dives again beneath the surface To the bottom of the river,
Deep, the wounds upon the body Of the monster of Tuoni.
Soars, and sails, and quickly circles, Swoops again upon the monster,
Both his eyeballs flashing lightning; With his beak of steel and copper
Firmly planted are his talons In the rocks and in his victim,
Lifts the pike above the waters, From Tuoni’s coal-black river,
Thus the third time does the eagle
Thus at last the eagle catches Mana’s pike, the worst of fishes,
From the river of Tuoni; None could see Manala’s river,
Hardly could one see through ether, For the feathers of the eagle,
Then the bird of copper talons
To the pine-tree’s topmost branches, To the fir-tree plumed with needles,
Ate the body of his victim, Left the head for Ilmarinen.
“O thou bird of evil nature, What thy thought and what thy motive?
Evidence of my successes; Thoughtless eagle, witless instinct,
But the bird of metal talons
Rising higher into ether, Rising, flying, soaring, sailing,
Made the vault of ether tremble, Split apart the dome of heaven,
Tore the Moon-horns from their sockets, Disappeared beyond the Sun-land,
Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Of the ever-dismal Northland, Thus addressed the ancient Louhi: “Let this head forever serve thee
Evidence of hero-triumphs; I have caught the pike of Mana,
Three my victories in Death-land, Three the tests of magic heroes;
Give to me the Maid of Beauty?” Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Badly is the test accomplished,
From his neck the head is severed, Of his body thou hast eaten,
These the words of Ilmarinen: “When the victory is greatest,
From the river of Tuoni, From the kingdom of Manala,
Thus the third task is completed. Tell me is the maiden ready,
Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “I will give to thee my daughter,
For the suitor, Ilmarinen; Thou hast won the Maid of Beauty,
Fit companion of thy fireside, Help and joy of all thy lifetime.”
And the babe this tale related. “There appeared within this dwelling,
From the East came flying hither, From the East, a monstrous eagle,
While the other swept the ocean; With his tail upon the waters,
Looked about, and eager watching, Flew around, and sailing, soaring,
Knocked three times with beak of copper On the castle-roof of iron;
“Then the eagle, looking round him,
Flew then to the mothers’ castle, Loudly rapped with heavy knocking
But the eagle could not enter.
“Then the eagle, looking round him,
Flew then to the virgins’ castle, Knocked again with beak of copper,
Easy for him there to enter; Flew upon the castle-chimney,
Pulled the clapboards from the studding, Tore the linen from the rafters,
Near the walls of many colors, On the cross-bars gaily-feathered,
Looked upon their golden ringlets, Looked upon the snow-white virgins,
On the fairest of the daughters, On the maid with pearly necklace,
Perched awhile, and looked, admiring, Swooped upon the Maid of Beauty,
On the whitest, on the fairest, On the stateliest and grandest,
Of the dismal Sariola; Grasped her in his mighty talons,
Maid of fairest form and feature, Maid adorned with pearly necklace,
Fragrant flowers upon her bosom, Scarlet band around her forehead,
Fairest maiden of the Northland.”
When the babe his tale had ended: “Tell me how, my child beloved,
Hast obtained the information, How her flaxen ringlets nestled,
How the virgin’s gold was lauded. Shone the silver Sun upon thee,
From the floor the child made answer: “Thus I gained the information,
To the home of the distinguished, To the guest-room of the maiden,
He that sailed the magic vessel; Better-name enjoyed the mother,
She that kneaded wheaten biscuits, Fed her many guests in Northland.
“Thus the information reached me,
Heard the virgin had arisen: Once I walked within the court-yard,
At an early hour of morning, Ere the Sun had broken slumber;
Blackened wreaths of smoke came rising From the chamber of the maiden,
There the maid was busy grinding, Moved the handles of the millstone
Like the ducks the side-holes sounded, And the sifter like the goldfinch,
“Then a second time I wandered
In the forest was the maiden Rocking on a fragrant hillock,
And in copper kettles, yellow.
“Then a third time did I wander
There I saw thy daughter weaving, Heard the flying of her shuttle,
Heard the rattling of her treddles, Heard the whirring of her yarn-reel.”
“Now alas! beloved daughter, I have often taught this lesson: ‘Do not sing among the pine-trees,
Do not hang thy head in walking, Do not bare thine arms, nor shoulders,
Hide thy beauty and thy power.’
“This I told thee in the autumn,
Sang thee in the budding spring-time, Sang thee when the snows were falling: ‘Let us build a place for hiding,
Where may weave my fairest daughter, Where my maid may ply her shuttle,
By the heroes of the Northland, By the suitors of Wainola.’”
Fourteen days the young child numbered: “Easy ’tis to hide a war-horse
Hard indeed to hide a maiden, Having lovely form and features!
In the middle of the ocean, Keep within thy lovely maiden,
Not long hidden canst thou keep her. Maidens will not grow and flourish,
Will not live without their suitors, Will not thrive without their wooers;
Neither on the land nor water.”
Head down-bent and heavy-hearted, Wanders to his native country,
To the plains of Kalevala, Chanting as he journeys homeward: “I have passed the age for wooing,
Woe is me, a witless minstrel, That I did not woo and marry,
When my hand was warm and welcome! Youth dethrones my age and station,
When a hero goes a-wooing With a poor but younger brother.
Does not wed in early manhood, In his youth does not be master
Thus the ancient Wainamoinen
“Old men must not go a-wooing, Must not swim the sea of anger,
Must not run a race for glory, With the younger sons of Northland.”
THE Brewing OF Beer.
Songs of wedding-feasts and dances, Sing the melodies of wedlock,
Sing of Ilmarinen’s marriage To the Maiden of the Rainbow,
Sing the drinking-songs of Pohya.
In Pohyola’s halls and chambers, In the courts of Sariola;
Great indeed the preparations For the marriage of the daughter,
For the drinking of the strangers, For the feeding of the poor-folk,
Grew an ox in far Karjala,
Was the ox that grew in Suomi; But his size was all-sufficient,
And his head was over Kemi, Horns in length a hundred fathoms,
Seven days it took a weasel To encircle neck and shoulders;
From one horn-tip to the other, Did not stop between for resting.
From the tail to reach the shoulders, But he could not gain the horn-tip
This young ox of huge dimensions,
Was conducted from Karjala To the meadows of Pohyola;
At his head and neck a thousand. When the mighty ox was lassoed,
Peacefully the monster journeyed By the bays of Sariola,
To the clouds arose his shoulders, And his horns to highest heaven.
Could a butcher be discovered That could kill the ox for Louhi,
In her hosts of giant people, In her rising generation,
Came a hero from a distance,
And these words the gray-beard uttered: “Wait, O wait, thou ox of Suomi,
Then I’ll smite thee on thy forehead, Break thy skull, thou willing victim!
Browse the woods of Sariola, Bare our pastures, fields, and forests;
Through the length and breadth of Northland, On the borders of this ocean!”
Started out the ox to slaughter, When Palwoinen swung his war-club,
Flashed his flaming eyes upon him; To the fir-tree leaped the hero,
Hid the gray-haired Wirokannas.
One to kill the ox of Suomi, In the country of Karelen,
In the quiet fields of Ehstland, On the battle-fields of Sweden,
In the magic fens of Turya; Seek him in Tuoni’s empire,
Long the search, and unsuccessful, On the blue back of the ocean,
There arose from out the sea-waves,
On the white-capped, roaring breakers, From the water’s broad expanses;
Nor belonged he to the smallest; Made his bed within a sea-shell,
Hero old, with hands of iron, And his face was copper-colored;
Like the full corn from the kernel. On his head a hat of flint-stone,
In his hand a golden cleaver, And the blade was copper-handled.
Found the magic ox a slayer. Nothing has been found so mighty
As the sea-god saw his booty,
Hurled him to his knees before him, Quickly felled the calf of Suomi,
Bountifully meat was furnished; Filled at least a thousand hogsheads
And a thousand weight of suet, For the banquet of Pohyola,
In Pohyola was a guest-room,
Was in length a hundred furlongs, And in breadth was nearly fifty;
Crowed at break of early morning, No one on the earth could hear him;
None could hear him at the other.
Hastens to the hall and court-room, In the centre speaks as follows: “Whence indeed will come the liquor,
Who will make the mead abundant, For the people of the Northland,
To her drinking-feast and nuptials? Cannot comprehend the malting,
Nor the origin of brewing.” Spake an old man from his corner: “Beer arises from the barley,
And the fire gives no assistance. Hop-vine was the son of Remu,
Cultivated in the loose soil, Scattered like the evil serpents
On the Osmo-fields and borders. There the young plant grew and flourished,
Clinging to the rocks and alders.
“Man of good-luck sowed the barley
And the barley grew and flourished, Grew and spread in rich abundance,
On the Osmo plains and highlands, On the fields of Kalew-heroes.
“Time had travelled little distance,
Barley in the fields was singing, And from Kalew’s well the water,
‘Let us join our triple forces, Join to each the other’s powers;
Little use in working singly, Better we should toil together.’
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
Takes the golden grains of barley, Taking six of barley-kernels,
Filling seven cups with water, On the fire she sets the caldron,
Lets them steep, and seethe, and bubble Brewing thus the beer delicious,
On the foggy promontory, On the island forest-covered;
Into hogsheads made of oak-wood.
“Thus did Osmotar of Kalew
Could not generate the ferment. Thinking long and long debating,
‘What will bring the effervescence, Who will add the needed factor,
May ferment and be delightful?’
“Kalevatar, magic maiden,
Swiftly moving, lightly stepping, In her trimly-buckled sandals,
Turns one way, and then another, In the centre of the caldron;
From the bottom lifts the fragment, Turns it in her fingers, musing: ‘What may come of this I know not,
In the virgin hands of Kapo, Snowy virgin of the Northland!’
“Kalevatar took the splinter
Who by unknown force and insight, Rubbed her hands and knees together,
Thus instructed she her creature, Gave the squirrel these directions: ‘Snow-white squirrel, mountain-jewel,
Haste thee whither I would send thee, Into Metsola’s wide limits,
Hasten through the heavy tree-tops, Wisely through the thickest branches,
Thus escape the bird of heaven. Bring me ripe cones from the fir-tree,
Bring them to the hands of Kapo, For the beer of Osmo’s daughter.’
“Quickly hastened forth the squirrel,
Swiftly hopping on its journey From one thicket to another,
From the pine-tree to the willow, From the sorb-tree to the alder,
Crossed the eagle-woods in safety, Into Metsola’s wide limits,
There perceived three magic pine-trees, There perceived three smaller fir-trees,
Was not captured by the eagle, Was not mangled in his talons;
Cut the shoots of pine-tree branches, Hid the cones within his pouches,
Brought them to the hands of Kapo, To the magic virgin’s fingers.
Laid them in the beer for ferment, But it brought no effervescence,
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
Deeply thought and long considered: ‘What will bring the effervescence,
That the beer may foam and sparkle, May ferment and be refreshing?’
“Kalevatar, sparkling maiden,
Softly moving, lightly stepping, In her trimly-buckled sandals,
Turns one way and then another, In the centre of the caldron,
Takes it from its place of resting, Looks upon the chip and muses: ‘What may come of this I know not,
In the hands of magic Kapo, In the virgin’s snow-white fingers.’
“Kalevatar took the birch-chip
Gave it to the white-faced maiden. Kapo, by the aid of magic,
And produced a magic marten, And the marten, golden-breasted;
Gave the marten these directions: ‘Thou, my golden-breasted marten,
Haste thou whither I may send thee, To the bear-dens of the mountain,
Gather yeast upon thy fingers, Gather foam from lips of anger,
Bring it to the hands of Kapo, To the hands of Osmo’s daughter.’
“Then the marten golden-breasted,
Quickly bounding on his journey, Lightly leaping through the distance
Leaping over rocky fissures, To the bear-dens of the mountain,
Where the wild-bears fight each other, Where they pass a dread existence,
In the fastnesses of mountains; From their lips the foam was dripping,
This the marten deftly gathered, Brought it to the maiden, Kapo,
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
Used the beer-foam as a ferment; But it brought no effervescence,
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
‘Who or what will bring the ferment, That my beer may not be lifeless?’
“Kalevatar, magic maiden,
Softly moving, lightly stepping, In her trimly-buckled sandals,
Turns one way and then another, In the centre of the caldron,
Lifts it in her snow-white fingers, Turns it o’er and o’er, and muses: ‘What may come of this I know not,
In the hands of mystic Kapo, In the snowy virgin’s fingers?’
“Kalevatar, sparkling maiden,
Kapo, by the aid of magic, Rubbed the pod upon her knee-cap,
From the pod within her fingers, Kapo thus addressed her birdling: ‘Little bee with honeyed winglets,
Fly thou whither I direct thee, To the islands in the ocean,
Where asleep a maid has fallen, Girdled with a belt of copper;
By her lips are fragrant flowers, Herbs and flowers honey-laden;
Gather honey on thy winglets, From the calyces of flowers,
Bring it to the hands of Kapo, To the hands of Osmo’s daughter.’
“Then the bee, the swift-winged birdling,
On his journey to the islands, O’er the high waves of the ocean;
Journeyed all the next day onward, Till the third day evening brought him
To the water-cliffs and grottoes; Found the maiden sweetly sleeping,
Girdled with a belt of copper, In a nameless meadow, sleeping,
By her side were honeyed grasses, By her lips were fragrant flowers,
Dipped its winglets in the honey, Dipped its fingers in the juices
Brought the honey back to Kapo, To the mystic maiden’s fingers.
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
Kapo mixed the beer and honey, And the wedding-beer fermented;
From the bottom of the vessels, Upward in the tubs of birch-wood,
Till it touched the oaken handles, Overflowing all the caldrons;
Sank away in sand and gravel.
“Time had gone but little distance,
Ere the heroes came in numbers To the foaming beer of Northland,
Ere all others Lemminkainen Drank, and grew intoxicated
On the honey-drink of Kalew.
“Osmotar, the beer-preparer,
Spake these words in saddened accents: ‘Woe is me, my life hard-fated,
Have not brewed the beer in wisdom, Will not live within its vessels,
“From a tree-top sings the redbreast,
‘Do not grieve, thy beer is worthy, Put it into oaken vessels,
Firmly bound with hoops of copper.’
“Thus was brewed the beer of Northland,
This the origin of brewing Beer from Kalew-hops and barley;
Of the ancient beer of Kalew, Said to make the feeble hardy,
Famed to cheer the broken-hearted, Make the aged young and supple,
Make the brave men ever braver, Fill the heart with joy and gladness,
Fill the tongue with ancient legends, Only makes the fool more foolish.”
Heard how beer was first fermented, Heard the origin of brewing,
Many oaken tubs and barrels; Filled but half the largest vessels,
Added also hops abundant; Well she mixed the triple forces
Heated stones for months succeeding, Thus to boil the magic mixture,
Burned the wood of many forests, Emptied all the springs of Pohya;
And the wells gave up their waters, Thus to aid the hostess, Louhi,
From the water, hops, and barley, And from honey of the islands,
For Pohyola’s great carousal And rejoicings at the marriage
To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen, Metal-worker of Wainola.
Fire, upon the promontory, Black smoke rising to the heavens
Fills with clouds the half of Pohya, Fills Karelen’s many hamlets;
This the chorus of the women: “Whence are rising all these smoke-clouds,
Is not like the smoke of camp-fires, Is too large for fires of shepherds!”
Journeyed in the early morning For some water to the fountain,
In the region of Pohyola, These the words the mother uttered: “’Tis the smoke of battle-heroes,
Even Ahti, island-hero,
Also known as Kaukomieli, Looked upon the scene in wonder,
“I would like to see this nearer, Learn the cause of all this trouble,
Whether smoke from heat of battle, Or the bonfires of the shepherds.”
Studied long the rising smoke-clouds; Came not from the heat of battle,
Heard they were the fires of Louhi Brewing beer in Sariola,
Long and oft looked Lemminkainen, Strained in eagerness his vision,
Looked abashed and envy-swollen, Spake these words upon his island: “O beloved, second mother,
Brew thy beer of honey-flavor, Make thy liquors foam and sparkle,
Brew it well for Lemminkainen, For his marriage in Pohyola
Finally the beer was ready,
Stored away in casks and barrels, There to rest awhile in silence,
In the copper-banded vessels, In the magic oaken hogsheads,
Then the hostess of Pohyola Skilfully prepared the dishes,
In the boiling-pans and kettles, Ordered countless loaves of barley,
All the delicacies of Northland, For the feasting of her people,
For the nuptial songs and dances, At the marriage of her daughter
When the loaves were baked and ready,
Time had gone but little distance, Scarce a moment had passed over,
Loudly rapped, and sang, and murmured: “Come, ye heroes, come and take me,
Make you sing the songs of wisdom, That with honor ye may praise me,
Straightway Louhi sought a minstrel,
That the beer might well be lauded, Might be praised in song and honor.
Also brought a pike from ocean, But the salmon had no talent,
Teeth of pike and gills of salmon Were not made for singing legends.
Magic minstrel, beer-enchanter, Thus to praise the drink of heroes,
And a boy was brought for singing; But the boy had little knowledge,
Children’s tongues are filled with questions, Children cannot speak in wisdom,
Stronger grew the beer imprisoned
Locked behind the copper faucets, Boiled, and foamed, and sang, and murmured: “If ye do not bring a singer,
That will sing my praise deserving, I will burst these bands of copper,
Will not serve the best of heroes Till he sings my many virtues.”
Called a trusted maiden-servant, Sent her to invite the people
These the words that Louhi uttered: “O my trusted, truthful maiden,
Call together all my people, Call the heroes to my banquet,
Ask the blind and deaf, and crippled, Ask the young, and ask the aged;
To the highways, and the by-ways, Urge them to my daughter’s wedding;
In my boats upon the waters, In my sledges bring the halting,
Ask the whole of Sariola, Ask the people of Karelen,
Famous bard and wisdom-singer; But I give command explicit
Not the island-dweller, Ahti!” This the question of the servant: “Why not ask wild Lemminkainen,
Louhi gave this simple answer: “Good the reasons that I give thee
Must not have an invitation To my daughter’s feast and marriage:
Lemminkainen fosters trouble, Skilful fighter of the virtues;
He would bring but pain and sorrow, He would jest and jeer at maidens
Cannot ask the evil-minded!” Thus again the servant questions: “Tell me how to know this Ahti,
That I may not ask him hither; Do not know the isle of Ahti,
Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Easy ’tis to know the wizard,
Ahti lives on yonder island, On that point dwells Lemminkainen,
Far at sea his home and dwelling.”
Spread the wedding-invitations To the people of Pohyola,
Asked the friendless, asked the homeless Asked the laborers and shepherds,
Asked the deaf, the dumb, the crippled, Asked the young, and asked the aged,
Did not give an invitation To the reckless Lemminkainen,
Ilmarinen’S Wedding-Feast.
Ancient dame of Sariola, While at work within her dwelling,
Heard the rattle of the sledges; To the northward turned her glances,
And her thoughts ran on as follow: “Who are these in bright apparel,
Are they friends or hostile armies?”
Looked again and well considered, Drew much nearer to examine,
Found that they were friends and suitors. In the midst was Ilmarinen,
When the hostess of Pohyola
She addressed the words that follow: “I had thought the winds were raging,
Thought the pebbles in commotion, Or perchance the ocean roaring;
Drew still nearer and examined, Found the winds were not in battle,
Found the ocean was not roaring, Nor the pebbles in commotion;
With his heroes and attendants, Heroes counted by the hundreds.
“Should you ask of me the question,
Mid the hosts of men and heroes, I should answer, I should tell you: ‘As the hazel-bush in copses,
As the Moon among the planets; Drives the groom a coal-black courser,
Flying like the hungry raven, Graceful as the lark at morning,
Twitter on the birchen cross-bow; There are seven bluebirds singing
Noises hear they in the court-yard,
To the court comes Ilmarinen, With his body-guard of heroes;
Not too far in front of others, Not too far behind his fellows.
“Hie ye hither, men and heroes, Haste, ye watchers, to the stables,
Lower well the racer’s breast-plate, There undo the straps and buckles,
And conduct the suitor hither, Give my son-in-law good welcome!”
Into Louhi’s yard and stables, And descended from his snow-sledge.
“Come, thou servant of my bidding, Best of all my trusted servants,
From the shafts adorned with silver, From the curving arch of willow,
Tie the white-face to the manger, Treat the suitor’s steed with kindness,
By his soft and shining bridle, By his halter tipped with silver;
On the bottoms soft and even, On the borders of the snow-banks,
“Lead the hero’s steed to water,
Where the living streams are flowing, Sweet as milk of human kindness,
Underneath the shade of aspens.
“Feed the courser of the suitor,
On the summer-wheat and clover, In the caldron steeped in sweetness;
In the boxes lined with copper, At my manger richly furnished,
Tie him with a silk-like halter, To the golden rings and staples,
Set in beams of birch and oak-wood; Feed him on the hay the sweetest,
Give the best my barns can furnish.
“Curry well the suitor’s courser
Brush his hair with silken brushes, Put his mane and tail in order,
Blankets wrought in gold and silver, Buckles forged from shining copper.
“Come, ye small lads of the village,
With your auburn locks uncovered, From your hands remove your mittens,
Through the door without his stooping, Lifting not the upper cross-bar,
Moving not the birchen casings, Great the hero who must enter.
“Ilmarinen is too stately,
Not the son-in-law and bridegroom, Till the portals have been heightened;
Than the door-ways of the mansion.”
Tore away the upper cross-bar, That his cap might not be lifted;
That the hero might not stumble; Made the birch-wood portals wider,
Easy entrance for the suitor.
As the bridegroom freely passes Through the doorway of her dwelling: “Thanks are due to thee, O Ukko,
Let me now my halls examine; Make the bridal chambers ready,
Softest furs upon my benches, Birchen flooring scrubbed to whiteness,
Then the hostess of Pohyola
Did not recognize her chambers; Every room had been remodeled,
All the halls were newly burnished, Hedge-hog bones were used for ceilings,
Bones of wolverine for door-sills, For the cross-bars bones of roebuck,
Alder-wood, the window-casings, Scales of trout adorned the windows,
All the seats were made of silver, All the floors of copper-tiling,
On the floor were silken mattings, Every fire-place set in copper,
On each shelf were colored sea-shells, Kalew’s tree was their protection.
Chosen suitor from Wainola, These the words of Ilmarinen: “Send, O Ukko, health and pleasure
To this mansion richly fashioned!” Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Let thy coming be auspicious
To the home of thine affianced, To this dwelling lowly fashioned,
“Come, ye maidens that should serve me,
Bring me fire upon the birch-bark, Light the fagots of the fir-tree,
Chosen suitor of my daughter, Fairy Maiden of the Rainbow,
Whether they are blue or sable, See if they are warm and faithful.”
Brought the fire upon the birch-bark, Brought it on the tips of pine-wood;
Roll and roar about the hero, Blackening the suitor’s visage,
“Bring the fire upon a taper, On the waxen tapers bring it!”
Quickly brought the lighted tapers, Made the suitor’s eyeballs glisten,
Made his eyes of sable color Sparkle like the foam of waters,
Colored as the ocean jewels, Iridescent as the rainbow.
“Come, ye fellows of the hamlets,
To the highest seat at table, To the seat of greatest honor,
Looking on my bounteous tables, Facing all the guests of Northland.”
Served her guests in great abundance, Richest drinks and rarest viands,
On his platters, honeyed biscuit, And the sweetest river salmon,
All the dainties of Pohyola. Then the helpers served the others,
With the varied food of Northland. Spake the hostess of Pohyola: “Come, ye maidens from the village,
In the urns with double handles, To the many guests in-gathered,
Thereupon the merry maidens
From the copper-banded vessels, For the wedding-guests assembled;
On the beard of Ilmarinen, On the beards of many heroes.
Of the wondrous beer of barley, Spake the beer in merry accents
Through the tongue of many a hero, Through the tongue of Wainamoinen,
Of the Northland bards and minstrels, These the words of the enchanter: “O thou beer of honeyed flavor,
Let some hero sing thy praises, Sing thy worth in golden measures;
Let the bridegroom sound thy virtues! Have our songs thus quickly vanished,
Evil then has been the brewing, Then the beer must be unworthy,
Does not move the merry minstrel, That the golden guests are joyless,
Never will these benches echo Till the bench-guests chant thy virtues;
Till the floor-guests sing in concord; Nor the windows join the chorus
All the tables will keep silence Till the heroes toast thy virtues;
Till the chimney-guests have chanted.”
Thus the little boy made answer: “I am small and young in singing,
Be that as it may, my seniors, Since the elder minstrels sing not,
Nor the hostess lead the singing, I will sing my simple stories,
To the pleasure of the evening, To the joy of the invited.”
And the gray-beard thus made answer: “Not the time for children’s singing,
Children’s songs are filled with trifles, Filled with shrewd and vain deceptions,
Leave the songs and incantations To the ancient wizard-singers;
To the minstrel of Wainola, To the hero of the Northland,
Thereupon Osmoinen answered: “Are there not some sweeter singers
That will clasp their hands together, Sing the ancient songs unbroken,
Make these ancient halls re-echo For the pleasure of the evening,
From the hearth-stone spake, the gray-beard “Not a singer of Pohyola,
That was better skilled in chanting Legends of the days departed,
In my years of vain ambition; Then I chanted tales of heroes,
Sang the ballads of my people, In the vales and on the mountains,
Sweet my voice and skilled my singing, All my songs were highly lauded,
Easy-flowing like the waters, Easy-gliding as the snow-shoes,
“Woe is me, my days are ended,
All its sweetness gone to others, Flows no more like rippling waters,
Now my songs are full of discord, Like the rake upon the stubble,
Like the boat upon the sea-shore!”
Spake these words in magic measures: “Since no other bard appeareth
I will sing some simple legends, Sing my garnered store of wisdom,
With my tales of ancient story, Since a bard I was created,
Do not ask the ways of others, Follow not the paths of strangers.”
Song’s eternal, wise supporter, Then began the songs of pleasure,
Filled the rooms with wondrous singing; Sang the ancient bard-magician
Did not fail in voice nor legends, All the wisest thoughts remembered.
Sang the joy of all assembled, To the pleasure of the evening,
To the happiness of heroes; All the guests were stilled in wonder
At the songs of the magician.
When his wonder-tales had ended: “l have little worth or power,
Little consequence my singing, Mine abilities as nothing,
Should intone his wisdom-sayings, Sing the source of good and evil,
Sing the legends of omniscience, Sing his songs in full perfection.
Sing the sands to ruddy berries, Sing the pebbles into barley,
Sing to salt the rocks of ocean, Into corn-fields sing the forests,
Sing to bread the hills and mountains, Sing to eggs the rounded sandstones;
He could turn the keys of nature, And produce within thy pastures,
Stables filled with fleet-foot stallions, Kine in every field and fallow;
For the bride a coat of ermine, For the hostess, shoes of silver,
“Grant O Ukko, my Creator,
Grant thy blessing on our feasting, Bless this company assembled,
For the happiness of Northland! May this bread and beer bring joyance,
May they carry full contentment To the people of Pohyola,
May the hours we spend in singing, In the morning, in the evening,
Hear us in our supplications, Grant to us thy needed blessings,
To the people here assembled, To the host and to the hostess,
To the sons upon the waters, To the daughters at their weavings,
To the shepherds in the fenlands, That our lives may end in honor,
Ilmarinen’s magic marriage To the Maiden of the Rainbow,
The Bride’S Farewell.
When the many guests had feasted, At the wedding of the Northland,
Spake the hostess of Pohyola To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen: “Wherefore, bridegroom, dost thou linger,
Sittest for the father’s pleasure, For affection of the mother,
For the beauty of the daughter? Noble son-in-law and brother,
Long already for the virgin, Thine affianced is not ready,
Only are her tresses braided.
“Chosen bridegroom, pride of Pohya,
Long already for the virgin, Thy beloved is preparing,
“Famous artist, Ilmarinen,
Long already for the virgin, Thy beloved is not ready,
Spake again the ancient Louhi: “Chosen suitor of my daughter,
Wait no longer for the virgin, Thy beloved now is ready,
Fairy Maiden of the Rainbow.
“Beauteous daughter, join thy suitor,
Very near is the uniting, Near indeed thy separation.
Near the door he waits to lead thee, Guide thee to his home and kindred;
Restless champs his silver bridle, And the sledge awaits thy presence.
“Thou wert anxious for a suitor,
Wert in haste to take his jewels, Place his rings upon thy fingers;
To his sledge, with happy footsteps, Hie in haste to join the bridegroom,
With thy chosen life-companion, With thy suitor, Ilmarinen.
Hast not raised thine eyes above thee, Beauteous maiden of the Northland.
Full of wailing thine engagement, And thy marriage full of sorrow,
Thou art leaving now forever, Leaving also friends and kindred,
“O how beautiful thy childhood,
Nurtured like a tender flower, Like the strawberry in spring-time;
Warm thy fires and rich thy table; From the fields came corn in plenty,
Wheat and barley in abundance, Fish, and fowl, and hare, and bacon,
“Never wert thou, child, in sorrow,
All thy cares were left to fir-trees, All thy worry to the copses,
All thy sighing to the lindens, All thy thinking to the aspens
Light and airy as the leaflet, As a butterfly in summer,
Beautiful as vernal flowers.
“Now thou leavest home and kindred,
Goest to another mother, Other sisters, other brothers,
To the servant-folk of strangers, From thy native hills and lowlands.
Happier thy mother’s hearth-stone; Other horns will there be sounded,
Other hinges there be creaking; There the doors thou canst not enter
Canst not tend the fires and ovens As will please the minds of strangers.
“Didst thou think, my fairest maiden,
Couldst return, if thou shouldst wish it, To thy father’s court and dwelling?
Wilt thou leave thy mother’s chambers, Leave thy sisters and thy brothers,
Long the time the wife must wander, Many months and years must wander,
Even though the mother liveth. Great, indeed, must be the changes
Changed, thy friends and nearest kindred, Changed, thy father’s ancient dwellings,
Other birds will sing thy praises!”
Then the daughter spake, departing: “In my early days of childhood
‘Art a virgin, yet no virgin, Guided by an aged mother,
In the mansion of a father! Only wilt become a virgin,
Only when thou wedst a hero, One foot on the father’s threshold,
That will speed thee and thy husband To his native vales and highlands!’
“I have wished thus many summers,
Hoped for this as for the flowers, Welcome as the birds of spring-time.
Very near is my departure, One foot on my father’s threshold,
With my husband to his people; Cannot understand the reason
Cannot leave thee now with gladness, Cannot go with great rejoicing
Where as maiden I have lingered, From the courts where I was nurtured,
From my faithful mother’s counsel. Now I go, a maid of sorrow,
Like the bride of Night in winter, Like the ice upon the rivers.
“Such is not the mind of others,
Others do not leave unhappy, Have no tears, nor cares, nor sorrows,
Carry to my grave great sadness, Heart as dark as Death’s black river.
“Such the feelings of the happy,
Like the early dawn of spring-time, Like the rising Sun in summer;
With my young heart filled with terror; Happiness is not my portion,
Like the dark rift of the storm-cloud, Like the cheerless nights of winter!
Dreary too the autumn evening, Still more dreary is my future!”
Ever guarding home and kindred, Spake these words of doubtful comfort: “Dost thou, beauteous bride, remember,
These the words that I have taught thee: ‘Look not joyfully for suitors,
Look not in the eyes of charmers, At their feet let fall thy vision.
He that hath an eye for beauty, Offers little that will comfort;
In his mouth dwells dire Tuoni.’
“Thus, fair bride, did I advise thee,
Should there come the best of suitors, Noblest wooers, proudest lovers,
Let thine answer be as follows: ‘Never will I think it wisdom,
To become a second daughter, Linger with my husband’s mother;
Never wander forth to bondage, At the bidding of a bridegroom:
Wife and slave to any hero, Never will I be submissive
“Fairest bride, thou didst not heed me,
Didst not listen to my counsel; Wittingly thy feet have wandered
Hastened to thy suitor’s snow-sledge, To the bear-dens of thy husband,
Carried to his native country, To the bondage of his people,
Thou hast left thy mother’s dwelling, To the schooling of the master;
Little else than constant torture; Ready for thee are his bridles,
Were not forged for any other; Soon, indeed, thou’lt feel the hardness,
Feel thy second father’s censure, And his wife’s inhuman treatment,
Quail before thy haughty sister.
“Listen, bride, to what I tell thee:
Wert thy father’s pride and pleasure, ‘Moonlight,’ did thy father call thee,
‘Sea-foam’ did thy brother call thee, And thy sister called thee ‘Flower.’
Goest to a second mother, Often she will give thee censure,

Rarely will she give thee counsel, Never will she sound thy praises. ‘Brush-wood,’ will the father call thee, ‘Sledge of Rags,’ thy husband’s mother, ‘Flight of Stairs,’ thy stranger brother, ‘Scare-crow,’ will the sister call thee,
Then wilt think of my good counsels, Then wilt wish in tears and murmurs,
That as smoke thy soul had risen, That as sparks thy life had vanished.
From thy nest to circle homeward, Canst not fall and die like leaflets,
Like the smoke thou canst not vanish.
“Youthful bride, and darling sister,
Hast exchanged thy loving father, Thou hast left thy faithful mother
Hast exchanged thy loving brother, Hast renounced thy gentle sister,
Hast exchanged thy snow-white covers For the rocky couch of sorrow;
For the waters of Wainola; Hast renounced these sandy sea-shores
Northland glens thou hast forsaken For thy husband’s barren meadows;
For the stubble-fields and deserts.
“Thou, O maiden, hast been thinking
Neither work, nor care, nor sorrow, From this night would be thy portion,
Not to sleep art thou conducted, Not to happiness, nor joyance,
And thy day-attendant, trouble; Often thou wilt drink of sorrow,
“When at home thou hadst no head-gear,
When thy couch was not of linen, No unhappiness came nigh thee;
Linen breeds bad dispositions, Linen brings but deeps of anguish,
“Happy in her home, the maiden,
Like the master in his mansion, Happy with her bows and arrows. ’Tis not thus with married women;
To the prisoners of Moskva, Held in bondage by their masters.
“As a wife, must weep and labor,
When the next hour passes over, Thou must tend the fire and oven,
Must direct thy master’s servants. When thine evening meal is ready,
In the brain of perch and salmon, In the mouths of ocean whiting,
Canst not learn it from thy mother, Mother dear of seven daughters;
Where were born the human instincts, Where were born the minds of heroes,
Whence the beauty of her tresses, Why all life revives in spring-time.
“Weep, O weep, my pretty young bride.
Weep great rivers from thine eyelids, Floods of tears in field and fallow,
Weep thy rooms to overflowing, Shed thy tears in great abundance,
To thy native hills and valleys, When thou visitest thy father
On his arm a withered tassel.
“Weep, O weep, my lovely maiden,
Weep great rivers from thine eyelids; If thou dost not weep sincerely,
To thy Northland home and kindred, When thou visitest thy mother
In her arms a barley-bundle.
“Weep, O weep, sweet bride of beauty,
If thou dost not weep in earnest, Thou wilt weep on thy returning
When thou visitest thy brother Lying wounded by the way-side,
“Weep, O weep, my sister’s daughter,
If thou dost not weep sufficient, Thou wilt weep on thy returning
When thou visitest thy sister Lying, prostrate in the meadow,
When the ancient maid had ended,
Straightway fell to bitter weeping, Spake these words in deeps of sorrow: “O, ye sisters, my beloved,
Playmates of my early summers, Listen to your sister’s counsel:
Why my mind is so dejected, Why this weariness and sadness,
Cannot understand the meaning Of this mighty weight of sorrow!
I had hoped for greater pleasures, I had hoped to sing as cuckoos,
When I had attained this station, Reached at last the goal expectant;
Singing, merry on the hill-tops; I am like the songless blue-duck,
Swims upon the cold, cold ocean, Icicles upon her pinions.
“Ancient father, gray-haired mother,
Whither take this bride, thy daughter, That this sorrow may pass over,
Where this grief may turn to gladness? Better it had been, O mother,
Hadst thou clothed the colored sandstone, Rather than this hapless maiden,
For this keen and killing trouble.
“Many sympathizers tell me: ‘Foolish bride, thou art ungrateful,
Thou hast little cause for weeping.’
“O, deceive me not, my people,
For alas! I have more troubles Than the waterfalls have pebbles,
Than the Suomi-hills have berries; Never could the Pohya plow-horse
Shaking not his birchen cross-bar, Breaking not his heavy collar;
Heavy shod and stoutly harnessed, Draw this load of care and trouble.”
And the young child spake as follows: “Why, O fair bride, art thou weeping,
Leave thy troubles to the elk-herds, And thy grief to sable fillies,
Bear the burden of thine anguish, Horses have much larger foreheads,
And their necks are made for labor, Stronger are their bones and muscles,
There is little good in weeping, Useless are thy tears of sorrow;
Nor to banks of little rivers; Thou art led to fields of flowers,
Led away from beer of Pohya To the sweeter mead of Kalew.
On thy right side, Ilmarinen, Constant friend and life-protector,
Husband ready, steed in waiting, Gold-and-silver-mounted harness,
On the courser’s yoke and cross-bar; Thrushes also sing and twitter
Seven bluebirds, seven cuckoos, Sing thy wedding-march in concord.
“Be no longer full of sorrow,
Thou hast found a noble husband, Better wilt thou fare than ever,
Artist husband, metal-master, Bread-provider of thy table,
On the breast of the elk-hunter, By the side of the bear-killer.
Hast obtained a mighty hero; Never idle is his cross-bow,
Neither are his dogs in kennel, Active agents is his hunting.
In the early hours of morning He arises from his fare-couch,
Thrice within the sowing season, On his eyes the deer has fallen,
And his locks been combed by fir-boughs. Hasten homeward with thy husband,
Where his forests sing thy welcome.
“Ilmarinen there possesses
All the beasts that haunt the woodlands, All that feed upon the mountains,
Sheep and cattle by the thousands; Sweet the grass upon his meadows,
In the lowlands corn abundant, Wheat upon the elm-wood fallows,
Waving grain on many acres, On his mountains gold and silver,
Highlands filled with magic metals, Chests of jewels in his store-house,
Osmotar the Bride-Adviser.
Who will teach the Maid of Beauty, Who instruct the Rainbow-daughter?
Kalew’s fair and lovely virgin, Osmotar will give instructions
To the orphaned bride of Pohya, Teach her how to live in pleasure,
Win her second mother’s praises, Joyful in her husband’s dwelling.
Thus the anxious bride addresses: “Maid of Beauty, lovely sister,
Hear thou what thy sister teaches, Listen to her sage instructions:
Wander far away, my flower, Travel on enwrapped in colors,
From this house renowned and ancient, From thy father’s halls and court-yards
Hasten to his mother’s household; Strange, the rooms in other dwellings,
“Full of thought must be thy going,
Quite unlike thy home in Northland, On the meadows of thy father,
Singing through thy mother’s fenlands, Culling daisies with thy sister.
“When thou goest from thy father
Only three things leave behind thee: Leave thy day-dreams to thy sister,
To thy brother leave thy labors, Take all else that thou desirest.
Cast thy sighing to the pine-trees, And thy maidenhood to zephyrs,
Cast thy trinkets to the children, And thy leisure to the gray-beards,
Let them take them to the woodlands, Bury them beneath the mountain.
“Thou must hence acquire new habits,
Mother-love must be forsaken, Thou must love thy husband’s mother,
Kind words only must thou utter.
“Thou must hence acquire new habits,
Father-love must be forsaken, Thou must love thy husband’s father,
Kind words only must thou utter.
“Thou must hence acquire new habits,
Brother-love must be forsaken, Thou must love thy husband’s brother,
Kind words only must thou utter.
“Thou must hence acquire new habits
Sister-love must be forsaken, Thou must love thy husband’s sister,
Kind words only must thou utter.
“Never in the course of ages,
Wickedly approach thy household, Nor unworthily, thy servants,
Let thy dwellings sing good manners, And thy walls re-echo virtue.
And the best of men seek honor, Seek for honesty and wisdom;
If thine inmates fail in virtue, Then thy gray-beards would be black-dogs
All thy women would be witches, Wicked witches in thy chambers,
Crawling through thy husband’s mansion; All thy sisters would be famous
“Equal honors must be given
Lower must thy head be bended, Than within thy mother’s dwelling,
When thou didst thy kindred honor. Ever strive to give good counsel,
Bear a head upon thy shoulders Filled with wise and ancient sayings;
To behold the silver sunrise, Sharpen well thine ears at evening,
When he makes his second calling, Straightway thou must rise from slumber,
Should the rooster fail to call thee, Let the moonbeams touch thine eyelids,
Often go thou and consult them, Call upon the Moon for counsel,
From the stars divine thy future; When the Great Bear faces southward,
This is time to break with slumber, Seek for fire within the ashes,
Blow the fire through all the fuel. If no spark is in the ashes,
Speak these words to him on waking: ‘Give me fire, O my beloved,
Strike a little fire from flintstone, Let it fall upon my tinder.’
“From the spark, O Bride of Beauty,
In the holder, place the torch-light, Find thy pathway to the stables,
If thy husband’s cows be lowing, If thy brother’s steeds be neighing,
And the steeds for thee are calling, Hasten, stooping through the hurdles,
Feed thy husband’s cows with pleasure, Feed with care the gentle lambkins,
Hay, and barley, to the horses, Feed the calves of lowing mothers,
“Never rest upon the haymow,
When the kine are fed and tended, When the flocks have all been watered;
Like the snow-flakes to thy dwelling, There a crying babe awaits thee,
Cannot speak and tell his troubles, Speechless babe, and weeping infant,
Whether pain or cold distresses, Greets with joy his mother’s footsteps.
To thy husband’s rooms and presence, Early visit thou his chambers,
On thine arm a broom of birch-wood, In thy teeth a lighted taper,
Sweep thou then thy hero’s dwelling, Dust his benches and his tables,
“If the baby of thy sister
Show the little child attention, Bathe his eyes and smoothe his ringlets,
Shouldst thou have no bread of barley, In his hand adjust some trinket.
“Lastly, when the week has ended,
Benches, tables, walls, and ceilings; What of dust is on the windows,
All thy rooms must first be sprinkled, That the dust may not be scattered,
Sweep the dust from every crevice, Leave thou not a single atom;
Do not then forget the rafters, Lest thy home should seem untidy,
“Hear, O maiden, what I tell thee,
Never dress in scanty raiment, Let thy robes be plain and comely,
On thy feet wear tidy fur-shoes, For the glory of thy husband,
Tend thou well the sacred sorb-tree, Guard the mountain-ashes planted
Beautiful the mountain-ashes, Beautiful their leaves and flowers,
Thus the exiled one demonstrates That she lives to please her husband,
“Like the mouse, have ears for hearing,
Bend thy neck and turn thy visage Like the juniper and aspen,
Thus to guard thy feet from stumbling, That thou mayest walk in safety.
“When thy brother comes from plowing,
And thy husband from the woodlands, From his chopping, thy beloved,
Give to each a linen-towel, Speak to each some pleasant greeting.
“When thy second mother hastens
In her hand a corn-meal measure, Haste thou to the court to meet her,
Take the measure from her fingers, Happy, bear it to thy husband.
“If thou shouldst not see distinctly
Ask at once thy hero’s mother: ‘Second mother, my beloved,
By thy willing second daughter, Tell me how to best perform it.’
“This should be the mother’s answer: ‘This the manner of thy workings,
Stamp with diligence and courage, Grind with will and great endurance,
Fill the barley-pans with water, Knead with strength the dough for baking,
That thy ovens may be heated, Bake in love the honey-biscuit,
Rinse to cleanliness thy platters, Polish well thy drinking-vessels.
“If thou hearest from the mother,
That the cask for meal is empty, Take the barley from the garners,
When thou grindest in the chambers, Do not sing in glee and joyance,
To the mill give up thy singing, Let the side-holes furnish music;
Do not groan as if in trouble, Lest the father think thee weary,
That thy groans mean discontentment, That thy sighing means displeasure.
Take it to the casks in buckets, Bake thy hero’s bread with pleasure,
That thy biscuits may be worthy, That the dough be light and airy.
“Shouldst thou see a bucket empty,
On thine arm a silver-dipper, Hasten off to fill with water
Gracefully thy bucket carry, Bear it firmly by the handles,
Hasten like the air of autumn; Do not tarry near the streamlet,
That the father may not fancy, Nor the ancient dame imagine,
Hast admired thy form and features, Hast admired thy grace and beauty
In the crystal streamlet’s eddies.
“Shouldst thou journey to the woodlands,
Do not go with noise and bustle, Gather all thy sticks in silence,
That the father may not fancy, And the mother not imagine,
And thy noise from discontentment.
“If thou goest to the store-house
Do not tarry on thy journey, On the threshold do not linger,
And the mother not imagine, That the meal thou hast divided
“If thou goest to the river,
There to cleanse thy pans and buckets, Lest thy work be done in neatness,
Rinse thy pitchers to perfection, Spoons, and forks, and knives, and goblets,
Closely watch the food-utensils, That the dogs may not deface them,
That the eagles may not steal them, That the children may not break them;
Many little heads and fingers, That will need thy careful watching,
“When thou goest to thy bathing,
In the bath-room clean and smokeless; Do not, linger in the water,
That the father may not fancy, And the mother not imagine,
Rolling in the laps of comfort.
“From thy bath, when thou returnest,
Speak to him the words that follow: ‘Father of my hero-husband,
Everything in perfect order; Go and bathe for thine enjoyment,
I will lend thee needed service.’
“When the time has come for spinning,
Do not ask the help of others, Look not in the stream for knowledge,
Nor the spindle from the sisters, Nor the weaving-comb from strangers.
With thine own hand ply the shuttle, Loosely wind the skeins of wool-yarn,
Wind them deftly in the shuttle; Fit the warp upon the rollers,
Swiftly ply the weaver’s shuttle, Weave good cloth for all thy vestments,
From the finest wool of lambkins, One thread only in thy weaving.
“Hear thou what I now advise thee:
From the barley’s new-grown kernels, Brew it with the magic virtues,
Do not stir it with the birch-rod, Stir it with thy skilful fingers;
Do not let the seed bring evil, Keep the dogs outside the brew-house,
Nor the wild-beasts of the mountains, When thou goest to thy brewing,
“Should some stranger come to see thee,
Ever does the worthy household Have provisions for the stranger,
Ample for the dinner-table; Seat the stranger in thy dwelling,
Entertain the guest with kindness, While his dinner is preparing.
When his farewell has been spoken, Lead him only to the portals,
That thy husband may not fancy, And the mother not imagine,
“Shouldst thou ever make a journey
There to gain some needed object, While thou speakest in the hamlet,
That thou shamest not thy kindred, Nor disgrace thy husband’s household.
“Village-maidens oft will ask thee,
‘Does thy husband’s mother greet thee As in childhood thou wert greeted,
Do not answer in negation, Say that she has always given
Given thee the kindest greetings, Though it be but once a season.
“Listen well to what I tell thee:
To thy husband’s distant dwelling, Thou must not forget thy mother,
Her that nurtured thee in childhood, Many sleepless nights she nursed thee;
Numberless the times she rocked thee; Tender, true, and ever faithful,
She that can forget her mother, Can neglect the one that nursed her,
In the kingdom of Tuoni; In Manala she would suffer,
Should her mother be forgotten; Should her dear one be neglected,
And Tuoni’s sons revile her, They will ask her much as follows: ‘How couldst thou forget thy mother,
Great the pain thy mother suffered, Great the trouble that thou gavest
Into life for good or evil, When she gave thee earth-existence,
When she fed thee in thy childhood, When she taught thee what thou knowest,
Since thy mother is forgotten!’”
Near the fire a beggar-woman, One that knew the ways of people,
“Thus the crow calls in the winter: ‘Would that I could be a singer,
But, alas! my songs are worthless, Cannot charm the weakest creature;
Leave the songs to the musicians, Those that live in golden houses,
Homeless therefore I must wander, Like a beggar in the corn-fields,
