“Hear now, sister, what I tell thee,
Follow not his mind, nor fancies, As my husband’s mind I followed;
Sprouting like a rose in spring-time, Growing like a slender maiden,
Like the playmates of my childhood, Like the goslings of my father,
Like my brother’s water-younglings, Like the bullfinch of my sister;
Like the berry of the meadow, Played upon the sandy sea-shore,
Sang all day adown the valley, Thrilled with song the hill and mountain,
Lived and frolicked in the woodlands.
“Into traps are foxes driven
Into traps, the cunning ermine; Thus are maidens wooed and wedded,
Thus created is the virgin, Thus intended is the daughter,
Subject also to his mother.
“Then to other fields I hastened,
Like a cranberry for roasting, Like a strawberry for dinner;
All the aspens tried to cut me, All the willows tried to seize me,
Thus I journeyed to my husband, Thus I travelled to his dwelling,
Then there were, as was reported, Six compartments built of pine-wood,
And the mansion filled with garrets, Studding all the forest border,
Streamlets bordered fields of barley, Filled with wheat and corn, the islands,
Rye unthrashed in great abundance, Countless sums of gold and silver,
When my journey I had ended, When my hand at last was given,
Seven poles as rails for fencing. Filled with anger were the bushes,
All the walks were lined with trouble, Evil-tempered were the forests,
Hundred others of unkindness. Did not let this bring me sorrow,
Long I hoped to find some favor, Strove most earnestly for kindness;
There I tried some chips to gather, Knocked my head against the portals
“At the door were eyes of strangers,
Green with envy in his cabin, Evil heroes in the back-ground,
From each tongue the sparks out-flying, Flying from my second father,
Did not let this bring me trouble, Tried to live in peace and pleasure,
In humility I suffered, Skipped about with feet of rabbit,
Late I laid my head to slumber, Early rose as if a servant,
Could not merit love nor honor, Though I had dislodged the mountains,
“Then I turned the heavy millstone,
Ground the barley-grains in patience, That the mother might be nourished,
What might please her taste and fancy, From her gold-enamelled platters,
“As for me, the hapless daughter,
On the table near the oven, Ate I from the birchen ladle;
Gathered in the lowland meadows, Baked them into loaves for eating;
Thirsty, sipped it from the dipper, Ate of fish the worst in Northland,
Rocking in my boat of birch-bark; Never ate I fish or biscuit
“Blades I gathered in the summers,
Like the laborers of heroes, Like the servants sold in bondage.
Evermore to me was given Flail the heaviest and longest,
On the shore the strongest beater, And the largest rake in haying;
No one thought that I could suffer, Though the best of heroes faltered,
“Thus did I, a youthful housewife,
Drenched myself in perspiration, Hoped for better times to follow;
Knowing neither rest nor pleasure. I was blamed by all the household,
Now about my awkward manners, Now about my reputation,
Words unkind were heaped upon me, Fell like hail on me unhappy,
Like the heavy hail of spring-time. I did not despair entirely,
Underneath the tongue of malice, But the old-one spoiled my temper,
Then my husband grew a wild-bear, Grew a savage wolf of Hisi.
“Only then I turned to weeping,
Thought of all my former pleasures Of the happy days of childhood,
Of my mother’s peaceful cottage, Then began I thus to murmur: ‘Well thou knowest, ancient mother,
How to train thy tender shootlet; Did not know where to ingraft it,
In the very worst of places, On an unproductive hillock,
Where it could not grow and flourish, There to waste its life, in weeping,
Worthier had been my conduct, In the regions that are better,
In compartments that are larger, Living with a loving husband,
Shoe of birch-bark was my suitor, Shoe of Laplanders, my husband;
Voice and visage like the jackdaw, Mouth and claws were from the black-wolf,
Had I known that mine affianced Was a fount of pain and evil,
Been a pine-tree on the highway, Been a linden on the border,
Grown a beard of ugly bristles, Head of loam and eyes of lightning,
For my limbs the trunks of aspens.’
“This the manner of my singing
Thus I sang my cares and murmurs Thus my hero near the portals
Then he hastened to my chamber; Straightway knew I by his footsteps,
Knew it by his steps implanted; All the winds were still in slumber,
Fluttered round his head in fury, While his horrid mouth stood open;
In one hand a branch of willow, In the other, club of alder;
Aimed the cudgel at my forehead.
“When the evening had descended,
Took he in his hand a whip-stalk, With a whip-lash made of deer-skin,
Only made for me unhappy.
“When at last I begged for mercy,
By his side I courted slumber, Merciless, my husband seized me,
Beat me with the whip of torture, Deer-skin-lash and stalk of birch-wood.
In the coldest night of winter, But the husband fleetly followed,
Grasped me by my streaming tresses, Tore my ringlets from my forehead,
To the freezing winds of winter. What the aid that I could ask for,
Made I shoes of magic metals, Made the straps of steel and copper,
Long I listened at the portals, Hoping he would end his ravings,
But he did not seek for resting, Did not wish to still his fury.
As an outcast from his cabin, I was forced to walk and wander,
This the substance of my thinking: ‘I will not endure this torture,
Will not bear this cruel treatment, Such contempt I will not suffer
In this nest of evil Piru.’
“Then I said, ‘Farewell forever!’
To my much-loved home and husband; Started forth upon a journey
Over swamps and over snow-fields, Wandered over towering mountains,
To my brother’s welcome meadows, To my sister’s home and birthplace.
“There were rustling withered pine-trees,
Countless ravens there were cawing, All the jackdaws harshly singing,
‘Thou hast here a home no longer, This is not the happy homestead
“Heeding not this woodland chorus,
Of my childhood’s friend and brother, Where the portals spake in concord,
This their saddened song and echo: ‘Wherefore dost thou journey hither,
To thy father’s old dominions? Here unhappiness awaits thee,
Dead and gone to visit Ukko, Dead and gone thy faithful mother,
While his wife is chill and heartless!’
“Heeding not these many warnings,
Were my weary feet directed, Laid my hand upon the door-latch
But the latch was cold and lifeless. When I wandered to the chamber,
There I saw the heartless hostess, But she did not give me greeting,
Proud, alas! was I unhappy, Did not make the first advances,
And my hand I did not proffer; Laid my hand upon the oven,
On the coal I laid my fingers, All the latent heat had left it.
Lay outstretched before the fire-place, Heaps of soot upon his shoulders,
Thus the brother asked the stranger, Questioned thus his guest politely: ‘Tell me what thy name and station,
“This the answer that I gave him: ‘Hast thou then forgot thy sister,
Not recall his mother’s daughter? We are children of one mother,
In one nest were hatched and nurtured.’”
“Then the brother fell to weeping,
To his wife the brother whispered, Whispered thus unto the housewife: ‘Bring thou beer to give my sister,
“Full of envy, brought the sister
Water for the infant’s eyelids, Soap and water from the bath-room.
“To his wife the brother whispered,
‘Bring thou salmon for my sister, For my sister so long absent,
“Thereupon the wife obeying,
That the children had been eating, And the house-dogs had been licking,
“Then I left my brother’s dwelling,
To my mother’s home deserted; Onward, onward did I wander,
Dragged my body on in anguish, To the cottage-doors of strangers,
For the care of the neglected, For the needy of the village,
“There are many wicked people,
Many women evil-minded, That malign their sex through envy.
That belie the best of maidens, Prove the innocent are guilty
Speak aloud in tones unceasing, Speak, alas! with wicked motives,
Through the tongues of self-pollution. Very few, indeed, the people
That will bid the stranger welcome; Very few to treat her kindly,
Few to offer her a shelter From the chilling storms of winter,
Coats of ice her only raiment!
“Never in my days of childhood,
Never would believe the story, Though a hundred tongues had told it,
That such evil things could happen, That such misery could follow,
Who has tried to do her duty, Who has tried to live uprightly,
Thus the young bride was instructed,
Thus by Osmotar, the teacher.
The Bride’S Farewell.
Gives the wedding-guests this counsel, Speaks these measures to the bridegroom: “Ilmarinen, artist-brother,
Of my mother’s sons the dearest, Gentlest, truest, bravest, grandest,
Of the Maiden of the Rainbow, Of thy beauteous life-companion:
Praise forever thy good fortune; If thou praisest, praise sincerely,
Good the bride that Ukko gives thee, Graciously has God bestowed her.
Praise her virtues to thy mother, Let thy heart rejoice in secret,
Lovely Maiden of the Rainbow!
“Brilliant near thee stands the maiden,
Happy under thy protection, Beautiful as golden moonlight,
Strong to do thy kindly bidding, Labor with thee as thou wishest,
Keep thy home in full perfection, Spin for thee the finest linen,
Make for thee the softest raiment, Make thy weaver’s loom as merry
Make the shuttle glide in beauty Like the ermine of the woodlands;
As the squirrel spins the acorn; Village-maidens will not slumber
While she plies the graceful shuttle.
“Bridegroom of the Bride of Beauty,
Forge thyself a scythe for mowing, Furnish it with oaken handle,
Hammer it upon thine anvil, Have it ready for the summer,
Take thy bride then to the lowlands, Mow the grass upon thy meadows,
Make the reeds and grasses rustle, Toss the fragrant heads of clover,
When the silver sun is shining.
“When the time has come for weaving,
Give to her the spools and shuttles, Let the willing loom be worthy,
Give to her what may be needed, That the weaver’s song may echo,
May be heard within the village, That the aged may remark it,
‘Who is she that now is weaving, What new power now plies the shuttle?’ “Make this answer to the question: ‘It is my beloved weaving,
“Shall the weaver’s weft be loosened,
Do not let the weft be loosened, Nor the weaver’s loom be tightened;
Of the Moon beyond the cloudlets; Such the spinning of the maidens
Of the daughters of the Great Bear, Of the daughters of the Evening.
“Bridegroom, thou beloved hero,
When thou goest on a journey, When thou drivest on the highway,
Fairest bride of Sariola, Do not lead her as a titmouse,
Into unfrequented places, Into copses of the borders,
Into unproductive marshes; Let her wander not, nor stumble
Never in her father’s dwelling, Never in her mother’s court-yard,
Stumbled hard against the fences, Run through brier-fields, nor brambles,
“Magic bridegroom of Wainola,
Never let thy young wife suffer, Never let her be neglected,
Never leave her unattended. Never in her father’s mansion,
Has she sat alone in darkness, Has she suffered for attention;
Sat and rocked, in peace and plenty, Evenings for her father’s pleasure,
Never mayest thou, O bridegroom, Lead the Maiden of the Rainbow
There to grind the bark for cooking, There to bake her bread from stubble,
Never in her father’s dwelling, Never in her mother’s mansion,
There to bake her bread from sea-grass. Thou shouldst lead the Bride of Beauty
There to draw the till of barley, Grind the flour and knead for baking,
Wheaten flour for honey-biscuits.
“Hero-bridegroom of Wainola,
To regret her day of marriage; Never make her shed a tear-drop,
Should there ever come an evening When thy wife shall feel unhappy,
Hitch the fleet-foot to the snow-sledge, Take her to her father’s dwelling,
Never in thy hero-lifetime, Never while the moonbeams glimmer,
Never treat her as thy servant; Do not bar her from the cellar,
Never in her father’s mansion, Never by her faithful mother
“Honored bridegroom of the Northland,
If thou treatest well thy young wife, Worthily wilt thou be treated;
When thou visitest her father, Thou shalt meet a cordial welcome.
“Censure not the Bride of Beauty,
Never say in tones reproachful, She was born in lowly station,
Honored are thy bride’s relations, From an old-time tribe, her kindred;
Each one’s portion was a kernel; When they sowed a cask of flax-seed,
Never, never, magic husband, Treat thy beauty-bride unkindly,
Strike her not with thongs of leather; Never has she wept in anguish
Stand before her like a rampart, Be to her a strong protection,
Let thy father not upbraid her, Never let thy guests offend her;
They may need the master’s censure; Do not harm the Bride of Beauty,
Three long years hast thou been wooing, Hoping every mouth to win her.
“Counsel with the bride of heaven,
Kindly teach thy bride in secret, In the long and dreary evenings,
Teach one year, in words of kindness, Teach with eyes of love a second,
If she should not heed thy teaching, Should not hear thy kindly counsel
Cut a reed upon the lowlands, Cut a nettle from the border,
In the fourth year, if she heed not, Threaten her with sterner treatment,
Use not yet the thongs of leather, Do not touch her with the birch-whip.
Should she pay thee no attention, Cut a rod upon the mountains,
Hide it underneath thy mantle, That the stranger may not see it,
Shame her thus to do her duty, Strike not yet, though disobeying.
Still refuse to heed thy wishes, Then instruct her with the willow,
In the closet of thy dwelling, In the attic of thy mansion;
Do not conquer her in public, Lest the villagers should see thee,
And the forests learn thy troubles. Touch thy wife upon the shoulders,
Do not touch her on the forehead, Nor upon the ears, nor visage;
Or a blue mark on her eyelids, Then her mother would perceive it,
All the village-workmen see it, And the village-women ask her ‘Hast thou been in heat of battle,
Or perchance the wolves have torn thee, Or the forest-bears embraced thee,
And the bear be thy protector?’”
On the hearth-stone lay a beggar, And the old man spake as follows: “Never, never, hero-husband,
Follow not her inclinations, As, alas! I did, regretful;
Veal, and beer, and best of butter, Fish and fowl of all descriptions,
Wheat from all the distant nations, All the dainties of the Northland;
Gave my wife no satisfaction, Often came she to my chamber,
With a visage fierce and frightful, With her eyeballs flashing anger,
Ever speaking words of evil, Using epithets the vilest,
Then I sought for other measures, Used on her my last resources,
And she spake in tones endearing; Cut a juniper or willow,
When with lash my wife I threatened, Hung she on my neck with kisses.”
Thus the last advices given.
Beauteous bride of Ilmarinen, Sighing heavily and moaning,
Spake these words from depths of sorrow: “Near, indeed, the separation,
Near the time for my departure; O the anguish of the parting,
From these walls renowned and ancient, From this village of the Northland,
Where my faithful mother taught me, Where my father gave instruction
When my years were few and tender! As a child I did not fancy,
From the confines of this cottage, From these dear old hills and mountains,
Since I now cannot escape it; Empty is the bowl of parting,
And my husband’s sledge is waiting, With the break-board looking southward,
“How shall I give compensation,
All the kindness of my mother, All the counsel of my father,
All my sister’s warm affection? Gratitude to thee, dear father,
For the comforts of thy table, For the pleasures of my childhood!
For thy tender care and guidance, For my birth and for my culture,
Gratitude to thee, dear brother, Gratitude to thee, sweet sister,
To my many friends and playmates!
“Never, never, aged father,
Never, ye, my kindred spirits, Never harbor care, nor sorrow,
Since thy child has gone to others, To the distant home of strangers,
From her father’s fields and firesides. Shines the Sun of the Creator,
Glitter all the stars of heaven, In the firmament of ether,
Not upon my father’s uplands, Not upon my home in childhood,
“Now the time has come for parting
From my brother’s welcome hearth-stone, From the chambers of my sister,
Now I leave the swamps and lowlands, Leave the grassy vales and mountains,
Leave the shores and sandy shallows, Leave the white-capped surging billows,
Where the mermaids sing and frolic; Leave the swamps to those that wander,
Leave the forests to the weary, Leave the heather to the rover,
Leave the alleys to the beggar, Leave the court-yards to the rambler,
Leave the matting to the sweeper, Leave the highways to the roebuck,
Leave the lowlands to the wild-geese, And the birch-tree to the cuckoo.
Journey southward with my husband, To the arms of Night and Winter,
“Should I once again, returning,
Mother would not hear me calling, Father would not see me weeping,
Weeping o’er my buried father, On their graves the fragrant flowers,
Verdure from my mother’s tresses, From the gray-beard of my father.
“Should I visit Sariola,
No one here would bid me welcome. Nothing in these hills would greet me,
By the fence a clump of osiers, And a land-mark at the corner,
When a child of little stature.
“Mother’s kine perhaps will know me,
Which I oft have fed and tended, Lowing now at my departure,
Sure my mother’s kine will welcome Northland’s daughter home returning.
Steeds that I have often ridden, When a maiden free and happy,
In the pasture of my brother, In the stable of my father;
Bid Pohyola’s daughter welcome. Brother’s faithful dogs may know me,
Dogs that I have taught to frolic, That now mourn for me departing,
In their kennels cold and cheerless; Sure my brother’s dogs will welcome
But the people will not know me, When I come these scenes to visit,
Though unchanged remain the rivers, Though untouched the flaxen fish-nets
“Fare thou well, my dear old homestead,
It would give me joy unceasing Could I linger here forever.
Leading to my father’s mansion; It would give me joy unceasing
Fare ye well, familiar gardens Filled with trees and fragrant flowers;
Could I linger here forever. Send to all my farewell greetings,
Greet the meadows with their daisies, Greet the borders with their fences,
Greet the streams with trout disporting, Greet the hills with stately pine-trees,
Fare ye well, ye streams and lakelets, Fertile fields, and shores of ocean,
All ye lindens of the valleys, All ye beautiful stone-lindens,
All ye junipers and willows, All ye shrubs with berries laden,
Arms of elms, and oaks, and alders, Fare ye well, dear scenes of childhood,
Ending thus, Pohyola’s daughter
Left the darksome Sariola, With her husband, Ilmarinen,
But the youth remained for singing,
“Hither came a bird of evil, Flew in fleetness from the forest,
Came to win the Maid of Beauty; Took away our fairest flower,
Won her with his youth and beauty, With his keys of ancient wisdom.
Who conduct us to the rivers? Now the buckets will be idle,
Now unswept will lie the matting, And unswept the halls of birch-wood,
Dark the handles of the pitchers, Fare thou well, dear Rainbow Maiden.”
Hastened homeward with the daughter Of the hostess of Pohyola,
Fleetly flew the hero’s snow-sledge, Loudly creaked, and roared, and rattled
By the side of Honey-inlet, On the back of Sandy Mountain.
Like the winds the sledge flew onward, On the yoke rang hoops of iron,
Loudly creaked the bands of willow, All the birchen cross-bars trembled,
In the racing of the fleet-foot, In the courser’s gallop homeward;
Journeyed still the third day onward, In one hand the reins of magic,
One foot resting on the cross-bar, And the other in the fur-robes.
Quickly did the highways shorten, Till at last upon the third day,
There appeared the blacksmith’s furnace, Nearer, Ilmarinen’s dwelling,
Clouds of smoke to lofty heaven, From the village of Wainola,
From the chimneys of the hero, From the home of the successful.
Wainamoinen’S Wedding-Songs.
Long had they been watching, waiting, For the coming of the blacksmith,
Weary were the eyes of watchers, Waiting from the father’s portals,
Weary were the young knees standing At the gates of the magician;
Tramping to the walls and watching; Worn and torn, the shoes of heroes,
Now at last upon a morning
Heard they from the woods the rumble Of a snow-sledge swiftly bounding.
She the lovely Kalew-daughter, Spake these words in great excitement: “’Tis the sledge of the magician,
From the dismal Sariola, By his side the Bride of Beauty!
Welcome to thy mother’s hearth-stone, To the dwelling of thy father,
Straightway came great Ilmarinen
To the fireside of his father, To his mother’s ancient dwelling.
On the newly-bended collar; Sweetly called the sacred cuckoos
Merry, jumped the graceful squirrel On the oaken shafts and cross-bar.
Beauteous daughter of Wainola, Spake these words of hearty welcome: “For the new moon hopes the village,
For the boat, the swelling water; I have not the moon expected,
I have waited for my hero, Waited for the Bride of Beauty;
Did not know but some misfortune, Some sad fate had overtaken
Thought the maiden growing weary, Weary of my son’s attentions,
To return to Kalevala, Ere his foot-prints had departed
Every morn I looked and listened, Constantly I thought and wondered
When it would return triumphant To his home, renowned and ancient.
Hobbled to these shores awaiting, With a sledge of but two pieces,
Had it brought my son beloved, Had it brought the Bride of Beauty.
Looking out from morn till even, Watching with my head extended,
With my eyelids widely opened, Waiting for my son’s returning
To this narrow place of resting. Finally am I rewarded,
Bringing home my son and hero, By his side the Rainbow maiden,
Pride and joy of Sariola.
“Wizard-bridegroom of Wainola,
Lead him to the well-filled manger, To the best of grain and clover;
Greetings send to all thy people. When thy greetings thou hast ended,
To our hero in his absence. Hast thou gone without adventure
Searching for the Maid of Beauty? Didst thou scale the hostile ramparts,
Passing o’er her mother’s threshold, Visiting the halls of Louhi?
“But I know without the asking,
Comest from the North a victor, On thy journey well contented;
Thou hast razed the hostile portals, Thou hast stormed the forts of Louhi,
On thy journey to Pohyola, To the village of the father.
In thine arms, the Rainbow-maiden, At thy side, the pride of Northland,
Who has told the cruel story, Who the worst of news has scattered,
That in vain thy steed had journeyed? Not in vain has been thy wooing,
To the dismal homes of Lapland; He has journeyed heavy laden,
Dripping foam from lips and nostrils, Through the bringing of the maiden,
“Come, thou beauty, from the snow-sledge,
Do not linger for assistance, Do not tarry to be carried;
If too proud the one in waiting, Rise thou, graceful, like a young bird,
On the tan-bark scarlet-colored, That the herds of kine have evened,
Smoothened by the tails of horses. Haste thou here with gentle footsteps,
On the tiles of even surface, On thy second father’s court-yard,
To thy brother’s place of resting, To thy sister’s silent chambers.
Step across this waiting threshold, Enter thou these halls of joyance,
Underneath this roof of ages. During all the winter evenings,
Sang the tiling made of ivory, Wishing thou wouldst walk upon it;
Hoping thou wouldst walk beneath it, And the windows often whistled,
Even on this merry morning, Even on the recent evening,
On the sea-shore ran the children, Near the walls the maidens waited,
There to watch the young bride’s coming, Coming with her hero-husband.
“Hail, ye courtiers of Wainola,
Hail to thee, Wainola’s hamlet, Hail, ye halls with heroes peopled,
Hail to thee, sweet golden moonlight, Hail to thee, benignant Ukko,
Never has there been in Northland Such a wedding-train of honor,
“Bridegroom, thou beloved hero,
And remove the silken muffler, Let us see the honey-maiden,
Seven years hast thou been wooing, Hast thou brought the maid affianced,
Sought one fairer than the moonlight, Sought a mermaid from the ocean?
See the answer to my question: Thou hast brought the sweet-voiced cuckoo,
Plucked the sweetest flower of Northland, Culled the fairest of the jewels,
Sat a babe upon the matting,
“Brother, what is this thou bringest, Aspen-log or trunk of willow,
Bridegroom, well dost thou remember, Thou hast hoped it all thy life-time,
Thou a thousand times hast said it, Better far than any other,
Nor the magpie from the border, Nor the scarecrow from the corn-fields,
What has this one done of credit, In the summer that has ended?
Where the mittens she has woven? Thou hast brought her empty-handed,
In thy chests the mice are nesting, Long-tails feeding on thy vestments,
Lakko, hostess of Wainola,
Hears the young child’s speech in wonder, Speaks these words of disapproval: “Silly prattler, cease thy talking,
Let all others be astonished, Heap thy malice on thy kindred, must not harm the Bride of Beauty,
False indeed is this thy prattle, All thy words are full of evil,
From the lips of one unworthy. Excellent the hero’s young bride,
Like the strawberry in summer, Like the daisy from the meadow,
Like the bluebird from the aspen, Like the redbreast from the heather,
Never couldst thou find in Ehstland Such a virgin as this daughter,
With such dignity of carriage, With such arms of pearly whiteness,
Neither is she empty-handed, She has brought us furs abundant,
Richest weavings of Pohyola. Many beauteous things the maiden,
Spun and woven with her fingers; Dresses of the finest texture
Bleached them in the days of spring-time, Dried them at the hour of noon-day,
For our heads the softest pillows, For our comfort woollen blankets,
To the bride speaks gracious Lakko: “Goodly wife, thou Maid of Beauty,
In thy father’s distant country; Here thou shalt be praised forever
Thou shalt never suffer sorrow, Never give thy heart to grieving;
Wert not fed beside the brooklets; Thou wert born ’neath stars auspicious,
Thou wert taken to the brewing Of the sweetest beer in Northland.
“Beauteous bride from Sariola,
Casks of corn, or wheat, or barley, Bringing rye in great abundance,
Good the plowing of thy husband, Good his sowing and his reaping.
“Bride of Beauty from the Northland,
Learn to labor with thy kindred; Good the home for thee to dwell in,
At thy hand will rest the milk-pail, And the churn awaits thine order;
Happy will the young bride labor, Easy are the resting-benches;
Like thy mother is the hostess, All the sons are like thy brothers,
“Shouldst thou ever have a longing
For thy father’s Northland salmon, For thy brother’s hazel-chickens,
Let thy hero-husband bring them. There is not in all of Northland,
Not a bird beneath the ether, Not a fish within the waters,
That thy husband cannot capture. It is well here for the maiden,
Need not turn the heavy millstone, Need not move the iron pestle;
For the rye, the swifter current, While the billows wash the vessels
Thou hast here a lovely village, Finest spot in all of Northland,
In the uplands, fields of beauty, With the lake-shore near the hamlet,
Where the goslings swim and frolic, Water-birds disport in numbers.”
Were refreshed with richest viands, Given food and drink abundant,
On the sweetest loaves of barley, On the best of wheaten biscuits,
Many things were on the table, Many dainties of Wainola,
In the platters deftly painted, Many cakes with honey sweetened,
Many bits of trout and whiting, Larger salmon carved in slices,
Rimmed with gold the silver handles, Beer of barley ceaseless flowing,
In the cellar flows profusely, Beer for all, the tongues to quicken,
Who is there to lead the singing, Lead the songs of Kalevala?
The eternal, wise enchanter, Quick begins his incantations,
“Golden brethren, dearest kindred, Ye, my loved ones, wise and worthy
Listen to my simple sayings: Rarely stand the geese together,
Not together stand the brothers, Nor the children of one mother,
“Shall we now begin the singing,
Singers can but sing their wisdom, And the cuckoo call the spring-time,
Only dyes the earth in beauty; So the goddesses of weaving
Ever sing the youth of Lapland In their straw-shoes full of gladness,
Or of blue-moose they have eaten. Wherefore should I not be singing,
Of the biscuits of Wainola, Of the bread of Kalew-waters?
In their straw-shoes filled with joyance, Drinking but a cup of water,
Wherefore should I not be singing, And the children not be chanting
Brewed from barley in perfection, Dressed in quaint and homely costume,
Wherefore should I not be singing, And the children too be chanting
In these halls renowned and ancient? This the place for men to linger,
Near the foaming beer of barley, Honey-brewed in great abundance,
Near, the nets for trout and whiting, Here where food is never wanting,
Here Wainola’s sons assemble, Here Wainola’s daughters gather,
Here they live without regretting, In the life-time of the landlord,
“Who shall first be sung and lauded?
Let us praise the bridegroom’s father, Let the hero-host be chanted,
Him who built upon the mountains, Him who brought the trunks of lindens,
Brought them to the best of places, Joined them skilfully together,
For this famous hero-dwelling, Walls procured upon the lowlands,
From the woodlands beams of oak-wood, From the berry-plains the studding,
And the mosses from the fenlands. Trimly builded is this mansion,
Here a hundred men have labored, On the roof have stood a thousand,
As this roof was tightly jointed. Here the ancient mansion-builder,
Lost in storms his locks of sable, Scattered by the winds of heaven.
On the rocks his gloves forgotten, Left his hat upon the willows,
Oftentimes the mansion-builder, In the early hours of morning,
Unperceived by all the village, Has arisen from his slumber,
Combed his locks among the branches, Bathed his eyes in dews of morning.
“Thus obtained the pleasant landlord
Fill his benches with magicians, Fill his windows with enchanters,
Fill his floors with ancient speakers, Fill his ancient court with strangers,
Thus the Kalew-host is lauded.
“Now I praise the genial hostess,
Fills with plenty all her tables, Bakes the honeyed loaves of barley,
With her arms of strength and beauty, Bakes her bread in copper ovens,
Feeds them on the toothsome bacon, On the trout, and pike, and whiting,
On the dainties of Wainola.
“Often has the faithful hostess
Ere the crowing of the watcher, To prepare the wedding-banquet,
Brew the honey-beer of wedlock. Excellently has the housewife,
Brewed the beer from hops and barley, From the corn of Kalevala,
Stirred the beer with graceful fingers, At the oven in the penthouse,
Neither did the prudent hostess, Beautiful, and full of wisdom,
Lest the beer should taste of black-earth, Be too bitter in the brewing;
Went alone at hour of midnight, Was not frightened by the black-wolf,
“Now the hostess I have lauded,
Now the honored hero-bridegroom, Best of all the village-masters.
Raiment brought from distant nations, Tightly fitting to his body;
To the floor it hangs in beauty, Trailing from his neck and shoulders,
Peeping through his outer raiment, Woven by the Moon’s fair daughters,
Dressed in neatness is the suitor, Round his waist a belt of copper,
Ere the early fires were lighted, Ere the fire had been discovered.
On his feet are silken stockings, Silken ribbons on his ankles,
Dressed in beauty is the bridegroom, On his feet are shoes of deer-skin,
Like the blue-duck on the sea-waves, Like the thrush among the willows,
Well adorned the hero-suitor, With his locks of golden color,
Hero-hat upon his forehead, Piercing through the forest branches,
Bought with countless gold and silver, Priceless is the suitor’s head-gear.
“Now the bridegroom has been lauded,
Day-companion in her childhood, In the maiden’s magic mansion.
From the village of Tanikka? Thence was never brought the playmate,
Has she come from distant nations, From the waters of the Dwina,
Not from Dwina came the maiden, Did not sail across the waters;
As a strawberry of sweetness, On the fields the child of beauty,
Thence has come the young bride’s playmate, Thence arose her fair companion.
Small her lips of scarlet color, Like the maiden’s loom of Suomi;
Like the twinkling stars of heaven; Beam the playmate’s throbbing temples
Trinkets has the bride’s companion, On her neck a golden necklace,
On her arms are golden bracelets, Golden rings upon her fingers,
Loops of gold upon her temples, And with pearls her brow is studded.
When her jeweled ear-rings glistened; Thought the Sun had left his station
Thought a ship was homeward sailing When her colored head-gear fluttered.
Playmate of the Rainbow-maiden.
“Now I praise the friends assembled,
If the old are wise and silent, All the youth are free and merry,
Never was there in Wainola, Never will there be in Northland,
All the children speak in joyance, All the aged move sedately;
Like the hoar-frost of the morning, Like the welcome dawn of spring-time,
Silver then was more abundant, Gold among the guests in plenty,
Money-bags along the valleys, For the friends that were invited,
All the friends have now been lauded, Each has gained his meed of honor.”
Song-deliverer of Northland, Swung himself upon the fur-bench
Straightway hastened to his hamlet, Singing as he journeyed onward,
Singing one day, then a second, All the third day chanting legends.
Hung the sledge upon a birch-stump, Broke it into many pieces,
Double were the runners bended, All the parts were torn asunder,
Then the good, old Wainamoinen
“Is there one among this number, In this rising generation,
In the passing generation, That will go to Mana’s kingdom,
There to get the magic auger From the master of Manala,
Or a second sledge may fashion?”
Was the answer of the aged: “Not among the youth of Northland,
Is there one of ample courage, That has bravery sufficient,
To the kingdom of Tuoni, To Manala’s fields and castles,
Wherewithal to mend thy snow-sledge, Build anew thy sledge of magic.”
The eternal wisdom-singer, Went again to Mana’s empire,
Crossed the sable stream of Deathland, To the castles of Manala,
Brought the instrument in safety. Straightway sings old Wainamoinen,
In the forest, slender birches, And beside them, mighty oak-trees,
Moulds them by his will and power, Makes anew his sledge of magic.
Binds him to his sledge securely, Seats himself upon the cross-bench,
To the manger filled and waiting, To the stable of his master;
Famous bard and wise enchanter, To the threshold of his dwelling,
Origin of the Serpent.
Near the Kauko-point and harbor, Plowed his fields for rye and barley,
Heard with quickened ears an uproar, Heard the village in commotion,
Heard the foot-steps on the ice-plain, Heard the rattle of the sledges;
Knew it was Pohyola’s wedding, Wedding of the Rainbow-virgin.
Shook his sable locks in envy, Turned his hero-head in anger,
Through his pallid face and temples; Ceased his plowing and his sowing,
On his steed he lightly mounted, Straightway galloped fleetly homeward
To his mother old and golden, Gave his mother these directions,
“My beloved, faithful mother, Quickly bring me beer and viands,
Food and drink for me abundant, Have my bath-room quickly heated,
That I may refresh my body, Dress myself in hero-raiment.”
Brings her hero food in plenty, Beer and viands for the hungry,
Quick she heats the ancient bath-room, Quickly sets his bath in order.
Ate his meat with beer inspiring, Hastened to his bath awaiting;
With the many-colored bunting; Quick the hero laved his temples,
Quick returning to his mother, Spake in haste the words that follow: “My beloved, helpful mother,
To the store-house on the hill-top, Bring my vest of finest texture,
Bring my suit of magic colors, Thus to make me look attractive,
First the ancient mother asked him,
“Whither dost thou go, my hero? Dost thou go to hunt the roebuck,
Shoot the squirrel in the woodlands?”
Also known as Kaukomieli: “Worthy mother of my being,
Chase the lynx upon the mountains, Shoot the squirrel on the tree-tops;
To the feasting of her people. Bring at once my purple vestments,
Let me don it for the marriage Of the maiden of the Northland.”
And the wife forebade the husband; Two of all the best of heroes,
Strongly urged wild Lemminkainen Not to go to Sariola,
To the marriage-feast of Northland, “Since thou hast not been invited,
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen.
“Where the wicked are invited, There the good are always welcome,
I am constantly reminded By this sword of sharpened edges,
That Pohyola needs my presence.”
Sought again to stay her hero: “Do not go, my son beloved,
Full of horrors are the highways, On the road are many wonders,
Thrice destruction hovers over!”
These the words of Kaukomieli: “Death is seen by aged people,
Death can never frighten heroes, Heroes do not fear the spectre;
Tell that I may understand thee, Name the first of all destructions,
Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “I will tell thee, son and hero,
But because the truth is worthy; I will name the chief destruction,
When thou hast a distance journeyed, Only one day hast thou travelled,
Stream of fire of wondrous beauty, In the stream a mighty fire-spout,
On the rock a fiery hillock, On the top a flaming eagle,
Sharpens too his bloody talons, For the coming of the stranger,
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen,
“Women die beneath the eagle, Such is not the death of heroes;
That will heal the wounds of eagles; Make myself a steed of alders,
That will stride ahead majestic; As a duck I’ll drive behind him,
Underneath the flaming eagle, With his bloody beak and talons.
Name the second of destroyers.” Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “This the second of destroyers:
Only two days hast thou travelled, Comes a pit of fire to meet thee,
Eastward far the pit extending, Stretches endless to the westward,
Glowing with the heat of ages; Hundreds has this monster swallowed,
Hundreds with their trusty broadswords, Thousands on their fiery chargers.”
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli: “Never will the hero perish
Know I well the means of safety, Know a remedy efficient:
On the snow-clad fields, a hero, Drive the snow-man on before me,
Drive him through the fiery furnace, With my magic broom of copper;
Follow close the magic image, Thus escape the frightful monster,
With my flowing beard untangled. Ancient mother of my being,
Name the third of the destroyers.” Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “This the third of fatal dangers:
Hast thou travelled one day longer, To the portals of Pohyola,
There a wolf will rise to meet thee, There the black-bear sneak upon thee;
Hundreds in their jaws have perished, Have devoured a thousand heroes;
Since thy form is unprotected?”
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli: “Let them eat the gentle lambkins,
They cannot devour this hero; I am girded with my buckler,
Armlets wear I of the master, From the wolf and bear protected,
I can meet the wolf of Lempo, For the bear I have a balsam,
For the wolf, forge chains of iron; I will smite them as the willow,
Thus I’ll gain the open court-yard, Thus triumphant end my journey.”
“Then thy journey is not ended, Greater dangers still await thee,
Horrors three within thy pathway; Three great dangers of the hero
These the worst of all thy dangers: When thou hast still farther wandered,
Where the walls are forged from iron, And from steel the outer bulwark;
Back again to earth returning; Double spears are used for railings,
On each rail are stinging adders; Lizards too adorn the bulwarks,
Hissing lizards, venomed serpents, Jump and writhe upon the rampart,
On the greensward lie the monsters, On the ground the things of evil,
Hissing, striking, crawling, writhing; One more horrid than the others,
Longer than the longest rafters, Larger than the largest portals;
Lifts his head in awful menace, Raises it to strike none other
Spake the warlike Lemminkainen,
“By such things the children perish, Such is not the death of heroes;
I can quench the flames of passion, I can meet the prowling wild-beasts,
I can heal the sting of adders, I have plowed the serpent-pastures,
While my hands were unprotected, Held the serpents in my fingers,
On my hands the blood of serpents, On my feet the fat of adders.
On the serpents of the Northland; With my heel I’ll crush the monsters,
I will banish them from Pohya, Drive them to Manala’s kingdom,
Walk the halls of Sariola!” Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “Do not go, my son beloved,
Through the Northland fields and fallows; There are warriors with broadswords,
Are on beer intoxicated, By the beer are much embittered;
On the tips of swords of magic; Greater heroes have been conjured,
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen: “Formerly thy son resided
Laplanders cannot enchant me, Nor the Turyalanders harm me;
Charm him with my magic powers, Sing his shoulders wide asunder,
Sing his collar-bone to pieces, Sing his breast to thousand fragments.”
“Foolish son, ungrateful wizard, Boasting of thy former visit,
Once in Northland thou wert living, In the homesteads of Pohyola;
Tasted there the dog-tongue waters, Floated down the fatal current,
Thou hast seen Tuoni’s river, Thou hast measured Mana’s waters,
Had it not been for thy mother! What I tell thee well remember,
Filled with stakes thou’lt find the court-yard, These to hold the heads of heroes;
Shouldst thou go to Sariola.” Spake the warlike Lemminkainen: “Fools indeed may heed thy counsel,
Those of seven conquest-summers Cannot heed such weak advising.
Bring my magic mail of copper, Bring me too my father’s broadsword,
Long it has been cold and idle, Long has lain in secret places,
Long been asking for a bearer.”
Took his ancient battle-armor, Took his father’s sword of magic,
Tried its edge upon the sorb-tree; In his hand the blade was bended,
Like the juniper in summer. Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “There is none in Pohya’s hamlets,
That with me can measure broadswords, That can meet this blade ancestral.”
Took the strongest from the rafters, Spake these words in meditation: “I shall recognize as worthy,
That can bend this mighty cross-bow, That can break its magic sinews,
Lemminkainen, filled with courage,
Dons his mighty mail of copper, To his servant speaks as follows: “Trusty slave, and whom I purchased,
Quick prepare my fiery charger, Harness well my steed of battle;
To the banquet-fields of Lempo.”
Hitches well the noble war-horse, Quick prepares the fire-red stallion,
“I have done what thou hast hidden, Ready harnessed is the charger,
Comes the hour of the departing
Right hand ready, left unwilling, All his anxious fingers pain him,
All his members give permission; Starts the hero on his journey,
At the threshold of the dwelling, At the highway of the court-yard: “Child of courage, my beloved,
If thou goest to the feasting, Shouldst thou reach the great carousal,
Drink the goblet to the middle, Always give the half remaining,
To another more unworthy; In the lower half are serpents,
Feeding on the slimy bottom.”
Gives her son these sage directions, On the border of the court-yard,
“If thou goest to the banquet, Shouldst thou reach the great carousal,
Take but half a stride in walking, Give the second half to others,
Only thus thou’lt be a hero, Thus become a son immortal;
Bravely move about the chambers, In the gatherings of heroes,
Thereupon wild Lemminkainen
Of his battle-sledge of wonder, Raised his pearl-enamelled birch-rod,
And the steed flew onward fleetly, Galloped on his distant journey.
When a flight of hazel-chickens Quick arose before his coming,
There were left some feathers lying, Feathers of the hazel-chickens,
These the reckless Lemminkainen Gathered for their magic virtues,
Did not know what things might happen On his journey to Pohyola;
In a strait all things are useful.
Galloped farther on the highway, When his courser neighed in danger,
Then the stout-heart, Lemminkainen, Handsome hero, Kaukomieli,
Craned his neck and looked about him. Found it as his mother told him,
Ran the fire-stream like a river, Ran across the hero’s pathway.
In the cataract a fire-rock, On the rock a fiery hillock,
From his throat the fire was streaming To the crater far below him,
Glowing with a fiery splendor; Long he looked upon the hero,
Then the eagle thus addressed him: “Whither art thou driving, Ahti,
Kaukomieli spake in answer: “To the feastings of Pohyola,
To the banquet of her people; Move aside and let me journey,
Let this wanderer pass by thee, I am warlike Lemminkainen.”
Screaming from his throat of splendor: “Though thou art wild Lemminkainen,
Through my fire-throat let thee journey, Through these flames shall be thy passage
To Pohyola’s great carousal!”
Thinks himself in little trouble, Thrusts his fingers in his pockets,
Quickly takes the magic feathers, Feathers from the hazel-chickens,
Rubs them with his magic fingers, Whence a flight of birds arises,
Large the bevy of the young birds. Quick the wizard, Lemminkainen,
Thus to satisfy his hunger, Thus to quench the fire out-streaming.
Thus escapes the first of dangers, Passes thus the first destroyer,
With his whip he strikes his courser,
Straightway speeds the fiery charger, Noiselessly upon his journey,
Till the flying steed in terror Neighs again and ceases running.
Cranes his neck and looks about him, Sees his mother’s words were truthful,
Lo! before him yawned a fire-gulf, Stretching crosswise through his pathway;
To the west an endless distance, Filled with stones and burning pebbles,
Little heeding, Lemminkainen
“Ukko, thou O God above me, Dear Creator, omnipresent,
From the east, dispatch a second, From the south send forth a third one;
Sew their edges well together, Fill thou well the interspaces,
Let it fall from upper ether, Fall upon the flaming fire-pit,
Mighty Ukko, the Creator,
Dwelling in the courts of heaven, Sent a storm-cloud from the north-west,
From the south despatched a third one, Let them gather from the south-west,
Filled their many interspaces, Sent a snow-fall high as heaven,
Sent it seething to the fire-pit, On the streams of burning matter;
Grows a lake with rolling billows. Quick the hero, Lemminkainen,
From one border to the other, Thus escapes his second danger,
Then the reckless Lemminkainen
Snapped his whip above his racer, And the steed flew onward swiftly,
O’er the highway to Pohyola; Galloped fast and galloped faster,
When the stallion loudly neighing, Stopped and trembled on the highway.
Raised himself upon the cross-bench, Looked to see what else had happened;
In the passage-way a black-bear, At the high-gate of Pohyola,
Thereupon young Lemminkainen,
Thrusts his fingers in his pockets, Seeks his magic pouch of leather,
Rubs it firmly in his fingers, In his hands it falls to powder;
When a flock of sheep arises, Goats and sheep of sable color;
And the wild-bear aids the slaughter, While the reckless Lemminkainen
Gallops on a little distance, To the court of Sariola,
And of steel the rods and pickets, In the earth a hundred fathoms,
Double-pointed spears projecting; On each spear were serpents twisted,
Lizards mingled with the serpents, Tails entangled pointing earthward,
Writhing, hissing mass of evil.
Deeply thought and long considered: “It is as my mother told me,
Stretching from the earth to heaven; Downward deep are serpents creeping,
High as highest flight of eagles, Higher still the wall shoots upward.”
Little cares, nor feels disheartened, Draws his broadsword from its scabbard,
Hews the wall with might of magic, Breaks the palisade in pieces,
Chops the serpent-wall to fragments; Through the breach he quickly passes
In the way, a serpent lying,
Longer than the longest rafters, Larger than the posts of oak-wood;
And a thousand tongues, the monster, Eyes as large as sifting vessels,
Teeth as large as hatchet-handles, Back as broad as skiffs of ocean.
Straightway through this host opposing, Through the hundred heads of adders,
Spake the magic Lemminkainen: “Venomed viper, thing of evil,
Thou that crawlest in the stubble, Through the flower-roots of Lempo,
Sent thee from thine evil coverts, Sent thee hither, crawling, writhing,
Who bestowed thy mouth of venom, Who insisted, who commanded,
Who thy tail has given action? Was this given by the father,
Or the eldest of the brothers, Or the youngest of the sisters,
“Close thy mouth, thou thing of evil,
In a circle wrap thy body, Coil thou like a shield in silence,
Let this wanderer pass by thee, Or remove thyself entirely;
Quick retreat to bog and stubble, Hide thyself in reeds and rushes,
Like a ball of flax enfolding, Like a sphere of aspen-branches,
Roll thyself to yonder mountain; In the heather is thy dwelling,
Shouldst thou raise thy head in anger, Mighty Ukko will destroy it,
With his death-balls made of iron!”
When the monster, little heeding, Hissing with his tongue in anger,
Pounces with his mouth of venom At the head of Lemminkainen;
Speaks the master-words of knowledge, Words that came from distant ages,
Words his mother learned in childhood, These the words of Lemminkainen: “Since thou wilt not heed mine order,
Puffed with pride of thine own greatness, Thou shall burst in triple pieces.
I will hunt thine ancient mother, Sing thine origin of evil,
Suoyatar, thine ancient mother, Thing of evil, thy creator!
“Suoyatar once let her spittle
This was rocked by winds and waters, Shaken by the ocean-currents,
Rocked in water seven summers, On the blue-back of the ocean,
Lengthwise did the billows draw it, And the sunshine gave it softness,
On the coast the waters left it.
“Then appeared Creation’s daughters,
On the roaring shore of ocean, There beheld the spittle lying,
‘What would happen from this spittle, Should the breath of the Creator
Breathe the breath of life upon it, Give the thing the sense of vision?’
“The Creator heard these measures,
‘Evil only comes from evil, This is the expectoration
Therefore would the thing be evil, Should I breathe a soul within it,
“Hisi heard this conversation,
Made himself to be creator, Breathed a soul into the spittle,
Thus arose the poison-monster, Thus was born the evil serpent,
“Whence the life that gave her action?
Whence then was her heart created? From the heart-throbs of her mother.
From the foam of rolling waters. Whence was consciousness awakened?
Whence arose her head of venom? From the seed-germs of the ivy.
From the flaxen seeds of Lempo. Whence the evil ears for hearing?
Whence then was her mouth created? This from Suoyatar’s foam-currents.
From the spear of Keitolainen. Whence arose thy fangs of poison?
Whence then was thy back created? From the carbon-posts of Piru.
From the brain of the hobgoblin. Whence arose thy writhing entrails?
“This thine origin, O Serpent,
Vilest thing of God’s creation, Writhing, hissing thing of evil,
With the shade of earth and heaven, With the darkness of the storm-cloud.
Clear the pathway of this hero. I am mighty Lemminkainen,
To the feastings and carousals, In the halls of darksome Northland.”
Hundred-eyed and heinous monster, Crawled away to other portals,
Might proceed upon his errand, To the dismal Sariola,
In the banquet-halls of Pohya.
THE Unwelcome Guest.
Brought the Islander and hero, Also known as Lemminkainen,
Through the darkling deeps of Kalma, To the homesteads of Pohyola,
Now must I relate his doings, Must relate to all my hearers,
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli, Wandered through Pohyola’s chambers,
How the hero went unbidden To the feasting and carousal,
Lemminkainen full of courage,
Stepped across the ancient threshold, To the centre of the court-room,
Walls and ceilings creaked and murmured.
These the words that Ahti uttered: “Be ye greeted on my coming,
Listen, all ye hosts of Pohya; Is there food about this homestead,
Beer to give a thirsty stranger?”
At the east end of the table, Gave this answer to the questions: “Surely is there in this homestead,
Never will this host refuse thee, Shouldst thou act a part becoming,
Waiting near the birchen rafters, In the spaces by the kettles,
Then the reckless Lemminkainen
“Lempo may perchance come hither, Let him fill this lowly station,
That with soot he may be blackened. Never has my ancient father,
Stood upon a spot unworthy, At the portals near the rafters;
Food and shelter gladly furnished, And a room for his attendants,
Hooks provided for his snow-shoes, Halls in waiting for his helmet.
What my father found before me?”
Walked around the dining table, Sat upon a bench and waited,
And the kettle creaked beneath him. Spake the reckless Lemminkainen: “As a guest am I unwelcome,
Bring no dishes to the stranger?”
Then addressed the words that follow: “Lemminkainen, thou art evil,
Thou hast not the look of kindness, Thou wilt give me throbbing temples,
All our beer is in the barley, All the malt is in the kernel,
And our dinner has been eaten; Yesterday thou shouldst have been here,
Whereupon wild Lemminkainen
Shook his coal-black locks and answered: “All the tables here are empty,
All the beer has left the goblets, Empty too are all the pitchers,
O thou hostess of Pohyola, Toothless dame of dismal Northland,
And thy feast is ill-conducted, Like the dogs hast thou invited;
Wheaten loaves of greatest virtue, Brewed thy beer from hops and barley,
Six the hamlets thou hast honored, Nine the villages invited
Thou hast asked the poor and lowly, Asked the hosts of common people,
Asked a multitude of beggars, Toilers by the day, and hirelings;
Asked the maids with braided tresses, I alone was not invited.
Since I sent thee kegs of barley? Others sent thee grain in cupfuls,
While I sent thee fullest measure, Sent the half of all my garners,
Of the grain that I had gathered. Even now young Lemminkainen,
Has no beer, no food, no welcome, Naught for him art thou preparing,
Nothing brewing in thy cellars For the hero of the Islands,
Ilpotar, the ancient hostess,
“Come, my pretty maiden-waiter, Servant-girl to me belonging,
Bring some beer to give the stranger!”
Washer of the banquet-platters, Rinser of the dinner-ladles,
And she laid some food in kettles, Only bones and heads of whiting,
Crusts of bread and bits of biscuit. Then she brought some beer in pitchers,
That the stranger, Lemminkainen, Might have drink, and meat in welcome,
Then the maiden spake as follows: “Thou art sure a mighty hero,
Here to empty all our vessels!”
Closely handled all the pitchers, Looking to the very bottoms;
In the centre adders swimming, On the borders worms and lizards.
Filled with anger, spake as follows: “Get ye hence, ye things of evil,
With the bearer of these pitchers, With the maid that brought ye hither,
Ere the day-star seeks the ocean! O thou wretched beer of barley,
Into disrepute hast fallen, But I’ll drink thee, notwithstanding,
Then the hero to his pockets
Searching in his pouch of leather; Quick withdraws a hook for fishing,
Through the worthless beer of barley; On his fish-book hang the serpents,
Catches frogs in magic numbers, Catches blackened worms in thousands,
Quickly draws his heavy broad sword, And decapitates the serpents.
When the wizard speaks as follows: “As a guest am I unwelcome,
That is worthy of a hero; Neither has a ram been butchered,
Worthy food for Lemminkainen.”
Answered thus the Island-minstrel: “Wherefore hast thou journeyed hither,
Spake in answer Lemminkainen: “Happy is the guest invited,
Listen, son of Pohylander, Host of Sariola, listen:
Give me worthy drink for money!”
In bad humor, full of anger, Conjured in the earth a lakelet,
Thus addressed the Island-hero: “Quench thy thirst from yonder lakelet,
Little heeding, Lemminkainen
“I am neither bear nor roebuck, That should drink this filthy water,
Ahti then began to conjure,
Bull with horns of gold and silver, And the bull drank from the lakelet,
Then the landlord of Pohyola There a savage wolf created,
To destroy the bull of magic. Lemminkainen, full of courage,
Set him on the floor before him To attract the wolf’s attention.
Conjured there a dog of Lempo, Set him on the floor before him
Lemminkainen, full of mischief, Conjured on the roof a squirrel,
He might catch the dog’s attention. But the master of the Northland
And he drove the magic squirrel From his seat upon the rafters.
Made a fox of scarlet color, And it ate the golden marten.
Conjured there a hen to flutter Near the fox of scarlet color.
Thereupon a hawk created, That with beak and crooked talons
Spake the landlord of Pohyola,
“Never will this feast be bettered Till the guests are less in number;
Get thee hence, thou evil stranger, Cease thy conjurings of evil,
Haste away, thou wicked wizard, To thine Island-home and people!”
“Thus no hero will be driven, Not a son of any courage
Will be driven from thy banquet.”
Snatched his broadsword from the rafters, Drew it rashly from the scabbard,
“Ahti, Islander of evil, Thou the handsome Kaukomieli,
Let our skill be fully tested; Surely is my broadsword better
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “That my blade is good and trusty,
Has on many bones been tested; Be that as it may, my fellow,
Let our swords be fully tested, Let us see whose blade is better.
Tested well this sword in battle, Never failing in a conflict.
Then he grasped his mighty broadsword,
Hanging from his belt of copper. Standing on their hilts their broadswords,
Found the sword of Northland’s master Longer than the sword of Ahti
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen. “Since thou hast the longer broadsword,
I am ready for thy weapon.”
With the wondrous strength of anger, Tried in vain to slay the hero,
Chipped the splinters from the rafters, Cut the ceiling into fragments,
Thereupon brave Kaukomieli,
“Have the rafters thee offended? What the crimes they have committed,
Listen now, thou host of Northland, Reckless landlord of Pohyola,
In these chambers filled with women; We shall stain these painted rafters,
Let us go without the mansion, In the field is room for combat,
Blood looks fairer in the court-yard, Better in the open spaces,
To the yard the heroes hasten,
Spread it on the field of battle; On the ox-skin stand the swordsmen.
“Listen well, thou host of Northland, Though thy broadsword is the longer,
Thou shalt have the first advantage; Use with skill thy boasted broadsword
Ere thy head be chopped in pieces; Strike with skill, or thou wilt perish,
Thereupon Pohyola’s landlord
Struck a heavy blow in anger, Struck a second, then a third time,
Could not draw a single blood-drop From the veins of Lemminkainen,
Spake the handsome Kaukomieli: “Let me try my skill at fencing,
Let my honored blade be tested!” But the landlord of Pohyola,
Strikes in fury, strikes unceasing, Ever aiming, ever missing.
Swings his mighty blade of magic, Fire disports along his weapon,
Glistens from the hero’s broadsword, Balls of fire disporting, dancing,
Overflow upon the shoulders Of the landlord of Pohyola.
“O thou son of Sariola, See! indeed thy neck is glowing
Like the rising Sun in ocean!”
Thoughtless host of darksome Northland, To behold the fiery splendor
Quick as lightning, Lemminkainen, With his father’s blade of battle,
With united skill and power, Lopped the head of Pohya’s master;
As the ear falls from the corn-stalk, As one strikes the fins from salmon,
Of the landlord of Pohyola, Like a ball it rolled and circled.
Hundreds were the sharpened pillars, And a head on every picket,
Quick the victor, Lemminkainen, Took the head of Pohya’s landlord,
Then the Islander, rejoicing,
Quick returning to the chambers, Gave this order to the hostess: “Evil maiden, bring me water,
From the blood of Northland’s master, Wicked host of Sariola.”
Fired with anger, threatened vengeance, Conjured men with heavy broadswords,
Hundred warriors with their javelins, And a thousand bearing cross-bows,
For the death of Lemminkainen. Kaukomieli soon discovered
That his presence was unwelcome At the feasting of Pohyola,
The Mother’S Counsel.
Wild magician, Lemminkainen, Also known as Kaukomieli,
From the banquet-halls of Louhi, From the ever-darksome Northland,
Stormful strode he from the mansion, Hastened like the smoke of battle,
Left his crimes and misdemeanors In the halls of ancient Louhi.
Seeking for his tethered courser, Anxious looked in field and stable,
Found a black thing in the fallow, Proved to be a clump of willows.
Who will give him wise directions, Guide the wizard out of trouble,
Keep his magic head from danger From the warriors of Northland?
And a din from other homesteads, From the battle-hosts of Louhi,
Of the homesteads of Pohyola.
Handsome Islander and hero, Changing both his form and features,
Changing to another body, Quick became a mighty eagle,
Tried to fly to highest heaven, But the moonlight burned his temples,
Then entreating, Lemminkainen,
This the prayer that Ahti uttered: “Ukko, God of love and mercy,
Wise Director of the lightning, Thou the Author of the thunder,
Give to me thy cloak of vapor, Throw a silver cloud around me,
Hasten to my native country, To my mother’s Island-dwelling,
With a mother’s grave forebodings.”
Flew and soared on eagle-pinions, Looked about him, backwards, forwards,
In his eyes the fire of splendor, Like the eyes of Pohyalanders,
And the gray-hawk thus addressed him: “Ho! there! hero, Lemminkainen,
With the hero-heads of Northland?”
These the words of Kaukomieli: “O thou gray-hawk, bird of beauty,
Fly as fast as wings can bear thee; When thou hast arrived in safety,
Tell the archers and the spearmen, They will never catch the eagle,
To his Island-home and fortress.”
Straightway to his mother’s cottage, In his face the look of trouble,
Ahti’s mother ran to meet him, When she spied him in the pathway,
These the words the mother uttered: “Of my sons thou art the bravest,
Wherefore then comes thine annoyance, On returning from Pohyola?
At the feast and great carousal? At thy cups, if thou wert injured,
Thou shalt have the cup thy father Brought me from the hero-castle.”
“Worthy mother, thou that nursed me, If I had been maimed at drinking,
Would have slain a thousand heroes, Would have taught them useful lessons.”
“Wherefore then art thou indignant, Didst thou meet disgrace and insult,
Buy thou then a better courser With the riches of thy mother,
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “Faithful mother of my being,
If for him my heart was injured, I the landlord would have punished,
All of Pohya’s strongest riders.” Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “Tell me then thy dire misfortune,
On his journey to Pohyola? Have the Northland maidens scorned thee,
If the maidens scorned thy presence, If the women gave derision,
Thou canst scorn a thousand women.” Said the reckless Lemminkainen: “Honored mother, fond and faithful,
Or the maidens laughed derision, I the maidens would have punished,
Lemminkainen’s mother answered: “Wherefore then are thou indignant,
On returning from Pohyola? Was thy feasting out of season,
Were thy dreams of evil import When asleep in darksome Northland?”
“Aged women may remember What they dream on beds of trouble;
Since I left my Island-cottage. My beloved, helpful mother,
Flour and salt in great abundance, Farther must thy hero wander,
Leave his pleasant Island-dwelling, Journey from this home of ages;
Sharpening their spears and lances, For the death of Lemminkainen.”
Hurriedly she asked the reason: “Why the men their swords were whetting,
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen,
“Therefore do they whet their broadswords, Therefore sharpen they their lances:
At his heart are aimed their lances. In the court-yard of Pohyola,
Fierce the battle waged against me; But I slew the Northland hero,
Quick to arms rose Louhi’s people, All the spears and swords of Northland
All of Pohya turned against me, Turned against a single foeman.”
“I had told thee this beforehand, I had warned thee of this danger,
To the hostile fields of Northland. Here my hero could have lingered,
Lived forever with his mother, With his mother for protection,
Here no war would have arisen, No contention would have followed.
Whither will my loved one hasten, To escape thy fierce pursuers,
From thy sins to hide in safety, From thy crimes and misdemeanors,
That thy body be not mangled, That thy locks be not outrooted?”
“Know I not a spot befitting, Do not know a place of safety,
That will give me sure protection From the crimes by me committed.
Where to flee wilt thou advise me?” This the answer of the mother: “I do not know where I can send thee;
Or a juniper in lowlands? Then misfortune may befall thee;
Cut in splints for candle-lighters; And the juniper is often
Go a birch-tree to the valleys, Or an elm-tree to the glenwood?
Misery may overtake thee; Often is the lowland birch-tree
Often is the elm-wood forest Cleared away for other plantings.
Cranberry upon the heather, Strawberry upon the mountains,
Even there will trouble find thee, There misfortune overtake thee,
Silver-tinselled girls would get thee. Be a pike then in the ocean,
Then would trouble overtake thee, Would become thy life-companion;
Catch thee in his net of flax-thread, Catch thee with his cruel fish-hook.
Or a black-bear in the thickets? Even then would trouble find thee,
Sable hunters of the Northland Have their spears and cross-bows ready
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen: “Know I well the worst of places,
Where misfortune’s eye would find me; Since thou gavest me existence,
Whither shall I flee for safety, Whither hide from death and danger?
Dire misfortune hovers o’er me; On the morrow come the spearmen,
Ahti’s head their satisfaction.” This the answer of the mother: “I can name a goodly refuge,
Name a distant ocean-island, Where my son may live in safety.
There thy head cannot be severed; But an oath as strong as heaven,
Thou wilt not for sixty summers Join in war or deadly combat,
Wishest gold and silver treasures.” Spake the grateful Lemminkainen: “I will swear an oath of honor,
Draw my sword in the arena, Test the warrior in battle;
On my breast two scars of broadsword, Of my former battles, relics,
On the battle-fields of Northland, In the wars with men and heroes.”
“Go thou, take thy father’s vessel, Go and hide thyself in safety,
In the tenth, sail to the centre, To the island, forest-covered,
Where thy father went before thee, Where he hid from his pursuers,
In the darksome days of battle; Good the isle for thee to dwell in,
Hide one year, and then a second, In the third return in safety
To thy father’s ancient mansion, To my hero’s place of resting.”
THE Isle OF Refuge.
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli, Took provisions in abundance,
Hastened to the Isle of Refuge, Sailed away across the oceans,
“Fare thee well, mine Island-dwelling, I must sail to other borders,
Till the second summer passes; Let the serpents keep the island,
Let the blue-moose roam the mountains, Let the wild-geese eat the barley.
When the warriors of the Northland, From the dismal Sariola,
Asking for my head in vengeance, Say that I have long departed,
When the barley had been garnered.”
Threw the vessel to the waters, From the iron-banded rollers,
On the masts the sails he hoisted, Spread the magic sails of linen,
And prepared to sail his vessel, One hand resting on the rudder.
These the words of Lemminkainen: “Blow, ye winds, and drive me onward,
Toward the island in the ocean, That my bark may fly in safety
To the far and nameless island!”
Rocked the vessel o’er the billows, O’er the blue-back of the waters,
Blew two months and blew unceasing, Blew a third month toward the island,
Sat some maidens on the seaside,
Turned about in all directions, Looking out upon the billows;
And a second for her father, And a third one, anxious, waited
There they spied young Lemminkainen, There perceived the hero’s vessel
It was like a hanging cloudlet, Hanging twixt the earth and heaven.
Thus they spake to one another: “What this stranger on the ocean,
Art thou one of our sea-vessels? Wert thou builded on this island?
To the island-point of landing That thy tribe may be discovered.”
Rocked his vessel o’er the billows, Drove it to the magic island,
On the sandy shore and harbor.
These the words that Ahti uttered: “Is there room upon this island,
Where my bark may lie at anchor, Where the sun may dry my vessel?”
Dwellers on the Isle of Refuge: “There is room within this harbor,
Where thy bark may lie at anchor, Where the sun may dry thy vessel;
Cylinders adorned with copper; If thou hadst a hundred vessels,
We would give them room in welcome.”
Rolled his vessel in the harbor, On the cylinders of copper,
“Is there room upon this island, Or a spot within these forests,
From the coming din of battle, From the play of spears and arrows?”
“There are places on this island, On these plains a spot befitting,
Hero-son of little valor. Here are many, many castles,
Though there come a thousand heroes, Though a thousand spearmen follow,
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “Is there room upon this island,
Where this son may fell the forest, And may cultivate the fallow?”
“There is not a spot befitting, Not a place upon the island,
Not the smallest patch of birch-wood, Thou canst bring to cultivation.
All these woods have been apportioned, Fields and forests have their owners.”
These the words of Kaukomieli: “Is there room upon this island,
Where to sing my songs of magic, Chant my gathered store of wisdom,
Answered thus the Island-maidens: “There is room upon this island,
Thou canst sing thy garnered wisdom, Thou canst chant thine ancient legends,
In the forest, in the castle, On the island-plains and pastures.”
To intone his wizard-sayings; Sang he alders to the waysides,
On the oak-trees sang he branches, On each branch he sang an acorn,
On each roller, sang a cuckoo; Then began the cuckoos, calling,
Copper fell from every feather, And each wing emitted silver,
Sang again young Lemminkainen, Conjured on, and sang, and chanted,
Sang the stones to pearls resplendent, Robed the groves in iridescence,
Many-colored as the rainbow. Sang again the magic minstrel,
On the well a golden cover, On the lid a silver dipper,
That the maids might lave their eyelids. On the plains he conjured lakelets,
Golden-cheeked and silver-headed, Sang the feet from shining copper;
Stood entranced at Ahti’s wisdom, At the songs of Lemminkainen,
Spake the singer, Lemminkainen,
“I would sing a wondrous legend, Sing in miracles of sweetness,
I were seated at the table. If I sing not in the castle,
Then I sing my songs to zephyrs, Fling them to the fields and forests.”
“On this isle are castle-chambers, Halls for use of magic singers,
Where thy singing will be welcome, Where thy songs will not be scattered
Nor thy wisdom lost in ether.”
With the maidens to the castle; There he sang and conjured pitchers
Sang and conjured golden goblets Foaming with the beer of barley;
Bowls of honey-drink abundant, Sweetest butter, toothsome biscuit,
All the dainties of the Northland, Wherewithal to still his hunger.
Was not ready for the banquet, Did not yet begin his feasting,
For a knife of golden handle; Quick he sang the precious metals,
To the blade a golden handle, Straightway then began his feasting,
Charmed the maidens on the island.
Roamed throughout the island-hamlets, To the joy of all the virgins,
Wheresoe’er he turned his footsteps, There appeared a maid to greet him;
There his hand was kindly taken; When he wandered out at evening,
There the maidens bade him welcome; There was not an island-village
In each castle seven daughters, And the daughters stood in waiting,
Only one of all the maidens Whom he did not greet with pleasure.
Spent three summers in the ocean, Spent a merry time in refuge,
To the pleasure of the maidens, To the joy of all the daughters;
She a poor and graceless spinster, On the isle’s remotest border,
Then he thought about his journey
To the cottage of his father. There appeared the slighted spinster,
Spake these words to Lemminkainen: “O, thou handsome Kaukomieli,
Since this maiden thou hast slighted, May the winds destroy thy vessel,
On the ocean-rocks and ledges!”
Did not heed the maiden’s murmurs, Did not rise before the dawning
To the pleasure of the maiden Of the much-neglected hamlet.
He resolved to leave the island, He resolved to waken early,
Long before the time appointed, He arose that he might wander
Bid adieu to all the maidens, On the morn of his departure.
Walking through the village path-ways To the last of all the hamlets;
Where three dwellings were not standing; Saw he none of all the dwellings
Saw he none of all the heroes, Who was not engaged in grinding
For the death of Lemminkainen. And these words the hero uttered: “Now alas! the Sun arises
On the frailest of the heroes, On the saddest child of Northland;
Might protect me from all evil, Though a hundred foes assail me,
Then he left the maids ungreeted,
Of the nameless Isle of Refuge, With his farewell-words unspoken,
Toward his magic bark at anchor; But he found it burned to ashes,
Lighted by the slighted spinster. Then he saw the dawn of evil,
Saw destruction round about him. Straightway he began rebuilding
New and wondrous, full of beauty; But the hero needed timber,
Found the smallest bit of lumber, Found of boards but seven fragments,
Found six pieces of the distaff; With these fragments builds his vessel,
Builds the bark with secret knowledge, Through the will of the magician;
Strikes a second, builds the centre, Strikes a third with wondrous power,
Thereupon the ship he launches,
And these words the hero utters: “Like a bubble swim these waters,
Loan me of thy magic feathers, Three, O eagle, four, O raven,
Lest it flounder in the ocean!”
Seats himself upon the bottom Of the vessel he has builded,
Head depressed and evil-humored, Cap awry upon his forehead,
That he could not dwell forever In the castles of the daughters
Spake the minstrel, Lemminkainen,
“Leave I must this merry island, Leave her many joys and pleasures,
Leave her dances and her daughters, To the joys of other heroes;
All the maidens on the island, Save the spinster who was slighted,
Will regret my quick departure; They will miss me at the dances,
In the homes of merry maidens, On my father’s Isle of Refuge.”
Long lamenting, loudly calling To the hero sailing homeward: “Whither goest, Lemminkainen,
Dost thou leave from inattention, Is there here a dearth of maidens,
Sang the magic Lemminkainen
This in answer to their calling: “Leaving not for want of pleasure,
Beautiful the island-maidens, Countless as the sands their virtues.
I am longing for my home-land, Longing for my mother’s cabins,
For the raspberries of Kalew, For the maidens of my childhood,
Then the merry Lemminkainen
Winds arose and drove his vessel On the blue-back of the ocean,
Toward the island of his mother. On the shore were grouped the daughters
On the rocks sat the forsaken, Weeping stood the island-maidens,
Weep the maidens of the island While the sail-yards greet their vision,
Do not weep to lose the sail-yards, Nor to lose the copper-beltings;
For the fleeing Kaukomieli Guiding the departing vessel.
Sorely weeps, and loud-lamenting, Weeps while he can see the island,
Does not mourn the island-mountains, Weeps he only for the maidens,
Thereupon sailed Kaukomieli
Sailed one day, and then a second, But, alas! upon the third day,
And the sky was black with fury. Blew the black winds from the north-west,
Tore away the ship’s forecastle, Tore away the vessel’s rudder,
Thereupon wild Lemminkainen Headlong fell upon the waters;
With his hands and feet, the rowing; Swam whole days and nights unceasing,
Till at last appeared a cloudlet, Growing cloudlet to the westward,
Into land within the ocean.
Hastened to a magic castle, Found therein a hostess baking,
And these words the hero uttered: “O, thou hostess, filled with kindness,
Couldst thou guess my name and station, Thou wouldst hasten to the storehouse,
Bring the best of thy provisions, Bring me fish, and veal, and bacon,
Set for me a wholesome dinner, Wherewithal to still my hunger,
Days and nights have I been swimming, Buffeting the waves of ocean,
And the billows gave me shelter.”
Hastened to the mountain storehouse, Cut some butter, veal, and bacon,
Brought the best of her provisions, Brought the mead and beer of barley,
Wherewithal to still his hunger, Quench the thirst of Lemminkainen.
Straightway was a magic vessel Given by the kindly hostess
Bark of beauty, new and hardy, Wherewithal to aid the stranger
To the cottage of his mother.
On the blue-back of the ocean; Sailed he days and nights unceasing,
Of his own loved home and country; There beheld he scenes familiar,
Saw his former shipping-stations, Saw he many ancient landmarks,
Saw the pine-trees on the hill-tops, Saw the willows in the lowlands;
Nor the dwellings of his mother. Where a mansion once had risen,
Shrubs were growing on the homestead, Junipers within the court-yard.
“In this glen I played and wandered, On these stones I rocked for ages,
Frolicked on these woodland-borders, When a child of little stature.
Where the castles of my father? Fire, I fear, has found the hamlet,
Then he fell to bitter weeping,
Wept the third day without ceasing; Did not mourn the ancient homestead,
Wept he for his darling mother, Wept he for the dear departed,
Then he saw the bird of heaven,
And he asked the bird this question: “Mighty eagle, bird majestic,
Where my mother may have wandered, Whither I may go and find her!”
Only knew that Ahti’s people Long ago together perished;
That his people had been scattered By the swords, and spears, and arrows,
Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “Faithful mother, dear departed,
Art thou dead and turned to ashes, Didst thou perish for my follies,
Junipers above thy body, Alders watching o’er thy slumbers?
This the recompense of folly! Fool was I, a son unworthy,
With the landlord of Pohyola. To my tribe came fell destruction,
Through my crimes and misdemeanors.”
Anxious, looked in all directions, And beheld some gentle foot-prints,
Where the heather had been beaten. Quick as thought the path he followed,
O’er the hills, and through the valleys, To a forest, vast and cheerless;
Still a greater distance travelled, To a dense and hidden glenwood,
Found therein a sheltered cabin, Found a small and darksome dwelling
In the midst of triple pine-trees; And within he spied his mother,
Lemminkainen loud rejoices,
These the words that Ahti utters: “Faithful mother, well-beloved,
Happy I, that thou art living, That thou hast not yet departed
To the islands of the blessed, I had thought that thou hadst perished,
Hadst been slain with bows and arrows. Heavy are mine eyes from weeping,
Since I thought my mother slaughtered For the sins I had committed!”
“Long, indeed, hast thou been absent, Long, my son, hast thou been living
Roaming on the secret island, Living at the doors of strangers,
Refuge from the Northland foemen.” Spake the hero, Lemminkainen: “Charming is that spot for living,
Rainbow-colored was the forest, Blue the glimmer of the meadows,
Golden were the heather-blossoms; All the woodlands dripped with honey,
Honey flowed from birch and sorb-tree, Milk in streams from fir and aspen,
Charming there to live and linger, All their edibles delicious.
Great the fear for all the maidens, All the heroes filled with envy,
Thought that all the island-maidens, Thought that all the wives and daughters,
Gave thy son too much attention; Thought the stranger, Lemminkainen,
Yet the virgins I avoided, Shunned the good and shunned the evil,
As the black-wolf shuns the sheep-fold, As the hawk neglects the chickens.”
THE Frost-Fiend.
Handsome hero, Kaukomieli, Hastens as the dawn is breaking,
To the resting-place of vessels, To the harbor of the island,
Hears the wailing of the rigging, And the ships intone this chorus: “Must we wretched lie forever
Here to dry and fall in pieces? Ahti wars no more in Northland,
Even should he thirst for silver, Should he wish the gold of battle.”
With his gloves adorned with copper, And addressed the ships as follows: “Mourn no more, my ships of fir-wood,
To the wars ye soon may hasten, Hasten to the seas of battle;
Ere to-morrow’s morn has risen.”
Hastened to his aged mother, Spake to her the words that follow: “Weep no longer, faithful mother,
Should he leave for scenes of battle, For the hostile fields of Pohya;
