And my soul is well determined, To avenge the shameful insult
Gave to thee, defenseless woman.”
Warns her son again of danger: “Do not go, my son beloved,
There the jaws of Death await thee, Fell destruction lies before thee!”
Still determined, speaks as follows: “Where may I secure a swordsman,
To assist me in the combat? Often I have heard of Tiera,
This one I will take to help me, Magic hero of the broadsword;
Will protect me from destruction.”
On the way to Tiera’s hamlet, These the words that Ahti utters
“Dearest friend, my noble Tiera, My beloved hero-brother,
When we fought and bled together, On the battle-fields of Northland?
Where there were not seven mansions, In each mansion seven heroes,
Whom we did not slay with broadswords, Victims of our skill and valor.”
Whittling out a javelin-handle; Near the threshold sat the mother
Near the portal stood the brother Working on a sledge of birch-wood;
Washing out their varied garments.
From the threshold spake the mother, From the portals spake the brother,
“Tiera has no time for combat, And his broadsword cannot battle;
Still unveiled his bride awaits him.”
Lying by the fire was Kura, Hastily one foot was shoeing,
From the hook he takes his girdle, Buckles it around his body,
Not the largest, nor the smallest, Buckles on his mighty scabbard,
On each javelin pranced a charger, Wolves were howling from his helmet,
Tiera poised his mighty javelin, Launched the spear upon its errand;
To the border of the forest, O’er the clay-fields of Pohyola,
Through the distant hills of Northland. Then great Tiera touched his javelin
Pledged his aid to Lemminkainen, As his combatant and comrade.
Pushed his boat upon the waters; Like the serpent through the heather,
Sails the boat away to Pohya, O’er the seas of Sariola.
Sends the black-frost of the heavens To the waters of Pohyola,
Gave the black-frost these directions: “Much-loved Frost, my son and hero,
Hasten whither I may send thee, Go wherever I command thee,
Lemminkainen’s bark of magic, On the broad back of the ocean,
Freeze the wizard in his vessel, Freeze to ice the wicked Ahti,
Never waken while thou livest, Or at least till I shall free him,
Frost, the son of wicked parents,
Hastens off to freeze the ocean, Goes to fasten down the flood-gates,
As he hastens on his journey, Takes the leaves from all the forest,
Robs the flowers of their colors. When his journey he had ended,
Gained the sea-shore curved and endless, On the first night of his visit,
Freezes too the shore of ocean, Freezes not the ocean-billows,
On the sea a finch is resting, Bird of song upon the waters,
Neither is his head endangered. When the second night Frost lingered,
He became a fierce intruder, Fearless grew in his invasions,
Sends the fiercest cold of Northland, Turns to ice the boundless waters.
Grew the ice on sea and ocean, Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
Froze the hero’s ship of beauty, Cold and lifeless bark of Ahti;
Freeze him lifeless as his vessel, Asked the minstrel for his life-blood,
Then the hero, Lemminkainen,
Hurled the black-frost to the fire-god, Threw him to the fiery furnace,
Then addressed the frost as follows: “Frost, thou evil son of Northland,
Let my members not be stiffened, Neither ears, nor feet, nor fingers,
Thou hast other things to feed on, Many other heads to stiffen;
Let this minstrel pass in safety, Freeze the swamps, and lakes, and rivers,
Let the cold stones grow still colder, Freeze the willows in the waters,
Let the bark peel from the birch-trees, Let the pines burst on the mountains,
Do not let his locks be stiffened.
“If all these prove insufficient,
Let the hot stones freeze asunder, Let the flaming rocks be frozen,
Freeze to ice the iron mountains; Stiffen well the mighty Wuoksi,
Freeze the sacred stream and whirlpool, Let their boiling billows stiffen,
Tell thy lineage of evil. Well I know thine evil nature,
Whence thou camest, where thou goest, Know thine ancestry of evil.
Wert conceived upon the willows, Near the borders of Pohyola,
Sin-begotten was thy father, And thy mother was Dishonor.
“While in infancy who fed thee
Surely thou wert fed by adders, Nursed by foul and slimy serpents;
Cradled thee in roughest weather, In the worst of willow-marshes,
Evil-born and evil-nurtured, Grew to be an evil genius,
And the infant still was nameless, Till the name of Frost was given
“Then the young lad lived in hedges,
Lived in springs in days of summer, On the borders of the marshes,
Stormed among the glens and forests, Raged among the sacred birch-trees,
Froze the trees, the shoots, the grasses, Evened all the plains and prairies,
Made the stalks drop down their blossoms, Peeled the bark on weeds and willows.
“Thou hast grown to large proportions,
Dost thou labor to benumb me, Dost thou wish mine ears and fingers,
Do not strive to freeze this hero, In his anguish and misfortune;
Fire to drive thee from my presence, In my shoes lay flaming faggots,
Heated sandstones in my rigging; Thus will hold thee at a distance.
To the farthest Northland borders; When thy journey is completed,
Freeze the caldrons in the castle, Freeze the coal upon the hearthstone,
On its mother’s lap, the infant, Freeze the colt beside its mother.
“If thou shouldst not heed this order,
To the carbon-piles of Hisi, To the chimney-hearth of Lempo,
Lay thee on the iron anvil, That thy body may be hammered
May be pounded into atoms, Twixt the anvil and the hammer.
“If thou shouldst not heed this order,
Know I still another kingdom, Know another spot of resting;
Lead thy tongue to warmer climates, There a prisoner to suffer,
Till thy spirit I deliver, Till I go myself and free thee.”
Saw the magic bird of evil Hovering above his spirit,
These the words the Frost-fiend uttered: “Let us now agree together,
Never in the course of ages, Never while the moonlight glimmers
If thou hearest that I bring thee Cold to freeze thy feet and fingers,
Hammer me upon the anvil Of the blacksmith, Ilmarinen;
Banish me to lands of summer, There a prisoner to suffer,
Thereupon wild Lemminkainen
Frozen in the ice of Northland, Left his warlike boat forever,
To the borders of Pohyola, And the mighty Tiera followed
On the ice they journeyed northward Briskly walked upon the ice-plain,
Till the closing of the third day, When the Hunger-land approached them,
Here the hardy Lemminkainen
This the hero’s prayer and question: “Is there food within this castle,
To refresh us on our journey, Mighty heroes, cold and weary?
Found no food within the castle, Neither fish, nor fowl, nor bacon,
“May the fire destroy these chambers, May the waters flood this dwelling,
Then they hastened onward, onward,
Over by-ways long untrodden, Over unknown paths and snow-fields;
Reckless hero, Kaukomieli, Pulled the soft wool from the ledges,
Wove them into magic stockings, Wove them into shoes and mittens,
In the stinging cold of Northland.
That would guide their wayward footsteps, And the hero spake as follows: “O thou Tiera, friend beloved,
Wandering for days together, Through these Northland fields and forests?”
“We, alas! have come for vengeance, Come for blood and retribution,
To the dismal Sariola, Here to leave our souls and bodies,
In the dreariest of places, In this sun-forsaken country!
Never learn it, never tell it, Which the pathway that can guide us
To the Pohya-plains to perish, In the home-land of the ravens,
Often do the Northland vultures Hither come to feed their fledgelings;
Bits of flesh and blood of heroes; Often do the beaks of ravens
Often do the eagle’s talons Carry bones and trembling vitals,
In their rocky homes and ledges.
“Oh! my mother can but wonder,
Where her reckless son is roaming, Where her hero’s blood is flowing,
Whether in the heat of battle, Or upon the waves of the ocean,
Or along some forest by-way. Nothing can her mind discover
Only think that he has perished. Thus the hoary-headed mother
‘Where is now my son beloved, In the kingdom of Manala?
Harrow well the fields of Kalma! Now the bow receives its respite
Bow and arrow now are useless, Now the merry birds can fatten
Bears may live in dens of freedom, On the fields may sport the elk-herds.’”
“Thus it is, mine aged mother, Thou that gavest me existence!
Hatched and reared thy flights of white-swans, All of them the winds have scattered,
One flew hither, and one thither, And a third one, lost forever!
Of our better days together, When I wandered like the flowers,
Many saw my form majestic, Many thought me well-proportioned.
Into evil days have fallen, Since I see but storms and darkness!
Then we did not weep and murmur, Did not fill our hearts with sorrow,
When the virgins twined their tresses; Then the women joined in joyance,
Whether bridegrooms choose discreetly, Whether they were wise or unwise.
“But we must not grow disheartened,
Here we are not yet enchanted, Not bewitched by magic singing,
Sink and perish on our journey. Full of youth we should not suffer,
Whom the wizards have enchanted, Have bewitched with songs of magic;
Bury them within their dungeons, Hide them spell-bound in their cabins.
And bewitch their magic offspring, Bring their tribes to fell destruction.
Bow submission to a wizard, Offer worship to magicians.
These the thoughts his son advances: ‘Guard us, thou O great Creator,
With thine arms of grace protect us, Help us with thy strength and wisdom,
Keep aright the thoughts of women, Keep the old from speaking evil,
Be to us a help forever, Be our Guardian and our Father,
From the ways of their Creator, From the path that God has given!’”
Made from cares the fleetest racers, Sable racers from his sorrows,
From his sacred pains made saddles. To the saddle, quickly springing,
To his dear and aged mother; And his comrade, faithful Tiera,
Now departs wild Lemminkainen,
From these ancient songs and legends; Only guides his faithful Kura
While these lays and incantations Shall be turned to other heroes.
Kullerwoinen Son of Evil.
Hatched and raised some swans and chickens, Placed the chickens in the brushwood,
Came an eagle, hawk, and falcon, Scattered all her swans and chickens,
And a second into Ehstland, Left a third at home in Pohya.
Soon became a thriving merchant; He that journeyed to Karyala
He that hid away in Pohya Took the name of Untamoinen,
To the heart-pain of his mother.
In the waters of Kalervo; Kullerwoinen sees the fish-nets,
Then Untamo, evil-minded, Angry grew and sighed for vengeance,
Bared his mighty arms for battle, For the stealing of his salmon,
Long they battled, fierce the struggle, Neither one could prove the victor;
He himself was fiercely beaten.
On the second and the third days, Kalerwoinen sowed some barley
Untamoinen’s sheep in hunger Ate the crop of Kullerwoinen;
Tore Untamo’s sheep in pieces; Then Untamo sorely threatened
Of his brother, Kalerwoinen, To exterminate his tribe-folk,
To out-root his race and kingdom; Conjures men with broadswords girded,
Fashions youth with spears adjusted, Bearing axes on their shoulders;
Hastens to begin a battle, Bring a war upon his brother.
Sat beside her chamber-window, Looking out along the highway,
“Do I see some smoke arising, Or perchance a heavy storm-cloud,
Near the ending of the prairie?”
Nor indeed a heavy storm-cloud, It was Untamoinen’s soldiers
Warriors of Untamoinen Came equipped with spears and arrows,
Slew his tribe and all his kindred, Burned to ashes many dwellings,
Only left Kalervo’s daughter, With her unborn child, survivors
And she led the hostile army To her father’s halls and mansion,
Gave the heroes home-attentions.
Ere a boy was born in magic Of the virgin, Untamala,
Him the mother named Kullervo, “Pearl of Combat,” said Untamo.
Fatherless, the magic infant, In the cradle of attention,
But he rocked himself at pleasure, Rocked until his locks stood endwise;
Rocked the third from morn till noontide; But before the third day ended,
Forwards, backwards, upwards, downwards, Kicks in miracles of power,
Creeping from beneath his blankets, Knocks his cradle into fragments,
Seemed that he would grow a hero, And his mother, Untamala,
When he found his strength and reason, Would become a great magician,
When three months the boy had thriven,
“When my form is full of stature, When these arms grow strong and hardy,
Of Kalervo and his people!”
Speaks these words to those about him: “To my tribe he brings destruction,
Then the heroes well considered,
How to kill the magic infant, That their tribe may live in safety.
Finally, they all consenting, He was placed within a basket,
Taken to the reeds and rushes, Lowered to the deepest waters,
When three nights had circled over,
Went to see if he had perished In his basket in the waters;
Had not perished in the rushes; He had left his willow-basket,
In his hand a rod of copper, On the rod a golden fish-line,
Measuring the deeps beneath him; In the sea was little water,
Untamoinen then reflected,
“Whither shall we take this wonder, Lay this prodigy of evil,
Where the boy will sink and perish?”
To collect dried poles of brushwood, Birch-trees with their hundred branches,
Ordered that a pyre be builded, That the boy might be cremated,
High they piled the arid branches, Dried limbs from the sacred birch-tree,
Knots and branches full of resign; Filled with bark a thousand sledges,
Piled the brushwood to the tree-tops, Set the boy upon the summit,
Burned one day, and then a second, Burned the third from morn till evening.
To inspect the pyre and wizard, There to learn if young Kullervo
There they saw the young boy sitting On a pyramid of embers,
Raking coals of fire about him, To increase their heat and power;
Not a ringlet singed nor shrivelled.
Thus addressed his trusted heralds: “Whither shall the boy be taken,
That destruction may o’ertake him. That the boy may sink and perish?”
Crucified him in the branches, That the wizard there might perish.
Untamoinen spake as follows: “It is time to send my heralds
There to learn if young Kullervo Lives or dies among the branches.”
And the heralds brought this message: “Young Kullervo has not perished,
Of the oak-tree where we hung him. In the oak he maketh pictures
Pictures hang from all the branches, Carved and painted by Kullervo;
With their swords and spears adjusted, Fill the branches of the oak-tree,
Who can help the grave Untamo
To Untamo’s tribe and country, Since he will not die by water,
Finally it was decided That his body was immortal,
In despair grave Untamoinen
“Wilt thou live a life becoming, Always do my people honor,
Shouldst thou render servant’s duty, Then thou wilt receive thy wages,
Thou canst wear the golden girdle, Or endure the tongue of censure.”
Had increased in strength and stature, He was given occupation,
Made to rock the infant’s cradle. These the words of Untamoinen: “Often look upon the young child,
Wash his linen in the river, Give the infant good attention.”
Nurses one day then a second; On the morning of the third day,
Blinds its eyes and breaks its fingers; And when evening shadows gather,
Throws its body to the waters, Breaks and burns the infant’s cradle.
“Never will this fell Kullervo Be a worthy nurse for children,
Do not know how I can use him, What employment I can give him!”
He must fell the standing forest, And Kullervo gave this answer: “Only will I be a hero,
I am young, and fair, and mighty, Far more beautiful than others,
Thereupon he sought the blacksmith,
“Listen, O thou metal-artist, Forge for me an axe of copper,
Wherewith I may fell the forest, Fell the birch, and oak, and aspen.”
Forges him an axe of copper, Wonderful the blade he forges.
Grinds his blade from morn till evening, And the next day makes the handle;
To the upward-sloping mountain, To the tallest of the birches,
There he swings his axe of copper, Swings his blade with might of magic,
With one blow he fells the oak-tree, With a second blow, the linden;
By the hatchet of Kullervo. Then the wizard spake as follows: “This the proper work of Lempo,
In the birch he sank his hatchet,
Called aloud in tones of thunder, Whistled to the distant mountains,
When Kullervo spake as follows: “May the forest, in the circle
In the earth be lost forever! May no tree remain unlevelled,
Never while the moonlight glimmers, Where Kullervo’s voice has echoed,
Where the ground with seed is planted, And the grain shall sprout and flourish,
May the ears of corn be blasted!”
Went to look at early evening, How Kullervo was progressing,
Little was the work accomplished, Was not worthy of a hero;
“Young Kullervo is not fitted For the work of clearing forests,
To my lands he brings destruction; I shall set him making fences.”
Of a fence for Untamoinen; Took the trunks of stately fir-trees,
Cut the tallest in the woodlands, For the railing of his fences;
From the longest of the lindens; Made the fence without a pass-way,
And Kullervo spake these measures: “He that does not rise as eagles,
Cannot cross Kullervo’s pickets, Nor the fences he has builded.”
To inspect the young boy’s labors, View the fences of Kullervo;
Not a wicket in his fences; From the earth the fence extended
These the words of Untamoinen: “For this work he is not fitted,
Is so high that none can cross it, And there is no passage through it:
Young Kullervo, quick preparing,
Threshed the rye to finest powder, Threshed the barley into atoms,
Untamoinen went at evening,
View the work of Kullerwoinen; Found the rye was ground to powder,
And the straw to worthless rubbish.
Spake these words in bitter accents: “Kullerwoinen as a workman
Whatsoever work he touches Is but ruined by his witchcraft;
In Karyala I shall sell him To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Untamoinen sells Kullervo,
To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen, To the master of the metals,
Seven worn and worthless sickles, Three old caldrons worse than useless,
Recompense, indeed, sufficient For a boy that will not labor
Kullervo As a Shepherd.
Of the blacksmith, Ilmarinen, Purchased slave from Untamoinen,
With a head of golden ringlets, In his shoes of marten-leather,
Asked the host for work at morning, In the evening asked the hostess,
“Give me work at early morning, In the evening, occupation,
Then the wife of Ilmarinen,
Thinking long, and long debating, How to give the youth employment,
Finally a shepherd made him, Made him keeper of her pastures;
Baked a biscuit for the herdsman, Baked a loaf of wondrous thickness,
And the upper-half of barley, Baked a flint-stone in the centre,
Then she gave it to the shepherd, Food to still the herdsman’s hunger;
“Do not eat the bread in hunger, Till the herd is in the woodlands!”
Sent her cattle to the pasture, Thus addressing Kullerwoinen: “Drive the cows to yonder bowers,
That they there may feed and fatten, Fill themselves with milk and butter,
On the distant hills and mountains, In the glens among the birch-trees,
In the golden pine-tree forests, In the thickets silver-laden.
“Guard them, thou O kind Creator,
Shelter them from every danger, And protect them from all evil,
From the paths of peace and plenty. As at home Thou didst protect them
Guard them now beneath the heavens, Shelter them in woodland pastures,
To the joy of Northland’s hostess, And against the will of Lempo.
“If my herdsman prove unworthy,
Let the pastures be their shepherds, Let the alders guard the cattle,
Let the willow drive them homeward, Ere the hostess go to seek them,
Should the birch-tree not protect them, Nor the aspen lend assistance,
Nor the willow drive them homeward, Wilt thou give them better herdsmen,
Be their kindly shepherdesses. Thou hast many lovely maidens,
In the Ether’s spacious circles, Beauteous daughters of creation.
“Summer-daughter, magic maiden,
Pine-tree daughter, Kateyatar, Pihlayatar, of the aspen,
Daughter of the glen, Millikki, And the mountain-maid, Tellervo,
Keep them from the evil-minded, Keep them safe in days of summer,
While the tender leaves are whispering, While the Earth is verdure-laden.
“Summer-daughter, charming maiden,
Spread abroad thy robes of safety, Spread thine apron o’er the forest,
And protect the unprotected, That no evil winds may harm them,
Guard my flocks from every danger, Keep them from the hands of wild-beasts,
From the springs that bubble trouble, From the swiftly running waters,
That they may not find misfortune, May not wander to destruction,
Though against God’s best intentions, Though against the will of Ukko.
“From a distance bring a bugle,
Bring the honey-flute of Ukko, Play the music of creation,
Play the flowers on the highlands, Charm the hills, and dales, and mountains,
Fill the forest-trees with honey, Fill with spice the fountain-borders.
“For my herds give food and shelter,
Give them drink at honeyed fountains Feed them on thy golden grasses,
From the springs of life and beauty, From the crystal-waters flowing,
From the uplands green and golden, From the glens enriched in silver.
On the four sides of the willow, That the cows may drink in sweetness,
That their milk may flow in streamlets; Let the milk be caught in vessels,
Be not given to Manala.
“Many are the sons of evil,
Give their milk to evil-doers, Waste it in Tuoni’s empire;
That can get the milk from Mana; Never did my ancient mother
Never in the courts for wisdom; She obtained her milk from Mana,
Sweet-milk from the greater distance, From the kingdom of Manala,
Brought it in the dusk of evening, Through the by-ways in the darkness,
That it should not find destruction.
“This the language of my mother,
‘Whither does the cow’s gift wander, Whither has the milk departed?
Banished to the distant village, Gone to feed the hamlet-lover,
Disappeared within the woodlands, Scattered o’er the hills and mountains,
It shall never go to Mana, Never go to feed the stranger,
Neither shall it feed the forest, Nor be lost upon the mountains,
Nor be mingled with the waters; It is needed for our tables,
“Summer-daughter, maid of beauty,
Give Suotikki tender fodder, To Watikki, give pure water,
Fresh provisions to Tuorikki, From Mairikki let the milk flow,
Coming from the tips of grasses, From the tender herbs and leaflets,
From the mother of the forest, From the meadows sweetly dripping,
From the heath of flower-maidens, From the verdure-maiden bowers,
From the virgin of the heavens, That the milk may flow abundant
To the keeping of Kullervo.
“Rise thou virgin of the valley,
Rise thou maiden of the fountain, Beautiful, arise in ether,
And my roaming herds besprinkle, That my cows may drink and flourish,
Of the shepherdess of evening.
“O Millikki, forest-hostess,
Send the tallest of thy servants, Send the best of thine assistants,
Through the pleasant days of summer, Given us by our Creator.
“Beauteous virgin of the woodlands,
Fair Tellervo, forest-maiden, Softly clad in silken raiment,
Do thou give my herds protection, In the Metsola dominions,
Shield them with thy hands of beauty, Stroke them gently with thy fingers,
Make them shine like fins of salmon, Grow them robes as soft as ermine.
“When the evening star brings darkness,
Send my lowing cattle homeward, Milk within their vessels coursing,
When the Sun has set in ocean, When the evening-bird is singing,
“Ye that carry horns, now hasten
Ye enriched in milk go homeward, To the hostess now in waiting,
Forest-beds are full of danger; When the evening comes in darkness,
Building fires to light the pathway On the turf enriched in honey,
“Thou, O Tapio’s son, Nyrikki,
Cut the fir-trees on the mountains, Cut the pines with cones of beauty,
Cover well the sloughs of quicksand, In the swamps and in the lowlands,
On their long and dismal journey, To the clouds of smoke may hasten,
If the cows heed not this order, Do not hasten home at evening,
Cut a birch-rod from the glenwood, From the juniper, a whip-stick,
Standing on the ash-tree mountain, Drive my wayward, lowing cattle,
When the evening-star is rising.
“Thou, O Otso, forest-apple,
Let us make a lasting treaty, Make a vow for future ages,
Wilt not eat my milk-providers; That I will not send my hunters
Never in the days of summer, The Creator’s warmest season.
“Dost thou hear the tones of cow-bells,
Hide thyself within the meadow, Sink upon the turf in slumber,
Crouch within some alder-thicket Climb between the mossy ledges,
Flee away to other mountains, Till thou canst not hear the cow-bells,
“Listen, Otso of the woodlands,
To approach the herd of cattle Thou thyself art not forbidden,
Must not touch my herd in summer, Must not harm my harmless creatures.
Amble through the milky pastures, From the tones of bells and shepherds.
Go thou quickly to the marshes; Should my cattle browse the lowlands,
Should they feed upon the uplands, Thou must hasten to the valley;
Thou must feed upon the summit.
“Wander like the golden cuckoo,
Like a little fish in ocean; Hide thy claws within thy hair-foot,
That my herd may not be frightened, May not think themselves in danger.
Let them journey home in order, Through the vales and mountain by-ways,
Harming not my harmless creatures.
“Call to mind our former pledges,
Near the waterfall and whirlpool, In the ears of our Creator.
In the circuit of the summer, To approach the land of cow-bells,
But to thee it was not granted, Otso never had permission
To begin a work of evil. Should the blinding thing of malice
Should thy bloody teeth feel hunger, Throw thy malice to the mountains,
Sink thy teeth within the aspens, In the dead limbs of the birches,
Should thy hunger still impel thee, Go thou to the berry-mountain,
Feed thy hunger on the ant-hills, Eat the red roots of the bear-tree,
Not the grass my herd would feed on. Or if Metsola’s rich honey
On the hills of golden color, On the mountains filled with silver,
Other drink for thirsting Otso, Everlasting will the food be,
“Let us now agree in honor,
That our lives may end in pleasure, May be merry in the summer,
Though our food must be distinctive. Shouldst thou still desire to fight me,
Let our wars be on the snow-fields. Swamps will thaw in days of summer,
Therefore shouldst thou break this treaty, Shouldst thou come where golden cattle
We will slay thee with our cross-bows; Should our arrow-men be absent,
And among them is the hostess, That can use the fatal weapon,
Thus will end the days of trouble That thou bringest to our people,
“Ukko, ruler in the heavens,
Metamorphose all my cattle, Through the mighty force of magic,
If the enemy should wander, Near my herd in days of summer.
“If I had been born an Otso,
At the feet of aged women; Elsewhere there are hills and valleys,
Where the lazy bear may wander, Where the indolent may linger;
That thy tender flesh may lessen, In the blue-glen’s deep recesses,
Thou canst move through fields of acorns, Through the sand and ocean-pebbles,
Through the woodlands on the sea-coast, To the Northland’s farthest limits,
There ’tis well for thee to lumber, There to live will be a pleasure.
Stockingless in days of autumn, On the blue-back of the mountain,
“If thou canst not journey thither,
Hasten on a little distance, In the bear-path leading northward.
To the honey-plains of Kalma, Swamps there are in which to wander,
There are Kiryos, there are Karyos, And of beasts a countless number,
Fattening within the forest. Be ye gracious, groves and mountains,
Peace and plenty to my cattle, Through the pleasant days of summer,
“Knippana, O King of forests,
Watch thy dogs in fen and fallow, Lay a sponge within one nostril,
That they may not scent my cattle; Tie their eyes with silken fillets,
May not see my cattle grazing.
“Should all this seem inefficient,
Let them run to other forests, Let them hunt in other marshes,
From these far outstretching borders, Hide thy dogs within thy caverns,
Tie them with thy golden fetters, With thy chains adorned with silver,
May not do a deed of mischief.
“Should all this prove inefficient,
Wise director, full of mercy, Hear the golden words I utter,
From the alder make a muzzle, For each dog within the kennel;
Cast a band of purest copper; Should the copper prove a failure,
Should the iron snap asunder, In each nose a small-ring fasten,
Chain thy dogs in forest-caverns, That my herd may not be injured.”
Life-companion of the blacksmith, Opened all her yards and stables,
Placed them in the herdman’s keeping, In the care of Kullerwoinen.
Kullervo and the Cheat-Cake.
Laid his luncheon in his basket, Drove the herd to mountain-pastures,
To their grazings in the woodlands, Speaking as he careless wandered: “Of the youth am I the poorest,
Evil luck to me befallen! I, alas! must idly wander
As a watch-dog for the cattle!”
In a sunny spot selected, Singing, chanting words as follow: “Shine, O shine, thou Sun of heaven,
On the herdsman of the blacksmith, On the head of Kullerwoinen,
Not in Ilmarinen’s smithy, Nor the dwellings of his people;
Cuts the best of wheaten biscuit, Honey-cakes she cuts in slices,
Only dry bread has the herdsman, Eats with pain the oaten bread-crusts,
Feeds upon the worst of straw-bread, Pine-tree bark, the bread he feeds on,
Drinking from the tips of grasses! Go, O Sun, and go, O barley,
Hide within the mountain pine-trees, Go, O wheat, to yonder thickets,
To the junipers and alders, Safely lead the herdsman homeward
To the honeyed cakes and viands!”
Kullerwoinen’s song and echo, Ilmarinen’s wife was feasting
On the toothsome cakes of barley, On the richest of provisions;
For the herdsman, Kullerwoinen; Set apart some wasted fragments,
For the shepherd, home returning.
Sang this song to Kullerwoinen: “’Tis the time for forest-dinners,
Of the herds to eat his viands, Eat the good things from his basket!”
Looked upon the Sun’s long shadow, Straightway spake the words that follow: “True, the singing of the song-bird,
Time to eat my basket-dinner.”
Called his herd to rest in safety, Sat upon a grassy hillock,
Took therefrom the arid oat-loaf, Turned it over in his fingers,
Spake these words of ancient wisdom: “Many loaves are fine to look on,
On the inside, chaff and tan-bark!”
Drew his knife to cut his oat-loaf, Cut the hard and arid biscuit;
Well imbedded in the centre, Breaks his ancient knife in pieces;
Saw his magic knife had broken, Weeping sore, he spake as follows: “This, the blade that I hold sacred,
Relic of my mother’s people! On the stone within this oat-loaf,
I my precious knife have broken. How shall I repay this insult,
What the wages for deception?” From a tree the raven answered: “O thou little silver buckle,
Why art thou in evil humor, Wherefore sad in thy demeanor?
Take a birch-rod from the valley, Drive thy herd across the lowlands,
To the wolves let one half wander, To the bear-dens, lead the other;
Sing the bears down from the mountains, Call the wolves thy little children,
Drive them like a cow-herd homeward, Drive them home like spotted cattle,
Thus thou wilt repay the hostess For her malice and derision.”
These the words of Kullerwoinen: “Wait, yea wait, thou bride of Hisi!
Mourn the keep-sake thou hast broken? Thou thyself shalt mourn as sorely
From the tree he cuts a birch-wand,
Drives the herd across the lowlands, Through the quicksands of the marshes,
To the bear-dens leads the other; Calls the wolves his little children,
Changes all his herd of cattle Into wolves and bears by magic.
Telling that the night is coming. Quick the wizard, Kullerwoinen,
Hastens through the forest homeward, Drives the wolves and bears before him
To the herd he speaks as follows, As they journey on together: “Tear and kill the wicked hostess,
When she comes to view her cattle, When she stoops to do her milking!”
From an ox-bone makes a bugle, Makes it from Tuonikki’s cow-horn,
Plays a song upon his bugle, Plays upon his flute of magic,
Six times near the coming gate-ways.
Long had waited for the coming Of her herd with Kullerwoinen,
Waited for the new-made butter, Heard the footsteps in the cow-path,
Spake these joyous words of welcome: “Be thou praised, O gracious Ukko,
But I hear a bugle sounding, ’Tis the playing of my herdsman,
Bursting all our ears with music!”
To the hostess spake as follows: “Found the bugle in the woodlands,
All thy herd are in the passage, All thy cows within the hurdles,
This the time to do the milking!”
Thus addressed an aged servant: “Go, thou old one, to the milking,
Do not ask for mine assistance, Since I have to knead the biscuit.”
“Always does the worthy hostess, Ever does the wisdom-mother
Tend the cows within the hurdles!”
Built a field-fire in the passage, Went to milk her cows awaiting,
Spake these happy words of greeting: “Beautiful, my herd of cattle,
Hair as soft as fur of ermine, Peaceful waiting for the milk-pail!”
Milks one moment, then a second, Then a third time milks and ceases;
Quick attack the hostess milking, And the bears lend their assistance,
With their teeth and sharpened fingers. Kullerwoinen, cruel wizard,
Thus repaid her evil treatment.
Cried aloud in bitter anguish, Thus addressed the youth, Kullervo: “Evil son, thou bloody herdsman,
Driven bears within my hurdles!” These the words of Kullerwoinen: “Have I evil done as shepherd,
Baked a stone inside my oat-cake, On the inside, rock and tan-bark,
Treasure of my mother’s household, Broken virtue of my people!”
“Noble herdsman, Kullerwoinen, Change, I pray thee, thine opinion,
From the bears and wolves release me, Save me from this spell of torture;
Give the best of milk and butter, Set for thee the sweetest table;
Need not labor for thy keeping. If thou dost not free me quickly,
I shall sink into the Death-land, Shall return to Tuonela.”
“It is best that thou shouldst perish, Let destruction overtake thee,
Room for all the dead in Kalma, There the worthiest must slumber,
Ilmarinen’s wife made answer: “Ukko, thou O God in heaven,
Test the weapon by thy wisdom, Lay an arrow forged from copper,
Rightly aim thy flaming arrow, With thy magic hurl the missile,
Pierce the heart of Kullerwoinen With the lightning of the heavens,
Kullerwoinen prays as follows: “Ukko, God of truth and justice.
Slay the wife of Ilmarinen, Kill in her the worst of women,
Lest she wander hence in freedom, To perform some other mischief,
Quick as lightning fell the hostess,
Fell and perished in the hurdles, On the ground before her cottage;
Cherished wife of Ilmarinen, Once the Maiden of the Rainbow,
Pride and joy of Kalevala!
Kullervo Finds His Tribe-Folk.
In his beauteous, golden ringlets, In his magic shoes of deer-skin,
Wandered forth upon his journey, Ere the blacksmith heard the tidings
Of his wife and joy-companion, Lest a bloody fight should follow.
Blowing on his magic bugle, Joyful left the lands of Ilma,
Made the distant hills re-echo, Made the swamps and mountains tremble,
To the music of his cow-horn, In its wild reverberations,
Songs were heard within the smithy, And the blacksmith stopped and listened,
Hastened to the open court-yard, If perchance he might discover
What was sounding through the forest. Quick he learned the cruel story,
Saw the hostess dead before him, Knew his beauteous wife had perished,
In the court-yard of his dwelling. Thereupon the metal-artist
Wept through all the dreary night-time, Deep the grief that settled o’er him,
Could not stay his tears of sorrow.
Straying, roaming, hither, thither, Wandered on through field and forest,
When the darkness settled o’er him, When the bird of night was flitting,
The forsaken sat and rested On a hillock of the forest.
“Why was I, alas! created, Why was I so ill-begotten,
Lost among the ether-spaces? Others have their homes to dwell in,
As the evening gathers round them: But my home is in the forest,
And my bath-room is the rain-cloud.
“Never didst thou, God of mercy,
Give an infant birth unwisely; Wherefore then was I created,
Motherless and lone to wander? Thou, O Ukko, art my father,
As the sea-gull on the ocean, As the duck upon the waters,
Shines as bright upon the sparrow, Gives the joy-birds song and gladness,
Nevermore will shine the sunlight, Never will the moonlight glimmer
Do not know my hero-father, Cannot tell who was my mother;
Left me in the sand to perish. Young was I and small of stature,
Dead, my father and my mother, Dead, my honored tribe of heroes;
Stockings filled with frosts of ages, Let me on the freezing ice-plains
From the giddy heights of mountains Let me tumble to destruction.
“O, thou wise and good Creator,
I shall never fall and perish On the ice-plains, in the marshes,
Not while I have arms of virtue That can serve my honored kindred!”
To the village of Untamo, To avenge his father’s murder,
And the troubles of his tribe-folk. These the words of Kullerwoinen: “Wait, yea wait, thou Untamoinen,
When I meet thee in the combat, I will slay thee and thy kindred,
Came a woman on the highway,
To Kullervo spake as follows: “Whither goest, Kullerwoinen,
Kullerwoinen gave this answer: “I have thought that I would journey
To the village of Untamo, To avenge my father’s murder,
And the troubles of my tribe-folk.” Thus the gray-haired woman answered: “Surely thou dost rest in error,
And thy mother still is living With thy father in the Northland,
“O, thou ancient dame beloved,
Tell me where my father liveth, Where my loving mother lingers!”
“Yonder lives thine aged father,
On the farthest shore of Northland, On the long-point of the fish-lake!”
“Tell me, O thou woodland-mother,
How to find mine honored tribe-folk.”
“Easy is the way for strangers:
Hasten to the river-border, Travel one day, then a second,
To the north-west, thou must journey. If a mountain comes to meet thee,
Westward hold thy weary journey, Till thou comest to a river,
Travel to the river border, Where three water-falls will greet thee;
On the point thou’lt see a cottage Where the fishermen assemble;
With thy mother and her daughters, Beautiful thy maiden sisters.”
Hastens northward on his journey, Walks one day, and then a second,
To the north-west walks Kullervo, Till a mountain comes to meet him,
Westward, westward, holds his journey, Till he sees a river coming;
Walks along the streams and rapids Till three waterfalls accost him;
On the point he spies a cottage, Where the fishermen assemble.
Quick he passes through the portals Of the cottage on the headland,
No one knows the youth, Kullervo, No one knows whence comes the stranger,
These the words of young Kullervo: “Dost thou know me not, my mother,
I am hapless Kullerwoinen, Whom the heroes of Untamo
When my height was but a hand-breadth.” Quick the hopeful mother answers: “O my worthy son, beloved,
Hast thou with thy mind of magic, Wandered through the fields of Northland
As one dead I long have mourned thee, Had supposed thee in Manala.
Had two good and beauteous daughters, Two of these have long been absent,
For the wars my son departed, While my daughter strayed and perished;
Yet my daughter still is absent.” Kullerwoinen asked his mother: “Whither did my sister wander,
This the answer of the mother: “This the story of thy sister:
To the mountains went my daughter, Where the lovely maiden vanished,
Died some death beyond my knowledge, Nameless is the death she suffered.
No one mourns her as her mother, Walks and wanders, mourns and searches,
Therefore did the mother wander, Searching for thy lovely sister,
Ran the glenways like the adder, Searched one day and then a second,
Till she reached the mountain-summit, There she called and called her daughter,
Called to her who had departed: ‘Where art thou, my lovely maiden,
“Thus I called, and sought thy sister,
Thus the hills and valleys echoed: ‘Call no more, thou weeping mother,
Nevermore in all thy lifetime, Never in the course of ages,
At her brother’s landing-places, In her father’s humble dwelling.’”
Kullervo’S Evil Deeds.
In his blue and scarlet stockings, Henceforth lingered with his parents;
Could not gain a higher wisdom, Could not win a better judgment;
Early rocked in stupid cradles, By a nurse of many follies,
To his work went Kullerwoinen,
First, Kullervo went a-fishing, Set his fishing-nets in ocean;
Kullerwoinen spake as follows: “Shall I pull with all my forces,
Or with weakness of the aged?”
And he answered thus Kullervo: “Pull with all thy youthful vigor;
Thou couldst not destroy this vessel, Couldst not row this boat to fragments.”
Rowed with all his youthful vigor, With the mighty force of magic,
Ribs of juniper he shattered, Rowed the aspen-oars to pieces.
Saw the work of Kullerwoinen, He addressed his son as follows: “Dost not understand the rowing;
Bands of juniper and willow, Rowed my aspen-boat to pieces;
This, perchance, will suit thee better.”
Hastened to his work as bidden, Drove the salmon to the fish-nets,
“Shall I with my youthful vigor Scare the salmon to the fish-nets,
Shall I drive them to their capture?” Spake the master of the fish-nets: “That would be but work of women,
In the frighting of the salmon!”
Scares the salmon with the forces Of his mighty arms and shoulders,
Stirs the water thick with black-earth, Beats the scare-net into pieces,
When the aged sire, Kalervo,
To his son these words he uttered: “Dost not understand this labor,
Canst not scare the perch and salmon To the fish-nets of thy father;
Torn my scare-net into tatters, Beaten into pulp the whiting,
Beaten into bits my wedges. Leave the fishing to another;
Pay my yearly contribution; See if thou canst better travel,
Thereupon the son, Kullervo,
In his magic shoes of deer-skin, In his locks of golden color,
Pay the tribute for his people. When the youth had paid the tribute,
He returned to join the snow-sledge, Took his place upon the cross-bench,
And began his journey homeward; Rattled on along the highway,
Wainamoinen’s hills and valleys, And his fields in cultivation.
On her snow-shoes came a virgin, O’er the hills of Wainamoinen,
Quick the wizard-son, Kullervo,
Thus addressed the charming maiden: “Come, sweet maiden, to my snow-sledge,
As she ran, the maiden answered: “Let the Death-maid sit beside thee,
Thereupon the youth, Kullervo,
Fleet as wind he gallops homeward, Dashes down along the highway;
Gallops onward, onward, onward, O’er the broad-back of the ocean,
Comes a winsome maid to meet him,
On the far outstretching ice-plains; Quick the wizard checks his racer,
Chanting carefully these measures: “Come, thou beauty, to my snow-sledge,
Tauntingly the maiden answered: “Take Tuoni to thy snow-sledge,
Sit with thee, and rest, and linger!”
Struck his fiery, prancing racer, With the birch-whip of his father.
Galloped on the highway homeward; O’er the hills the snow-sledge bounded,
Kullerwoinen, wild magician, Measures, on his journey homeward,
And the fertile plains of Pohya. Comes a beauteous maid to meet him,
On the heather of Pohyola, O’er the Pohya-hills and moorlands.
Holds the bridle of his courser, Charmingly intones these measures: “Come, fair maiden, to my snow-sledge,
Eat with me the golden apples, Eat the hazel-nut in joyance,
Eat the dainties that I give thee.”
With the tin-pin on her bosom: “I have scorn to give thy snow-sledge,
Cold is it beneath thy fur-robes, And thy sledge is chill and cheerless.
Wicked wizard of the Northland, Drew the maiden to his snow-sledge,
Quickly in his furs enwrapped her; And the tin-adorned made answer,
“Loose me from thy magic power, Let me leave at once thy presence,
Lest I say the prayer of evil; Free me now as I command thee,
Throw these fur-robes to the north-winds.”
Evil wizard and magician, Opens all his treasure-boxes,
Shows her silken wraps of beauty, Silken hose with golden borders,
Jewelry that dims the vision, Blunts the conscience of the virgin.
Gold entices from uprightness. Kullerwoinen, wicked wizard,
One hand on the reins of leather, One upon the maiden’s shoulder;
Pass the night in merry-making.
When the second day was dawning, Then the maid addressed Kullervo,
“Of what tribe art thou descended, Of what race thy hero-father?
This, Kullervo’s truthful answer: “Am not from a mighty nation,
But my lineage is worthy: Am Kalervo’s son of folly,
Hapless son of cold misfortune. Tell me of thy race of heroes,
This the answer of the maiden: “Came not from a race primeval,
But my lineage is worthy; Am Kalervo’s wretched daughter,
Am a maid of contradictions, Hapless daughter of misfortune.
“When a child I lived in plenty
To the woods I went for berries, Went for raspberries to uplands,
Gathered one day then a second; But, alas! upon the third day,
Forestward the highways led me, All the footpaths, to the woodlands.
Wept one day and then a second, Wept the third from morn till even.
There I called in wailing accents, And the woodlands gave this answer,
‘Call no longer, foolish virgin, All thy calls and tears are useless;
Far away, thy home and people.’
“On the third and on the fourth days,
Constantly I sought to perish; But in vain were all my efforts,
If this wretched maid had perished, In the summer of the third year,
She had blossomed as a flower, Knowing neither pain nor sorrow.”
When she bounded from the snow-sledge, Rushed upon the rolling river,
To the fiery stream and whirlpool. Thus Kullervo’s lovely sister
To her death by fire and water, Found her peace in Tuonela,
Then the wicked Kullerwoinen
Wailed, and wept, and heavy-hearted, Spake these words in bitter sorrow: “Woe is me, my life hard-fated!
Shamed the daughter of my mother; Woe to thee, my ancient father!
Wherefore was I born and nurtured, Why this hapless child’s existence?
Had he never seen the daylight, Or, if born, had never thriven
Death has failed to do his duty, Sickness sinned in passing by me,
When the seventh day had ended!”
Of his prancing royal racer, Mounts the silver-headed fleet-foot,
Gallops only for a moment, When he halts his foaming courser
In the court-yard stood the mother, Thus the wicked son addressed her: “Faithful mother, fond and tender,
Smoked my life out in the chamber, In a winding-sheet hadst thrown me
In the fire hadst set my cradle, After seven nights had ended,
Had the village-maidens asked thee: ‘Where is now the little cradle,
This had been a worthy answer: ‘I have burned the wizard’s cradle,
In the bath-room corn is sprouting, From the barley malt is brewing.’”
Asks her wizard-son these questions: “What has happened to my hero,
Comest thou as from Tuoni, From the castles of Manala?”
“Infamous the tale I bring thee, My confession is dishonor:
Met thy long-lost, wayward daughter, Did not recognize my sister,
When the taxes had been settled, When the tribute had been gathered,
Whom I witless led to sorrow, This my mother’s long-lost daughter.
Quick she bounded from the snow-sledge, Hastened to the roaring waters,
To the fiery stream and whirlpool, Hastened to her full destruction.
“Now, alas! must I determine,
Where thy sinful son may perish; Tell me, all-forgiving mother,
Let me stop the black-wolf’s howling, Let me satisfy the hunger
Let the shark or hungry sea-dog Be my dwelling-place hereafter!”
“Do not go to stop the howling Of the hungry wolf of Northland;
Growling in his forest-cavern; Let not shark, nor vicious sea-dog
Spacious are the rooms of Suomi, Limitless the Sawa-borders,
Man’s misdeeds to hide for ages, With his sins and evil actions.
In the border-land of Kalma, Even nine for magic heroes,
Till they quiet all his mourning.”
Answers thus his grieving mother: “Shall not haste to hide from sorrow,
To the jaws of death I hasten, To the open courts of Kalma,
To the battle-fields of heroes. Untamoinen still is living,
Unavenged my father’s grievance, Unavenged my mother’s tortures,
Kullerwoinen’S Victory and Death.
In his purple-colored stockings, Now prepares himself for battle;
Sharpens well his trusty weapon, And his mother speaks as follows: “Do not go, my son beloved,
Struggle not with hostile spearsmen. Whoso goes to war for nothing,
Undertakes a fatal issue; Those that war without a reason
Easy prey to bows and arrows. Go thou with a goat to battle,
’Tis the goat that will be vanquished, And the roebuck will be slaughtered;
Victor, with but little honor!” These the words of Kullerwoinen: “Shall not journey through the marshes,
On the home-land of the raven, Where the eagles scream at day-break.
Bravely will I fall in battle, Fall upon the field of glory,
And the clang and clash of armies, Beautiful the strife for conquest!
To the kingdom of Tuoni, To the realm of the departed,
This the answer of the mother: “If thou diest in the conflict,
Who will give thy sire protection?” These the words of Kullerwoinen: “Let him die upon the court-yard,
“Who then will protect thy mother,
“Let her die within the stable,
“Who then will defend thy brother,
“Let him die within the forest,
“Who will comfort then thy sister,
“Let her sink beneath the waters,
Where the brook flows on in beauty, Like a silver serpent winding
Thereupon the wild Kullervo
To his father speaks, departing: “Fare thou well, my aged father!
When thou hearest I have perished, Fallen from thy tribe forever,
Thus the father speaks in answer: “I shall never mourn the downfall
Shall not weep when thou hast perished; Shall beget a second hero
That will think and act in wisdom.” Kullerwoinen gives this answer: “Neither shall I mourn thy downfall,
I shall make a second father, Make the head from loam and sandstone,
Make the beard from withered sea-grass, Make the feet from roots of willow,
Thereupon the youth, Kullervo,
“Fare thou well, beloved brother! Wilt thou weep for me departed,
Fallen on the field of battle?” This the answer of the brother: “I shall never mourn the downfall
Shall not weep when thou hast perished; I shall find a second brother,
This is Kullerwoinen’s answer: “Neither shall I mourn thy downfall,
I shall form a second brother, Make the head from dust and ashes,
Make the beard from withered verdure, Make the form from pulp of birch-wood.”
“Fare thou well, beloved sister! Surely thou wilt mourn my downfall,
When thou hearest I have fallen In the heat and din of battle,
But the sister makes this answer: “Never shall I mourn thy downfall,
I shall seek a second brother, Seek a brother, purer, better,
Kullerwoinen thus makes answer: “Neither shall I mourn thee fallen,
I shall form a second sister, Make the head from whitened marble,
Make the tresses from the rainbow, Make the ears from ocean-flowers,
“Fare thou well, beloved mother,
Wilt thou weep when I have perished, Fallen on the field of glory,
Thus the mother speaks in answer: “Canst not fathom love maternal,
Bitterly I’ll mourn thy downfall, I would weep if thou shouldst perish,
I would weep in court or cabin, Sprinkle all these fields with tear-drops,
Weep to melt the snows of Northland, Make the hillocks green with weeping,
Weep three years in bitter sorrow O’er the death of Kullerwoinen!”
Went rejoicing to the combat; In delight to war he hastened
Shouting loudly on the heather, Singing o’er the hills and mountains,
Blowing war upon his bugle.
When a messenger appearing, Spake these words to Kullerwoinen: “Lo! thine aged sire has perished,
Hasten home and do him honor, Lay him in the lap of Kalma.”
“Has my aged father perished, There is home a sable stallion
Lay him in the lap of Kalma.”
Calling war upon his bugle, Till a messenger appearing,
“Lo! thy brother too has perished, Dead he lies within the forest,
Home return and do him honor, Lay him in the lap of Kalma.”
“Has my hero-brother perished, There is home a sable stallion
Lay him in the lap of Kalma.”
Over vale and over mountain, Playing on his reed of battle,
Brought the warrior these tidings: “Lo! thy sister too has perished,
Where the waters flow in beauty, Like a silver serpent winding
Home return and do her honor, Lay her in the lap of Kalma.”
“Has my beauteous sister perished, Fallen from my race forever,
That will take her to her resting, Lay her in the lap of Kalma.”
Through the fens he went rejoicing, Sounding war upon his bugle,
Brought to him these words of sorrow: “Lo! thy mother too has perished,
Home return and do her honor, Lay her in the lap of Kalma.”
“Woe is me, my life hard-fated, That my mother too has perished,
Made my couch a golden cover, Twirled for me the spool and spindle!
When his mother’s life departed; May have died upon the mountains,
Lave the dead form of my mother In the crystal waters flowing;
Tie her hands with silken ribbon, Take her to the grave of ages,
Bury her with songs of mourning, Let the singers chant my sorrow;
While Untamo goes unpunished, Fell destroyer of my people.”
Still rejoicing, to the combat, Sang these songs in supplication: “Ukko, mightiest of rulers,
Grant to me thy matchless weapon, And against a thousand armies
Ukko gave the youth his broadsword,
To the wizard, Kullerwoinen. Thus equipped, the mighty hero
Burned their villages to ashes; Only left the stones and ovens,
Then the conqueror, Kullervo,
To the cabin of his father, To his ancient fields and forests.
And the forests were deserted; No one came to give him greeting,
Laid his fingers on the oven, But he found it cold and lifeless;
That his mother lived no longer; Laid his hand upon the fire-place,
Then he knew to satisfaction That his sister too had perished;
Found no boats upon the rollers; Then he knew to satisfaction
Then he looked upon the fish-nets, And he found them torn and tangled;
That his father too had perished.
Wept one day, and then a second, On the third day spake as follows: “Faithful mother, fond and tender,
In this wilderness of trouble? But thou dost not hear my calling,
Though my tear-drops speak lamenting, Though my heart bemoans thine absence.
To Kullervo speaks these measures: “Thou has still the dog remaining,
Follow thou the faithful watcher, Let him lead thee to the woodlands,
To the caverns of the wood-nymphs; There the forest maidens linger,
Give my hero joyful greetings.”
Hastens onward through the forest, Journeys on through fields and fallows;
Till he comes upon the summit Where he met his long-lost sister;
Finds the glen-wood filled with sorrow, Finds the heather shedding tear-drops,
O’er the ruin of his sister.
Grasps the handle of his broadsword, Asks the blade this simple question: “Tell me, O my blade of honor,
Drink the blood of Kullerwoinen?”
Well divining his intentions: “Why should I not drink thy life-blood,
Since I feast upon the worthy, Drink the life-blood of the righteous?”
Wicked wizard of the Northland, Lifts the mighty sword of Ukko,
Firmly thrusts the hilt in heather, To his heart he points the weapon,
Pouring out his wicked life-blood, Ere he journeys to Manala.
This the end of Kullerwoinen, Born in sin, and nursed in folly.
As he hears the joyful tidings, Learns the death of fell Kullervo,
“O, ye many unborn nations, Never evil nurse your children,
Never trust them to the foolish! If the child is not well nurtured,
Though he grow to years of manhood, Bear a strong and shapely body,
Never eat the bread of honor, Never drink the cup of wisdom.”
Ilmarinen’S Bride of Gold.
Wept one day, and then a second, Wept the third from morn till evening,
Once the Maiden of the Rainbow; Did not swing his heavy hammer,
Made no sound within his smithy, Made no blow upon his anvil,
Then the blacksmith spake as follows: “Woe is me, unhappy hero!
Long the days, and cold, and dreary, Longer still the nights, and colder;
In the morning still am weary, Have no longing for the morning,
Have no pleasure in the future, All my pleasures gone forever,
Slaughtered by the hand of witchcraft! Often will my heart-strings quiver
When I wake at dreamy midnight, Half-unconscious, vainly searching
Wifeless lived the mourning blacksmith,
Wept one month and then another, Wept three months in full succession.
Gathered gold from deeps of ocean, Gathered silver from the mountains,
Filled with faggots thirty sledges, Burned the birch-wood into ashes;
Laid the gold upon the embers, Lengthwise laid a piece of silver
Or the fleet-foot hare in winter; Places servants at the bellows,
Eagerly the servants labor, Gloveless, hatless, do the workmen
Ilmarinen, magic blacksmith,
Thus to mould a golden image, Mould a bride from gold and silver;
Faithless stand they at the bellows. Wow the artist, Ilmarinen,
Blows one day, and then a second, Blows the third from morn till even;
Looks around the oven-border, Hoping there to see an image
Comes a lambkin from the furnace,
Wearing hair of gold and copper, Laced with many threads of silver;
At the beauty of the image. This the language of the blacksmith: “May the wolf admire thy graces;
Born from molten gold and silver!”
To the furnace threw the lambkin; Added gold in great abundance,
Added other magic metals, Set the workmen at the bellows;
Gloveless, hatless, do the workmen Fan the flames within the furnace.
Works unceasing with his metals, Moulding well a golden image,
But the workmen fail their master, Faithless do they ply the bellows.
Fans the flames by force of magic; Blows one day, and then a second,
When he looks within the furnace, Looks around the oven-border,
Rising from the molten metals. From the flames a colt arises,
Hoofs are formed of shining copper. All rejoice but Ilmarinen
This the language of the blacksmith: “Let the bears admire thy graces;
Born of many magic metals.”
Drives the colt back to the furnace, Adds a greater mass of silver,
Sets the workmen at the bellows. Eagerly the servants labor,
Fan the flames within the furnace.
Works unceasing at his witchcraft, Moulding well a golden maiden,
But the workmen fail their master, Faithlessly they ply the bellows.
Fans the flames with magic powers, Blows one day, and then a second,
Then he looks within his furnace, Looks around the oven-border,
Coming from the molten metals. From the fire a virgin rises,
Beautiful in form and feature. All are filled with awe and wonder,
Ilmarinen, metal-worker, Forges nights and days unceasing,
Feet he forges for the maiden, Hands and arms, of gold and silver;
Neither can her arms embrace him. Ears he forges for the virgin,
Forges her a mouth of beauty, Eyes he forges bright and sparkling;
And the eyes are not for seeing. Spake the artist, Ilmarinen: “This, indeed, a priceless maiden,
Could she breathe the breath of Ukko!”
On his silken couch of slumber, On his downy place of resting.
Makes it ready for his service, Binds together silken brushes,
Wherewithal to lave the image, Lave the golden maid of beauty.
Ilmarinen, hoping, trusting, Laid his golden bride to slumber,
Ordered many silken wrappings, Ordered bear-skins, three in number,
Thus to keep him warm in slumber, Sleeping by the golden image
Warm the side of Ilmarinen That was wrapped in furs and blankets;
By his bride of gold and silver; One side warm, the other lifeless,
Spake the artist, Ilmarinen: “Not for me was born this virgin
I shall take her to Wainola, Give her to old Wainamoinen,
Comfort to him in his dotage.”
Takes the virgin to Wainola, To the plains of Kalevala,
“O, thou ancient Wainamoinen, Look with favor on this image;
Beautiful in form and feature, Suited to thy years declining!”
Looked in wonder on the virgin, On the golden bride of beauty,
“Wherefore dost thou bring this maiden, Wherefore bring to Wainamoinen
Spake in answer Ilmarinen: “Wherefore should I bring this image,
I have brought her as companion To thy life in years declining,
When thy days are full of trouble!” Spake the good, old Wainamoinen: “Magic brother, wonder-forger,
To the flames, thy golden image, Forge from her a thousand trinkets.
Take her to the plains of Pohya, That for her the mighty powers
Worthy trophy for the victor; Not for me this bride of wonder,
I shall never wed an image Born from many magic metals,
Never wed a golden virgin.” Then the hero of the waters
Spake these words of ancient wisdom: “Every child of Northland, listen,
Never bow before an image Born of molten gold and silver;
Never while the moonlight glimmers, Choose a maiden of the metals,
Cold the lips of golden maiden, Silver breathes the breath of sorrow.”
Ilmarinen’S Fruitless Wooing.
The eternal metal-artist, Lays aside the golden image,
Throws the harness on his courser, Binds him to his sledge of birch-wood,
Snaps the whip above the racer, Thinking once again to journey
There to woo a bride in honor, Second daughter of the Northland.
Journeyed one day, then a second, So the third from morn till evening,
On the plains of Sariola.
Standing in the open court-yard, Spied the hero, Ilmarinen,
“Tell me how my child is living, How the Bride of Beauty prospers,
Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Thus addressed the Northland hostess: “O, thou dame of Sariola,
Since, alas! in Tuonela Sleeps the Maiden of the Rainbow,
Underneath the fragrant heather, In the kingdom of Manala.
For the fairest of thy virgins. Beauteous hostess of Pohyola,
For my former wife’s compartments, For the chambers of her sister.”
Spake these words to Ilmarinen: “Foolish was the Northland-hostess,
In the bloom of youth and beauty To the blacksmith of Wainola,
Like a lambkin to the slaughter! I shall never give my daughter,
Bride of thine to be hereafter, Life-companion at thy fireside.
To the cataract and whirlpool, To the river of Manala,
Then the blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Shook his sable locks in anger, Entered to the inner court-room,
Spake these measures to the daughter: “Come with me, thou bright-eyed maiden,
Lived and lingered in contentment, Baked for me the toothsome biscuit,
Kept my dwelling-place in order.”
Thus he sang to Ilmarinen: “Uninvited, leave this mansion,
Once before thou camest hither, Only bringing pain and trouble,
Fairest daughter of my mother, Do not give this suitor welcome,
Nor admire his form and features. In his mouth are only wolf-teeth,
In his shoes art only bear-claws, In his belt a hungry dagger;
Only worn by the unworthy.”
To the blacksmith, Ilmarinen: “Follow thee this maid will never,
Thou hast slain the Bride of Beauty, Once the Maiden of the Rainbow,
I deserve a better suitor, Wish a truer, nobler husband,
Have a better home-protection; Never will I sweep the cottage
Then the hero, Ilmarinen,
Turned his head away, disdainful, Shook his sable locks in anger,
Held her in his grasp of iron, Hastened from the court of Louhi,
In his sleigh he seats the virgin, Snugly wraps her in his fur-robes,
Gallops on the high-road homeward; With one hand the reins he tightens,
Speaks the virgin-daughter, weeping: “We have reached the lowland-berries,
Leave me here to sink and perish As a child of cold misfortune.
If thou dost not quickly free me, I will break thy sledge to pieces,
Ilmarinen makes this answer: “When the blacksmith builds his snow-sledge,
Therefore will the beauteous maiden Never beat my sledge to fragments.”
Wept and wailed in bitter accents, Wrung her hands in desperation,
“If thou dost not quickly free me, I shall change to ocean-salmon,
“Thou wilt never thus escape me,
Then the maiden of Pohyola
Wrung her hands in desperation, Spake again to Ilmarinen; “If thou dost not quickly free me,
Mid the rocks become an ermine!”
“Thou wilt never thus escape me,
Then the beauty of the Northland,
Wrung her hands in desperation, Spake once more to Ilmarinen: “Surely, if thou dost not free me,
Hide myself within the storm-clouds.”
“Neither wilt thou thus escape me,
They had gone but little distance,
Frighted at some passing object; And the maiden looked in wonder,
Spake these words to Ilmarinen: “Who has run across our highway?”
“’Tis the timid hare”, he answered.
Sobbed, and moaned, in deeps of sorrow, Heavy-hearted, spake these measures: “Woe is me, ill-fated virgin!
If the hare I could but follow To his burrow in the woodlands!
Than the robes of Ilmarinen.”
Tossed his head in full resentment, Galloped on the highway homeward;
When again his courser halted, Frighted at some passing stranger.
In the snow beheld some foot-prints, Spake these measures to the blacksmith: “Who has crossed our snowy pathway?”
“’Tis a fox”, replied the minstrel.
Moaned again in depths of anguish, Sang these accents, heavy-hearted: “Woe is me, ill-fated maiden!
With the cunning fox to wander, Than with this ill-mannered suitor;
Than the robes of Ilmarinen.”
Shut his lips in sore displeasure, Hastened on the highway homeward;
When again his courser halted.
In the snow beheld some foot-prints, Spake these words to the magician: “Who again has crossed our pathway?”
“’Tis the wolf”, said Ilmarinen.
Fell again to bitter weeping, And intoned these words of sorrow: “Woe is me, a hapless maiden!
Brighter far would be my future, If these tracks I could but follow;
Than the furs of Ilmarinen, Faithless suitor of the Northland.”
Closed his lips again in anger, Shook his sable locks, resentful,
And the steed flew onward swiftly, O’er the way to Kalevala,
Sad and weary from his journey,
Fell upon his couch in slumber, And the maiden laughed derision.
Head confused, and locks dishevelled, Spake the wizard, words as follow: “Shall I set myself to singing
Shall I now enchant this maiden To a black-wolf on the mountains,
Shall not send her to the woodlands, All the forest would be frighted;
All the fish would flee in terror; This my sword shall drink her life-blood,
Quick the sword feels his intention,
Speaks these words to Ilmarinen: “Was not born to drink the life-blood
Of a fair but helpless virgin.”
Filled with rage, began his singing; Sang the very rocks asunder,
Sang the maiden to a sea-gull, Croaking from the ocean-ledges,
Screeching on the sandy sea-coast, Flying to the winds opposing.
Ilmarinen joined his snow-sledge, Whipped his steed upon a gallop,
To his home in Kalevala.
Comes to meet him on the highway, Speaks these words to the magician: “Ilmarinen, worthy brother,
From the dismal Sariola? Does Pohyola live and prosper?”
“Why should not Pohyola prosper? There the Sampo grinds unceasing,
Grinds one day the flour for eating, Grinds the second flour for selling,
Thus it is Pohyola prospers. While the Sampo is in Northland,
There is growth of every virtue, There is welfare never-ending.”
“Ilmarinen, artist-brother, Where then is the Northland-daughter,
For whose hand thou hast been absent?” These the words of Ilmarinen: “I have changed the hateful virgin
Now she calls above the waters, Screeches from the ocean-islands;
Vainly calling for a suitor.”
Wainamoinen’S Sailing.
Spake these words to Ilmarinen: “O thou wonder-working brother,
There to gain the magic Sampo, There to see the lid in colors.”
“Hard indeed to seize the Sampo, Neither can the lid be captured
From the dismal Sariola. Louhi took away the Sampo,
To the stone-mount of Pohyola; Hid it in the copper mountain,
Many young roots sprout around it, Grow nine fathoms deep in sand-earth,
In the cataract a second, And a third beneath the castle
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Brother mine, and wonder-worker,
That we may secure the Sampo; Let us build a goodly vessel,
Bring away the lid in colors, From the stone-berg of Pohyola,
Where the miracle lies anchored.” Ilmarinen thus made answer: “By the land the way is safer,
Ghastly Death upon his shoulder; On the sea the waves will drift us,
Then our hands must do the rowing, And our feet must steer us homeward.”
“Safe indeed by land to journey, But the way is rough and trying,
Lovely is the ship on ocean, Beautiful to ride the billows,
Sailing in a trusty vessel; Should the West-wind cross our pathway,
Be that as it may, my brother, Since thou dost not love the water,
Forge me now the sword of battle, Forge for me the mighty fire-sword,
Frighten all the Northland people, As we journey for the Sampo
To the never-pleasant Northland, To the dismal Sariola.”
The eternal forger-artist, Laid the metals in the furnace,
In the hot-coals, gold and silver, Rightful measure of the metals;
Lustily they plied the bellows. Like the wax the iron melted,
Like the water ran the silver, And the liquid gold flowed after.
The eternal wonder-forger, Looks within his magic furnace,
There beholds the fire-sword forming, Sees the blade with golden handle;
Lays it on his heavy anvil For the falling of the hammer;
Well the heavy sword he tempers, Ornaments the hero-weapon
Wainamoinen, the magician,
Lifts admiringly the fire-sword, Then these words the hero utters: “Does the weapon match the soldier,
Yea, the blade and hilt are molded To the wishes of the minstrel.”
On the blade the sun is shining, On the hilt the bright stars twinkle,
On the handle plays a kitten, On the sheath a dog is barking.
Tests it on the iron-mountain, And these words the hero utters: “With this broadsword I could quickly
Cut the flinty rocks asunder.” Spake the blacksmith, Ilmarinen: “Wherewith shall I guard from danger,
From the ills by land and water? Shall I wear an iron armor,
Stronger is a man in armor, Safer in a mail of copper.”
To the never-pleasant Northland; Wainamoinen, ancient minstrel,
Hasten to the field and forest, Searching for their fiery coursers,
With a harness on their shoulders. In the woods they find a race;
Ready for his master’s service. Wainamoinen, old and trusty,
Throw the harness on the courser, Hitch him to the sledge of conquest,
Drive along the broad-sea’s margin Till they hear some one lamenting,
Near the landing-place of vessels.
Speaks these words in wonder, guessing: “This must be some maiden weeping,
Let us journey somewhat nearer, To discover whence this wailing.”
Hoping thus to find a maiden Weeping on the sandy sea-shore.
But a vessel, sad, and lonely, Waiting on the shore and wailing.
“Why art weeping, goodly vessel, What the cause of thy lamenting?
Is thy rigging ill-adjusted? Dost thou weep since thou art anchored
Thus the war-ship spake in answer: “To the waters would this vessel
As a happy maiden journeys To the cottage of her husband.
Weep because I lie at anchor, Weep and wail because no hero
Free to ride the rolling billows. It was said when I was fashioned,
That this bark should be for battle, Should become a mighty war-ship,
Priceless goods across the ocean. Never have I sailed to conquest,
Other vessels not as worthy To the wars are ever sailing,
Three times in the summer season Come they home with treasures laden,
I, alas! a worthy vessel, Many months have lain at anchor,
Am decaying in the harbor, Never having sailed to conquest;
In my hull their dwelling-places, And ill-omened birds of heaven
Frogs and lizards of the forest Play about my oars and rudder;
Were he but a valley birch-tree, Or an aspen on the heather,
And the dogs beneath them barking!”
Thus addressed the ship at anchor: “Weep no more, thou goodly vessel,
Thou shalt sail to Sariola, Sing the war-songs of the Northland,
Wert thou built by the Creator, Thou canst sail the roughest waters,
Dost not need the hand to touch thee, Dost not need the foot to turn thee,
Thus the weeping boat made answer: “Cannot sail without assistance,
Sail unaided o’er the waters, Sail across the waves undriven.”
“Should I lead thee to the broad-sea, Wilt thou journey north unaided,
Sail without the aid of south-winds, Sail without the helm to guide thee?”
“Cannot sail without assistance, Neither can my brother-vessels
Sail without the help of south-winds, Nor without the helm to guide them.”
“Wilt thou run with aid of oarsmen When the south-winds give assistance,
This the answer of the war-ship: “Quickly can I course these waters,
When my sails are filled with south-winds, All my goodly brother-vessels
When the master holds the rudder.”
Left the racer on the sea-side, Tied him to the sacred birch-tree,
Rolled the vessel to the waters, Sang the ship upon the broad-sea,
“O thou vessel, well-appearing From the mighty oak constructed,
As in view thou art commanding?” Thus the goodly ship made answer: “Strong am I to carry treasures,
I can bear a hundred oarsmen, And of warriors a thousand.”
Then began his wondrous singing. On one side the magic vessel,
Bearded youth with strength of heroes, Sang them into mail of copper.
Sang he silver-tinselled maidens, Girded them with belts of copper,
Sings again the great magician, Fills the magic ship with heroes,
Sings them into narrow limits, Since the young men came before them.
Near the last beam of the vessel, Steered his goodly boat in joyance,
“Glide upon the trackless waters, Sail away, my ship of magic,
Speed thou like a dancing bubble, Like a flower upon the billows!”
Set the young men to the rowing, Let the maidens sit in waiting.
Bend the oars and try the row-locks, But the distance is not lessened.
Set the maidens to the rowing, Let the young men rest in waiting.
Bend the aspen-oars in rowing, But the distance is not lessened.
Set the old men to the rowing, Let the youth remain in waiting.
Bend and try the oars of aspen, But the distance is not lessened.
Grasped the oars with master-magic, And the boat leaped o’er the surges,
Far and wide the oars resounded, Quickly was the distance lessened.
Ilmarinen sped his vessel, Benches, ribs, and row-locks creaking,
Flap the sails like wings of moor-cocks, And the prow dips like a white-swan;
Loud the oars and rigging rattle.
Sitting by the bending rudder, Turns his magic vessel landward,
Where appears a Northland-village. On the point stands Lemminkainen,
Ahti, wizard of Wainola, Wishing for the fish of Pohya,
For his perilous adventures, Hard at work upon a vessel,
Near the hunger-point and island, Near the village-home deserted.
Good the wizard’s eyes for seeing; Casts his vision to the South-east,
Sees afar a wondrous rainbow, Farther on, a cloudlet hanging;
And the cloudlet a delusion; ’Tis a vessel swiftly sailing, ’Tis a war-ship flying northward,
On the far-extending waters, At the helm the master standing,
Spake the reckless Lemminkainen: “Do not know this wondrous vessel,
Coming from the distant Suomi, Rowing for the hostile Pohya.”
Called aloud in tones of thunder O’er the waters to the vessel;
With the music of his calling: “Whence this vessel on the waters,
Spake the master of the vessel
“Who art thou from fen or forest, Senseless wizard from the woodlands,
Magic war-ship of Wainola? Dost not know him at the rudder,
Spake the wizard, Lemminkainen: “Well I know the helm-director,
Wainamoinen, old and trusty, At the helm directs the vessel;
Whither is the vessel sailing, Whither wandering, my heroes?”
“We are sailing to the Northland, There to gain the magic Sampo,
From the stone-berg of Pohyola, From the copper-bearing mountain.”
“O, thou good, old Wainamoinen, Take me with thee to Pohyola,
Since thou goest for the Sampo, Goest for the lid in colors;
When thy wisdom calls for fighting; I am skilled in arts of warfare!”
Gave assent to Ahti’s wishes; Thereupon wild Lemminkainen
Bringing floats of aspen-timber, To the ships of Wainamoinen.
Speaks to reckless Lemminkainen: “There is aspen on my vessel,
And the boat is heavy-laden. Wherefore dost thou bring the aspen
Lemminkainen gave this answer: “Not through caution sinks a vessel,
Seas abound in hidden dangers, Heavy storms arise and threaten
That would brave the angry billows.” Spake the good, old Wainamoinen: “Therefore is this warlike vessel
Trimmed and bound in toughest iron, That the winds may not destroy it,

Onward steered his goodly vessel, From the isle of Lemminkainen,
Steered his war-ship through the waters, Sang it o’er the ocean-billows,
On the banks were maidens standing,
“List the music on the waters! What this wonderful rejoicing,
Far more beautiful this singing, This rejoicing on the waters,
Wainamoinen, the magician,
Steered one day along the sea-shore, Steered the next through shallow waters,
Then the reckless Lemminkainen
He had heard along the fire-stream Near the cataract and whirlpool,
“Cease, O cataract, thy roaring, Cease, O waterfall, thy foaming!
Sitting on the rocks in water, On the stone-blocks in the river,
In your arms and still their anger, That our ships may pass in safety!
Thou that livest in the sea-foam, Swimming, rise above the waters,
Gather well the foam and billows In thine arms and still their fury,
Ye, O rocks beneath the current, Underneath the angry waters,
Sink below our magic vessel, That our ship may pass in safety!
“Should this prayer prove inefficient,
Bore an outlet with thine auger, Cut a channel for this vessel
That our ship may pass in safety! Should all this prove unavailing,
Change to moss these rocky ledges, Change this vessel to an air-bag,
It may float, and pass in safety!
“Virgin of the sacred whirlpool,
Spin from flax of strongest fiber, Spin a thread of crimson color,
That the thread our ship may follow, And our vessel pass in safety!
Of the ocean-winds and sea-foam, Take thy helm endowed with mercy,
Hasten through these floods enchanted, Passing by the house of envy,
That our ship may pass in safety!
“Should this prayer prove inefficient,
Guide our vessel with thy fire-sword, Guide it with thy blade of lightning,
Through the cataract and whirlpool, That our ship may pass in safety!”
Steered his boat through winds and waters, Through the rocky chinks and channels,
And the vessel passed in safety Through the dangers of the current,
As it gains the open waters, Gains at length the broad-lake’s bosom,
On some object firmly anchored. Thereupon young Ilmarinen,
Plunges in the lake the rudder, Struggles with the aid of magic;
Cannot free it from its moorings.
Thus addresses his companion: “O thou hero, Lemminkainen,
See on what this boat is anchored, See on what our craft is hanging,
In the broad-lake’s deepest soundings, If upon some rock or tree-snag,
Thereupon wild Lemminkainen
Peering through the crystal waters, Spake and these the words he uttered: “Does not rest upon a sand-bar,
But upon the back and shoulders Of the mighty pike of Northland,
