Thus the wicked hostess answered: “All my power has departed,
All my hope is in the deep-sea; In the waters lies my Sampo!”
Home departed, weeping, wailing, To the land of cold and darkness;
Of the Sampo to her people; Carried she the lid to Pohya,
Hence the poverty of Northland, And the famines of Pohyola.
Hastened to the broad-sea’s margin, Stepped upon the shore in joyance;
Fragments of the lid in colors, On the borders of the waters,
Gathered well the Sampo-relics From the waters near the fog-point,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen:,
“Grant, O Ukko, our Creator, Grant to us, thy needful children,
That our lives may be successful, That our days may end in honor,
On the prairies of Wainola, In the homes of Kalevala!
“Ukko, wise and good Creator,
Shelter and protect thy people From the evil-minded heroes,
That our country’s plagues may leave us, That thy faithful tribes may prosper.
Be the helper of thy children, In the night a roof above them,
That the sunshine may not vanish, That the moonlight may not lessen,
And destructive hail pass over. Build a metal wall around us,
Build of stone a mighty fortress On the borders of Wainola,
As their dwelling-place forever, Sure protection to thy people,
Nor the thieves break through and pilfer, Never while the moonlight glistens,
To the plains of Kalevala.”
Birth of the Second Harp.
Long reflecting, sang these measures: “It is now the time befitting
Time for me to touch the harp-strings, Time to sing the songs primeval,
In these homes of Kalevala; But, alas! my harp lies hidden,
To the salmon’s hiding-places, To the dwellings of the whiting,
Where the Northland-pike assemble. Nevermore will I regain it,
Joy and music gone forever!
“O thou blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Thickly set the teeth of copper, Many fathoms long the handle;
Search the broad-sea to the bottom, Rake the weeds and reeds together,
That I may regain my treasure, May regain my harp of fish-bone
From the caverns of the salmon, From the castles of Wellamo.”
The eternal metal-worker, Forges well a rake of iron,
And a thousand long the handle, Thickly sets the teeth of copper.
Takes the rake of magic metals, Travels but a little distance,
To the copper-banded rollers, Where he finds two ships awaiting,
Wainamoinen, old and faithful,
“Go, thou boat of master-magic, Hasten to the willing waters,
And without the hand to move thee; Let my will impel thee seaward.”
On the cylinders of oak-wood, Quick descended to the waters,
Wainamoinen, the magician,
Raked up all the water-flowers, Bits of broken reeds and rushes,
Did not find his harp of fish-bone, Lost forever to Wainola!
Left the waters, homeward hastened, Cap pulled down upon his forehead,
“Nevermore shall I awaken With my harp-strings, joy and gladness!
Charm the people of the Northland With the harp of his creation!
O’er the hills of Kalevala!”
Went lamenting through the forest, Wandered through the sighing pine-woods,
Heard a juniper complaining; Drawing nearer, waits and listens,
“Wherefore, brother, art thou weeping, Merry birch enrobed in silver,
Art thou shedding tears of sorrow, Since thou art not led to battle,
Wisely does the birch make answer: “This the language of the many,
That I only live in pleasure, That my silver leaves and tassels
That I have no cares, no sorrows, That I have no hours unhappy,
I am weeping for my smallness, Am lamenting for my weakness,
Stand here motionless for ages, Stand alone in fen and forest,
Others hope for coming summers, For the beauties of the spring-time;
Dread the changing of the seasons, I must give my bark to others,
Often come the Suomi children, Peel my bark and drink my life-blood:
Come and steal my belt of silver, Of my bark make berry-baskets,
Oftentimes the Northland maidens Cut my tender limbs for birch-brooms,
Into brooms to sweep their cabins; Often have the Northland heroes
Three times in the summer season, In the pleasant days of spring-time,
On my silver trunk and branches, Robbed me of my life for ages;
This my happiness in summer, And my winter days no better!
Sorrow settles on my visage, And my face grows white with anguish;
And the hoar-frost bring me sadness, Blast my tender leaves and tassels,
Rob me of my silver raiment, Leave me naked on the mountain,
Spake the good, old Wainamoinen: “Weep no longer, sacred birch-tree,
Thou shalt have a better fortune; I will turn thy grief to joyance,
Then the ancient Wainamoinen
Fashioned in the days of summer, Beautiful the harp of magic,
On the fog-point in the Big-Sea, On the island forest-covered,
And the frame-work from the aspen. These the words of the magician: “All the archings are completed,
Whence the hooks and pins for tuning, That the harp may sing in concord?”
Skyward grew with equal branches, On each twig an acorn growing,
On each ball a singing cuckoo. As each cuckoo’s call resounded,
From the songster’s throat of joyance; From each throat came liquid music,
Flowing to the hills and hillocks, To the silvery vales and mountains;
That the harp might play in concord. Spake again wise Wainamoinen: “I the pins have well completed,
Now I need five strings for playing, Where shall I procure the harp-strings?”
Journeyed through the fen and forest. On a hillock sat a maiden,
And the maiden was not weeping, Joyful was the sylvan daughter,
That the eventide might hasten, In the hope that her beloved
Wainamoinen, old and trusted,
Asked her for her golden ringlets, These the words of the magician: “Give me, maiden, of thy tresses,
I will weave them into harp-strings, To the joy of Wainamoinen,
Thereupon the forest-maiden
Gave him of her golden ringlets, And of these he made the harp-strings.
To the people of Wainola.
And the minstrel, Wainamoinen, Sits upon the rock of joyance,
Turns the arch up, looking skyward; With his knee the arch supporting,
Runs his fingers o’er the harp-strings, And the notes of pleasure follow.
The eternal wisdom-singer, Plays upon his harp of birch-wood.
Wide the harp of joy re-echoes; Mountains dance and valleys listen,
Stones are hurled upon the waters, Pebbles swim upon the Big-Sea,
Alders skip about the heather, And the aspen sways in concord.
Straightway leave their shining needles, Hasten forward like the current,
That they may enjoy and wonder. Laugh the younger men and maidens,
Flying swift to bear the playing, To enjoy the common pleasure,
Aged men and bearded seniors, Gray-haired mothers with their daughters
Creeps the babe in full enjoyment As he hears the magic singing,
All of Northland stops in wonder, Speaks in unison these measures: “Never have we heard such playing,
Never since the earth was fashioned, As the songs of this magician,
Far and wide the sweet tones echo,
O’er the seven islands echo; Every creature of the Northland
Listen to the songs of gladness, To the harp of Wainamoinen.
Fall upon their knees and wonder At the playing of the minstrel,
All the songsters of the forests Perch upon the trembling branches,
Of the harp of Wainamoinen. All the dwellers of the waters
Swim against the shore and listen To the playing of the minstrel,
All the little things in nature, Rise from earth, and fall from ether,
To the notes of the enchanter, To the songs of the magician,
Plays the singer of the Northland,
Plays one day, and then a second, Plays the third from morn till even;
In the dwellings of his people, Till the floors and ceilings echo,
Till the windows speak and tremble, Till the portals echo joyance,
As he journeys through the forest, As he wanders through the woodlands,
Birch and willow bend obeisance, Beech and aspen bow submission;
To the measure of his playing, To the notes of the magician.
Sings upon the mead and heather, Glen and hill his songs re-echo,
And the shrubs attune their voices To the music of the harp-strings,
Birth of the Nine Diseases.
Heard the word in Sariola, Heard the news with ears of envy,
That Osmoinen’s wealth increases, Through the ruins of the Sampo,
Thereupon her wrath she kindled, Well considered, long reflected,
For the people of Wainola, For the tribes of Kalevala.
Thus entreats the god of thunder: “Ukko, thou who art in heaven,
With thine iron-hail of justice, With thine arrows tipped with lightning,
Let them die the death deserving; Let the men die in the forest,
The blind daughter of Tuoni,
Worst of all the Death-land women, Ugliest of Mana’s children,
All the ills and plagues of Northland, Black in heart, and soul, and visage,
Made her couch along the wayside, On the fields of sin and sorrow;
To the source of stormy weather, To the chilling winds of morning.
Heavy-laden grew Lowyatar, Through the east-wind’s impregnation,
Long she bore her weight of trouble, Many morns she suffered anguish,
Makes her couch within the forest, On a rock upon the mountain;
By the mountain-springs and fountains, By the crystal waters flowing,
By the cataract and fire-stream; But her burden does not lighten.
Knew not where to look for succor, How to lose her weight of sorrow,
Spake the Highest from the heavens,
“Is a triangle in Swamp-field, Near the border of the ocean,
In the dismal Sariola; Thither go and lay thy burden,
There the Laplanders await thee, There will bid thy children welcome.”
Blackest daughter of Tuoni, Mana’s old and ugly maiden,
To the chambers of Pohyola, To the ancient halls of Louhi,
There to leave her evil offspring.
Old and toothless witch of Pohya, Takes Lowyatar to her mansion;
To the bath-rooms of her chamber, Pours the foaming beer of barley,
That their movements may be secret, Speaks these measures to Lowyatar: “Faithful daughter of Creation,
First and last of ancient mothers, Hasten on thy feet to ocean,
Take the sea-foam from the waters, Take the honey of the mermaids,
That thy labors may be lightened.
“Should all this be unavailing,
Hasten hither, thou art needed, Come thou to thy child in trouble,
Take thy golden-colored sceptre, Charm away opposing forces,
Open all resisting portals, That the great and small may wander
Through the courts and halls of freedom.”
Wicked witch of Tuonela, Was delivered of her burden,
Underneath the golden covers. Thus at last were born nine children,
From Lowyatar, blind and ancient, Ugly daughter of Tuoni.
Guards her children in affection, As an artist loves and nurses
Thus Lowyatar named her offspring,
Ulcer, Plague, and dread Consumption, Gout, Sterility, and Cancer.
Blind Lowyatar quickly banished, Drove away as an enchanter,
To engender strife and envy.
Banished all the other children To the fog-point in the ocean,
Banished all the fatal creatures, Gave these wicked sons of evil
To the youth of Kalevala, For the Kalew-tribe’s destruction.
Young and aged, men and heroes, With the worst of all diseases,
Sick and dying is Wainola.
Wise and wonderful enchanter, Hastens to his people’s rescue,
To a conflict with Tuoni, To destroy the evil children
Wainamoinen heats the bath-rooms, Heats the blocks of healing-sandstone
Gathered by the sacred river; Water brings in covered buckets
Brooms he brings enwrapped with ermine, Well the bath the healer cleanses,
Then a honey-heat he wakens, Fills the rooms with healing vapors,
Glowing in the heat of magic, Thus he speaks in supplication: “Come, O Ukko, to my rescue,
Give these vapor-baths new virtues, Grant to them the powers of healing,
Drive away these fell diseases, Banish them to the unworthy,
Keep this heat in healing limits, That it may not harm thy children,
When I pour the sacred waters On the heated blocks of sandstone,
Laden with the balm of healing. Let the stream of magic virtues
From this bath enrolled in sea-moss, That the guiltless may not suffer,
Till the Master gives permission, Until Ukko sends his minions,
To destroy my trusting people. Let the hostess of Pohyola,
Suffer from a gnawing conscience, Suffer for her evil doings.
Lose his magic skill and weaken, Should he prove of little service
To deliver from these evils, Then may Ukko be our healer,
“Omnipresent God of mercy,
Hasten hither, thou art needed, Hasten to thine ailing children,
To dispel these fell diseases, Drive destruction from our borders.
Bring to me thy blade of lightning, That I may subdue these evils,
Send these pains, and ills, and tortures, To the empire of Tuoni,
To the islands of the wicked, To the caverns of the demons,
To the hidden beds of iron, That the rocks may fall and sicken,
Rocks and metals do not murmur At the hands of the invader.
“Torture-daughter of Tuoni,
At the junction of three rivers, Turning rocks of pain and torture,
Through the virtues of the blue-stone; Lead them to the water-channels,
Where the winds can never find them, Where the sunlight never enters.
“Should this prayer prove unavailing,
Come and heal my dying people, Still their agonies and anguish,
Give them healthful rest and slumber; These diseases take and banish,
To thy caves within the mountains, To the summit of the Pain-rock,
In the mountain is a touch-stone, Lucky-stone of ancient story,
Through this pour these pains and tortures, Wretched feelings, thoughts of evil,
Tribulations, and misfortunes, That they may not rise at evening,
Ending thus, old Wainamoinen,
Rubbed his sufferers with balsams, Rubbed the tissues, red and painful,
Balsams made of herbs enchanted, Sprinkled all with healing vapors,
“Ukko, thou who art in heaven, God of justice, and of mercy,
Send a dark cloud from the north-west, From the north let fall a third one,
Balsam from the great Physician, To remove this plague of Northland.
Only comes from my Creator; Lend me, therefore, of thy wisdom,
Save them from the fell destroyer. If my hands should fall in virtue.
God alone can save from trouble. Come to us with thine enchantment,
That my people may not perish; Give to all alleviation
In the morning, in the evening, Let their wasting ailments vanish;
Nevermore to visit Northland, Never in the course of ages,
O’er the lakes of Kalevala.”
The eternal wisdom-singer, Thus expelled the nine diseases,
Healed the tribes of Kalevala, Saved his people from destruction.
Otso the Honey-Eater.
To the village of the Northland, That Wainola had recovered
From her sicknesses and sorrows.
Toothless dame of Sariola, Envy-laden, spake these measures: “Know I other means of trouble,
I will drive the bear before me, From the heather and the mountain,
Drive great Otso from the glen-wood On the cattle of Wainola,
Thereupon the Northland hostess
From his cavern to the meadows, To Wainola’s plains and pastures.
To his brother spake as follows: “O thou blacksmith, Ilmarinen,
Forge a lancet triple-pointed, Forge the handle out of copper,
Slay the mighty bear of Northland, That he may not eat my horses,
Nor the flocks upon my pastures.”
Forged a spear from magic metals, Forged a lancet triple-pointed,
Forged the spear in wondrous beauty. On one side a bear was sitting,
On the blade an elk lay sleeping, On the shaft a colt was running,
Snows had fallen from the heavens,
Or the hare, in days of winter, And the minstrel sang these measures: “My desire impels me onward
To the homes of forest-maidens, To the courts of the white virgins;
Labor with the woodland-forces.
“Ruler of the Tapio-forests,
Help me clear these boundless woodlands. O Mielikki, forest-hostess,
Call thy dogs and well enchain them, Set in readiness thy hunters,
“Otso, thou O Forest-apple,
Learn that Wainamoinen follows, That the singer comes to meet thee;
Let thy teeth remain in darkness, That they may not harm the minstrel,
Mighty Otso, much beloved, Honey-eater of the mountains,
On the turf and in thy caverns; Let the aspen wave above thee,
O’er thy head for thy protection. Rest in peace, thou much-loved Otso,
Like the partridge at her brooding, In the spring-time like the wild-goose.”
Heard his dog bark in the forest, Heard his hunter’s call and echo,
“Thought it was the cuckoo calling, Thought the pretty bird was singing;
Not the liquid notes of songsters, ’Twas my dog that called and murmured, ’Twas the echo of my hunter
On the border of the woodlands.”
Finds the mighty bear in waiting, Lifts in joy the golden covers,
Lifts his honey-paws in wonder, Then addresses his Creator: “Be thou praised, O mighty Ukko,
Givest me the Forest-apple, Thanks be paid to thee unending.”
“Otso, thou my well beloved, Honey-eater of the woodlands,
I have not the force to slay thee, Willingly thy life thou givest
Thou hast from the tree descended, Glided from the aspen branches,
In the fog-days, smooth the branches. Golden friend of fen and forest,
Pride of woodlands, famous Light-foot, Leave thy cold and cheerless dwelling,
Leave thy couch among the willows, Hasten in thy purple stockings,
Come among the haunts of heroes, Join thy friends in Kalevala.
Thou shalt dwell in peace and plenty, Thou shalt feed on milk and honey,
Haste away from this thy covert, From the couch of the unworthy,
Of Wainola’s ancient dwellings. Haste thee onward o’er the snow-plain,
Skip beneath these birchen branches, As a squirrel in the summer,
Wainamoinen, the magician,
O’er the snow-fields hastened homeward, Singing o’er the hills and mountains,
With his friend, the famous Light-foot, With the Honey-paw of Northland.
Heard the playing of the hunter, Heard the songs of Wainamoinen;
Men and maidens, young and aged, From their cabins spake as follows: “Hear the echoes from the woodlands,
Hear the flute-notes of the songsters, Hear the pipes of forest-maidens!”
Soon appears within the court-yard. Rush the people from their cabins,
“Has a mine of gold been opened, Hast thou found a vein of silver,
Does the forest yield her treasures, Give to thee the Honey-eater?
Give to thee the lynx and adder, Since thou comest home rejoicing,
Wainamoinen, ancient minstrel,
“For his songs I caught the adder, Caught the serpent for his wisdom;
Singing, playing, on my snow-shoes. Not the mountain lynx, nor serpent,
The Illustrious is coming, Pride and beauty of the forest, ’Tis the Master comes among us,
Welcome, Otso, welcome, Light-foot, Welcome, Loved-one from the glenwood!
Open wide the gates of entry; If the bear is thought unworthy,
This the answer of the tribe-folk: “We salute thee, mighty Otso,
Welcome to our courts and cabins, Welcome, Light-foot, to our tables
We have wished for thee for ages, Waiting since the days of childhood,
For the singing of the wood-nymphs, For the coming of dear Otso,
Waiting for the year of plenty, Longing for it as for summer,
As the sledge for beaten highways, As the maiden for her suitor,
Sat at evening by the windows, At the gates have sat at morning,
Near the granaries in winter, Till the snow-fields warmed and vanished,
Till the earth grew green and blossomed, Thinking all the while as follows: ‘Where is our beloved Otso,
Has he gone to distant Ehstland, To the upper glens of Suomi?’”
“Whither shall I lead the stranger, Whither take the golden Light-foot?
To the house of straw conduct him?” This the answer of his tribe-folk: “To the dining-hall lead Otso,
Famous Light-foot, Forest-apple, Pride and glory of the woodlands,
Fear not curly-headed virgins, Clad in silver-tinselled raiment;
When dear Otso joins their number, When the hero comes among them.”
“Grant, O Ukko, peace and plenty Underneath these painted rafters,
Thanks be paid to gracious Ukko!” Spake again the ancient minstrel: “Whither shall we lead dear Otso,
This the answer of his people: “Hither let the fur-robed Light-foot
Let the Honey-paw be welcomed To the hearth-stone of the penthouse,
That we may admire his fur-robe, May behold his cloak with joyance.
Let not anger swell thy bosom As thy coat we view with pleasure;
Shall not make it into garments To protect unworthy people.”
Pulled the sacred robe from Otso, Spread it in the open court-yard,
Laid them in the heating caldrons, In the copper-bottomed vessels.
On the crane were hooks of copper, On the hooks the broiling vessels
Seasoned with the salt of Dwina, From the Saxon-land imported,
From the salt-sea brought in shallops.
From the fire are swung the kettles On the crane of polished iron;
Is the bear displayed in dishes, Golden dishes, decorated;
Were the tables newly fashioned; Drinking cups were forged from copper,
Filled the vessels to their borders With the choicest bits of Light-foot,
Spake the ancient Wainamoinen: “Ancient one with bosom golden,
Metsola’s most lovely hostess, Hostess of the glen and forest,
Stalwart youth in cap of scarlet, Tapio’s most beauteous virgin,
Metsola with all her people, Come, and welcome, to the feasting,
All sufficient, the provisions, Food to eat and drink abundant,
Plenty more to give the village.” This the question of the people: “Tell us of the birth of Otso!
Was he nurtured in the bath-room Was his origin ignoble?”
“Otso was not born a beggar, Was not born among the rushes,
Honey-paw was born in ether, In the regions of the Moon-land,
With the daughters of creation.
“Through the ether walked a maiden,
On the border of the heavens, In her stockings purple-tinted,
In her hand she held a wool-box, With a hair-box on her shoulder;
And the hair upon the rivers; These are rocked by winds and waters,
Bear them to the sandy sea-shore, Land them near the woods of honey,
“Fair Mielikki, woodland hostess,
Took the fragments from the sea-side, Took the white wool from the waters,
Laid the bundle in her basket, Basket made from bark of birch-wood,
With the chains of gold she bound it To the pine-tree’s topmost branches.
Rocked to life the tender baby, Mid the blossoms of the pine-tree,
Thus the young bear well was nurtured, Thus was sacred Otso cradled
In the middle of the forest.
“Sacred Otso grew and flourished,
Short of feet, with crooked ankles, Wide of mouth and broad of forehead,
But his claws were not well fashioned, Neither were his teeth implanted.
Spake these words in meditation: ‘Claws I should be pleased to give him,
Would he not abuse the favor.’
“Swore the bear a promise sacred,
Hostess of the glen and forest, And before omniscient Ukko,
That he would not harm the worthy, Never do a deed of evil.
Wisest maid of Tapiola, Sought for teeth and claws to give him,
From the juniper and oak tree, From the dry knots of the alder.
Would not render goodly service.
“Grew a fir-tree on the mountain,
And the fir had silver branches, Bearing golden cones abundant;
Teeth and claws of these she fashioned In the jaws and feet of Otso,
Then she freed her new-made creature, Let the Light-foot walk and wander,
Let him amble through the forest, Roll upon the plains and pastures;
How to move with graceful motion, How to live in ease and pleasure,
In the moors and in the marshes, On the borders of the woodlands;
Stockingless to run in autumn; How to rest and sleep in winter
Underneath the sheltering fir-tree, Underneath the pine’s protection,
With the juniper and willow. This the origin of Otso,
Whence the sacred booty cometh.” Thus again the people questioned: “Why became the woods so gracious,
Why is Tapio so humored, That he gave his dearest treasure,
Honey-eater of his kingdom? Was he startled with thine arrows,
Wainamoinen, the magician,
“Filled with kindness was the forest, Glen and woodland full of greetings,
Fair Mielikki, forest hostess, Metsola’s bewitching daughter,
Gladly led me on my journey, Smoothed my pathway through the glen-wood.
Pointing me to Otso’s caverns, To the Great Bear’s golden island.
“When my journeyings had ended,
Had no need to launch my javelins, Did not need to aim the arrow;
Lost his balance in his cradle, In the fir-tree where he slumbered;
Freely gave his life to others.
“Mighty Otso, my beloved,
Take thy fur-cap from thy forehead, Lay aside thy teeth forever,
Close thy mouth and still thine anger, While thy sacred skull is breaking.
“Now I take the eyes of Otso,
Lest their former powers shall weaken; Though I take not all his members,
“Now I take the ears of Otso,
Lest their former powers shall weaken; Though I take not all his members,
“Now I take the nose of Otso,
Lest its former powers shall weaken; Though I take not all his members,
“Now I take the tongue of Otso,
Lest its former powers shall weaken; Though I take not all his members,
“Now I take the brain of Otso,
Lest his consciousness should fail him, Lest his former instincts weaken;
Not alone must this be taken.
“I will reckon him a hero,
That will loosen Otso’s fingers From their settings firmly fastened.”
To perform the task demanded. Therefore ancient Wainamoinen
Loosens all the claws of Light-foot, With his fingers strong as copper,
Speaking to the bear these measures: “Otso, thou my Honey-eater,
Onward, onward, must thou journey From thy low and lonely dwelling,
Go, my treasure, through the pathway Near the herds of swine and cattle,
To the high and rising mountains, To the spruce-trees filled with needles,
There remain, my Forest-apple, Linger there in lasting slumber,
To the pleasure of the shepherd.”
Wainamoinen, old and truthful, Hastened from his emptied tables,
“Whither hast thou led thy booty, Where hast left thy Forest-apple,
Hast thou left him on the iceberg, Buried him upon the snow-field?
Laid him low beneath the heather?” Wainamoinen spake in answer: “Have not left him on the iceberg,
There the dogs would soon devour him, Birds of prey would feast upon him;
Have not buried him in heather; There the worms would live upon him,
Thither I have taken Otso, To the summit of the Gold-hill,
Laid him in his silken cradle In the summit of a pine-tree,
Rock him to his lasting slumber, To the pleasure of the hunter,
To the east his lips are pointing, While his eyes are northward looking;
For the fierceness of the storm-winds Would destroy his sense of vision.”
Touched again his harp of joyance, Sang again his songs enchanting,
To the joy of morn arising. Spake the singer of Wainola: “Light for me a torch of pine-wood,
That my playing may be joyous And my wisdom-songs find welcome.”
Wise and worthy Wainamoinen, Sweetly sang, and played, and chanted,
Ending thus his incantation: “Grant, O Ukko, my Creator,
May enjoy another banquet In the company of Light-foot;
Kalevala’s feast with Otso!
“Grant, O Ukko, my Creator,
That the notches in the pine-tree May direct my faithful people
That great Tapio’s sacred bugle May resound through glen and forest;
May be heard in field and hamlet, To the joy of all that listen!
Ring throughout the fen and forest, Through the hills and dales of Northland
To awaken song and gladness In the forests of Wainola,
On the meads of Kalevala, For the coming generations.”
Louhi Steals Sun, Moon, and Fire.
Touched again his magic harp-strings, Sang in miracles of concord,
Melodies arose to heaven, Songs arose to Luna’s chambers,
And the Moon has left her station, Drops and settles in the birch-tree;
Settles in the fir-tree branches, Comes to share the common pleasure,
To the harp of Wainamoinen.
Northland’s old and toothless wizard, Makes the Sun and Moon her captives;
From her cradle in the birch-tree, Calls the Sun down from his station,
Carries them to upper Northland, To the darksome Sariola;
In a rock of many colors; Hides the Sun, to shine no longer,
Thereupon these words she utters: “Moon of gold and Sun of silver,
Of Pohyola’s dismal mountain; Shine no more to gladden Northland,
Drawn by coursers nine in number, Sable coursers of one mother!”
And the silver Sun had hidden In the iron-banded caverns,
From the regions of Wainola, Left the mansions cold and cheerless,
Night was king and reigned unbroken, Darkness ruled in Kalevala,
Hard to live without the moonlight, Harder still without the sunshine;
When the Sun and Moon desert him.
Lived in wonder at the darkness; Long reflected, well considered,
What this accident in nature To the Moon upon her journey;
Why has disappeared the moonlight. Then great Ukko walked the heavens,
In his purple-colored vestments, In his silver-tinselled sandals,
Looking for the silver sunshine. Lightning Ukko struck in darkness
Shot the flames in all directions, From his blade of golden color,
Into Ether’s starry pastures.
Ukko hid it in the cloud-space, In a box of gold and silver,
Gave it to the ether-maidens, Called a virgin then to rock it,
That a second sun might follow. On the long-cloud rocked the virgin,
Rocked the fire of the Creator, In her copper-colored cradle,

“I have come for Mariatta,
Spake the wife of old Ruotus,
“Occupied are all our chambers, All our bath-rooms near the reed-brook;
Is a stable in the forest, For the flaming horse of Hisi;
Fitting birth-place for the hero From the wife of cold misfortune,
Thereupon the servant, Piltti,
Spake these measures, much regretting. “There is not a place befitting,
Spake the wife of old Ruotus: ‘Occupied are all the chambers,
In the mount of fire are couches, Is a stable in the forest,
In the stable is a manger, Fitting birth-place for the hero
Worthy couch for Mariatta.’”
Mariatta, virgin-mother, Fell to bitter tears and murmurs,
“I, alas! must go an outcast, Wander as a wretched hireling,
Hasten to the burning mountain, To the stable in the forest,
Near the flaming steed of Hisi!”
Outcast from her father’s dwelling, Gathered up her flowing raiment,
Hastened forth in pain and sorrow To the stable in the woodlands,
Spake these words in supplication: “Come, I pray thee, my Creator,
Come to me and bring protection To thy child, the virgin-mother,
In this hour of sore affliction. Come to me, benignant Ukko,
Lest thy guiltless child should perish, Die the death of the unworthy!”
Had arrived within the stable Of the flaming horse of Hisi,
“Breathe, O sympathizing fire-horse, Breathe on me, the virgin-mother,
Let thy pleasant warmth surround me, Like the vapor of the morning;
Find a refuge in thy manger!”
Breathed the moisture of his nostrils On the body of the virgin,
Gave her warmth and needed comforts, Gave his aid to the afflicted,
There the babe was born and cradled
Of the virgin, Mariatta, Pure as pearly dews of morning,
There the mother rocks her infant, In his swaddling clothes she wraps him,
Carefully the babe she nurtures, Well she guards her much-beloved,
Her beloved gem of silver.
Vanished while the mother slumbered. Mariatta, lone and wretched,
Hastened off to seek her infant. Everywhere the mother sought him,
Her beloved gem of silver; Sought him underneath the millstone,
Underneath the sieve she sought him, Underneath the willow-basket,
Long she sought her golden infant, Sought him on the fir-tree-mountain,
Looks within the clumps of flowers, Well examines every thicket,
Lifts the branches of the alder.
And the star she thus beseeches: “O, thou guiding-star of Northland,
Dost thou know and wilt thou tell me Where my darling child has wandered,
Thus the star of Northland answers: “If I knew, I would not tell thee; ’Tis thy child that me created,
In the cold to shine forever, Here to twinkle in the darkness.”
And the Moon she thus beseeches: “Golden Moon, by Ukko fashioned,
Dost thou know and wilt thou tell me Where my darling child has wandered,
Speaks the golden Moon in answer: “If I knew I would not tell thee; ’Tis thy child that me created,
All alone at eve to wander On my cold and cheerless journey,
Shining for the good of others.”
Falls again to bitter weeping, Hastens on through fen and forest,
Comes the silver Sun to meet her,
“Silver Sun by Ukko fashioned, Source of light and life to Northland,
Where my darling child has wandered, Where my holy babe lies hidden?”
“Well I know thy babe’s dominions, Where thy holy child is sleeping,
’Tis thy child that me created, Made me king of earth and ether,
Set me here to shine at midday, Makes me shine in silver raiment,
Yonder is thy golden infant, There thy holy babe lies sleeping,
Hidden in the reeds and rushes.”
Virgin-mother of the Northland, Straightway seeks her babe in Swamp-land,
Takes the young child on her bosom To the dwelling of her father.
Gathered strength, and light, and wisdom, All of Suomi saw and wondered.
When the mother named him, Flower, Others named him, Son-of-Sorrow.
Sought the priesthood to baptize him, Came an old man, Wirokannas,
Bringing to the babe his blessing; And the gray-beard spake as follows: “I shall not baptize a wizard,
With the drops of holy water; Let the young child be examined,
Lest he prove the son of witchcraft.”
Called the ancient Wainamoinen, The eternal wisdom-singer,
To report him good or evil.
Carefully the child examined, Gave this answer to his people: “Since the child is but an outcast,
Since the berry is his father; Let him lie upon the heather,
Let him live upon the mountains; Take the young child to the marshes,
Then the child of Mariatta,
“O, thou ancient Wainamoinen, Son of Folly and Injustice,
Falsely hast thou rendered judgment. In thy years, for greater follies,
Thou wert not unjustly punished. In thy former years of trouble,
For thy selfish life a ransom, Thus to save thee from destruction,
To be murdered for thy follies. In thy former years of sorrow,
In the deep and boundless blue-sea, To escape thy persecutions,
Wert not banished by thy people.”
Of the wilderness the ruler, Touched the child with holy water,
Gave him rights of royal heirship, Free to live and grow a hero,
King and Master of Karyala.
Recognized his waning powers, Empty-handed, heavy-hearted,
To the people of Wainola; Sang himself a boat of copper,
At the helm sat the magician, Sat the ancient wisdom-singer.
O’er the blue-back of the waters, Singing as he left Wainola,
“Suns may rise and set in Suomi, Rise and set for generations,
Will recall my wisdom-sayings, Hungry for the true religion.
Watch for me at dawn of morning, That I may bring back the Sampo,
Bring again the golden moonlight, Bring again the silver sunshine,
Thus the ancient Wainamoinen,
Left his tribe in Kalevala, Sailing o’er the rolling billows,
Sailing through the dusk of evening, Sailing to the fiery sunset,
To the lower verge of heaven; Quickly gained the far horizon,
There his bark he firmly anchored, Rested in his boat of copper;
Left his songs and wisdom-sayings, To the lasting joy of Suomi.
Bid my weary tongue keep silence, Leave my songs to other singers.
After many hours of labor; Even sickles will grow weary
Waters seek a quiet haven After running long in rivers;
At the dawning of the morning; Therefore I should end my singing,
For the pleasure of the evening, For the joy of morn arising.
Often heard the words repeated: “Worthy cataracts and rivers
Thus the wise and worthy singer Sings not all his garnered wisdom;
Than to sing them out of season.
Do I roll up all my legends, Roll them in a ball for safety,
In their narrow place of resting, Lest the songs escape unheeded,
While the teeth remain unparted, And the weary tongue is silent.
Chant them in the glen and forest, Sing them on the hill and heather?
Lies beneath the meadow, sleeping, Hears my ancient songs no longer,
Only will the forest listen, Sacred birches, sighing pine-trees,
Alder-trees that love to hear me, With the aspens and the willows.
Young was I, and low of stature; Like the cuckoo of the forest,
Like the lark I learned to twitter, Learned to sing my simple measures,
Stern and cold, without affection; Drove me helpless from my chamber
To the north-side of her cottage, Where the chilling winds in mercy
As a lark I learned to wander, Wander as a lonely song-bird,
Quietly o’er hill and heather; Walked in pain about the marshes,
Learned the music of the ocean, And the echoes of the woodlands.
Many women live to censure, Many speak with evil motives;
Curse me for my wretched singing, Blame my tongue for speaking wisdom,
Blame the songs and curse the singer. Be not thus, my worthy people,
Unpretending as a minstrel. I have never had the teaching,
Never learned the tongues of strangers, Never claimed to know much wisdom.
Nature was my only teacher, Woods and waters my instructors.
Save in childhood with my mother, When beneath her painted rafters,
By the work-bench of my brother, By the window of my sister,
In my early days of childhood.
This may point the way to others, To the singers better gifted,
For the coming generations, For the rising folk of Suomi.
A-ha’va. The West-wind; the father of the swift dogs. Ah’ti. The same as Lemminkainen.
Ah’to-la. The water-castle of Ahto and his people. Ah’to-lai’set. The inhabitants of Ahtola.
Ai’no (i’no). Youkahainen’s sister. An’te-ro. A goddess of the waves. Ai’nue-lake. The lake into which the Fire-child falls.
An’te-ro. Another name for Wipanen, or Antero Wipunen. Dus’ter-land. The Northland; Pimentola.
Fire-Child. A synonym of Panu. Frost. The English for Pakkanen.
Hal’ti-a (plural Haltiat). The Genius of Finnish mythology. Het’e-wa’ne. The Finnish name of the Pleiades. Hi’si (original Hiisi). The Evil Principle; also called Jutas, Lempo, and Piru.

Hor’na. A sacred rock in Finland. I’ku-Tur’so. An evil giant of the sea. Il’ma-ri’nem. The worker of the metals; a brother of Wainamoinen. Il’ma-tar. Daughter of the Air, and mother of Wainamoinen. Il’po-tar. Believed to be the daughter of the Snow flake; the same as Louhi.
In’ger-land. The present St. Petersburg. Ja’men (Ya’men). A river of Finland.

Jou’ka-hai’nen (You-ka-hai’nen). A celebrated minstrel of Pohyola. Jou-ko’la (You-ko’la). The home or dwelling of Youkahainen. Ju-ma’la (You-ma’la). Originally the heavens, then the god of the heavens, and finally God. Ju’tas (yu’tas). The Evil Principle; Hisi, Piru, and Lempo are synonyms, Kai’nto-lai’nen. A son of the god of metals; from his spear came the tongue of the serpent.
Ka-le’va (Kalewai’nen). The father of heroes; a hero in general. Kal’e-va’la (kaleva, hero, and la, the place of). The land of heroes; the name of the epic poem of Finland.
Kal-e’vo. The same as Kaleva. Ka’lew. Often used for Kaleva.
Kam’mo. The father of Kimmo. Kan’ka-hat’ta-ret. The goddesses of weaving. Ka’pe. A synonym of Ilmatar, the mother of Wainamoinen.

Ka-re’len. A province of Finland. Kar-ja’la, (karya’la). The seat of the waterfall, Kaatrakoski. Kat’e-ja’tar (kataya’tar). The daughter of the Pine-tree. Kat’ra-kos’ki (Kaatrakos’ki). A waterfall in Karjala.
Kau’ko-miel’li. The same as Lemminkainen. Kaup’pi. The Snowshoe-builder; Lylikki.

Kim’mo. A name for the cow; the daughter of Kammo, the patron of the rocks. Ki’npu-ki’nvi. The name of the rock at Hell-river, beneath which the spirits of all diseases are imprisoned. Kir’kon-Woe’ki. Church dwarfs living under altars.
Knip’pa-no. Same as Tapio. Koot’a-moi’nen. The Moon.
Kul-ler’vo. The vicious son of Kalervo. Kul’ler-woi’nen. The same as Kullervo.

Kun. The Moon, and the Moon-god. Kun’tar. One of the daughters of the Moon. Ku’ra (Kuura). The Hoar-frost; also called Tiera, a ball of ice. Kul-lik’ki (also Kyl’li). The Sahri-maiden whom Lemminkainen kidnapped.
Lak-ko. The hostess of Kalevala. Lem’min-kai’nen. One of the brothers of Wainamoinen; a son of Lempi.
Lem’po. The Evil Principle; same as Hisi, Piru, and Jutas. Lin’nun-ra’ta (Bird-way). The Milky-way.
Low-ya’tar. Tuoni’s blind daughter, and the originator of the Plagues. Lu’on-no’tar. One of the mystic maidens, and the nurse of Wainamoinen.
Ly-lik’ki (Lyylik’ki). Maker of the snow-shoe. Maan-e’mo (man-e’mo). The mother of the Earth. Ma’hi-set (Maa’hi-set). The invisibly small deities of Finnish mythology.
Ma’na. A synonym of Tuoni, the god of death. Man’a-lai’nen. The same as Mana. Masr’i-at’ta (marja, berry). The Virgin Mary of Finnish mythology.
Meh’i-lai’nen. The honey-bee. Mel’a-tar. The goddess of the helm. Met’so-la. The same as Tapiola, the abode of the god of the forest,
Mi-merk’ki. A synonym of Mielikki. Mosk’va. A province of Suomi.
Ne’wa. A river of Finland. Ny-rik’ki. A son of Tapio.
Os-noi’nen. A synonym of Wainola’s hero. Os’mo-tar. The daughter of Osmo; she directs the brewing of the beer for Ilmarinen’s wedding-feast.
Ot’so. The bear of Finland. Poe’ivoe. The Sun, and the Sun god.
Pak’ka-nen. A synonym of Kura. Pal-woi’nen. A synonym of Turi, and also of Wirokannas. Pa’nu. The Fire-Child, born from the sword of Ukko. Pa’ra. A tripod-deity, presiding over milk and cheese.

Pen’i-tar. A blind witch of Pohyola; and the mother of the dog. Pik’ku Mies. The water-pigmy that felled the over-spreading oak-tree for Wainamoinen. Pil’a-ya’tar (Pilaja’tar). The daughter of the Aspen; and the goddess of the Mountain-ash.
Pi’nmen-to’la. A province of Finland; another name for Pohyola. Pi’nru. The same as Lempo, Jutas, and Hisi.

Poh’ya (Poh’ja). An abbreviated form for Pohyola. Poh-yo’la (Poh-jo’la). The Northland; Lapland. Pok-ka’nen. The Frost, the son of Puhuri; a synonym of Tiera. Puh-hu’ri. The North-wind; the father of Pakkanen.
Re’mu. The same as Remmen. Ru-o’tus. A persecutor of the Virgin Mariatta.

Sah’ri (Saari). The home of Kyllikki. Sam’po. The jewel that Ilmarinen forges from the magic metals; a talisman of success to the possessor; a continual source of strife between the tribes of the North.
Sa’ra. The same as Sariola. Sar’i-o’la. The same as Pohyola.
Sa’wa (Sa’wo). The eastern part of Finland. Sim’a Pil’li (Honey-flute). The flute of Sima-suu.
Sin’e-tar. The goddess of the blue sky. Si-net’ta-ret. The goddesses of dyeing.
Suo’mi (swo’mi). The ancient abode of the Finns. Suo’ne-tar (swone-tar). The goddess of the veins.
Suo’ya-tar (Syo’jatar). The mother of the serpent. Su’ve-tar (Suve, summer). Goddess of the South-wind
Taeh’ti. The Polar Star. Ta-he’tar. The daughter of the Stars.
Ta-ni’nka. A magic mansion of Pohja. Ta’pi-o. The god of the forest.
Ter’he-ne’tar. Daughter of the Fog. Tie’ra. Same as Kura; the Hoar-frost.
Tu’a-me’tar. Daughter of the Alder-tree. Tu-le’tar (Tuule’tar). A goddess of the winds. Tu-lik’ki (Tuullk’ki). One of the daughters of Tapio.
Tuo’nen Poi’nka. The son of Tuoni. Tu’o-ne’tar. The hostess of Death-land; a daughter of Tuoni.

Tu’ri (Tuuri). The god of the Honey-land. Turja (tur’ya). Another name for Pohya. Tur’ya-lan’der. An epithet for one of the tribe of Louhi. Tur’ya (Tyrja). A name for the waterfall of Rutya. Uk’ko. The Great Spirit of Finnish mythology; his abode is in Jumala. Uk’on-koi’nva (Ukko’s dog). The messenger of Ukko; the butterfly.
Un’du-tar. Goddess of the fog. U’ni. The god of sleep.
Un-ta’mo. The god of dreams; the dreamer; a brother of Kalervo, and his enemy.
Un’to. The same as Untamo. Utu-tyt’to. The same as Undutar. Wai’nam-oi’nen (Vainamoinen). The chief hero of the Kalevala; the hero of Wainola, whose mother, Ilmatar, fell from the air into the ocean.
Wai-no’la. The home of Wainamoinen and his people; a synonym of Kalevala.

Wet’e-hi’nen. An evil god of the sea. Wi-pu’nen (Vipu’nen). An old song-giant that swallowed Wainamoinen searching for the “lost words.” Wi’nro-kan’nas (Virokan’nas). Ruler of the wilderness; the slayer of the huge bull of Suomi; the priest that baptizes the son of Mariatta. Wo’ya-lan’der (Vuojalan’der). An epithet for Laplander. Wuok’sen (Vuo’ksen). A river in the east of Finland. Wuok’si. The same as Wuoksen.
THE END.
